nl_description:
Scoping the inpatient warehouse rebuild for a 900-bed tertiary centre. Volumes first, because they drive the partitioning: eleven years of history, about 1.4 million admission episodes, and the nurse-observation feed alone lands roughly 34 million rows a year.

Patients are identified internally by a UUID and externally by MRN; we hold date of birth, sex and blood group and nothing else demographic. An admission episode pins a patient to a specific bed, and beds sit in wards -- each ward has a named specialty and a fixed bed complement, and some beds are flagged isolation-capable. Every episode has an attending clinician (registered practitioners, each with a registration number, a grade and a specialty of their own), an admitted timestamp, a discharge timestamp, a derived length of stay in days, an admission source and a discharge disposition. Internal moves between beds are recorded as their own event with a from-bed, a to-bed, a timestamp and a reason -- we lose that history today and it is the main reason for the rebuild.

Coding is many-to-many. An episode carries several ICD-10 codes; each code, with its description and chapter, recurs across thousands of episodes; one of an episode's codes is flagged primary and the rest are sequenced.

Observations are heart rate, systolic BP, temperature in Celsius, SpO2 as a percentage and the computed NEWS2 aggregate, stamped to the second against the episode. Prescribing is one order per drug per episode -- dose in mg, doses per day, start and stop timestamps, and the prescriber -- and the drug catalogue itself carries an ATC code and a controlled-substance flag.

Distributions we have already measured: length of stay is log-normal, log-mean 1.1, log-variance 0.8. Heart rate is roughly normal at 82 with an SD of 14, temperature normal at 36.9 with SD 0.6. Admission source splits 61% emergency department, 24% elective, 9% inter-hospital transfer, 6% other. Drug usage is brutally long-tailed -- rank frequency fits a Zipf with exponent near 1.6.

Checks to enforce: SpO2 between 50 and 100, NEWS2 between 0 and 20, length of stay never negative. A controlled drug may only be prescribed by a clinician at consultant grade. Any observation with systolic below 90 or saturation below 92 must carry a NEWS2 of 5 or more.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: the nurse-observation feed alone lands roughly 34 million rows a year
Heart rate is roughly normal at 82

nl_description:
I run a small allergy clinic on my own, two mornings and three afternoons a week, and the whole thing is currently held together by a filing cabinet and a spreadsheet my old receptionist built. I have got maybe eleven hundred people on the books and I see a dozen or so a day, so this is not a big system, but I would like it to stop being a spreadsheet.

The people who come in -- I say patients, the letters from the hospital say clients, it is the same thing -- I need their name, when they were born, a phone number, and who sent them, because nearly everyone arrives on a referral from their GP and I write down which surgery. There are only about a dozen surgeries round here that ever send me anybody, no two of them are called the same thing, and each one sits in one town, so I would rather hold the surgery once with its name and its town than write the same address out four hundred times. I also want the date I first saw them, because for the insurers that matters -- and nothing in the diary is ever earlier than that date, since that is what the date means.

Then the appointments. Date and time obviously, and whether it was a first consultation or a follow-up, because those are different lengths and different money. A first one takes about forty minutes and a follow-up twenty; across everything it averages out to something like twenty-eight minutes with maybe eight minutes of slop either side. A first visit is 120 and a follow-up is 70, no negotiation -- the price follows the type of visit and nothing else -- and nothing in this place ever costs less than 70 or more than 120. My receptionist worked out that of every hundred booked slots, 87 turn up, 8 simply do not bother, and the other 5 ring beforehand and cancel, which at least lets me fill it.

The clinical bit is the skin prick testing. In one appointment we might test a dozen allergens, and for each one there is the allergen itself and the size of the weal in millimetres. I work off a standard list -- the grass and tree pollens, the house dust mite, the cat, the dog, the moulds, the peanut and so on. Every thing on that list has its own name, which is unique, the group it belongs to, and the size we count as a positive for that particular one: three millimetres for most of them, five for the moulds because they are so unreliable. Every sheet also gets a saline prick as a control and I write that reading down too, because a reading only counts as a positive if it beats the saline by at least three millimetres as well as making the size on the list for that allergen. Most of the readings are basically nothing at all with a long tail up to the big reactors -- if you averaged every reading I have ever taken you would get about two and a half millimetres, and obviously it cannot go below zero. One more thing: whichever of the two nurses does the pricking initials the sheet, and I would like to keep that, it has saved me twice.

What I do not need is any of the hospital's coding nonsense. I do not bill insurers directly, the patients claim it back themselves, so there is no invoicing in this at all -- the fee on the appointment is the whole of the money side, and the card machine handles the rest. And before you ask: no, I do not want a portal, I do not want an app, and the last person who built me something put the date of birth in American order and I did not notice for a year. Whatever this ends up being, it needs to survive me typing into it at half past six on a Friday with the lights off.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: There are only about a dozen surgeries round here that ever send me anybody
I have got maybe eleven hundred people on the books
across everything it averages out to something like twenty-eight minutes
if you averaged every reading I have ever taken you would get about two and a half millimetres

nl_description:
I look after reporting for a dental group -- fourteen practices at the moment, three more in the pipeline. Roughly 400,000 registered patients across the group and we book something like 2.6 million treatment lines a year, so it is not enormous, but it is well beyond what the current spreadsheets cope with.

Each practice has a name, a town and a number of chairs. Practice names are unique across the group and each practice is in one town. Chair counts run from three to nine and it is honestly pretty flat across that range -- there is no typical size. Dentists sit at a practice, have a GDC number that is unique to them, and some are flagged as specialists. The dentists themselves do not move around: each one works at their own practice and nowhere else, so the practice recorded on an appointment is always just the dentist's practice. For patients we hold the name, date of birth, the date they registered with us and which practice is their home one -- though they can be seen anywhere in the group, and that is exactly the bit that breaks the old reports.

An appointment ties a patient to a dentist at a practice at a time. Slots are 15, 30 or 60 minutes -- about half are 30, a bit over a quarter are 15 and the remaining fifth are the hour-longs. There is a status on the appointment, something like booked, attended, cancelled, failed-to-attend; I would have to check the exact list with the software people. A specialist's list is always booked in hour slots, no exceptions.

Under an appointment we record the individual items of work. Each one points at a treatment code from a central list -- the code carries a description, an NHS band and a standard fee -- plus the tooth it was done on and what we actually charged. Tooth numbering runs 1 to 48 because the children's teeth live in the same scheme. Any band 3 item is charged at least 282.80. Two rules about the money that nobody has written down before: we never charge below the standard fee on the list, and on the private side, where the price does move, we cap ourselves at twice the list price.

Fees are very skewed with a long right tail; the log of the charged fee sits around 3.9 with a log-variance of about 0.7. Patient mix is 55% NHS, 31% private and 14% on our own payment plan.

The front desk takes the money at the end of the appointment, and I want that as its own thing rather than smeared across the treatment lines: what was due on the day, what they actually paid, the date it was taken and how. You cannot pay more than was due -- the shortfall gets chased separately and that is a different system -- and nothing is ever taken before the appointment itself, we do not do deposits. Roughly 64% goes on a card, a quarter is the plan direct debit and the rest is cash.

Oh -- we also flag when an appointment ends in a referral out to an implant specialist we do not employ. There is more to it than a flag really: we write down which specialist we sent them to, the date, the reason, and whether they took the case. The referral is dated the day of the appointment or later, never before. I am not sure that belongs in the same place, but it is on the form so it needs to land somewhere.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: Roughly 400,000 registered patients across the group
we book something like 2.6 million treatment lines a year

nl_description:
Dispensing warehouse spec. 480 community pharmacies, 61 million dispensing events last year, about 5 million new fact rows a month, so date partitioning throughout.

Stores carry a four-character store code -- unique, it is the natural key everyone quotes -- a region, an opening date and a 24-hour flag. Pharmacists have a home store, a council registration number that is unique to the individual, and exactly one per store is flagged superintendent. Customers are UUID-keyed with NHS number (also unique), date of birth, a prescription-charge exemption flag and, where they are exempt, the exemption code, which must be populated in that case -- the current extract has 200,000 rows flagged exempt with a blank code. The drug catalogue holds a product name, an ATC code, the controlled-drug schedule, a unit cost and a cold-chain flag; the product name is unique in the catalogue and carries its own ATC code and schedule with it.

A prescription is received at a store for a customer from an external prescriber code, with an issue date, a received timestamp and a source. It is never received before it was issued. It explodes into one or more dispensing rows: drug, dispensing pharmacist, the quantity written, the quantity actually dispensed, days supply, charge taken, dispense timestamp. We never dispense more than was written -- owings are a separate process -- and the dispense timestamp is never before the prescription was received.

Stock is per store per drug -- on-hand units, reorder point, last-counted timestamp -- and that pair is the natural key, no surrogate. On-hand is not maintained by update in place; it is reconciled from a stock movement ledger. A movement row is the store, the drug, a movement type (receipt, dispense, wastage, transfer), a signed unit delta and a timestamp, plus the dispensing row it came from where the movement was a dispense. A dispense movement is exactly the negative of the quantity dispensed on that line and is never dated before that dispense; a receipt movement is always positive.

Measured: dispensing by product is near-Zipf, exponent 1.35. Quantity dispensed is Poisson-like around 28. Charge amount is log-normal, log-mean 2.2, log-variance 0.9, and never negative. Source is 78% EPS, 15% paper, 7% repeat dispensing.

Enforce: on-hand units never negative; days supply between 1 and 90; Schedule 2 controlled drugs dispensed only by the superintendent pharmacist; cold-chain lines carry a reorder point of at least 12 units, since those deliveries are twice weekly.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: 200,000 rows flagged exempt with a blank code

nl_description:
This is for replacing the reporting layer on the LIMS at a regional pathology network. Scale, since you asked: we take work from just over 900 client sites -- GP surgeries, community clinics and three acute trusts -- and we report something like 19 million individual test results a year.

Work arrives as a specimen. A specimen belongs to a patient, and on the patient we hold a lab number -- one lab number, one patient, that is how we look them up -- a date of birth and sex. It was requested by a named doctor, with their specialty, who works at one of the client sites; a doctor is attached to exactly one site, so the site we stamp on the specimen is really just the requesting doctor's site. The specimen also has a type, a collection time and a receipt time, and it is never received before it was collected. Sites have a name (unique, and we lean on that), a type and exactly one courier route; there has been talk of tracking the individual courier run that brought the bag in, but for now the route on the site is all we get. We also mark a specimen rejected, with a reason, when it turns up haemolysed or unlabelled -- and if it is rejected there has to be a reason recorded, because the current system lets that through empty and it is a standing audit finding.

Priority is routine or urgent, plus the STAT ones the wards ring through: about 82% routine, 15% urgent, 3% STAT. A STAT specimen has to be reported within four hours.

Tests are identified by a test code with a name, an owning department, a unit and a turnaround target in hours. The name is unique as well and it carries the department and the unit with it, which is why the department is not on the result. We are measured on turnaround against that target: a routine test has to come back inside the target, and an urgent one inside half of it. Doctors mostly order panels rather than individual tests, and a panel is just a named bundle of test codes with a display order -- panel names are unique too, and the same test code shows up in several panels, so that pairing is its own thing. On average a specimen ends up carrying 7.4 tests and the count behaves like a Poisson; it is never fewer than one.

Each result records the numeric value, a high/low/normal flag, when it was reported -- never before the specimen was received -- the elapsed turnaround in hours and which analyser produced it, and that last one is just the analyser's serial off the instrument; we are deliberately not holding a list of the machines in here, the estates team has one and it is always wrong. Roughly 84% of results come back normal, 9% high and 7% low. The analytics team fitted turnaround to an exponential with a mean of about six hours.

Reference ranges are held per test code, split by sex and by an age band with a lower and an upper limit on the value. The upper limit is above the lower one and the top of the age band is above the bottom of it, which sounds obvious until you look at what is in there now. Ages in that table run 0 to 120. The high/low/normal flag is not typed in by anyone -- it is the value against the reference range for that test, so a high result sits above the upper limit, a low one below the lower limit, and a normal one between the two.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: 19 million individual test results a year
On average a specimen ends up carrying 7.4 tests

nl_description:
Imaging data mart. About 310,000 studies a year across two sites -- roughly 240 million images, though we hold counts, not pixels. The two sites each have a name and a town, and everything physical hangs off them.

Grain is the study: accession number (unique, one accession is one study and that is what external systems quote at us), patient, the scanner it ran on, the protocol that was run, modality, body part, a start timestamp, a duration in minutes, whether contrast was given, and the recorded dose in mGy. Duration means scan time, not room time; the two get conflated in the current reports and we are standardising on scan time. Below a study, one row per series with a series number, an image count and a slice thickness in mm.

Patients carry an MRN, date of birth, sex and weight in kg, since weight drives protocol selection. Scanners have a modality, a manufacturer, a room and, for the MR units, field strength in tesla; one scanner to a room, and a room is at one site, so the room number tells you the machine and the site both. Yes, modality lands on both the scanner and the study -- keep both; the study-level value is what the reports read and it does occasionally get overridden.

The protocol book comes across too, because at the moment it is a laminated sheet on the wall. Each protocol has a name (unique, and the name carries the modality, the body part and the dose ceiling with it), the modality and body part it is for, the weight window it is valid over as a lower and an upper weight, and a dose ceiling in mGy. The upper end of the window is above the lower end. A study records which protocol ran, and two things follow from that: the patient's weight has to sit inside the protocol's weight window, and the recorded dose must not exceed the protocol's ceiling, though physics being physics we allow a tenth over before it flags.

One report per study: the radiologist, a dictation timestamp -- never earlier than the study started -- the narrative text, a critical-finding flag and a status. Radiologists have a subspecialty and a consultant flag, and a critical finding must be signed off by a consultant. Somebody has asked for the referring clinician on the study too -- that lives in the RIS and we are deliberately not pulling it across this phase.

Shape: modality mix is 54% plain film, 21% CT, 14% MR, 9% ultrasound, 2% nuclear medicine. Study duration is log-normal, log-mean 2.6, log-variance 0.45, and never negative. Series image counts are heavy tailed, close to Zipf with exponent 1.9. Patient weight is normal, mean 78.5 kg, SD 17.

Constraints: a plain film never logs more than 20 mGy and never negative -- CT runs far higher, so that ceiling is modality-specific, not global. Slice thickness 0.5 to 10 mm. A series has at least one image.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: About 310,000 studies a year across two sites

nl_description:
OK so, background: we are a telehealth outfit, four years in, and last year we did just under 900,000 consultations. The database we are on was built by a contractor in a hurry and I want to start again properly before we sign the next enterprise deal.

We have members. The doctors insist on calling them patients, and honestly the app says 'patient' in two screens and 'member' everywhere else, which tells you how carefully any of this was thought through. Either way -- somebody signs up with a name, an email, their date of birth, the country they are in, and they sit on one of our plans. We will not let two people share an email, so that is as good as a name badge. We keep the sign-up date too, and the date they went onto the plan they are on now, which for most people is the same day they signed up and is never before it.

The plans are a short list and I want them held once, properly, because at the moment the price is typed into three different places. There is a free tier, a paid personal one, and the employer-sponsored one we bill differently; each has a name, the monthly price and the cut-off length for a call on that plan, because the free chats get closed at ten minutes and the personal ones do not. Roughly 58% of members are on the free tier, 26% personal and 16% employer. The employer-sponsored ones sit under an employer, and for those we hold the company, the country the contract is in, when the contract started -- nobody on that plan signed up before their company's contract did, and if they did it is a data error -- and how many seats they bought, which is never fewer than one.

The doctors are on a panel rather than employed by us. We need to know when each one joined the panel and which languages they speak -- right now that last one is a comma-separated string in a single box, which I am told is grim, but it is what we have. Licensing is the bit the contractor flattened and should not have: several of them are licensed in two or three countries, and for each licence there is the country, the licence number and the dates it runs between, the end being after the start. This matters because a doctor can only take a call from a member in a country the doctor holds a licence in -- that is a regulatory thing and I have the regulator's letter about it in a drawer.

Then the consultation, which is the thing everyone wants to report on. Somebody hits the button, that is a request time, and at some point they get connected, so there is a connect time -- after the request, obviously -- and a wait in between. Most people are through in a couple of minutes but a few sit there for ages -- the average wait comes out around four minutes and the tail is long, and it is never negative whatever the old reports say. The call itself is nine and a half minutes almost every time, plus or minus about three, and it never runs past the cut-off on the plan. We stamp the plan they were on at the time onto the call itself, because people upgrade mid-month and the old reports moved historic calls onto the new plan, which is how we ended up with three different answers about the free tier. It is video, phone or chat: video is about 62%, phone 29%, chat is the rest. Free-tier members only ever get chat, that one is a hard rule and it is the whole reason people upgrade.

At the end there is an outcome -- advice only, prescription, referral, or send them to A&E -- and the member rates the call one to five stars. People are generous: two thirds give five, about a fifth give four, and the bottom three ratings together are a bit over a tenth of everything.

When the doctor does prescribe, we log what the drug was, how much of it and when it was issued, one line per drug, and the issue time is never before the call connected. That gets handed to a partner pharmacy, but their system is not my problem.

Two things I want to be clear about because the last contractor got them wrong. First, a consultation is always exactly one member and exactly one doctor. We tried group sessions for physio, it went badly, and nobody is bringing it back. Second, doctors are not employees and I do not want payroll, rotas, or availability calendars in here -- the scheduling system does that and it can keep doing it. What I want is to be able to answer, in one query, how long people wait by plan and by country, and which doctors are getting the bad ratings.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: average wait comes out around four minutes
The call itself is nine and a half minutes almost every time

nl_description:
I am the practice lead at a small psychological therapies service -- nine therapists and around 600 people on the caseload at any one time, so we are talking thousands of rows, not millions. We are finally moving off paper diaries and a shared spreadsheet.

The people we see: on the clinical side we hold initials rather than full names, a date of birth, where the referral came from, and the dates we opened and closed the file. A file obviously does not close before it opened, though you would not know that from the spreadsheet.

Therapists have a modality -- CBT, EMDR, psychodynamic -- and an accreditation body, and the body follows from the modality: the CBT people are all with the same one, the EMDR people all with theirs, so it is really the modality that decides it rather than the individual. Everyone except the two most senior has a supervisor, and the supervisors are therapists here too, so I think that just points back at itself rather than being a separate thing. Nobody supervises themselves, before you ask.

Work is organised into episodes of care: one person, one therapist, an open date and a close date -- again, the close is never before the open -- a number of sessions planned, and a discharge reason at the end. A block is usually eight sessions, sometimes six, sometimes twelve; we do not plan fewer than six or more than twelve, that is a commissioning thing. The risk rating sits on the episode rather than on the person, because it genuinely does change between episodes and we got caught out by that in the old spreadsheet.

Then the sessions themselves. People write session, appointment or just meeting depending on who is filling the form in; they are all the same thing. Each one has a date -- never before the episode it belongs to opened and never after it closed -- a length, whether the person turned up, and whether it was in the room or over video. The standard hour is really fifty minutes -- about three quarters are that, then a chunk of thirty-minute check-ins, and the trauma work runs to eighty. Roughly four in five are attended, about 13% get cancelled and the remaining 8% are did-not-attends. If an episode is flagged high risk then the sessions have to be face to face, never remote.

We take outcome measures at sessions -- PHQ-9 mostly, GAD-7 on the anxiety pathway. Each one is the instrument name, a total score and the date it was taken, and since it is taken in the session it always carries that session's date; there is no such thing as a measure with a date of its own. PHQ-9 totals run 0 to 27; people arrive scoring around fifteen, give or take five or so, and the scores drift down over a block, though I could not put a number on the drift.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: around 600 people on the caseload at any one time
people arrive scoring around fifteen, give or take five or so

nl_description:
Right, so it is me and one other vet, plus Sandra on the desk. We have got about eighteen hundred animals on the books, maybe a bit fewer if you take out the ones we have not laid eyes on in three years.

Everything hangs off the owner, really -- name, mobile number, address, and the date they first registered with us. I say owner, Sandra says client, and the invoices say customer. Same person, three words for it, that is going to have to be sorted out at some point.

Each owner brings in one or more animals, sometimes a whole houseful. For the animal we want the name, what it is, the breed if we know it, roughly when it was born, its weight, whether it has been done, and the microchip number, which is unique to the animal and is the one thing on that record you can actually rely on. If we have got the breed then we do not really need to be told what it is as well -- a Labrador is a dog, a Persian is a cat -- but people type both in anyway. Weight is the awkward one -- the average across the whole book is about sixteen kilos, but that is a nonsense number: most of them are under ten, and then there is a handful of sixty-plus dogs dragging it upwards. Nothing under a hundred grams and nothing over ninety kilos, that much I can promise you.

What they are: about half dogs, call it 52%, then 38% cats, rabbits are 6%, and the rest is guinea pigs, a few birds and one very old tortoise.

Then the visits. The date, what they came in for, which of us saw them -- we just initial it, there are only two of us -- and the money. A consultation is 42 flat, or 78 if it is out of hours; nine times out of ten it is the 42. We sell food and flea treatment over the counter as well and that goes onto the same bill: Sandra writes each thing down as its own line, what it was and what we charged for it, and those lines add up to the retail part of the bill, so no one line is ever more than that. Then the bill itself is the consult plus the retail, and that is all it is -- so if they have bought anything at all then the bill comes to more than the consult fee on its own. And we note when the animal is next due for whatever it is -- boosters, a weight check, that sort of thing -- which is always some time after the visit we are writing it on, never before.

One thing I should say is that I do not want a stock system. I know that is the obvious next question. We buy the wormers from the wholesaler on a Tuesday, Sandra puts them in the cupboard and when the cupboard looks empty she buys more, and that has worked for nineteen years. The lines on the bill are enough. Same with lab work -- the bloods go off to an external lab and the results come back on paper and go in the folder, and I am not putting that in a computer for anyone.

What I actually want out of this is to be able to see, at the start of the week, which animals are overdue for something, and to be able to find an owner from a mobile number when they ring up and start talking without saying who they are, which happens roughly hourly -- so one number, one owner, and if two of them share a landline they will have to give me a mobile. Anything beyond that is a bonus.

variance.basis: variance = ln(1 + CV^2) for CV in [0.324, 3.166], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=70)

ground_truth_moments.evidence: we have got about eighteen hundred animals on the books
the average across the whole book is about sixteen kilos

nl_description:
Handover notes for the replacement clinical and operational data store. Read this as the whole estate rather than one extract: it swallows the three siloed feeds we run today (control room, fleet, clinical) and it has to carry the audit trail the last inspection said we did not have. Volume for sizing: 1.9 million emergency calls a year, 2.4 million dispatch legs against them, roughly 1.4 million patient encounters, and the vehicle telemetry feed on top of that at about 40 million position pings a month, which on its own is bigger than everything else combined.

GEOGRAPHY AND FLEET. The service is split into divisions, each with a name and the region it reports into. Stations sit in a division and carry a name, a location as latitude and longitude, and the date they opened; station names are unique across the service and a station never changes division, so the name tells you the division. Vehicles belong to a station and carry a call sign, an in-service date, a retirement date once they are stood down -- after the in-service date, naturally -- and a running odometer in km. The call sign is unique and has the station in it, so from a call sign you know both the vehicle and its station. Each vehicle is of a vehicle type; the type list is short (double-crewed ambulance, rapid response car, hazardous area team and so on) and carries a description, the crew size the type must be staffed to, and whether the type can transport a patient at all. Every change of a vehicle's operational status is an event row -- the vehicle, the status it moved to, the timestamp and the crew member who keyed it -- and the status codes themselves are a short list with a description and a flag for whether that status counts as available. The position pings are just vehicle, timestamp, latitude, longitude and speed in kph. Equipment carried on a vehicle is inventoried: the vehicle, what the item is, a serial number, when it was last checked and when it expires, and nothing is signed off as checked after it has already expired. At the start of every shift -- so timestamped at or after the shift start -- the crew do a vehicle check, which is a row against the vehicle and the shift with a timestamp, who did it, whether it passed and a defect note; if it did not pass there has to be a defect note, and that is the one rule the current system silently lets through.

PEOPLE AND ROSTERING. A crew member has a home station, a name, a professional registration number that is unique to the individual, a joining date and a primary qualification. Qualifications are their own list with a description, a seniority rank and a flag for whether that qualification may administer drugs. Behind the primary one we hold every ticket a crew member holds -- the qualification, the date it was awarded and the date it expires, the expiry always after the award -- because a paramedic whose ticket has lapsed is not a paramedic. Training courses are separate from tickets: a course name, when it was completed and when the completion lapses, again after completion. Shifts are per vehicle: a shift type (that list carries a description and planned hours), a start, an end after the start, and the station the shift is run from -- and that station is always the vehicle's own station, we do not lend vehicles between stations. Crew are rostered onto shifts many to many, with a role recorded on each rostering (the role list is attendant, driver, observer and a couple of others) plus the times they actually signed on and off, which are not the shift times: sign-on is never before the shift starts and sign-off never before sign-on.

CONTROL ROOM. There are three control centres, each with a name, a region and a location, and control-room staff belong to exactly one of them with a name and a role. A call is the entry point: the receipt timestamp, the caller number, the location as reported plus the geocoded latitude and longitude, the postcode sector we geocoded into, a chief-complaint code, the triage category the call taker assigned, and the staff member who took it. We stamp the centre on the call as well, though since a staff member sits in one centre that value is really just the taker's centre. Chief-complaint codes are a coded list with a description, the triage category they default to, and a cardiac-arrest flag. Triage categories are a list too and carry the response target in seconds -- that is the number we are held to, and it belongs in the reference table rather than hard-coded in a report, which is how we got three different answers last year. Postcode sectors are held with the division that covers them and an urban/rural classification: a sector determines both, and that is the entire point of the table. Every change of state on a call is an event -- the call, the status, when it happened and which staff member -- so an upgraded, downgraded or duplicated call can be reconstructed; no call event predates the call itself.

DISPATCH. One row per vehicle assigned, so one call can generate several. It carries the call, the vehicle, the shift it was working, the triage category it was assigned under (calls get upgraded and we are measured on the category at the time of assignment, not the final one), the four timestamps we are measured on -- assigned, mobile, on scene, cleared, each one never before the one in front of it -- the derived response time in seconds, the on-scene minutes, and an outcome from a coded outcome list that also says whether that outcome involved a transport. The response time must beat the target seconds held on the triage category the leg was assigned under, and it is never negative. Note the shift already knows the vehicle, so the vehicle on the dispatch is strictly the shift's vehicle; keep the column for query convenience but it is derivable and it has been inconsistent in the old extract.

CLINICAL. Where a patient is actually treated we open an encounter against the dispatch: age, sex, presenting problem, the first set of observations copied up for reporting (GCS, systolic BP, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation as a percentage), whether they were transported and the receiving hospital -- and if they were transported there has to be a receiving hospital. The full series of observations lives below the encounter, one row per set with a timestamp and the same five measurements; the copy on the encounter is the earliest set and exists only because the reports were unusable without it. GCS is 3 to 15 wherever it appears. Hospitals carry a name, the trust that runs them -- a hospital site is in exactly one trust, so the site name gives you the trust -- trauma-centre and PCI capability flags, a location, and the number of ED bays, which is at least one. Arrival at hospital is its own row: the encounter, the hospital, when we arrived, when the patient was handed over and the handover minutes; handover is never before arrival. Handover time is log-normal, log-mean 2.9, log-variance 0.6, and it is the metric the trusts argue about.

Interventions performed during an encounter come from a coded list -- each code has a description and a paramedic-only flag -- and one encounter can have several of them, each with a timestamp and the crew member who performed it; a paramedic-only intervention must be performed by a crew member holding the paramedic qualification. Drugs are separate from interventions and have their own catalogue: a drug code that is unique in the catalogue, a name, a controlled-drug flag, the unit and the maximum single dose in milligrams. Every administration is a row -- the encounter, the drug, the dose in mg, the route, the time and who gave it. A dose never exceeds the drug's maximum single dose, and for a patient under sixteen it never exceeds half of it. A controlled drug may only be given by a paramedic. Drug usage is long-tailed, close to Zipf with an exponent around 1.5.

GOVERNANCE. A share of encounters go to clinical audit: the encounter, which crew member reviewed it, the date, a score and an outcome. Safeguarding referrals are raised off an encounter with a category, when it was raised, who raised it and the date it was sent on, which is never before it was raised. Complaints come in against a call with a category, the date received, the date closed and whether it was upheld; closed is never before received. And the audit trail: every change to any of this is a row naming the table, the record key, the action, the field, the old and the new value, the staff member who made the change and when. On an update the old value must be populated -- that is the inspection finding, and it is the reason this rebuild is funded.

Fitted distributions from the current extracts: response time in seconds is log-normal, log-mean 6.2, log-variance 0.35. On-scene time is roughly normal at 27 minutes with an SD of 9. Triage category splits 6% category 1, 31% category 2, 38% category 3, 19% category 4 and 6% category 5. Patient age is normal-ish, mean 58 with an SD of 22.

Hard rules restated, because they get lost in the prose: GCS 3 to 15; oxygen saturation is a percentage; response time never negative; a category 1 leg responded to within 420 seconds.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: about 40 million position pings a month
on-scene time is roughly normal at 27 minutes

domain: Retail Bank Accounts and Branch Network
nl_description:
I look after operations for a mid-sized bank -- we came out of a building society merger about a decade ago, and a fair bit of our record keeping is still held together with string, which is really why we are talking to you.

The centre of it all is the customer. For each one we hold their name, their date of birth, the address we post statements to, and the date they first joined us. We never delete a customer when they close everything down, we just stop them being active, because the auditors want the history.

Then there are the accounts. Current accounts, instant-access savings, and a small number of fixed-term savings bonds. About two thirds of what we hold open is a current account, roughly three in ten is instant access, and the rest -- maybe 4 percent -- is the fixed bonds. Those three are really a little list of products in their own right, and I wish we held them that way, because at the moment the rate and the deposit limits are written onto every single account record and they have drifted. What belongs to the product and not to the account is: a description of it, the rate it pays, and the smallest and largest amount you are allowed to put in. Get the product wrong and you get the rate wrong for eleven thousand people at once, which has happened.

Every account belongs to a branch, because our staff bonuses still depend on which branch owns the relationship, and each account has a sort code and an account number, the balance, the date it was opened, whether it is still open, and the rate it pays. The sort code on an account is simply the sort code of its branch -- there is nothing else in it -- and the rate on an account is whatever the rate is for its product; we do not do special rates for individuals, whatever anybody in the branches tells you. An account can be a joint account -- we have quite a lot of couples on our books -- so one account may have two or even three people named on it, and equally one person often has several accounts with us. That relationship is the thing our current system handles worst of all. We do at least want the date each person was named on each account, and that is never before the account was opened, nor before the person joined us.

Balances are all over the place. A typical current account sits somewhere around 2,400 pounds, but there is a very long tail of people holding far more than that. By rule an account is never allowed to go below minus 500 -- that is the arranged overdraft floor we set for everybody, no exceptions -- and the running balance after any movement is under the same floor. On the bonds the money in has to be at least 1,000 pounds and no more than 85,000, which is where the deposit protection stops; on the two other products there is no minimum and no maximum at all, and whatever the limits on the product are, the balance has to respect them.

Every movement of money has to be kept: the date and time it happened, the amount, whether it was money in or money out, a short description of what it was, and the running balance afterwards. Nothing can be dated before the account it sits on was opened. The median payment going out is about 38 pounds, though we process the occasional six-figure transfer and that skews everything. Across the whole book we are looking at something like three million of these a month, sitting on 610,000 open accounts.

A lot of our customers also have standing orders running -- a fixed amount going out to the same place on the same day each month. We keep which account it comes out of, who it pays, the amount, the day of the month it goes, the date it starts and whether it is still active. The day has to be between 1 and 28, because February taught us that, and a standing order is never set up before the account is open.

We have 84 branches, each with a name, the town it is in, and its own sort code -- the sort code is unique to the branch and tells you the branch and its town. Oh, and one more thing I keep forgetting -- every branch has a manager, and the manager is one of our own staff, and obviously they work out of the branch they manage. So we need basic staff records too: name, job title, which branch they work out of and the date they started. Nobody works out of two branches, so the person tells you the branch. Around 1,900 people all in.

On rates: the instant-access savings pay 3.1 percent and always have, the current accounts pay nothing at all, and the fixed bonds are on 4.6.

nl_description:
Handover pack for the mortgage origination store, Postgres 16. Read it as the whole origination estate rather than one extract: it swallows the four systems we run today -- the intermediary portal, the case-management box, the valuation panel's own database and the affordability spreadsheet that should never have existed -- and it has to carry the audit trail the last FCA visit said we did not have. Sizing: 1.2 million applications over five years of history against roughly 900,000 properties, about 2.9 million documents hanging off them, and a bureau pull on every case.

DISTRIBUTION AND THE BROKER PANEL. Roughly three in five cases reach us through an intermediary and the rest come direct, so the channel goes on every application. Broker firms are the unit we contract with: an FCA reference that is unique to the firm and is what compliance actually quotes, a firm name, the date they joined the panel, and the panel tier they sit in. Panel tiers are a short reference list -- a tier code, a description, the maximum procuration fee percentage that tier may be paid, and a flag for whether cases from that tier need a pre-submission review. Description and fee cap belong to the tier code and nothing else; they were copied onto the firm row in the old portal and we now have two different caps recorded against the same tier. Individual brokers sit under a firm with a name, their own FCA individual reference which is unique to the person, and the dates their authorisation runs from and to -- the end date, where there is one, is never before the start. A broker never moves firms: we close the row and open a new one, so the broker id tells you the firm. Not every product is sellable by every tier, and that is a genuine many-to-many -- a tier gives access to many products and a product is available to several tiers, with the date access opened recorded against each pairing.

Procuration fees are paid per completed case: the offer they are paid against, the broker who introduced it, the fee percentage, the fee amount and the date we paid it. A fee amount is never more than one percent of the advance on that offer.

APPLICANTS, INCOME AND AFFORDABILITY. Joint applications are out of scope for this release, so hold the cardinality at one applicant per application. Applicant rows are identity only -- name, date of birth, national insurance number, marital status -- and the NI number is unique, one row per person. An application is always against exactly one property and carries the channel, the submission timestamp, the requested advance, the requested term in months, a status, and a nullable FK to the broker who introduced the case; direct business leaves it null. Because the bureau score is a point-in-time pull we snapshot a credit score onto the application itself rather than onto the applicant, where it would rot.

Bureau pulls are their own rows all the same, because we have to be able to show what we saw and when: the application, the bureau name, the timestamp we pulled it, the score it returned and a count of adverse entries. A pull is never timestamped before the application was submitted. Scores are 300 to 999 wherever they appear, mean 780 with a standard deviation of 90.

Declared income is one row per source per applicant -- employment, self-employment, rental, pension -- with the gross annual amount, always positive, and a verified flag, because affordability is computed over the whole set rather than off a single figure. About 68 percent of sources are employment, 14 self-employment, 11 rental and 7 pension. Employment history is separate from income: the employer name, the job title, the contract type, and the dates the job started and ended, with the end date never before the start. Committed credit is one row per commitment: the lender name, the commitment type, the outstanding balance and the monthly payment -- and the monthly payment never exceeds the outstanding balance, because where it does the feed is wrong rather than the borrower unusual. Declared household expenditure hangs off the application by expenditure type with a monthly amount, always positive.

The affordability assessment is one row per application and it is where the numbers land: the total monthly income we allowed, the total monthly commitment, the disposable income -- which is exactly the total monthly income less the total monthly commitment -- the stressed payment at the stress rate, the income multiple, and whether it passed. An assessment only passes where the disposable income covers the stressed payment. The income multiple never exceeds 4.75; that is policy, not an advisory.

PROPERTY AND VALUATION. Property holds the address line, the postcode, a property type code, the year it was built, the tenure and the number of bedrooms. Property types are reference data: the code, a description, whether the type is acceptable for lending at all, and the maximum LTV allowed on it -- all three of which are properties of the code alone. Year built sits between 1600 and 2026; we have genuinely had a 17th-century listed building through, and we have also had 1067 typed in.

Valuations are their own table because a property can be valued more than once -- desktop first, then a physical inspection when the desktop comes back outside tolerance. Each valuation names the property, the valuer firm that did it, the valuation date, the method, and the estimated value, which is always positive. About 72 percent are desktop and 28 percent physical. Valuer firms carry a firm name, their panel status and the region they cover. Where a valuation raises conditions -- essential repairs, a retention, a specialist report -- each one is a row against that valuation with a condition type, a description and a flag for whether it is a retention.

PRODUCTS AND PRICING. Products are reference data: product code, product name, the initial rate, the fixed period in months, the reversion rate, the maximum LTV, the minimum and maximum advance, the arrangement fee, and the date the product was withdrawn where it has been. Initial rate, fixed period, reversion rate and maximum LTV are all functions of the product code alone. Pricing on top of that is a tiered lookup: each tier row names the product, the credit score floor, the LTV ceiling and the rate that combination prices at, and the rate depends on those three and nothing else -- there is no fourth factor, whatever the pricing paper implies. Above 900 with LTV at or below 60 prices at 3.99; above 900 with LTV over 60 prices at 4.29; anything scoring 700 or below prices at 5.75. The five-year fixes -- the products with a 60-month fixed period -- are only available up to 85 LTV.

UNDERWRITING. Underwriters have a name, a mandate level, and the maximum advance they are authorised to approve. When underwriting completes we write a decision row against the application: the decision, its timestamp, the underwriter, free-text notes, and a materialised submission-to-decision lag in days -- so the decision timestamp is always the submission timestamp plus that lag, and can never precede submission. Decisions run 62 percent accept, 23 decline, 15 refer, and the lag is exponential with a mean of 9 days. An underwriter may not accept a case whose requested advance is above their own authorised maximum. That is the finding from the internal audit, and it is the only reason the mandate level is in the data at all.

Conditions attached to a decision are rows: a condition code, a description, and the date it was satisfied, which is never before the decision was made. Referrals are separate: the application, a reason code, when it was raised, when it was resolved and who resolved it, with resolution never before it was raised. Where we lend outside policy the exception is recorded against the decision with the rule code it breaches, a justification, and who approved it.

DOCUMENTS AND CASE HISTORY. Document types are reference data -- the code, a description, whether the type is mandatory, and how many years we retain it -- and those three follow from the code. Payslips, bank statements, ID and the rest hang off the application with a document type, the upload timestamp, the verification timestamp and who verified it; verification never predates upload, and a mandatory document has to end up verified. Every status change on an application is an event row: the application, the status, when it happened, and who changed it -- and no event predates the application's own submission. We lose that history today and it is a large part of why the rebuild is funded.

OFFER, LEGAL AND DRAWDOWN. If the decision is an accept we write an offer naming the product we priced it on, the advance amount, the LTV, the term in months, the rate actually given, the arrangement fee, the date it was issued and the date it expires -- expiry always after issue. The advance never exceeds the requested advance on the application, never exceeds the product's maximum advance, never falls below its minimum advance, and the LTV never exceeds the product's maximum LTV. The rate given is never below the product's initial rate, because the tiers only ever load. The arrangement fee on the offer is the product's arrangement fee: we do not discount it case by case, and where the old system let someone do that it was an error rather than a feature. LTV sits in (0, 95] everywhere. Advance amounts are log-normal with a median near 210,000, and LTV clusters around 75 with a standard deviation of about 10.

Conveyancing: solicitor firms carry a firm name, an SRA number unique to the firm, and their panel status. A legal case is opened against an offer, names the solicitor firm, and carries the date they were instructed, the date searches came back, the exchange date and the completion date -- instruction never before the offer was issued, exchange never before instruction, completion never before exchange, and completion never after the offer expires, because an expired offer has to be re-issued rather than quietly completed. Drawdown is a row against the offer with the amount, the date it was disbursed and the account number it went to; the amount disbursed never exceeds the advance on the offer.

FINANCIAL CRIME. Every applicant is screened: the provider, the timestamp, the result, and a risk score from 0 to 100 that averages about 22 with a standard deviation of 15. Fraud alerts are raised against an application by rule code, with the timestamp it was raised, a severity, an outcome, and the date it was closed, never before it was raised.

AUDIT. Every change to any of this is a row naming the table, the record key, the action, the field, the old and the new value, who made the change, and when. On an update the old value must be populated. That is the inspection finding verbatim, and it is non-negotiable.

nl_description:
I'm the product analyst on our cards book and we are rebuilding the reporting layer from scratch, so here is roughly what has to be in it.

We issue to individuals. I call them cardholders, the ops team still says customers and means exactly the same people. We hold the usual on them: name, date of birth, the address on file, when they were onboarded, and an internal risk band that the scoring job writes back overnight. The band runs A through E and the book skews good -- A is about 18 percent of it, B is 31, C is 27, D is 16 and E is the remaining 8.

The bands themselves need to be a table, not five magic letters scattered through the code. Each band has the band code, a description of what it means, the credit limit we grant at that band and the APR we charge at it. Band A gets 15,000, band C gets 5,000, band E is capped at 1,000, and the limit and the APR belong to the band and to nothing else -- today they are hardcoded in three separate jobs and one of them is out of date.

A cardholder can have more than one card account. The account is where the credit limit, the APR, the statement day of the month and the current balance live, and we also stamp the risk band on the account, because the limit is granted per account and we need to know which band granted it. That band is always the cardholder's own band. The limit on an account is the limit for its band and the APR is the APR for its band -- there are no hand-set limits any more -- the balance never goes over the limit, and no account anywhere can carry a limit above 50,000, which is a board-approved ceiling and does not flex. The statement day is between 1 and 28.

Cards then sit under the account, physical and virtual, and there can be several of them -- a primary plus an authorised user, replacements after fraud -- each with its own last four digits, the date it was issued, an expiry date that is always after issue, a network and a status. Roughly 14 million cards live against about 9.5 million accounts.

Every authorisation that settles becomes a transaction against the card it was made on: the timestamp, the amount, the currency, the merchant, the MCC, and whether it was card-present. Nothing settles on a card before it was issued or after it has expired -- we do see attempts, but they do not become rows here. Volume is the real problem: we are a bit over 900 million settled transactions a year. Spend is extremely concentrated by merchant -- a handful of merchants take a wildly disproportionate share and it tails off very fast after them, a textbook power law. The amounts themselves are small and skewed, median somewhere around 24 dollars with the odd very large one. On the merchants we only need the legal name, a category code and the country they are acquired in.

Monthly we cut a statement per account: the period start and end, the opening and closing balance, the minimum payment due and the due date. One statement per account per period start, so that pair identifies it. The period end is after the period start, the due date is on or after the period end, a minimum payment is never less than 25 dollars, and it is never more than the closing balance it is asking for.

Payments against a statement are their own rows -- the statement, the amount, the date it cleared and the method -- and there can be more than one. A payment never clears before the period it is paying has even ended, it is never for more than the closing balance on that statement, and a payment clearing on or before the due date has to be at least the minimum payment due, otherwise the account is in arrears and the collections job picks it up.

We also track rewards redemptions -- which account, when, how many points were spent and what they were redeemed for -- and the cash value we book against it, which is a flat penny a point, so the cash value is the points spent times 0.01.

nl_description:
Motor claims mart for a personal-lines insurer. 6.8 million in-force policies and around 41 million claim-related rows across eight years of history, so partitioning and column ordering both matter.

Policyholder is the paying customer: integer surrogate key, name, date of birth, postcode, date of first policy. A policy is annual, keyed on policy_id, and carries inception and expiry dates -- expiry strictly after inception -- the annual premium as DECIMAL(10,2) and always positive, a voluntary excess, the total excess we actually hold, its cover type, and the single vehicle it covers; one vehicle per policy in this book, no multi-car. We also keep a denormalised annual claim count on the policy row for pricing pulls, which is never negative.

Cover types are a reference table rather than an enum on the policy: the cover type code -- TPO, TPFT, COMPREHENSIVE -- a description, a flag for whether the type includes own-damage cover at all, and the base excess the type carries. Description, own-damage flag and base excess are properties of the code alone; they were denormalised onto the policy row in the old mart and we found three different base excesses for TPFT. The total excess on a policy is exactly the voluntary excess plus the base excess of its own cover type.

Vehicles hold registration, make, model, year of manufacture, engine capacity in cc and a market value. Registration is unique -- one row per registration, and it determines the make and model, because we resolve both off the DVLA feed rather than off keying.

Named drivers are the genuine many-to-many: a driver appears on several policies (a spouse on both household cars) and a policy names one to four of them, so there is a junction keyed on (policy_id, driver_id) carrying the relationship to the policyholder and a main-driver flag. Driver rows themselves hold a licence number, a date of birth and years of driving experience. The licence number is unique to the driver and determines their date of birth, which is how we de-duplicate the same person arriving from two brokers.

A claim references both the policy and the driver who was at the wheel, and holds the incident date, the notification date, a notification lag in days that we materialise on write -- so the notification date is exactly the incident date plus that lag, and the lag is never negative -- the claim type, a reserve amount, the settled amount, a status, and the handler who owns it. Claim handlers have a name, a team and a settlement authority limit in pounds; no claim is settled for more than the authority limit of its own handler, which is the control the last internal audit asked for. A claim only carries a settled amount once its status is SETTLED. Every status change on a claim is an event row -- the claim, the status, when it happened and who changed it -- and no such event predates the notification of the claim itself; we cannot reconstruct that today.

Payments against a claim are separate rows -- amount, always positive, paid date, payee type -- because there are normally several, and no single payment exceeds the settled amount on its claim, nor is one dated before the claim was notified.

Where a third party is involved we record their name, their insurer and whether they were legally represented. Repairs go to a panel garage, so a claim optionally names one; garages have a name, a town and an hourly labour rate, and a garage name is unique within its town. The repair itself is now a row rather than a cost buried on the claim: the claim, the garage, the labour hours, the labour cost, the parts cost, the total cost, the date it was authorised and the date it completed. The labour cost is the labour hours times that garage's own hourly labour rate, the total cost is the labour cost plus the parts cost, and completion is never before authorisation.

Anything we suspect goes to the special investigations unit as its own row: the claim, the date it was referred, the date it closed, the outcome and a fraud score from 0 to 100. A referral is never dated before the claim was notified, and a closure never before the referral.

Distribution facts from the last full year. Annual premium is log-normal, median near 640. Cover type splits 71 percent comprehensive, 21 TPFT, 8 TPO. The annual claim count per policy is Poisson with lambda 0.14. Settled amount on a claim is log-normal with a median around 1,850. Driver experience is close to uniform between 1 and 45 years. The notification lag is exponential with a mean of 4 days.

Rules to enforce: voluntary excess is between 0 and 1,000; engine capacity between 600 and 6,500 cc; driving experience between 1 and 45 years; a fraud score between 0 and 100; anything notified more than 30 days after the incident is forced to status REFERRED_SIU; and on a third-party-only policy there is no own-damage cover at all, so the settled amount on those claims is capped at zero.

nl_description:
We are a small outfit -- we only write about 900 new policies a year -- so nobody here has ever needed a proper system, and honestly the spreadsheet has got away from us now.

What happens is that somebody applies for cover through one of our agents. The proposal (we call them proposals, the agents call them applications, the compliance folder says submissions, it is all the same piece of paper) comes in with the person's details, how much cover they are asking for, the term, and the date we received it. Then we go through underwriting. There is a medical questionnaire, sometimes a nurse's report, and a doctor's letter if we have asked for one. Somebody here reads all of that and prices it, and the answer is either standard rates, or we load it by some percentage, or once in a while we just decline.

The people we are covering. We keep the life assured's name, when they were born, whether they smoke, their height and their weight, and what they do for a living. Smoking matters more for pricing than anything else on that list. We do not see many smokers, maybe one in six. Heights come out about average for the population -- five foot nine, give or take three inches -- although I have never been sure whether we ought to be keeping that in feet or in centimetres, and over the years we have done both, which is part of the mess.

Cover amounts vary enormously. Most of what we write is modest, a couple of hundred thousand, but we have done a handful in the millions, so it is very skewed and there is no typical case really. The term is nearly always 25 years -- about six in ten of them -- and the rest splits evenly between 15 and 30.

The medical evidence is the fiddly part. One proposal can have several pieces of it, and for each piece we need to know what kind it was, when it arrived and a short summary of what it said. And the agents -- they are self-employed, there are eleven of them, we pay them a commission rate, and we absolutely have to know which agent brought each proposal in, because that is how they get paid.

Once a proposal is accepted it becomes a policy, with a start date, the monthly premium, and the sum assured, which is the cover amount again under a different name. Policies lapse when people stop paying, and about a fifth of them do.

Two things the regulator cares about. We do not cover anybody under 18 or over 74 at entry, and we will not write more than 3 million on a single life. And where we have loaded somebody for smoking, the loading is never less than 100 percent -- they pay at least double.

nl_description:
Spec for the settlement engine's operational store. Five tables. It was three until reconciliation asked for net positions per participant and the scheme rules stopped being something we could sensibly hard-code -- everything else still lives upstream in the ledger and we are not duplicating it.

A participant bank is identified by its BIC, eleven characters and unique across the estate, but give it an integer surrogate key as well because it sits on the hot path of every join. Beyond that: legal name, country ISO code, and the central-bank account number we settle against.

Schemes are reference data now rather than a check constraint. One row per scheme code -- SEPA_CT, SEPA_INST, CHAPS, FPS -- carrying a description, the maximum instruction amount the scheme rule allows, and the settlement window in minutes. That ceiling is null for the schemes that do not set one, and SEPA_INST is the only one where it bites in practice: 100,000. Where a scheme does set a ceiling, an instruction's amount is validated against the row for its own scheme rather than against a literal in code, because the SEPA figure has moved twice since we launched. Both the description and the window are properties of the scheme code alone and used to be copied onto every instruction row, which is how we ended up with two different windows for FPS.

A payment instruction is the row that matters. UUID primary key, the debtor participant, the creditor participant, amount as DECIMAL(18,2), a three-letter currency, a value date, its scheme, a status, and the timestamp we accepted it. We also stamp the inter-arrival gap in milliseconds on the row, because latency analytics used to need a self-join to compute it and that did not scale. A participant never settles against itself: a self-payment is a ledger correction and has no business in the clearing store. We ingest around 38 million instructions a day and retain thirteen months, so it is partitioned by value date.

Instructions are grouped into settlement batches for net settlement. A batch has an id, the cycle number it belongs to (we run six cycles a day), its scheme, its value date, the cut-off timestamp, the count of instructions it contains and the net settlement amount. Cycle number, scheme and value date together identify a batch uniquely -- that triple is the natural key and the id is convenience for the FK. Every instruction carries an FK to its batch, nullable until it has been assigned to one; once it is assigned, the instruction must share the batch's scheme and value date, and the timestamp we accepted it must not fall after that batch's cut-off, because a late arrival rolls into the next cycle instead.

Net positions are the table reconciliation actually reads: one row per batch and participant, keyed on that pair, holding total debits, total credits and the net, where the net is exactly the credits less the debits. Neither total is ever negative -- direction is already in which column it lands in.

Observed shape, from last quarter. Scheme mix is 46 percent SEPA_CT, 34 SEPA_INST, 14 FPS and 6 CHAPS. Instruction amounts are log-normal with a median of 118 euros. The inter-arrival gap within a cycle is exponential, mean 2.3 milliseconds. Instruction count per batch averages about 6.3 million.

Hard rules: an amount is strictly positive and no single instruction may exceed 999,999,999.99; the cycle number is 1 through 6; and a batch never holds fewer than one instruction.

nl_description:
Product owner here. We run a retail investing app -- about 480,000 funded accounts, doing something like 12 million orders a quarter -- so nothing exotic by volume, but the data model we inherited is a mess and we are re-specifying it properly this time.

Clients sign up, we KYC them, and we hold the name, email, date of birth, country of residence, their tax residency, the date they registered and the date they were verified. The email is unique -- it is how people log in, so there is exactly one client per email. Verification never predates registration, obviously, but the old system managed it twice. We want to keep every KYC check rather than just the final verified date: which provider we used, when we ran it, the result it came back with and the risk rating on it. A check is never dated before the client registered.

A client normally has one account, but a stocks-and-shares ISA and a general investment account are separate accounts, so allow several per client: each has an account type, a base currency, the cash balance, the date it was opened and how much has been paid into it in the current tax year. We do not open an account before the client is verified. Account types are their own small reference list now instead of a string on the account row -- the type code, a description, whether it is tax-wrapped, the annual subscription limit that applies to it, and whether it is commission-free. Description and subscription limit depend on the type code and nothing else, which is exactly why they should not have been sitting on 480,000 account rows. What has been paid in this tax year can never exceed the subscription limit on that account's own type; that check is currently a nightly report that nobody reads.

Instruments are the securities we let people trade -- ticker, name, ISIN, asset class (share, ETF, trust) and the exchange that lists it. The ISIN is the real identifier, one instrument per ISIN, and the ticker is just what we show. Exchanges have a code, a name, a country and their trading hours in local time; code determines name and country. Fills come back with a venue rather than an exchange, so venues are held separately too: a venue code, the venue name, which exchange it belongs to and whether it is a dark pool. Best-execution reporting is the only reason that table exists, and code determines both the name and the exchange.

An order is placed on an account for one instrument, with a side, an order type of market or limit, the quantity, the limit price where there is one, when it was placed, the status, and the notional value which we compute and stamp on the row -- for a limit order that is simply the quantity times the limit price. A market order carries no limit price at all. Commission we charge once per order rather than per fill, so that sits on the order too. Orders fill in pieces, and each fill is its own row: the executed quantity, the execution price, the venue and the fill timestamp. A fill is never timestamped before its order was placed, and no single fill is for more than the quantity the order asked for.

We snapshot positions per account and instrument -- the quantity held and the average cost, one row per account and instrument pair, and neither figure is ever negative. We also snapshot a closing price per instrument per day: the instrument, the date, the closing price -- always positive -- and the volume traded. There is one snapshot per instrument per date, and that pair determines the closing price; the app's charts and the position valuations both read it.

Cash in and out is its own ledger: the movement type (deposit, withdrawal, dividend, fee), the amount, the currency and the timestamp. A withdrawal is never for more than the cash balance sitting on the account it comes out of.

Watchlists are technically a nice-to-have but people love them. A client makes a named list with a created date and puts instruments on it; an instrument can be on many thousands of lists and a list holds many instruments, and we want to know when each one was added -- never before the list itself was created. Corporate actions get mentioned a lot by the ops team -- splits, dividends, that sort of thing, recorded against an instrument with an action type, an ex-date and a rate or amount. When a dividend actually pays out we book it per account: the corporate action, the account, the amount and the date it paid, which is never before the ex-date. One payment per account per action, so those two together are the key.

Shape of it: order flow is brutally concentrated, a few dozen tickers take almost everything and it drops off very steeply after those. Order sizes are small and skewed, median around 6 shares. Commission averages 1.10 with hardly any variation, call it 15p either side. Orders end up filled about 82 percent of the time, cancelled 13, rejected 5.

Rules rather than tendencies: a limit order always has a positive limit price on it; commission is zero on any ISA account, which was a promotion we launched and never turned off; and nothing below 1 pound notional or above 250,000 gets through the gate.

a.basis: within the range of Zipf exponents the specifications state (n=30)

std.basis: coefficient of variation in [0.006, 0.682], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=117), applied to the stated mean

nl_description:
Front-office store for the treasury FX desk. Low volume, high value: we book maybe 300 tickets a day and the whole thing is a few hundred thousand rows, so no partitioning and no sharding -- correctness beats throughput here.

A deal has an integer ticket id, the pair traded, a direction, the notional in USD, the all-in rate, a trade date, a value date, a materialised tenor in days, a product of SPOT / FORWARD / SWAP, the counterparty, and the trader who booked it. The tenor is stored rather than computed on read: it is the value date less the trade date, so the value date is always the trade date plus the tenor, and a negative tenor is how the old system used to let a value date land before its own trade date.

Currency pairs are a small reference table: base and quote ISO codes, the pip decimal places, and a flag for whether the pair is in today's tradeable set. There is exactly one row per base-and-quote combination, so that combination is the real key and the integer pair id is only there for the join; the pip places belong to the pair and nothing else. We do not book against a pair that is out of the tradeable set.

Counterparties carry a legal entity name, an LEI -- unique, one row per LEI, and it is the identifier the credit team actually quotes -- a jurisdiction, an internal credit rating and a notional limit. No ticket's notional may exceed the notional limit on its own counterparty. Note the desk also books internal transfers against our own book; treat those as a counterparty like any other, we are not modelling them separately whatever ops say.

Traders have a name, their booking authority limit in USD, and the desk they sit on. The desk is its own row now: a desk code, the desk name, the location it books out of, and the desk-level notional limit the treasurer signs off annually. Name, location and limit all follow from the desk code alone -- they used to live on the trader row and we predictably ended up with two spellings of the same desk. No trader's authority limit is ever set above the limit on their own desk, and no ticket's notional exceeds the authority limit of the trader who booked it. The 50 million figure people quote at me is just the most common authority level, not the rule.

Shape: notionals are log-normal with a median around 2.4 million USD. Product mix runs 58 percent spot, 33 forward, 9 swap. The all-in rate across the pairs we actually trade averages 1.19 with a standard deviation of 0.07 -- yes, that is a mixture across pairs rather than one clean distribution, but it is what we have.

Controls that have to be enforced in the data rather than in the UI: notional is positive and no single ticket exceeds 250 million; the tenor in days is never negative; and a spot ticket has a tenor of at most 2 days.

nl_description:
Right, so we buy debt. Portfolios come to us from banks and utilities, we buy them at a discount, and then we chase them. There are maybe 2.3 million of these accounts on our books at the moment, which is exactly why the spreadsheets have stopped working.

Every one of them is a person who owes money. We call them debtors, the letters call them customers, the client's own file will say account holder -- same thing, three names, and that inconsistency is half our problem. What we need on them: the name, the last known address, a phone number if we have got a working one, the date of birth where we know it, and the balance outstanding. Also whether we have flagged them as vulnerable, because that changes everything we are and are not allowed to do.

The balances are mostly small. Loads and loads of little ones and a handful of big ones that pay for the whole operation -- the average sits somewhere around 900 pounds but that average is honestly close to meaningless given how spread out it is.

Then there is the chasing. Every time we contact somebody, or try to, that is a record: when it was, how we did it -- letter, phone, SMS, email, doorstep -- which of our agents did it, and what came of it. Phone is still about half of everything we do, letters a quarter, and SMS and email make up most of what is left, with doorstep just a sliver of it now.

When somebody agrees to pay in instalments we set up an arrangement: how much, how often, when it starts, and whether they are keeping to it. About 60 percent break them, which is depressingly consistent year on year.

Oh, and the portfolios themselves matter for reporting: who we bought each batch from, when, what we paid for it, and its face value. Every account came in on one of them.

Rules from the FCA side, and these are not negotiable. We never set up an arrangement below 5 pounds. The interest we add to an account is capped at 8 percent. And where somebody is flagged vulnerable we do not add interest at all and we never, ever go doorstep.
