nl_description:
I do the reporting for our outwards reinsurance and I am trying to write down what a proper database for it would actually look like, because right now it is four spreadsheets and a shared drive and I am the only one who understands any of it.

We are the cedant. We buy protection on our own book, treaty by treaty. A treaty has a reference, the class of business it covers, the underwriting year, the inception and expiry dates of the period it runs for, whether it is proportional or excess-of-loss, the retention we keep ourselves, the limit sitting above that, and the estimated premium income we declared at inception. We only have about 40 live treaties -- it is a small programme -- but there are ten years of them, so call it 400 rows in total.

Now the awkward part, and it is precisely the bit the spreadsheets cannot do. A treaty is not placed with one reinsurer. It is placed across several of them -- we say reinsurers, the brokers say the market, the slips say participants, and they all mean the same firms -- and each one takes a percentage line. One reinsurer sits on many of our treaties, and each treaty has anywhere from three to twenty of them on it. Per placement we need the signed line, the written line, and the date they signed.

On the reinsurers themselves: legal name, domicile, and their financial strength rating. That rating drives an approved-for-placement flag we keep against them -- anything rated below A- is not approved, and an unapproved reinsurer cannot hold a line at all, it has to be zero. We also will not give any single reinsurer more than 25 percent of one treaty.

Premium and claims move against a treaty by quarter. Each statement has the quarter it covers, the ceded premium, the brokerage we paid away, the commission we got back, and the paid and outstanding losses. Recoveries we claim off a treaty are separate again: the underlying loss reference, the date, the amount claimed and the amount we actually recovered.

Brokers place all of this for us and we do need to know which broker placed each treaty, although we hold almost nothing else about them beyond the name.

The mix: about two thirds of what we buy is excess-of-loss and the rest is proportional. Signed lines are typically fairly small, averaging around 8 percent, with one or two big lines on each treaty carrying most of it. Ceded premium per statement runs in the low hundreds of thousands and is very variable. And on the excess-of-loss side we never write a retention below 250,000 -- there is no point, the attritional stuff stays with us.

nl_description:
Handover notes for the marketplace core, written up before the shard migration so the next person has something to read.

Two populations at the top and they are deliberately separate accounts. A seller carries a display name, the country code it trades from, the date it onboarded, a rolling average of the stars buyers have left it, and a suspension flag. A buyer is little more than an email, a signup timestamp and a country. Listings hang off a seller and off one node of the category tree, which is self-referencing -- each category row names its parent. On the listing itself: the ask price as DECIMAL, an integer quantity available, a status, the moment it went live, and a denormalised view counter that Redis owns and we flush hourly. Buyers watch listings; many buyers per listing, many listings per buyer, and the only payload on that pairing is when it was added.

Orders are buyer-level with a placed_at timestamp, a total and a status. Each line under an order points at exactly one listing and freezes quantity and unit price at checkout. Shipments are per line rather than per order, because sellers dispatch independently -- carrier code, dispatch time, delivery time. Reviews are also per line: the buyer who left it, a star rating and free text. Sellers are paid fortnightly, one row per seller per period, holding gross, our commission and a hold flag.

Distributions, measured: view counts are Zipf with exponent about 1.35, so a few thousand listings absorb most of the traffic and the tail never breaks single digits. Order totals are log-normal, log-mean 3.4, log-variance 0.9. Line quantity is Poisson, lambda 1.4. Stars land at 60 percent five, 22 percent four, 8 percent three, 4 percent two, 6 percent one. Seller rating averages cluster around 4.5 with a standard deviation near 0.4.

Invariants worth enforcing: stars are 1 to 5; quantity available never goes negative; ask price is at least 1.00 and hard-capped at 250,000, and outside the collectibles category the cap is 15,000; and any payout above 2,000 is held when the seller's average rating is under 4.0.

Volume, current: about 40 million live listings, 120 million orders a year, and shipments running slightly ahead of that.

So we've got three shops now. The original one on Bridge Street, then Cross Lane, then the little kiosk by the station which honestly barely counts but it's on the same card scheme. I want to know for each of them what it's called, where it is and roughly when we opened it, because I keep having to look that up. The names are all different so honestly the name is as good as a reference number for a shop, and it tells you the address and the opening date on its own.

The scheme itself is dead simple. Someone signs up, we take their name and a mobile number -- the mobile is what we look them up on at the counter, one number one person, no sharing, and from then on every time they come in and buy a drink they get a stamp. Ten boxes on the card, when it's full the next one's free. It lives in the app now rather than being a bit of card, so I need to know at any moment how many stamps a given regular is sitting on -- and they're spread all over the place, some are on nought because they've just claimed, some are on nine and pestering us, and it's pretty flat across the range in between. Most of them have a shop they treat as theirs and it'd be nice to have that written down against them. One thing that fell out of the old spreadsheet: a couple of people are down as joining before the shop they call their local had even opened, which can't be right, so nobody's join date should ever be earlier than the opening date of their shop.

The bit I actually care about is the visits. Every time one of our members buys something I want the date and time, which shop, what they spent, what they had, and how many stamps it earned them. On the what-they-had -- I don't need the whole order, just the main drink. Roughly a third of everything we sell is a latte. Flat whites are about a fifth, americanos a bit under that at eighteen percent, cappuccinos maybe fifteen, tea's small at eight or so, and then five percent is odds and ends -- hot chocolate, the babyccinos, that sort of thing. Spend per visit is normally about four pounds eighty and it's rarely more than a pound or so either side of that.

Stamps: one per drink, but if someone's buying a round we cap it at three in one go. And if they spend over a tenner in one transaction they get two stamps minimum -- we started that in January and it's stuck. And if somebody somehow spends nothing -- staff comping a drink for a regular, it happens -- then no stamp, zero. Claiming a free one costs exactly ten stamps, and I want the claim written down against the visit it happened on, with the date and what they actually took, coffee or cake or whatever they picked. Nobody can claim more stamps than they're actually sitting on, and a claim is never dated before the visit it belongs to -- the old sheet managed both of those and neither made any sense. The claim carries who it was as well, even though the visit already tells you that, because whoever's closing up reads the claims list on its own without opening anything else.

Scale-wise it's tiny, which is why the spreadsheet lasted this long. About eight hundred people signed up, we see maybe two hundred visits a day across all three, and the free ones are a handful a week.

Whoever's on shift does the stamping but I don't need to keep track of that.

nl_description:
Proposed schema for the merchandising and stock side, replacing the nightly AS/400 extract.

Style level and variant level have to be modelled separately -- that is the whole point of the exercise. A style belongs to a brand (brands have a name and a country of origin), and carries the style code the buyers use, a display name, a department -- womenswear, menswear, kids, outerwear, accessories -- a season code, and the list price. The thing that actually has a barcode is the variant: one row per size and colour combination under a style, with its own SKU and barcode. The SKU is composed -- style code, size, colour, in that order -- so the SKU on its own fixes all three; the barcode is unique to the variant; and the style code the buyers use is unique too and fixes the display name, the department and the list price. Stock is held per store per variant, that pair is the key, and each row carries what is on hand and what is reserved against click-and-collect, and reserved can never exceed on hand. Stores get a name, a city and a floor area in square metres.

Tills write one sale header per basket -- store, timestamp, basket total, payment method -- and one line per variant scanned, with quantity, the unit price that actually rang, and the discount percentage applied. The line also stamps the style id alongside the variant id, denormalised on purpose: every merchandising report groups by style and I am not paying for that join nine million times a year -- the variant determines the style, so the two can never disagree. Nothing rings above the style's list price, and because the discount is capped at 70 percent nothing rings below 30 percent of list either. Returns come back against a specific sale line and carry a timestamp, a reason code and the refund amount, which can never exceed what that line actually took -- unit price times quantity.

Numbers from the current warehouse. Size mix on variants sold: XS 7 percent, S 20, M 31, L 26, XL 12, XXL 4. Basket totals are log-normal, log-mean 4.0 and log-variance 0.6. Units per line is Poisson with lambda 1.2. We also keep a year-to-date unit count on the style, and it is brutally Zipfian -- exponent around 1.5 -- a couple of hundred styles out of the eleven thousand we list do most of the volume and the tail moves a handful of units a season. Return reasons split wrong size 46 percent, changed mind 24, faulty 12, not as pictured 11, arrived late 7.

Constraints for the DDL: on-hand can never be negative; the line discount sits between 0 and 70 percent; and anything sold at more than 50 percent off is final sale, so a return raised against such a line must refund zero.

Sizing: 340 stores, about 11 thousand styles, 95 thousand variants, roughly 9 million sale lines a year.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: roughly 9 million sale lines a year

nl_description:
Notes from the platform scoping session -- what the till and supply side actually has to hold. I've written it as prose because the modelling call is not mine to make.

Stores first. We run three formats and about 62 percent of the estate is convenience, roughly 30 percent supermarket and the remaining 8 percent superstore. Each store has a name, a city, the date it opened and its floor area.

Products sit in a department, and some departments are chilled, which changes how deliveries into store get handled, so that flag belongs on the department rather than being repeated. Each product comes from exactly one supplier, and on the product we hold the name, the unit it is sold by (each, kilo, litre), the shelf price and whether it is age restricted. Suppliers have a name, a nominal lead time in days, and we mark the ones who make our own-brand lines: own-brand partners are contractually inside three days, everyone else is allowed up to 21.

Promotions run more or less weekly -- a name, a start date, an end date and a mechanic, which is multibuy or price cut or meal deal. A promotion covers many products and a product can be in more than one at a time, and the promotional price is a property of that pairing, not of either side on its own.

The transactional core is the basket: which store, which till, the timestamp it went through, the total, the number of items on it, and the loyalty card if one was swiped. We hold no name against a card, only when it was registered, the postcode district and a declared household size, because that is all legal will let us keep. Basket lines point at a product and carry a quantity -- fractional for loose goods, so don't make it an integer -- the line amount, and whether the operator did the age check.

Two more things around the edges: deliveries arriving into a store from a supplier, with the arrival timestamp and a pallet count, and the waste log, which is store, product, date, units binned and a reason. Someone also asked for shelf-edge label printing but that is not this project.

Distributions we already know: basket totals are log-normal with log-mean 3.1 and log-variance 0.8; items per basket is Poisson around 14. Weekly units per product is a very long tail -- Zipf, exponent about 1.4 -- a couple of thousand lines out of the forty thousand we list drive most of the volume and thousands of others sell in ones and twos.

Non-negotiable: an age check has to be recorded on any line for an age-restricted product, and a basket has at least one item on it.

Volume: 1,100 stores, about 9 million baskets a week and something like 130 million basket lines a week behind them.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: something like 130 million basket lines a week behind them
items per basket is Poisson around 14

nl_description:
Product notes on the data behind the box, from the kick-off doc.

The people first. We have called them subscribers, customers and members in three different parts of the app and I have stopped fighting it -- it is one group of people, one list. What we hold on them: an email, the day they joined, which plan they are on, whether they are live or paused or gone, and their referral code. Both the email and the referral code are unique to the person -- we hand out one code each and people trade them, so it has to be. Plans, there are three of them, at twelve, twenty-eight and forty-five pounds a month, and the top one -- the forty-five -- ships two boxes a month rather than one, so the boxes-per-month figure belongs to the plan, and the plan name fixes both the price and that number.

Every month has an edition -- a theme, the month it goes out and what the box cost us to put together. There is exactly one edition a month, so the ship month picks the edition out on its own. The things inside a box belong to the edition rather than to any individual parcel, which took us a while to work out: a product name, the brand it came from and what it retails for on its own. A typical one is four pounds, most sit between two and eight, and occasionally we talk a brand into putting in something worth thirty -- so the tail is long on the expensive side. We do refuse an item whose stated retail value is more than three times what the whole edition cost to build, because a supplier once typed 400 where they meant 4.00 and it went out in the marketing.

Then the parcels themselves, one per person per edition, with the day it went out, the day it landed, which carrier took it, what the postage cost and where it got to. Nothing lands before it ships, which sounds too obvious to write down and was not true of the old export. Postage runs about 4.20 a parcel, plus or minus 80p.

Retention is the number the board asks about. Most people do not last. The average person is with us about seven months, but a big chunk cancel after a single box and a few have been here since the start, so it is the usual exponential-looking decay curve. I would rather have the months-active number sat on the person's record than derive it every time someone opens the dashboard.

Feedback comes in against a parcel -- a one-to-five rating and usually a comment, with the time it was submitted, which is always after that parcel shipped. The parcel already tells you whose it is, but we copy the person onto the feedback row too because support reads that list on its own. We get 41 percent fives, 34 percent fours, 15 percent threes, 6 percent twos and 4 percent ones.

Two rules that actually bite. Ratings are one to five. And if someone is paused nothing ships -- the parcel gets marked cancelled before the carrier collects it, we do not just delete the row.

Size: a bit over 90,000 active subscribers and about 1.4 million parcels sent since we started.

nl_description:
We're a producing house with two spaces. The main auditorium seats 480 and the studio upstairs is 90, and I know the studio is unreserved half the time but for this let's pretend every seat is a seat. Each one has a row letter, a number within the row, the price band it falls in -- and the band is really the row's, we band whole rows together, so every seat in row F of the main house is the same band -- and whether it's one of the wheelchair spaces, because the box office gets asked that constantly and currently the answer lives on a laminated plan. Seat numbers run from one up to however many that space holds, never past it. The two spaces have different names and that's enough to tell them apart, capacity and all.

A production runs for a few weeks -- it has a title, what sort of thing it is, a first night and a last night, and the last night is obviously not before the first. Inside the run there are the individual performances, each one in one of the two spaces at a particular date and time, and every one of them falls inside the run -- nothing plays before the first night or after the last, and we do need the matinees flagged because they price differently.

The people who book give us a name, an email and a postcode, and we note whether they're one of our members -- there are about 900 of those and they get priority booking, which is the main reason anyone joins. Priority is a fortnight: nothing goes on general sale until fourteen days before the performance, so anything booked earlier than that came from a member. The email is unique to a person, that's what the website logs them in with.

A booking is one person buying for one performance, and it comes in through the website, over the phone, at the window, or as a group sale. The website is about 58 percent of it now, phone 22, the window 18, and group sales are the last 2 percent. You can't book after the curtain's up, so a booking is always dated on or before its performance. We keep when the booking was made and how many days ahead of the performance that was -- that second number is just the gap between the two, so it follows from them, and that number is a horrible skew -- most of it arrives in the last fortnight, the average works out around eleven days, but every so often somebody books six months out. Under the booking sit the actual tickets, each one against a specific seat, with what was paid for it -- never more than the booking total, since the booking is the sum of them, whether a concession was applied and which one, and whether it was a comp.

Prices: the average ticket goes for about twenty-four pounds fifty, and the spread is maybe seven pounds either side. Nothing is ever over sixty-five. Comps are free, so nothing at all, not a nominal penny. And we only count something as a group sale if it's over two hundred pounds all in.

It really isn't a lot of data. Two hundred and fifty-odd performances a year, a few thousand tickets a month, and the mailing list is under a thousand people.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: the average works out around eleven days
the average ticket goes for about twenty-four pounds fifty

nl_description:
POS backend for eleven sites. Terse, because you've seen the last one.

A site has a name, a city and a nominal seat count. Tables within a site carry the code the floor staff shout at each other, a seat count of their own -- which never exceeds the site's nominal count, and the codes only have to be unique within a site, T4 exists in eleven places -- and a flag for the two private rooms. The menu is per site, because London prices diverge from everywhere else, and each item has a course, a price, an alcohol flag and a target prep time in minutes; the same dish name inside one site is one row with one price, and London's version of it is a different row -- the kitchen average is 12 with a standard deviation of about 4.

Recipes need modelling properly this time: an item is made of many ingredients, an ingredient goes into many items, and the quantity is a property of the pairing rather than of either end. Ingredients carry a unit of measure and an allergen code, both fixed by the ingredient name -- flour is grams and gluten wherever it turns up.

A tab is opened against a table and holds an open timestamp, a close timestamp -- never earlier than the open, and the audit team check that -- a cover count that cannot exceed the table's own seats, a subtotal, the tip, which the till refuses above a third of the subtotal as a fat-finger guard, the service charge percentage, and a channel -- 71 percent dine-in, 19 percent takeaway, 10 percent through a delivery app. Lines on the tab reference a menu item with a quantity, the unit price that rang -- staff can discount, so it sits at or below the menu price, never above it -- and a void flag, because voids have to survive for the audit rather than being deleted.

From last year's extract: covers per tab is Poisson, lambda 2.6; subtotals are log-normal with log-mean 3.6 and log-variance 0.5.

Business rules that need to be in the schema, not the app. A party on a normal table is 1 to 8 covers, but a private room booking is 10 to 22. Desserts are all priced between 4 and 9. Anything with alcohol in it rings up at 5.50 or more. And the service charge is exactly 12.5 percent whenever the cover count is 6 or above.

Volume is about 4 million tab lines a year across the estate.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: the kitchen average is 12 with a standard deviation of about 4

nl_description:
Half-finished spec for replacing the delivery whiteboard, which is, still, literally a whiteboard.

Six showrooms, three of which have a warehouse attached. Everything we sell comes from a supplier -- mostly Poland and Italy -- and the supplier's quoted lead time in weeks is the number the sales floor promises against, so it lives on the supplier; supplier names are unique and fix the country and that lead time. A range is bought as a whole from one supplier, so the range name tells you the supplier without looking at the item. An item has a name, the range it belongs to, its retail price, a weight, whether it's flat pack and whether it's a two-person carry. Weights are all over the place -- a lamp is two kilos and a corner sofa is ninety -- so it's a heavy log-normal, log-mean around 2.6 and log-variance 1.1. Flat pack is capped at 40 kilos, that's a warehouse rule and it's never been broken. Anything over forty is a two-person carry by definition, whether it's flat pack or not.

Customers give us a name, a phone number, an email -- one address one customer, we merged the duplicates last year -- and a postcode. An order is placed by one customer at one showroom on a date, and carries a total, the deposit we took and a status. The deposit is at least ten percent of the total and obviously never more than the total itself. Orders average around 900 pounds with a long right tail -- log-normal again, log-variance about 0.6. Lines on the order are an item and a quantity, usually one, Poisson with lambda 1.3, plus the unit price at the time of sale, which is at or below the item's retail price -- we discount, we don't mark up at the till.

Deliveries are the awkward part and the reason for the whiteboard. We build slots: a date, a start and end time for the window -- end after start, and yes someone did enter it backwards -- the van's registration, how many crew are on it and the maximum drops we'll allow. One van does one slot on a day, so the registration and the date together are the slot. Crews are two people 78 percent of the time and three the rest. A delivery then puts one order into one slot at a position in the run, and we record when it actually landed, whether the customer refused it on the doorstep, and whether they asked for assembly. No van does more than twelve drops in a day, so the position in the run is 1 to 12, and within a slot it never goes past that slot's own maximum. And any order over three thousand pounds gets assembly thrown in free, so those always come through flagged as assembly requested.

When something goes wrong we raise a complaint against the delivery -- the date it was raised -- on or after the day the delivery landed, never before -- a category, how it was resolved and any goodwill payment, which is capped at 250 pounds without a manager. Damaged goods is 41 percent of them, late 27, wrong item 14, missing parts 12, and 6 percent is everything else.

Deposits obviously can't be negative. We're doing about 40,000 orders a year and have roughly 300,000 deliveries on record.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: we're doing about 40,000 orders a year

nl_description:
Single-site community pharmacy, dispensing side only. The front-shop till is a different system and out of scope here.

Four things to hold. Drugs: a name, the form (tablet, capsule, liquid, cream), the strength in milligrams, whether it is a controlled drug, and the pack price we pay. Name, form and strength together are what a script actually names, and that triple is one row. Controlled status is a property of the substance, not of the pack -- every strength and form under one name carries the same flag. Strengths span orders of magnitude, 5mg through to 1000mg, so model it log-normal with log-mean 3.0 and log-variance 1.4. Patients: NHS number -- unique, it is the identifier the whole service runs on -- year of birth, and whether they are charge exempt -- we deliberately hold no name in that table.

Every dispensing event is a row: the patient, the drug, the date on the prescription itself, the date it went out -- which is never before the prescription date -- the quantity of units, the days supply it covers, what we charged, and whether it came off a repeat. Quantity is never below days supply; a day of treatment is at least one unit. Days supply is overwhelmingly 28 at 62 percent, with 12 percent at 7 days, 9 percent at 14, 11 percent at 56 and 6 percent at 84. Quantity of units is Poisson-ish around 30.

Two regulatory rules to encode. A controlled drug may not be dispensed for more than 30 days supply. And the prescription charge is 9.90 flat per item while exempt patients pay nothing, so the charge sits between 0 and 9.90 and must be exactly zero whenever the patient is exempt.

Separately the CD cabinet and the fridge get counted every week: the drug, the date, the units on the shelf, the figure the system thought was there, and the discrepancy, which is exactly the counted units minus the system figure -- we store it because every report wants it and nobody trusts a view. A shelf count is never negative.

It is small. About 1,800 patients on file and 2,500 items dispensed a month, so under half a million rows in total after eight years of trading.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: Quantity of units is Poisson-ish around 30.

nl_description:
I'll describe this the way I'd describe it to my mum, and you can turn it into whatever it needs to be.

It's a place where people sell their old stuff to other people. Everyone is the same kind of account -- I sell you my drill on Tuesday and bid on your bike on Friday -- so I really do not want two separate lists of people. Someone has the handle they picked -- taken once and that's it, nobody else can have it -- when they joined, the town they're in, and a feedback score out of five which is just the average of what people have said about dealing with them.

A listing is one thing someone has put up for auction. There's a title, roughly what kind of thing it is, the price they want to start at, and how long they want it to run. We let them pick anywhere from three to ten days and it comes out pretty evenly spread across the options, no real favourite. We also keep a count of how many people are watching it, how many times it's been looked at -- you can't have more people watching than have looked, watching is something you do after you've looked -- the day it went up, the day it finished, which is just the start day plus however many days they picked, and whether it actually went. The looking is wildly uneven -- maybe one listing in ten thousand gets tens of thousands of views because it hit the front page or somebody shared it, and the enormous majority sit at single digits forever, which is exactly the long tail everyone tells me to expect. Starting prices are lopsided the same way: the middle of the pack is about two pounds, loads of things go up at 99p, and then there's the odd thousand-pound thing that drags the average miles above what anyone actually starts at.

Bids: who bid, on what, when, how much, and whether it was one of the automatic ones where the system keeps bidding for you up to a limit you set. Nobody can bid below what the seller asked to start at, and nothing comes in after the thing has finished. If it sold there was at least one bid on it, by definition. Stuff that sells typically gets three or four bids -- some get thirty, plenty get one -- and I'd like that count sat on the listing so the page doesn't have to add it up every time somebody loads it.

Once a deal is done either side can leave feedback, which is stars out of five, a note, and the day it was left, and it hangs off the listing it was about -- never dated before the listing finished, and you only get one go, so one person leaves at most one lot of feedback on any one listing. Nearly everyone leaves five: three quarters of it is five stars, fifteen percent four, five percent three, and the ones and twos are about three and two percent between them.

Two things I know we need to actually stop people doing. The run length has to be inside that three to ten days. And anyone whose feedback score is under two can't bid more than a hundred pounds -- that came out of a fraud thing last year and it isn't negotiable.

Oh, and the pricey stuff, anything starting over five hundred quid, we always run for the full ten days.

It's big now, which is the whole problem: something like twelve million listings live at any one time and we took a quarter of a billion bids last year.

a.basis: within the range of Zipf exponents the specifications state (n=30)

variance.basis: variance = ln(1 + CV^2) for CV in [0.324, 3.166], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=70)

ground_truth_moments.evidence: something like twelve million listings live at any one time

nl_description:
Notes for the new parcel platform, replacing the two systems we run today. Sizing first because it decides the partitioning: roughly 40 million parcels a quarter, so scan events run into the hundreds of millions, against a claims tail that is trivial in row count and the thing legal asks about most.

NETWORK AND COMMERCIAL. Depots are either regional hubs or spoke branches -- each one has a three-letter code and sits in exactly one region, and a spoke never spans regions, so the code on its own tells you the region. Around 12,000 named contract accounts book against us. Commercial terms do not belong on the account, they belong on a contract: a contract reference unique across the book, the account it was written for, a committed monthly parcel volume, an agreed rate per parcel, the date it starts and the date it ends, which is never earlier than the date it starts. An account works through several contracts over the years, and the reference is what everything is looked up by, so from a reference you get both the account and the committed volume.

A booking (we call it a shipment) is one account sending from one origin depot to one destination postcode at one service level, timestamped at booking, carrying a declared value in money. We sell four service levels, each with its own service code, a promised transit day count and a hard per-parcel weight cap; the code determines both of those, because they are properties of the product and not of the booking.

A shipment holds one or more parcels. A parcel is barcoded, the barcode is unique and it is how the whole network refers to the thing, and it carries a dead weight in kg plus length, width and height in cm from which we derive a volumetric weight. We bill on the greater of the two, so the chargeable weight held on the parcel works like this: where the volumetric figure comes out above the dead weight, the chargeable weight is at least the volumetric figure; where it does not, the chargeable weight is at least the dead weight. Bulky-but-light freight is exactly what the old system got wrong.

OPERATIONS. A route belongs to a depot and has a route code -- the code begins with the depot's three-letter code, so the route code gives you the depot -- plus a day of week and a planned stop count. A route run pins one route to one driver and one vehicle on a given run date, with departure and return timestamps, the weight loaded at departure and the number of stops actually completed. A run never returns before it departed and never completes more stops than its route plans for. We plan loading to 95% of the vehicle's plated payload capacity and never go above that figure. Drivers have a name, a home depot and a licence class; vehicles record a registration that is unique, a type and a payload capacity, which runs from 750 kg panel vans up to 7.5 tonne rigids. Neither the driver nor the van is ever lent out, so on any run both of them belong to the same depot the route belongs to. The 7.5 tonne rigids may only be driven by a driver holding a C1.

Trunking between depots is a separate movement from delivery: a linehaul trip is one vehicle and one driver running from an origin depot to a destination depot -- never the same depot at both ends -- with departure and arrival timestamps, arrival never before departure, and the trailer fill as a percentage. Fill averages 78% with a standard deviation around 12.

Every parcel accumulates timestamped scan events at a depot. The scan type is a reference list in its own right: a code, a description and a flag for whether the type is terminal (delivered, returned, destroyed). The code determines both the description and that flag, and the flag having been hard-coded into reports instead is how we ended up with three different delivered counts last year. A parcel also has zero or more delivery attempts, each against a route run, numbered, timestamped, with an outcome. An attempt is timestamped inside the run that made it: never before the van left the depot and never after it came back.

CLAIMS. A customer claims against a shipment, naming the parcel, with a reason code, the time it was raised, the amount claimed, the time it was settled and what we settled at. A claim is never raised before the shipment was booked, settlement is never before the claim was raised, we never settle above the amount claimed, and on a loss claim we never pay above the declared value on the shipment. Claim amounts are log-normal, log-mean 3.9, log-variance 1.1.

Measured behaviour, from the current warehouse: dead weight is log-normal, log-mean 0.6, log-variance 0.8. Destination postcode frequency is Zipf with exponent 1.35 -- a few hundred postcodes carry most of the traffic. Planned stops per route are Gaussian, mean 92, sd 24. Attempt outcomes split 88% delivered, 7% carded, 2% refused, 2% missorted, 1% damaged.

Rules to enforce: nothing over 31.5 kg enters the network and nothing under 10 g. Route plans are never written below 40 or above 160 stops. Trailer fill is a percentage and behaves like one. Declared value is capped at 2,500 on the express service (promised transit of one day) -- other services have no cap. Next-day bookings are only accepted at hub depots. After a third failed attempt the parcel's next attempt outcome is recorded as returned to sender.

Right, so what we do is take chilled and frozen food off the suppliers and get it out to the shops. I'll try to explain it the way it actually works rather than the way the last lot wrote it down.

The suppliers are mostly UK but we've a fair few Dutch and Spanish ones too, so we do need to know which country each one is in -- it matters for the paperwork. No two of them are called the same thing, so the name on its own tells you which country the paperwork goes to. Every line we sell -- the product list, the buyers call it -- comes from one supplier and one only. For each line we hold the name, how many days of life it has when it arrives, what a case of it weighs, which temperature band it belongs in, and the holding temperature it's meant to sit at. That last one isn't really a property of the line if I'm honest -- it follows straight from the band. Chilled is chilled, they all want the same number, and when someone typed a different figure against one chilled line last spring it caused a right mess. Six in ten of our lines are chilled, three in ten frozen, and the rest are ambient bits that ride along on the same lorries.

We've four depots -- distribution centres if you want the official word, but nobody says that -- each in its own town. Every shop is served out of one depot, never two, and we keep the store's name and the town it's in. Because of that, if you know the shop on a run you already know which depot it went out of, which is why the two of them never disagree on a run and if they ever do the run's wrong.

We run six lorries of our own. Each one has its registration on the plate -- that's what everyone calls them by, so the plate tells you the lorry -- what it's allowed to carry in kilos, and the depot it's kept at. A lorry only ever goes out of the depot it's kept at.

A run goes from a depot to a shop on one of the lorries. We note whether it's a chilled run or a frozen run, when it left, when it got there -- never before it left, obviously -- how long it took door to door, and the weight of the load off the ramp. We don't go over what the lorry's allowed to carry, that's the law not us. Most runs are done inside a couple of hours but the odd one drags on for half a day if there's trouble on the motorway -- long tail, that, average is about an hour and three quarters.

On each run there's a list of what's on it: which line, how many cases, what the shop actually signed for when it turned up, the set point the cabinet is meant to be held at, and the weight of that line, which is just the cases times what a case weighs. The shop can't sign for more than we sent -- less, yes, that happens, that's a shortage and we credit it. A line is usually a dozen or so cases, fourteen on average. And the set point is never above the holding temperature the line wants; colder is fine, warmer is a rejected load.

The probes are the bit the auditors care about. Each one is stuck somewhere in the trailer -- front, middle, back of the box -- and it writes the temperature every few minutes against the run. They only write while the doors are shut, so every reading falls between the time the lorry left and the time it got there. Most of what comes back sits right around three degrees, within a degree either way. On a chilled run the probe should never read below zero or above five, that's the line the auditor draws. Anything frozen has to be set at minus eighteen or colder, no argument.

Shelf life is anywhere from three days to three weeks and it's pretty evenly spread across that. Nobody sends a zero-case line, obviously.

Volume-wise we're putting through something like four hundred thousand delivery lines a year and the probes throw off a couple of million readings on top of that.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: average is about an hour and three quarters

nl_description:
We're re-platforming the WMS for our two national fulfilment sites and I've been asked to write down what the data side has to hold. I'm an analyst, not a DBA, so treat the types as advisory.

Each site -- each warehouse, if you want the word that's on the door -- has a code and a floor area in square metres. Inside a site you have zones -- ambient, chilled and frozen -- and each zone has its own code and belongs to exactly one site. The zone code carries the site letter and the temperature class in it, which is handy: give me a zone code and I can tell you the site and the class without looking anything up. Zones contain bins; a bin has a location code that is unique across both buildings and has its zone in it, a capacity in units, and a flag for whether it's a pick face or a reserve location.

The stock table is the one people always get wrong. It is not one row per SKU. It is one row per bin and SKU together, because the same SKU legitimately sits in several bins at once and a bin can hold more than one SKU -- the row carries the quantity on hand and the date it was last cycle-counted, and the bin plus the SKU is what identifies it. We never book more units into a bin than the bin's capacity says it holds, and obviously on-hand can't go negative. A SKU itself has a code that is unique and is what everyone quotes, a description, a per-each weight in kg, a unit cost, and an ABC class from the annual review: 15% of our SKUs come out A, 30% B, 55% C.

Inbound is changing with this rebuild -- the buyers' purchase orders come into scope, they've lived in a spreadsheet up to now. A supplier has a name and a quoted lead time in days, which runs anywhere from 2 to 30 and is pretty flat across that. A purchase order is raised on one supplier for one site with a reference that is unique and is what goods-in quote on the phone, the date it was raised and the date we expect it, which is never earlier than the date it was raised. Its lines say which SKU and how many units we ordered -- never fewer than one.

A receipt is one delivery against one purchase order, at a site, with a timestamp. Its lines each satisfy one purchase order line, and say how many were received and which bin they got put away into. The SKU on a receipt line is really just whatever the purchase order line said -- goods-in can't substitute one code for another, and where the two have disagreed in the old spreadsheet it was always a keying error. Goods-in are allowed to take up to five percent over the quantity the purchase order line asked for, and not a unit more than that.

Outbound: an order arrives against a site with a placed timestamp, a ship-by date that is never before the day it was placed, and a priority. Order lines are SKU and quantity ordered -- typically one or two units, average 2.6. SKU demand is the classic long tail; when we fitted it the Zipf exponent came out about 1.2, and the top handful of codes really do account for most of the picks.

We release work in waves. A wave is raised for one zone at one site at a released timestamp and carries a line count -- normally around 220 lines, standard deviation about 60. Since a zone already belongs to a site, the site on the wave is just the zone's site and the two are never allowed to differ. Frozen is the exception on volume: a wave in a frozen zone is capped at 40 lines, because there is a limit to how long anyone should be stood in there.

Each pick task in a wave points at one order line and the bin it was picked from -- always a bin inside the wave's own zone, we don't send pickers wandering between temperature classes -- and records the picker's badge, the quantity actually picked, when it was picked, and whether it went short. A task never picks more than the order line asked for. If the picker brings back less than the line asked for the task is short, and if he brings back the lot it isn't. And we never let an A-class SKU sit below 20 eaches in any bin it's held in -- that's a replenishment trigger, not a nice-to-have.

Returns do come back through the buildings but they live in a different system entirely and are out of scope here.

Scale: about 60 million pick tasks a year across the two sites, roughly 9 million orders.

variance.basis: variance = ln(1 + CV^2) for CV in [0.324, 3.166], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=70)

ground_truth_moments.evidence: about 60 million pick tasks a year

nl_description:
Terminal operating system, data layer. Read this as the handover for the whole estate rather than the one extract we shipped last time: it swallows the berth planner, the yard system, the equipment log, the gate and the storage billing run, which are five separate boxes today and disagree with each other every month-end. Sizing for the partitioning argument: 3.1 million TEU a year, about 9 million crane moves, 2.6 million truck visits, and the reefer plug feed on top of that at roughly 30 million readings a month, which on its own is bigger than everything else combined.

INFRASTRUCTURE. Two terminals under one operator; each has a terminal code and a quay length in metres. A berth belongs to a terminal and carries a berth code that is unique across the operator, a maximum permissible draft and a berth length -- the code tells you the terminal, the draft and the length, which is exactly why the planner should read them off the reference row instead of a spreadsheet. Ours run from 8.5 m on the feeder berth to 17.5 m on the deep-water pair. The yard is blocks, each block belonging to a terminal with a block code, a slot count and a flag for whether the block is plugged for reefers. A slot sits in one block and is identified within that block by its row and its tier -- block, row and tier together are what the driver reads out and what identifies the slot -- and it carries the maximum tier that may be stacked in that position plus a flag for whether the slot has a reefer plug. Nothing is ever stacked above a slot's maximum tier. Gate lanes belong to a terminal too, with a lane code and a flag for whether the lane is inbound.

COMMERCIAL AND SCHEDULE. Vessels belong to a shipping line (line code plus name). A line runs service loops: a loop code that is unique across the book, a loop name and the rotation in days, and the loop code determines both the line and the rotation. A vessel is keyed on our own surrogate but carries the IMO number, which is unique to the hull and gives you our key and the line, plus a name, TEU capacity, length overall and its own maximum draft. Capacity is log-normal across our call mix, log-mean 8.6 and log-variance 0.45. We handle nothing shorter than 90 m LOA and nothing longer than 400 m.

A vessel call is one voyage number of one vessel at one berth on one loop, with the ETA, the actual arrival, the actual departure -- never before the arrival -- the draft declared on arrival and the planned discharge count. A call is only berthed where it fits: the declared draft never exceeds the berth's permissible draft and never exceeds the vessel's own maximum draft, and the vessel's length overall never exceeds the berth length. Anything over 340 m LOA can only be worked at a berth whose permissible draft is 16 m or more. Every change of state on a call is an event row -- the call, the status code, when it happened and the staff member who keyed it -- and the status codes are a short reference list carrying a description and a flag for whether that status counts as working.

CARGO. Box types are an ISO reference list: the ISO type code, a description, the nominal size in feet, a reefer flag and the maximum gross weight permitted for the type. A container is keyed internally, carries the container number (unique, and it is what everyone quotes), its ISO type, and then the size in feet and the reefer flag again, copied onto the box row because half our interfaces want them there; both follow from the type and must agree with it. Tare weight sits on the box. Size mix is 34% twenty-foot, 61% forty-foot, 5% forty-five.

Paperwork: a bill of lading carries a B/L number, the line that issued it, the consignee name, the declared commodity and the freight kind. A container visit is one box arriving on one discharge call against one bill of lading, sitting in one yard slot, with a discharge timestamp, a gate-out timestamp -- that is when the road haulier takes it, and it is never before the discharge -- the dwell in hours, the gross weight as landed and a flag for whether the visit is an import. Landed gross weight is always above the box's tare weight. Import dwell is exponentially distributed with a mean around 48 hours and is never negative. Reefers are a different matter: a plugged box must be off the terminal inside 24 hours, and a reefer box is only ever put down in a slot that has a plug.

Verified gross mass is its own row against the box: when it was weighed, the verified gross weight and the weighbridge code. A verified weight is never below the box's tare either, and that is precisely the check the old bridge software did not do.

Dangerous goods: the IMDG classes are a reference list with a description and a segregation flag, and one visit can carry several classes, each with its UN number and a flashpoint in Celsius -- the visit and the class together make the row.

Reefer monitoring writes a reading per plugged visit: a timestamp, the set point and the supply air temperature. Set points run from minus 30 to plus 15. Supply air is allowed to sit up to two degrees above the set point and no further; that tolerance is what every cargo claim turns on.

EQUIPMENT AND MOVES. Cranes belong to a terminal, have a crane code, a rated moves-per-hour that is Gaussian around 30 with sd 4, and a maximum outreach in rows. Move types are a reference list: the code, a description and whether the move counts as productive. Every crane move records the crane, the call it was worked against, the box, the move type, the gang that worked it and a timestamp -- 42% discharge, 40% load, 13% reshuffle, 5% hatch cover. A move is always timestamped inside its call, between the arrival and the departure. Note the gang already knows which crane it was assigned to, so the crane on the move row is strictly the gang's crane; keep the column for query convenience but it is derivable and it has been inconsistent in the old extract.

Yard equipment -- straddles, reach stackers, terminal tractors -- sits against a terminal with an equipment code, an equipment class and a commissioning date. Faults are raised against a piece of equipment with a fault code, when it was reported, when it was cleared (never before it was reported) and the downtime in hours, which is log-normal, log-mean 1.2, log-variance 0.9, and never negative. Planned maintenance is separate from faults: an order against the equipment with a raised timestamp, a completed timestamp that is never before it, a work type and the labour hours booked to it.

LABOUR. Job roles are a reference list with a description and a flag for whether the role requires a certificate. Terminal staff belong to exactly one terminal with a name, a role and a hire date. Certificates held are their own rows in a certification log -- the staff member, the certificate code, when it was awarded and when it expires, the expiry always after the award -- because a lashing certificate that has lapsed is no certificate. A work shift belongs to a terminal with a shift code, a shift date, a start and an end after the start. A gang is raised on a shift against one crane with a gang number and a foreman, and that crane is always at the same terminal the shift is run at; we do not work cranes across the water. Gang membership is many to many: the gang and the staff member together, with the role worked on that gang and the times they actually signed on and off, sign-off never before sign-on.

LANDSIDE. Hauliers carry a name and a licence number. A truck visit is one haulier's truck at one gate lane with the truck registration, an arrival, a departure after it and the turn time in minutes, which is Gaussian, mean 45 with sd 14 -- that is the number the hauliers' association quotes at us in every meeting. Each gate transaction sits on a truck visit, names the container visit it moved, a direction and the time it was processed, and that time falls inside the truck's own arrival and departure.

REGULATORY. Hold reasons are a reference list with a description and a flag for whether the reason blocks gate-out. A customs hold sits against a container visit with a reason code, a placed timestamp and a release timestamp never before it. Where the reason blocks gate-out, the box does not leave the terminal before the hold is released -- the gate-out is at or after the release.

BILLING. Tariffs carry a tariff code, the free days allowed, a storage rate per day and a reefer surcharge per day; the code determines the free days and the rate, and hard-coding either into the billing run is how we ended up rebating a whole quarter. A storage invoice is issued against a bill of lading with an issue date, the chargeable days on it and the invoice total, which is never negative. Its lines each name a container visit and the tariff applied, the chargeable days for that visit -- around four on average -- and the line amount, which is the chargeable days times the tariff's storage rate per day.

AUDIT. Every change to any of the above is an audit row naming the table, the record key, the action, the field, the old and the new value, the staff member who made the change and when. The last inspection was specifically about yard-position history we could not produce, so this part is not negotiable.

Rail sidings are coming in phase two; ignore them for now.

We're a forwarder -- we don't own a single aircraft or ship, we buy space and sell it on. What I want out of a new system is one place where a job lives from the day we open it to the day the last invoice goes out, because at the moment it's half in the accounts package and half in people's heads.

A job -- some of the older hands call it a file, and the operations lot say consignment, it's all the same thing -- belongs to one client. Clients are companies and we need to know where they are, country-wise, because that drives who can sign what. Each job has a mode: roughly half of what we do is air, a bit over a third is sea and the rest goes by road. It has a place it comes from and a place it goes to -- we write them as port or airport names, which I know is a bit rough -- and the date we opened it. We hold two weights on it: what the freight actually weighs on the scale, and the chargeable weight, which is the number everything else hangs off. The chargeable is never below the actual -- that's the whole trick of volumetric, a pallet of cushions weighs nothing and costs a fortune. The average job is about 500 kilos chargeable but the spread is enormous, we've had 20-tonne machinery moves and we've had a 30-kilo box of samples. We won't take anything under 30 kilos chargeable any more, mind -- it isn't worth the paperwork.

A job moves in legs. Each leg is with one carrier -- airlines, shipping lines, hauliers, all in the same list with which mode they are -- and legs are ordered, so leg one, leg two and so on, never a leg nought, with the date it went and the date it landed, which is never before the date it went, and how many days it took. Nothing on a job is dated before the day the job was opened, legs included; if it is, someone's fat-fingered the year again. Leg one is always on the mode the job was sold as -- if we sold it as an air job then leg one is with an airline, whatever happens after that. A leg usually clears in a week or so but plenty run much longer. If we're booking with a shipping line we never quote a leg at less than ten days, that's a hard rule from the commercial director after we got burned.

Charges are where the money is. The charge types are a fixed little list -- freight, fuel, handling, duty, our own fee -- and each type says what it is and whether it's a disbursement, meaning money we're only passing on rather than earning. Each charge sits on a job, has its type, what it cost us, the amount we billed, and the currency it was billed in. We never bill under what a thing cost us, and the boss's rule is never more than double it either. Duty is always billed in sterling, no exceptions. Most charge lines are a couple of hundred pounds but every so often you get one in the tens of thousands. Nothing is ever billed negative; if we've overcharged we raise a credit through the accounts package, not here.

The invoice is what the client actually gets. It goes out against the job with the date it was issued, the total on it, and one currency for the whole thing -- every charge that goes onto an invoice is billed in that invoice's currency, we don't mix. Totals are never negative and an invoice is never dated before the job was opened.

Documents hang off the job too -- the bill of lading or air waybill, the packing list, the certificate of origin, whatever the corridor wants -- with what kind it is and when it was issued.

Oh, and the cargo insurance is placed through an underwriter, but that's their paperwork, not ours, so leave it out.

We're opening somewhere north of two hundred thousand jobs a year now and each one throws off roughly a dozen charge lines.

nl_description:
Schema brief for the rail freight planning store. Nine entities, and I want the consist modelled properly this time.

Yards: a yard code that is unique and tells you the region, plus the region itself and a siding count. Locomotives: class designation, tractive effort in kN, fuel type (diesel or electric). Wagons: a running number that is unique and identifies the wagon and its type, the wagon type, tare weight and maximum payload, both in tonnes -- payload runs from 20 t on the oldest vans to 102 t on the new bulk hoppers, and on every wagon in the fleet the maximum payload is above the tare. The fleet is 34% hopper, 30% box van, 22% flat and 14% tank.

Commodities are a reference list rather than a free-text field this time: a commodity code, a description, a hazardous flag and a flag for whether the commodity has to travel in a tank wagon. The code determines all three, and anything flagged tank-only never goes in anything else.

A service is the timetabled product: a service code, an origin yard, a destination yard -- never the same yard at both ends -- a scheduled departure time, a distance in km which is uniform between 40 and 620 across the book, the maximum consist length the book allows for that service, and whether the route is wired throughout. The service code determines the origin, the destination, the distance and the scheduled departure; those four live in the book and not on the run. A run is one dated operation of a service behind one locomotive, with actual departure and arrival timestamps -- arrival never before departure -- a delay in whole minutes and the consist length, which never exceeds the maximum the service allows. Delay is exponentially distributed with a mean of about 12 minutes and is never negative -- early arrivals are recorded as zero. Consist length is Poisson with lambda 42. An electric locomotive is only ever rostered onto a service whose route is wired.

The consist itself is a many-to-many: a wagon appears in many runs over its life and a run has many wagons, so it is its own relation keyed on the run and the wagon together, carrying the wagon's position in the train, counted from the locomotive back, and a position never exceeds the consist length recorded on that run. Any run booked over 400 km must be assigned a locomotive rated at 300 kN or better.

Consignments are the customer-facing side: a customer (name, sector), a commodity code, the tonnage the customer booked, the tonnage actually loaded, an origin and destination yard that are never the same, and the wagon and run it travelled on. Loaded tonnage never exceeds the wagon's maximum payload and never exceeds the booked tonnage by more than 2%. Tonnage is Gaussian, mean 58, sd 12, and we accept nothing below 1 t or above 100 t. Hazardous commodities are filled to no more than 95% of the wagon's payload -- ullage. A consignment loaded into a tank wagon is always liquid bulk; the commodity code follows from the wagon type there.

Sizing: about 180,000 runs a year, a couple of million consignments over the seven-year retention window, and around 7.5 million consist rows.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: Delay is exponentially distributed with a mean of about 12 minutes
Consist length is Poisson with lambda 42

nl_description:
So this is for the courier side of the app and honestly the spec is a bit thin because the ops team keeps changing its mind. I'll give you what I'm confident about.

We've got about 220 riders on the books. Everyone calls them different things -- riders, couriers, delivery partners -- it's the same person, one record each. We hold their name, when they joined, what they ride (bike, moped or car), and a rating. The rating is out of five and some of the ops people put halves in, so it's not a whole number. Most riders sit at 4.6 or so, very few below 4, standard deviation is something like a third of a point. Nobody can be rated below one.

The zones are a proper little list now rather than three strings in the code: a zone code, the name we show in the app, and a flag for whether bikes are allowed in it. Out-of-town has that flag off -- it's too far to ride -- and central and north have it on. The flag lives on the zone, so if we open a fourth zone nobody has to touch the app.

A rider signs up for shifts. A shift is a date, a start and an end time (the end is after the start, we don't run shifts over midnight), and a zone. A rider on a bike is only ever given a shift in a zone that allows bikes. We also keep a count of drops on the shift; a busy shift is a dozen, which is about the average.

Drops belong to a shift. Each one has the delivery address, the merchant it came from, the rider -- which I'll admit is daft, because the shift already says who was working, and the two must always be the same person -- when the rider accepted it, when it was dropped (never before he accepted it), a status, the value of the order and the tip amount. Merchants have a name that the app won't let anyone duplicate, and each sits in one of our zones. A rider only gets offered drops from merchants in the zone he signed up for, so the merchant's zone and the shift's zone always match. Statuses: 94% of drops go through fine, about 4% get cancelled and the remaining 2% we mark failed. If a drop is cancelled there's no tip on it, obviously -- and no tip is ever negative. The app also won't let anyone tip more than half the order value, which finance asked for after someone tipped 200 quid on a burrito. Tips average around two pounds but loads of them are nothing at all, it's very skewed.

We've been talking about tracking the insulated bags each rider carries so we know who's got what, but nothing's decided, so don't build it.

This is a small dataset -- we only hold the live quarter, so about four thousand drops sitting in there at any time and a few hundred shifts a week.

nl_description:
Customs brokerage back end. Importers are keyed on our own surrogate but carry the EORI number, which is unique and gives you the importer and the country code, plus the legal name and that country code. Each importer may hold one deferment account with an account number that is unique across the estate and identifies both the account and the importer, a credit limit and a running balance; the balance never exceeds the limit, and an importer whose deferment limit is under 50,000 is put on prepay, which is a declaration-level status.

Modes of transport are held as the UN code with its description rather than being repeated as free text -- 48% road = 3, 34% sea = 1, 16% air = 4, 2% rail = 2.

A declaration belongs to one importer and records the MRN, which is unique and is what everything is looked up by, the mode as its UN code, a lodgement timestamp, the total customs value with its currency code, the total duty for the declaration, a status, and the number of item lines it carries -- line counts are Poisson with lambda 6. Customs value is log-normal, log-mean 8.9, log-variance 1.6, and cannot be negative.

Declaration lines hold the tariff measure version they were rated under, the commodity code, a free-text goods description, net mass in kg, the line value, the duty rate applied as a percentage and the resulting duty amount. The commodity code and the applied rate both come off the measure the line cites -- if they disagree with it, the line was rated against a measure that has since been superseded, which is the single most common reason we get a query. No individual line's value exceeds the declaration's total customs value. Applied duty rates are roughly uniform between 0 and 12% but the schema must tolerate anything from 0 to 25%, so a line's duty never exceeds a quarter of the line's value. Where a line's value is 135 or below, no duty is charged -- the duty amount is zero.

Tariff measures are a reference table: a measure identifier, the commodity code, the duty rate, a preference code and a valid-from date, one row per measure version.

Duty payments sit against the declaration: the deferment account it was taken from, the date it was paid, the amount and the method. Nothing is paid before the declaration was lodged, and no payment exceeds the total duty on the declaration.

Queries raised by customs sit against a declaration with a reason code, a raised timestamp -- never before the declaration was lodged -- a resolved timestamp that is never before the raised timestamp, and the hours it stayed open, which is exponential with a mean of about 22 hours.

Volumes: roughly 900,000 declarations and 5.5 million lines a year.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: line counts are Poisson with lambda 6.
the hours it stayed open, which is exponential with a mean of about 22 hours.

nl_description:
Returns desk tooling. Small piece of work, but the spreadsheet has finally fallen over so we need it in a database.

When a customer wants to send something back they raise a return with us. We take the order reference as a string -- the order itself lives in the webshop platform and we are not duplicating it here, so a reference is all we get -- plus the email they contacted us on, the date it was raised, a reason code and a status we move through as it progresses. Reasons break down about like this: 31% too small, 22% not as described, 20% changed their mind, 18% arrived damaged and 9% turned up too late to be useful.

One return can cover several items, and each item line names the SKU as a code, the quantity of units (nearly always one, occasionally two or three -- averages about 1.3, never zero), the unit price it was sold at, the grade we settle on -- people say condition and grade interchangeably, it's one field -- and the refund we agreed. A refund is never more than the line was actually worth, meaning the unit price times the units on it. Refunds average about 34.50 with most within twenty pounds either side, and we never agree a negative amount. Change-of-mind returns are the one case where finance caps us: no more than 250 back on those, whatever the item was worth.

Then the warehouse inspects each item -- one inspection per item line, with the date, who did it, an outcome and a flag for whether it went back into sellable stock. Just under six in ten come out fit to restock, about a fifth go to refurb, a sixth get scrapped and the last few percent go back to the vendor. Anything graded A goes straight back on the shelf; anything scrapped obviously does not, and anything the inspector marks restock does. If I'm honest that flag tells you nothing the outcome doesn't already say -- the outcome decides it every time -- but the warehouse screen writes both fields and I'm not going to win that argument this quarter.

Finance pay out once the inspection is done, and that payout is its own record: which inspection cleared it, which item line it belongs to, the date it was paid, the amount that actually went back and the method. The inspection already tells you the item line, so those two never disagree. Nothing is ever paid before the inspection date, and nobody pays out more than the refund we agreed on the line -- part payments happen, over-payments do not.

We see maybe 40 returns a week, so a couple of thousand rows a year -- this is not a big table by anyone's standard.

My son said I should write this down properly before I ring anyone, so here goes. We hold spare parts for industrial laundry machines and we send them out to the engineers who fix them. Been doing it since 1988 out of the same unit.

The parts. Everything has a part number stamped on it or printed on the bag, and a name, though half the names in the book are wrong and the lads just call them bits. No two things share a number, and the number is how you find the shelf spot -- each one lives somewhere on the racking and we write that spot down or we'd never find anything. We know what we charge for each and how many we've got, and there's a level written on the bin card where you're supposed to reorder. Most of them are a few pounds -- seals, clips, that sort of thing -- but the big drum assemblies run into the thousands, so it's a very lopsided list. And here's the thing nobody outside believes: it's the same forty or fifty numbers that account for nearly all the movement. The rest sit on that racking for years. Obviously we can't have a minus figure in the stock count, and nothing is ever priced below nothing.

Then the orders. An engineer rings up or emails, and we take his name -- we don't hold anything else about them, they work for the customers not for us -- the date, and how urgent it is. There's a card taped to the wall with the three urgencies on it, what each one means and how many days it gets: a breakdown is nothing, zero days, machine's dead and the factory's stopped; urgent is next day; normal we allow three days. The days on an order come straight off that card, they're not something we decide job by job, and if the card ever changes it changes for everything. About a quarter of orders come in urgent and one in twenty is a proper breakdown. The rest are just normal restock. We write down the day it actually went out too, and that's never before the day it was ordered, whatever the book looks like when someone's been filling it in on a Monday.

On the order there's a list of what he wants: which part, the quantity -- usually one or two, sometimes a handful -- and what we charged for that line. We charge the price on the part times how many he's having, and never more than that; if there's a deal to be done it comes off, it never goes on. We don't promise what isn't on the shelf either, so a line never asks for more than we've got in stock. The one rule we keep to is that we won't send more than two of anything over a thousand pounds on the same order, not without someone senior saying so, because if it's wrong we've a fortune sat in a van.

We get most of the parts from two places up north but that's just phone calls and invoices, there's nothing to keep about them.

It's not big. Three thousand and something part numbers, and maybe sixty orders a week.
