nl_description:
Handover notes for the student record system at a federated university. Whoever inherits this: it is the whole record, not just the enrolment screens, and the volumes are why it is being rebuilt -- about 210,000 active students, roughly 41 million historical enrolment rows, eleven faculties, and something like a quarter of a million assessment submissions in a single teaching term. Partitioning and shard boundaries are a live concern rather than a nicety.

Start with the organisation, because everything else hangs off it. Faculties sit at the top with a code, a name and a dean. A faculty owns departments, and a department has a short code, a name and the faculty it sits under; the department code is what every downstream system keys on, so treat it as fixing both the name and the owning faculty. Teaching space is owned centrally instead: a building has a building code, a building name and the campus it stands on, and because the code determines the campus the timetablers read the campus straight off a room label. Rooms hang off a building with a room number, a seat count and a type; building plus room number is the natural key and it settles the seat count. Seat counts run from 12 up to 480, except the Old Quad buildings (code 'OQ'), which never exceed 60. Estates take rooms out of service for refurbishment, so there is a closure row against a room with a from date, a to date and a reason, and the to date always falls after the from date.

The calendar is a term: a term code, the academic year it belongs to, a start date, an end date and an add/drop deadline. The term code determines all three dates -- people rely on that, and it is why the code turns up in half the reporting views. The end date is after the start, and the add/drop deadline sits between the two.

Two bits of reference data are worth knowing about before anything else. The first is the grade scale: a grade code, the grade points it carries on the 0.0 to 4.3 scale, and the minimum percentage that earns it. Senate signs the mapping off once a year and the grade code determines the points, so nothing else may hardcode a conversion. The second is the fee bands: a band code, the fee status it stands for -- home or overseas -- and a price per credit, where again the band code determines both the status and the price.

Departments own both the degree programmes and the course catalogue. A programme carries a name, a degree level and a required credit total: undergraduate programmes require 360 credits and postgraduate ones 180. Courses have a catalogue code, a title, an integer credit-hour value and a numeric level code from 100 up to 700. The catalogue code is issued once and fixes the title and the credit value for the life of the course, which matters because the code is what appears on a transcript. Prerequisite structure is course-to-course and many-to-many: a course may list several prerequisites, each with a minimum grade-point threshold the student must already have achieved, the same course can appear as a prerequisite for many others, and nothing is ever its own prerequisite. Separately, a programme lists which courses count toward it, with the year of study they are expected in and whether they are compulsory.

Instructors belong to one department and carry a staff number, a name, an academic rank, a hire date and an FTE somewhere between zero and one. The staff number identifies them.

Students matriculate against exactly one programme and keep a matriculation number that identifies them, an entry year, the fee band they were assessed into, and a running cumulative GPA on the same 0.0 to 4.3 scale; across the student body that GPA sits at 3.05 with a standard deviation of 0.52. We hold several addresses per student, each with a city and a country code and a flag for which one is current. Each student also gets an academic adviser drawn from the instructors, recorded as an assignment with the date it started and the date it ended, where an end date always follows the start. Registry keeps the student's status -- registered, intermitting, withdrawn -- as dated history rows rather than one mutable field, with a reason and an effective-from and an effective-to, the to again after the from.

Each term a course runs zero or more sections. A section belongs to one term, one course and one instructor of record, and carries a section number, a seat capacity, a live enrolled count and a delivery mode: in person about 62% of the time, hybrid 23%, fully online the rest. Course, term and section number together identify the section. Capacity is lognormal in shape, median near 40 with a thin tail of 500-seat lecture theatres; demand is brutally long-tailed and a Zipf law with exponent near 1.6 fits section enrolled counts well. The enrolled count is never allowed above the capacity. Graduate sections, meaning any section whose course level is 500 or above, are capped at 25 seats. Sections meet in weekly slots -- day of week, start and end clock times, and a room, the end after the start -- and beyond the instructor of record a section has a teaching team of demonstrators and markers, each attached with a role and a number of contracted hours.

An enrolment is one student on one section. It records the date it was made, a status, the letter grade and the grade points that letter converted to, and we stamp the term onto the row as well so enrolments can be filtered without joining out through the section. Student and section together are unique, and the letter grade on the row determines the points on it. An enrolment is never made after its term's add/drop deadline. Status changes are kept as their own history rows -- old status, new status, a timestamp and who did it -- because the audit team asked for it and the old system threw them away. When a section fills, students queue on a waitlist with an integer position and the timestamp they joined; we only queue anyone once the section's enrolled count has reached its capacity, and we stop the queue at half the section's capacity, because past that it is a lie.

Assessment is where most of the row count lives. Each section publishes assessments with a title, a kind, a maximum mark, a weighting percentage and a due timestamp. A submission is one per enrolment per assessment: the timestamp it came in, the mark, the marker, and a late flag. A mark never exceeds that assessment's maximum, an on-time submission arrives on or before the due timestamp, and a late one is capped at half the maximum under the penalty rules. Marks come out roughly normal, mean 61.4 with a standard deviation of 15.8. Written exams get a sitting: the assessment, a room, a start and an end timestamp, and the number of seats used, which cannot exceed the room's seat count. Attendance is taken per enrolment against a meeting slot, with a session date and a mark. Appeals sit against an enrolment with the date, the ground, an outcome and revised grade points, and an upheld appeal never lowers the grade points that were already there.

Progression is computed per student per term: credits attempted, credits earned, a term GPA and a progression decision. Credits earned never exceed credits attempted, and a full-time student clears about 55 credits in a term. An award is the end of it -- the student, the programme, the date, a classification, a final GPA and the total credits counted -- and we do not confer until those total credits reach the programme's required total. Classifications split roughly 28% firsts, 48% upper seconds, 19% lower seconds and 5% thirds. Credit brought in from elsewhere is recorded against the student and the course it maps onto, with the institution name, the credits granted and the date it was approved. Intermission is a leave-of-absence row with a start, an end after it, a reason and an approver.

Fees, finally. A student is invoiced per term with an issue date, a due date after it, an amount due, and a running amount paid that never goes above the amount due; the amount due is lognormal, log-mean around 9.1 with a log-variance of 0.4. Payments hang off the invoice with a date, an amount and a method, and no single payment exceeds the invoice's amount due. Scholarships carry a name, a funder, an annual value and the number of awards available; an award goes to a student for a given term and is never worth more than the scholarship's annual value.

nl_description:
I look after the office side of a two-form-entry primary school, so this is really about knowing where every child is and who to ring when something happens. Nothing here is big data -- 420 children on roll, about 700 parents and carers on the contact list, 45 staff including the lunchtime supervisors, and a register that adds a few thousand lines a term.

Every child has the obvious stuff. A first name and a surname, a birthday (which matters more than you would think, we sort by it for admissions), the date they joined us, which is always later than the birthday however hard the old import tried to prove otherwise, and whether they are entitled to free school meals -- that one drives funding so it has to be right. They sit in one class, and our classes are named after trees rather than year numbers, which confuses every supply teacher who walks in, so we keep the year group on the class as well as on the child -- and the two had better say the same thing, because when they disagree it is the child's record that is wrong. The tree name is what everybody actually uses and it tells you the year group and the room without looking anything else up, so the room sits on the class too, along with how many children are currently in it and the agreed limit we have signed up to for that class. The number in a class must never go past its agreed limit. Two classes in each of the seven year groups from Reception up to Year 6. Reception is always a bit smaller than the rest and the others are pretty much level -- out of the whole school Reception is maybe thirteen percent and each of the six other year groups is around fourteen and a half. Classes are meant to be thirty and mostly land within two or three either side. The legal cap is thirty-two, and for Reception we hold it to twenty-six because of the adult ratios.

Each class has a class teacher, who is one of the staff. Staff records are thin -- name, job title, when they started, and whether they are teaching staff or not, although the job title settles that last one on its own: a lunchtime supervisor is never teaching staff and a class teacher always is, so really we are storing the same fact twice.

The register is the big one. Twice a day, every child, a mark. Present is about ninety-four percent of all marks, authorised absence three and a half, late just under two, and unauthorised absence the little bit left over. When a child is late we are supposed to write down how many minutes, and late children are typically about eight minutes late, though some of the office team just tick it and move on, which I keep asking them not to do. We also never put a mark against a child for a day before the day they joined us, which sounds too obvious to say until you have seen what the old system let through. Obviously the minutes can never be a negative number, and if the mark says late then there had better be a number bigger than zero sitting next to it.

For the grown-ups we hold a name, how they are related to the child, a mobile number, an email if they will give us one, and an address. An adult can have more than one child here and a child can have more than one adult listed, and we flag which adult is the first person to ring.

Oh, and trips -- I nearly forgot. Someone books a trip for a class: the name of the trip, the day it got booked, the day of the trip itself -- which is never earlier than the day it was booked -- and what we are charging per child. That runs from four pounds for the museum walk up to about forty-five for the residential deposit, and it is never a negative number.

nl_description:
Backing store for a consumer online-course marketplace. Volume to design against: 6.4 million learners, 9.1 million enrolments and about 74 million lesson-progress rows. Learner and certificate identifiers are UUIDs; everything else is a surrogate bigint.

Learners have an email -- unique, it is the login -- an ISO country code, a signup timestamp and an account tier. Instructors are separate entities with a display name, a long-form bio, a revenue share percentage and a join date -- anyone who joined before 2019-01-01 is grandfathered onto a 70% share.

A course belongs to exactly one instructor and carries a title, a category, a list price of at most 199.99, a published timestamp and a free flag. A course cannot be published before its instructor joined, which sounds obvious and is nevertheless the constraint the migration broke. If a course is flagged free then every enrolment against it records a price paid of zero. Courses decompose into ordered modules and modules into ordered lessons, and the ordering is load-bearing rather than cosmetic: a module's index within its course identifies it, and a lesson's index within its module identifies the lesson. A lesson has a content kind and, where it is video, a duration in seconds that is lognormal with a median around nine minutes. Some lessons carry a quiz -- at most one per lesson, so the lesson identifies the quiz -- which has a pass mark percentage between 50 and 100 and a question count.

Enrolment is learner-to-course with an enrolment timestamp, the price actually paid and a completion percentage between 0 and 100. Completion is the ugly number: mean around 12% with an exponentially decaying shape. Paid prices cluster near $18 with a long right tail, lognormal again. On anything that is not flagged free, the price paid is bounded above by the list price and, however coupons and promotions stack, we never let checkout take more than half off, so it is also bounded below by half the list price. Progress is tracked per enrolment per lesson -- that pair is the key -- and stores watched seconds, which never exceed the lesson's own video duration, and a completion timestamp, which is never earlier than the enrolment it hangs off.

Quiz attempts are per learner per quiz with an attempt number, a start timestamp, a score percentage that comes out roughly normal at mean 71 with a standard deviation of 16, and a passed flag that is only ever set when the score reached that quiz's pass mark. Certificates are issued against an enrolment and carry an issue timestamp and a printable serial code that identifies the certificate on its own. One is only ever issued once that enrolment has reached 100% completion.

Reviews are one per learner per course, and that pair is what identifies the review: an integer 1-5 star rating, a free-text body and a submission timestamp. The rating histogram is the usual J shape -- 55% fives, 27% fours, 10% threes, and 4% each at two stars and one.

Coupons belong to a course and carry a code, an integer discount percentage, an expiry timestamp and a redemption cap. Any coupon on a course listed under $20 is capped at 25% off.

nl_description:
We are a small language school above a bakery. Three rooms, four tutors, and me. I want to stop running the whole thing off one spreadsheet that only I understand.

The people who come to us -- I will call them students, though the website says learners and the invoices say client, and it is all the same person. I need a name, a phone number, what their first language is, because that changes how you group a class, the level they are at, and when they first signed up. Levels are the usual A1 to C2 ladder, except our own website says beginner and improver, which map onto the bottom two rungs, and I would rather we settled on one set of words. Out of every ten people who walk through the door, three are complete beginners, another two and a bit are only just past that, two are properly intermediate, and it thins out fast above there -- upper intermediate is maybe one in seven and the very top level is about one in twenty-five.

We sell blocks, not individual lessons. A block is one language at one level, taught by one tutor, starting on a date, running for so many weeks, with a price, a number of seats in the room, a running count of how many are booked onto it -- which can never be more than the seats -- and the number of sessions in it. Most blocks are the ten-week one, about a quarter are the six-week version, and the rest are four-week intensives. The price depends only on the length -- tell me the number of weeks and I will tell you the price and the number of sessions without looking at anything else -- and it lands somewhere between a hundred and twenty and four hundred pounds, spread fairly evenly across that range. We never run a class with fewer than four booked or more than twelve in the room.

People book onto a block, and plenty of them do two or three different blocks over a year, so one person turns up against several blocks and a block obviously has several people on it. For each of those I want the date they booked, which is never before the day they first signed up with us, what they actually paid, because sometimes it is less than the list price and sometimes they pay in two goes, and how many sessions they turned up to. A ten-week block is ten sessions and people typically make about eight of them. The four-week intensive runs twice a week, so eight sessions is the ceiling on that one, and in general nobody can be marked down as having attended more sessions than the block actually has. What they paid is never more than the block's price either.

For the tutors I barely need anything. A name, which languages they can teach, and what we pay them an hour, which is between twenty-two and thirty-four depending on how long they have been with us.

Two hundred and sixty people on the books at the moment. Maybe nine hundred all told since we opened.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: A ten-week block is ten sessions and people typically make about eight of them.

nl_description:
I am the data analyst at a national exam board and I am specifying the awarding database that sits behind the summer session. Volume for context: around 640,000 candidates and just under 1.9 million marked scripts in a single session.

Candidates are entered through a centre. Each candidate has a candidate number, a name, a date of birth, and a flag for whether they have access arrangements. The centre has its own code, which determines its name, its region and its type, and the candidate number is prefixed with that code, so you can read the centre straight off the number. Type first -- about 61% of our entries come from state schools, 19% from FE colleges, 14% from independent schools, and the remaining 6% are private candidates who enter through an examination centre rather than a school.

What a candidate actually sits is a paper, and papers belong to a specification. A specification has a code, a subject, a qualification level and a total UMS value, and the spec code is what centres quote at us so it had better determine all three: A level specifications are marked out of 300 UMS. A paper has a number within its specification, a session code, a maximum raw mark and a percentage weighting toward the overall grade, plus the UMS ceiling that paper can contribute, which is the spec total scaled by the weighting. Specification, paper number and session code together identify the paper and settle its maximum raw mark.

The script is the row that matters. One candidate, one paper, a raw mark, the converted UMS mark, the examiner who marked it, the date it was marked, and a flag for whether it went through second marking. A candidate sits any one paper once, so candidate and paper together fix the raw mark and the UMS mark on the row. A raw mark never exceeds the paper's maximum raw mark and a UMS mark never exceeds the paper's UMS ceiling. Raw marks come out roughly normal, mean about 52.4 with a standard deviation near 17.1, and a raw mark is never negative. Every script marked by an assistant examiner is second marked -- that is a hard rule from the standards team.

Examiners have a name, a seniority, a subject, and an allocation count. A normal allocation is around 340 scripts and we cap anybody at 600, but senior examiners are held to 200 because they also moderate.

Grade boundaries are set per paper after marking closes: a grade letter and the minimum UMS needed for it, one figure per letter per paper. A boundary never sits above the paper's UMS ceiling, and by convention the A boundary never sits below eighty percent of that ceiling.

Finally, remarks. A candidate can ask for a script to be looked at again. We record the request date, which is never earlier than the day the script was marked, the fee -- a flat 42 pounds -- the outcome, and the change in mark, which averages a little under one mark upward with a tight spread of a couple of marks either side.

std.basis: coefficient of variation in [0.006, 0.682], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=117), applied to the stated mean

ground_truth_moments.evidence: Raw marks come out roughly normal, mean about 52.4 with a standard deviation near 17.1

nl_description:
Product owner in the accommodation office. We are replacing a 2009 Access database and I need the data model straight before anyone writes a screen.

The estate is eleven halls of residence, eleven thousand beds give or take, each one on a named campus, each with a postcode and a bed count -- the hall name is distinctive enough that it tells you the campus and the postcode on its own -- and each with a warden who lives on site and gets rung at three in the morning. We hold the warden's name and a contact number and honestly not much else, but it has to be its own thing because wardens move between halls and one warden can cover more than one over a career.

Inside a hall you have flats. A flat sits on a floor, has a code that identifies it within its hall, and has some number of bedrooms sharing a kitchen -- typically five or six of them. The floor is a property of the flat, not of the rooms, so every room in a flat is on the flat's floor and asking a room what floor it is on means asking its flat. Some flats are the accessible ones and those are always on the ground floor, which we number zero. Nothing anywhere in the estate goes above the fourteenth floor.

A room is a bed, basically. One occupant, a room code that identifies it within the flat, a type, a weekly rent, and a floor area we are now obliged to publish. Roughly four in ten rooms are en suite these days, about the same again are plain standard rooms with a shared bathroom, and the remaining thirteen percent are studios. Rent runs from about a hundred and ten a week for a standard room in the older halls up to two hundred and fifteen for a studio, and it is fairly flat across that range. No studio is ever under a hundred and eighty.

Then the residents. Tenants. Students. Whichever word you like, it is one record per person, keyed on the student number because that is the only thing that never changes, with a name, a year of study and whether they are international, because internationals and postgrads take the longer contract, meaning fifty-one weeks or more. First years are guaranteed a place so they are the bulk of it, about six in ten, and the other three years split what is left roughly evenly. The tenancy links a person to a room for a start and an end date, the end always after the start, and a room only ever has one tenancy beginning on any given date, with a length in weeks -- the standard is forty-four weeks and that is around seven in ten of them, the fifty-one-week contract is about a fifth, and there is a handful of thirty-eight-week deals left over from an old scheme. There is a deposit on it too, two hundred and fifty normally, four hundred if the room is a studio, and finance's rule of thumb is that a deposit never comes to more than three weeks' rent on the room, and a status field because people withdraw. Call it nine thousand seven hundred tenancies a year.

Maintenance I should mention, since the helpdesk feeds us jobs: against a room, with the date reported, a category, a priority, the target date the helpdesk stamps on from that priority, and the date it was closed. A closed job is closed on or after the day it was reported and on or before its target date, or somebody has to explain why. There are something like three hundred thousand of those in the archive and nobody has ever deleted one.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: eleven thousand beds give or take
something like three hundred thousand of those in the archive
nine thousand seven hundred tenancies a year

nl_description:
Circulation database for a university library system: eight branches, 2.4 million items and roughly 38 million loan rows accumulated since 1998, so the loan table wants range partitioning on the checkout timestamp.

Bibliographic records hold an ISBN, a title, a publication year -- anything from 1470 to the current year, we have incunabula -- a Dewey class, a language code, and a denormalised circulation count refreshed nightly. Circulation per bib record is textbook Zipf with an exponent near 1.35, so any capacity planning that assumes even demand across the catalogue is wrong. Items are the physical copies: one bib record, a barcode, a home branch, a shelf location, a status, and an acquisition cost that is roughly normal around 38.50 with a standard deviation of 14. Branches carry a code, a name and a seat count.

Borrowers have a card barcode, a category, a faculty, a registration date and a running outstanding-fines balance which is never negative. The category mix is 58% undergraduate, 21% postgraduate, 13% staff, 5% alumni and 3% external members.

A loan joins one item to one borrower with a checkout timestamp, a due date, a return timestamp and a renewal count of at most six. We stamp the entitled loan period onto the row at checkout, because entitlement is a function of borrower category -- undergraduates get 14 days and staff get 84 -- and we stamp the realised days out once the item comes back. Days out is exponentially distributed with a mean of about nine days.

Fines hang off a loan with an amount, the date they accrued and a waived flag. They run at 20p a day and are capped at 15 pounds, and in log space the amount sits around 0.9 with variance 0.8.

Holds are placed against a bib record rather than a specific item, with a queue position, the timestamp it was placed and an expiry date.

Financial aid team here, and honestly the current setup is three spreadsheets and a shared mailbox, so treat this as a green field.

The unit of work is an application. Someone -- we call them applicants, the decision letters say candidates, the students' union calls them students, all the same human being -- applies to a scheme. About forty-six thousand applicants a cycle and roughly a hundred and eighty thousand applications sitting in the system across eleven years of running it.

On the person we hold a student number, a name, the household income figure off the assessment (whatever they have declared, we do not audit it), their entry tariff points, their domicile for fee status, and a flag for care leavers. Median household income on the forms is about twenty-seven thousand and there is a long right tail running up past a hundred and something thousand, so it is nothing like symmetric. Entry tariff points average around thirty-four out of forty-five with a spread of five or so. Income obviously cannot be negative.

A scheme has a name, where the money comes from, an annual budget, the biggest single award it is allowed to make, and whether it is means tested. That maximum is never below two hundred and fifty and never above nine thousand.

The application itself is who, which scheme, when it came in, the decision, how much was awarded if anything, and the name of whoever assessed it -- just the name, we do not need a whole staff record for that. Roughly a third get awarded, about half are rejected outright, one in eleven is withdrawn by the applicant, and a few percent are still pending at any given moment. The typical award is around twelve hundred pounds and the shape is a sharp decay, masses of small awards and very few big ones. Nothing over nine thousand has ever gone out of the door. Means-tested awards top out at four thousand. And care leavers are never rejected outright, that is policy -- they get something or the application gets referred.

Awards are paid in instalments against terms, so there is a payment row with the date, the amount and which term it was for. Some schemes are one-off and some pay per term and the spreadsheet does not currently distinguish, which is half the reason we are doing this at all.

variance.basis: variance = ln(1 + CV^2) for CV in [0.324, 3.166], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=70)

ground_truth_moments.evidence: About forty-six thousand applicants a cycle
roughly a hundred and eighty thousand applications sitting in the system across eleven years
Entry tariff points average around thirty-four out of forty-five with a spread of five or so

nl_description:
I am director of development here -- fundraising, alumni relations, the events, all of it. What I have inherited was built for printing mailing labels, so let me just describe what we actually do and you can tell me what it needs to look like.

Our people are graduates of this place. We say alumni, the vice-chancellor says members, the old database calls them constituents, which nobody outside this office understands. Three hundred and forty thousand of them on file, going back to 1946, and something like one and a half million gift records behind that. For each person we need a name, the name they actually like being called, the year they finished, an email if we have a live one, and two flags that matter more than anything else in the system -- whether they have died, and whether they have asked us never to contact them again. We also keep a running lifetime giving total on the record, because it is the first thing anybody asks me.

A lot of them have more than one degree from us. Did their undergraduate here, came back for a masters. So the degrees have to sit separately from the person: the degree code, the subject, the year it was awarded and the class of honours.

Addresses are a mess and always will be. One person can have several on file and only one of them is the current one, and we need the country on it because that drives which tax scheme applies. Same shape for jobs -- the employer, the job title, the sector and when they started. We keep the history, because "she has just moved to a hedge fund" is exactly the sort of thing that changes an ask.

Fundraising is organised into campaigns. A campaign has a name, a target amount, a launch date, a close date and a cause area -- scholarships, buildings, research, that sort of split. Underneath a campaign we run appeals, which is the actual sending: which channel it went out on, when, how many people it went to, and how many replied.

Gifts come in against an appeal, from a person, into a fund. Funds have to be separate because the finance office insists on it -- a fund has a name, whether it is restricted or unrestricted, and the year it was opened. A gift into a restricted fund has to be at least a thousand pounds; that is the minimum to open a named restriction and finance will not budge. Most gifts are tiny, the median is around forty pounds, and then we get the occasional seven-figure one, so the spread is enormous. Nearly half arrive by direct debit, a third on a card, about one in nine still by cheque, then bank transfers at about nine percent, and a very small number as gifts of shares. Anything recurring is direct debit, always -- we do not offer recurring on any other method. And we do not record anything under a pound.

Pledges are a different animal from gifts. Someone signs up to give a total amount against a campaign over some number of instalments. A third pay in one go, most spread it over a year, some over three years and a few over five. We will not take a pledge under a hundred pounds.

Events: the reunions, the black-tie dinner, the regional drinks. A name, a date, a venue, how many we can fit in, and a ticket price which runs from free up to two hundred and fifty a head for the dinner. People say whether they are coming, some of them actually turn up, and they bring guests -- a bit under one guest each on average, and we cap it at two, or three if there is a good reason. One person goes to many events and one event has many people, obviously.

Last thing, and it always gets forgotten: some of them volunteer for us. Mentoring, chairing a regional branch, interviewing applicants. A role with a name and a start and end date against the person.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: Three hundred and forty thousand of them on file
one and a half million gift records behind that

nl_description:
Small driving school. Four tables at most, but I want the constraints living in the model rather than scattered through the booking app.

Pupils: name, provisional licence number, date of birth, the date they registered, and a denormalised running count of hours logged. That count averages about 45 by the time they sit the practical, standard deviation around 12.

Instructors: name, ADI badge number, the car's registration, what transmission it is, and an hourly rate somewhere between 32 and 44. Three of the nine cars are automatic only, and any lesson taught in one of those is logged with an automatic lesson type, because the rate card depends on it.

A lesson is one pupil, one instructor, a date, a start time, a duration in hours, the amount charged, and a lesson type. Types are the usual set -- standard, motorway, mock test, pass plus -- and I will admit the list has grown organically and nobody has ever written it down properly. Slot length: just over half are two hours, about a fifth are 90 minutes, the rest are single hours. Nothing shorter than an hour and nothing longer than three.

Test bookings: the pupil, the test centre, the date, whether it is theory or practical, the outcome, the attempt number, and the minor fault count for practicals. Pass rate is 48%, fails 49%, and about 3% get recorded as not taken -- weather, no-shows, examiner strikes. Minor faults average about 5.3 and more than 15 minors is an automatic fail regardless of anything else, though the column itself we allow up to 40 because of data entry from the paper sheets.

Scale is trivial: 260 active pupils, nine instructors, about 6,000 lessons a year.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: That count averages about 45 by the time they sit the practical

nl_description:
Handover document for the playback and rights estate, written up before I go. Read it as the whole platform rather than one warehouse extract: it now swallows the four systems we ran separately until last year -- the catalogue, the rights ledger, the encoding farm and the billing stack -- plus the playback telemetry that was always its own thing. Nothing here is aspirational; all of it is in production and all of it is what the next person inherits.

Volumes first, because they decide the partitioning. 78 million live billing accounts, up to six viewing profiles under each one, about 210,000 episodes in the catalogue, and the play-event stream lands roughly 1.4 billion rows a month. That table gets a UUID key and date partitioning; almost everything else is INTEGER surrogates, and the plans and the promotions key on their short codes because those codes appear in a dozen upstream systems and renumbering them is not on the table.

REFERENCE DATA. Countries are held with a name, the region they roll into for reporting and the currency code we bill them in -- the country determines both, and that is the entire reason the table exists rather than the values being copied around. Languages are just a code and a name. Content ratings are a code, a display label, the minimum age the rating implies and the rating region, since the same film carries different codes in different places; minimum ages run from 0 for a universal certificate up to 18. Genres are a code list with a name and nothing else. Device classes -- TV, mobile, web, tablet -- carry a description, whether the class supports HDR, and the highest ladder rung we will ever serve to that class, which is the ceiling the player is meant to respect. And the bitrate ladder itself is a table: six rungs, each with a label, the video bitrate in kbps and the resolution height. A rung number determines its bitrate and its resolution, and playback only ever names a rung.

CATALOGUE. A title has a name, a type (movie or series), a release year, a content rating and an original language, plus a denormalised total view count we refresh nightly and which is a textbook Zipf with exponent 1.15 -- a few hundred titles carry most of the platform. Series break into seasons with a season number, a season name and a first air date; episodes hang off a season with an episode number, a name, a runtime in minutes and an air date. Runtime is near-normal at mean 44 minutes with an sd of 13, it is never under 1 minute and we have never taken anything over 240. An episode never airs before its own season's first air date. Movies get one synthetic season and one synthetic episode, because playback always resolves to an episode and never to a title -- that decision is fifteen years old and everything downstream depends on it. Genre against title is genuinely many-to-many, so it is an association keyed on the pair. Credits are people -- a full name and a birth year -- linked to titles with the role they were credited in and a billing order; one person can be credited on the same title in more than one role, so the role is part of the key.

ENCODING. Every episode goes through the farm. An encode job is one row per episode with the submission timestamp, the completion timestamp, a job status, the source size in GB of the mezzanine we were handed and the output size in GB we produced; when a job reports complete, the completion is never before the submission and the output size never exceeds the source size, which is the check that caught the misconfigured ladder last spring. The outputs themselves are episode assets: one row per rung, with the file size in MB, the duration in seconds and the CDN path. Asset duration is meant to agree with the declared runtime -- it is never more than a couple of percent off sixty times the runtime in minutes, in either direction, and when it drifts further than that the manifest is wrong. Subtitle tracks are per episode with a language, a forced flag and an SDH flag; audio tracks likewise with a language, a channel layout and a descriptive-audio flag.

RIGHTS. Licensors have a name, the country they contract from and a contact email. A licence is one licensor and one title with a window start, a window end after it, a minimum guarantee amount and an exclusivity flag; a licence belongs to exactly one licensor, so the licence identifier alone tells you who we are paying. The territories a licence covers are many-to-many against countries, so that is its own row. Royalty statements are raised per licence per period: the period start and end, the qualified view count in that period, the amount due and the amount paid. A statement period sits inside the licence window at both ends, its end is after its start, the amount due is never below the licence's minimum guarantee, and the amount paid never exceeds the amount due. This is the part the licensors audit us on and it is the part the old ledger got wrong.

BILLING. Plans key on a short code and carry a display name, the monthly price, the ceiling on simultaneous streams and the highest ladder rung the plan is entitled to; the code determines all three, and most entitlement questions in the business resolve to that one row. Monthly price sits between 6.99 and 24.99. An account names its plan code, the date it signed up, its country, a contact email that is unique across the platform so the email alone identifies the account, and an account status. Profiles are what people actually use: a display name, a maturity ceiling expressed as an integer age, and a kids flag -- a kids profile is one whose maturity ceiling is under 16, and a play event from a kids profile never settles above rung 3. Devices are registered against the account with the device class, the registration timestamp and a last-seen timestamp; last seen is never before registration and registration is never before the account signed up. Payment methods sit on the account with a method type, the last four of the card and when they were added.

Invoices are one row per account per billing period: the billing country as at issue, the plan code billed, the period start and end, the amount, the currency and whether it cleared. The invoice currency always agrees with the currency the billing country uses -- an Indian account bills in INR, and nobody should be hard-coding that anywhere else. The amount never exceeds the plan's list monthly price, because promotions only ever discount. Payments point at an invoice and at the payment method used, with the timestamp and the amount paid; a payment never exceeds the invoice amount, is never dated before the invoice period opened, and if it comes in short then the invoice is not marked cleared. Promotions are a code, a description, a discount percentage between 5 and 100 and the window they are valid in; the code determines the discount and the window, the window end is after the start, and an account picks up a promotion on a date inside that window. Plan changes are kept as their own event history -- the account, an event type, the plan code involved and when it happened -- because we lose the churn story otherwise, and no event predates the account.

PLAYBACK. A play event carries the profile, the episode, the registered device, the device class the stream came from, the start timestamp, the seconds watched, the ladder rung it settled on and a completed flag. The device class on the row is redundant against the device -- the device tells you its class -- but the telemetry team wanted it inline and it stays. Seconds watched is lognormal, mu 6.9 and sigma-squared 0.8 in log space. It never exceeds sixty times the episode runtime, the rung never goes above what the device class allows, and we never log a play that starts before the episode aired. The completed flag is set once the viewer gets past ninety percent of the runtime, which in seconds is fifty-four times the runtime in minutes. Device class comes out 41 percent TV, 27 mobile, 19 web, 13 tablet. Playback errors are their own rows against a play event with an error code, when they happened and the rebuffered seconds; rebuffer seconds decay exponentially at about 0.15 per second, an error never predates the play it belongs to, and the rebuffered seconds cannot exceed the seconds actually watched. Watchlists are a profile against a title with the date added, and thumbs are a profile against a title with the thumbs value and when it was rated -- thumbs down is 1 and thumbs up is 2, one opinion per profile per title.

SUPPORT AND AUDIT. Support tickets are raised on an account with a category, the open timestamp, a close timestamp once resolved and the resolution minutes; resolution time is lognormal with log mean 4.4 and variance 1.1, a close is never before the open, and a ticket is never opened before the account existed. Finally the audit trail, which is the reason half of this got funded: every change to any table here is a row naming the table, the record key, the action, the field, the old and the new value, when it changed and the email of whoever changed it. On an update the old value must be populated. That was the finding, and it is the one rule I would not let anyone relax.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: play-event stream lands roughly 1.4 billion rows a month
six rungs, each with a label
Runtime is near-normal at mean 44 minutes

nl_description:
We're rebuilding the reporting side of the music app and I want the data model straight before the engineers start arguing about it.

The centre of everything is the stream: someone hit play on a track and we logged it. That is about 640 million rows a day right now, which is why nobody wants to touch it. Each one knows who listened, which track, when, how many milliseconds actually played, and where the play came from -- a playlist, an album page, search, radio, an artist page. We also flag whether the play was monetised, because royalties only count a play once at least thirty seconds have gone through, and that flag is what finance reads. Two things we have never checked and should: the milliseconds played cannot be more than the track's own duration in milliseconds, and a stream cannot be dated before the listener who played it signed up. Both of those exist in the current table and both are rubbish rows.

Listeners are what marketing calls users and what billing calls customers. Same people. We hold an email, the signup date, their country and whether they are on free or premium. Emails are unique, so an email picks out exactly one listener even though everything internal joins on the id. Free listeners are capped at 128 kbps and premium goes higher, and the stream row records the bitrate actually served, which is how we prove the cap works -- on a free listener's stream expect it between 64 and 128.

The catalogue is artists, their albums, and the tracks on those albums. Every track sits on exactly one album, and the album is what tells you the artist. We do not model record labels properly; there is a label name sitting on the album and that is as far as it goes, which annoys licensing every quarter -- the label is a fact about the album and about nothing else, so it just gets repeated. A track row carries the title, duration in seconds, an explicit flag and a running stream count. Duration averages 214 seconds with a standard deviation of about 62. The stream counts are the ugly part: our data-science people fitted a Zipf with exponent 1.2 and it holds up well. Artist monthly-listener figures are lognormal-ish, log mean around 8.5 with variance 2.1 -- the median artist is a few thousand and the top end is absurd.

Playlists belong to a listener, have a name and are public or not, and a track can obviously sit in any number of playlists, so we keep the position of each track inside each playlist along with when it was added. Positions start at 1. Nothing is added to a playlist before the playlist was created, and no playlist predates the listener who owns it -- the migration from the old app broke both of those and we are still finding rows.

The bit nobody wrote down last time is royalties. Every artist gets a statement per period: the period it covers, the total streams in that period, how many of those were monetised, what we owe and what we actually paid out, plus the date we paid. Monetised streams can never be more than total streams, we never pay out more than we owe, the period end is after the period start, and we never pay before the period has closed. That is the whole argument we have with the labels, once a quarter, and it is all four of those checks.

Other things to police: a clip under ten seconds is not a track, and we bounce uploads longer than thirty minutes. And play source breaks down roughly 38 percent playlist, 21 album, 16 search, 15 radio, 10 artist page.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: about 640 million rows a day right now
Duration averages 214 seconds with a standard deviation of about 62

nl_description:
So we run a podcast hosting outfit -- small, family-ish operation, three of us plus a contractor. Right now there are 340-something shows on the platform and I think about twenty-six thousand episodes all told, which sounds like a lot until you realise a big chunk of that is one true-crime show that has been going since 2016.

What I care about keeping straight is the shows and everything hanging off them. A show has a title, a category -- comedy, true crime, business, that sort of thing -- the date it launched, and a host. The category and the host go with the show and never change, so they live there. Some shows have two hosts and honestly we just type both names into the one field. Not elegant, but nobody has ever needed to search on it, so please do not build me a whole separate thing for hosts.

Episodes are where the detail is. Each one belongs to exactly one show, has its own title, the date it was recorded, the date it went out, how long it runs -- the duration, if you want the proper word -- and the download count our stats provider hands us. Obviously nothing goes out before it was recorded, and nothing goes out before the show it belongs to had launched, though I did find a handful of both in the old spreadsheet when I went looking. Length varies a lot but the average is about thirty-eight minutes, give or take a quarter of an hour either side. Nothing under three minutes goes out as a real episode -- those are trailers and we do not publish them here -- and the longest thing we have ever hosted was just shy of four hours. Downloads are wildly uneven: most episodes land somewhere around a thousand or two, and then every so often one gets picked up somewhere and does forty thousand.

The money side is the sponsor reads. An episode can carry more than one -- we have done three on a couple of the big ones -- and for each read we note which sponsor it was, where in the episode it sits (pre-roll, mid-roll, post-roll) and what we billed for it. Now, the sponsors themselves we do keep a proper little list of, because it is the same dozen names round and round: who they are, what industry they are in, the rate we agreed with them, and the dates the contract runs from and to. The agreed rate is a fact about the sponsor, not about any one read, and we never bill a read below it. The contract obviously ends after it starts, and we do not run a read for a sponsor in an episode that went out before we signed them or after the contract had run out -- that happened once and it was awkward. The rates run from two hundred and fifty dollars up to four thousand depending on the show, and pre-roll is the premium slot, so a pre-roll read never goes out under a thousand. And we would never sell the same sponsor the same slot twice in one episode, so that combination is unique.

Oh, and reviews. Listeners leave a star rating out of five plus a bit of text, and that is against the show rather than any particular episode, and never before the show launched. They skew high, as these things do -- about six in ten are five stars, roughly two in ten are four, and then there is a stubborn little clump of one-stars from people who are angry about something unrelated.

nl_description:
Product owner here, writing up the model for the paywall analytics rebuild. We are a metropolitan daily: 4.2 million registered readers, around 90 million article views a month, roughly 380 journalists on staff.

Readers register with an email and we keep the registration date, the city they gave us, and a status that says whether they are an active subscriber, lapsed, or have never paid. The email is unique across the whole reader base -- it is what we deduplicate on, so an email on its own identifies the reader even though the analysts join on the numeric id. A subscription is its own record because people churn and come back: it points at the reader and at the product they bought, and has a start date, an end date once it is over, the amount we bill monthly, and an active flag. An end date is always after the start date, and the amount we bill is never above the product's list price, because everything we do to a price is a discount.

Products are the four or five things we actually sell. A product code fixes the display name, the list monthly price and how many premium articles that product allows per month -- those three facts live on the product row and nowhere else, and if you find them copied onto a subscription somewhere then that is the bug. Prices sit between 4.99 and 34.99. The one called Digital Plus is 14.99 a month and every subscription on it bills exactly the product's list price -- there is no grandfathered pricing on that product, unlike the older ones.

Billing itself I had forgotten to write down. Every subscription raises an invoice per billing period: the period it covers, the amount we billed, the amount that actually came in and the date it was paid. The period end is after the period start, we never take more than we billed, we never bill more than the subscription's own monthly amount, and no payment is ever dated before the period it pays for opened. Finance reconciles on exactly those four things.

Editorial side. Journalists have a name, the desk they sit on and a hire date -- one desk each, nobody is split across two. Sections -- metro, business, sport, culture, opinion -- have a code, a display name, and one journalist who edits them; the code fixes both the name and the editor. An article belongs to exactly one section and carries a headline, a publish timestamp, a word count, a premium flag and a running page-view total. Bylines are shared often enough that the article-to-journalist link is many-to-many, with the byline order recorded on it, counting from 1 for the lead byline. Word counts average about 780 with a standard deviation of 340; the shortest thing we publish is a 120-word brief and features top out around 6,000. We never put anything under 400 words behind the paywall.

On traffic, a view row records the article, the reader, when it happened, how many seconds they were on the page and where they arrived from. Nothing is ever viewed before it was published or before the reader who viewed it had registered -- both of those show up in the old extract and both are junk rows. Time on page is exponentially distributed with a rate of 0.02 per second, so about fifty seconds on average. Referrers break down 44 percent search, 21 social, 19 direct, 12 our own newsletters and 4 aggregators. Page-view totals per article are lognormal, log mean 7.0 and variance 2.2. A paywall hit is logged separately whenever a metered reader gets stopped, with the reader, the article, the timestamp and whether they converted on the spot -- again never before the article was published -- and once someone converts there, that reader's status is active.

The newsletters are a smaller concern but they have grown a tail. Each newsletter has a name, a send day and a running subscriber count, and the name and the send day are fixed by the newsletter, not by the send. A reader can sign up to any number of them, so that pairing is its own record with the signup date, which is never before the reader registered. What we did not have before is the sends themselves: each time a newsletter goes out we now keep an edition row with the date it went, how many recipients it reached and how many of those opened it. Opens can never exceed recipients, and an edition never goes to more addresses than the newsletter has subscribers on it -- growth marketing kept quoting numbers that broke both.

Comments sit on articles, written by readers, with the body, the posted timestamp and a flagged marker for the moderators. Nothing is commented on before it published either.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: around 90 million article views a month

nl_description:
Telemetry schema for the shooter, post-mortem edition -- what we should have built the first time round.

Player identity is a UUID handed to us by the account service; locally we keep the platform, a region code, the creation timestamp and the current account level. Level is close to exponential with rate 0.045, so a mean somewhere around twenty-two and a thin tail of grinders. About 11 million players touch the game daily and the participation table takes roughly 2.3 billion rows a month, which is the constraint that shapes everything below.

A match is also a UUID, with the mode, the map code, the server region, a start timestamp and a duration in seconds. Duration is near-normal: mean 1080, sd 240. The modes are a proper reference list this time, not a string we compare against in six places: a mode code, a display name, whether it is ranked, and the shortest and longest a match in that mode is allowed to run. Ranked sits at eight minutes to an hour; casual allows a lobby to collapse in ninety seconds. Every match's duration falls inside the floor and the ceiling its own mode declares, and a mode's ceiling is above its floor -- the mode row is the only place either number should live. Participation is the many-to-many between match and player, keyed on that pair, and carries the team slot, kills, deaths, damage dealt and final placement. Kills per participant are Poisson with lambda 4.6. Placement runs 1 through 100 because that is the lobby size.

Store side: an item has a name, a rarity and a gem price, and rarity comes out 58 percent common, 27 rare, 11 epic, 4 legendary. Legendaries are priced at 2,400 gems and up, so a purchase of one never lands below that either. A purchase records the player, the item, the timestamp, the gems actually charged, the currency source and, since last patch, which timed offer it came through if it came through one at all. The offers are their own rows: an item, a cut price in gems, and the window the offer is live for. An offer price is never above the item's list gem price and an offer's window closes after it opens. Where a purchase names an offer, the gems charged are exactly that offer's price -- the price is a fact about the offer, not about the purchase -- and no purchase ever charges more than the item's list price or is stamped before the player account existed.

Client health is deliberately separate: sessions per player with start and end timestamps, the client version and a crash flag. A session ends after it starts and never starts before the player was created. A crash report hangs off a session with the stack hash, the OS build and when it arrived; a report only ever exists against a session whose crash flag is set, and it never arrives before the session began.

Anti-cheat signals also land in this cluster but they belong to another team's pipeline -- leave them out of scope here.

nl_description:
Notes from the platform standup -- someone asked me to write down what we actually store for the feed, so here goes, and be warned it is not tidy.

Members, users, accounts: three names for one thing, pick one and stick with it. Whatever you call them, they have a handle, a join date, a bit of profile text, and a follower count we keep denormalised because computing it live was killing us. Handles are unique and always have been, so a handle picks out one person on its own. There is a verified marker too. We only ever verify someone once they are past ten thousand followers -- that is a hard rule from trust and safety, no exceptions have ever been granted.

Following is directional, and it is the obvious pair-of-ids arrangement plus the date it happened. Nobody follows themselves -- the two ids on a follow row are never the same -- and a follow cannot be dated before either of the two accounts joined, which sounds too obvious to say until you look at what the 2019 import did. The follower curve is basically a power law: a handful of accounts are in the millions and the median person has a couple of dozen. Our analyst fits a Zipf around 1.1 and nobody has argued with him yet.

Posts belong to whoever wrote them -- exactly one author each, no shared posts -- and have the text, a timestamp and a like count. Nothing is posted before its author joined. Replies are just posts that point at another post, which the mobile team hates but it is what we have; a post is never its own parent, and a reply is never stamped earlier than the post it answers. We store the character count on the row because the limits differ -- a reply is capped at 280 characters, a top-level post can go to two thousand -- and having the count sitting there saves the feed ranker a computation. Like counts are lognormal, log mean about 1.9 with variance 1.8. None of these counts ever go negative, obviously: not the likes, not the follower counts, not the tag counters.

Reactions are a separate thing from the like count, before anyone asks. Each one is a member reacting to a post at a particular time with a type, and it never predates either the post or the member. It is mostly the plain like -- call it seventy-one percent -- then laugh at eleven, heart at nine, angry five, sad four. We are pushing about three hundred million reactions a month across roughly 900,000 active people.

Hashtags: we pull them out of the post text at write time and keep exactly one row per distinct tag text with a running use count on it, and a post can obviously carry several of them, so there is a link between the two sides.

New since last quarter, and the reason the storage bill jumped: the ranker now logs an impression every time it puts a post in front of somebody -- which post, which member, when it was shown and how many milliseconds it stayed on screen. Same rule as everything else, nothing is shown before the post existed or before the member joined. That table is far and away the biggest thing we have.

People can report posts as well, but that goes into a completely separate tool that Trust runs, so do not build it here.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: about three hundred million reactions a month

nl_description:
Right, I will try to explain this the way I would explain it to my sister.

We make a picture-sharing app. People sign up with a username -- everyone here calls them users, so I will too -- and the username is theirs alone, nobody can take one that is already gone. We know which country they are in from the phone, and we note the day they joined. There is something in the region of seven hundred thousand people signed up and I would guess forty million pictures sitting on the servers now, which the hosting bill certainly reflects. Most of them are American -- close to three in ten -- India is the next biggest at about a fifth, then Brazil around a ninth, Indonesia a bit less than that, and the rest is scattered everywhere else.

When you put a picture up you can write a caption, and we keep the time it went up, how big the file is, whether it is public or just for you, and the day it was last looked at. A picture belongs to exactly one person, the one who put it up, and it cannot have gone up before that person even joined -- I am told there are rows like that from the 2019 migration, which is exactly the sort of nonsense I want stopped. Nothing is last looked at before it was uploaded either. Sizes are mostly two or three megabytes but there is always someone uploading a monster off a proper camera, so we stop them at twenty-five meg. We also count views, and that is very lopsided: the ordinary picture gets a couple of dozen looks and then once in a while one travels round the world. If a picture is set to private it is not in the public feed at all, so its view count just sits at zero, and a count never goes below that anyway.

Then there are albums. We called them galleries for the first two years and half the team still does, so if you see 'gallery' in the old code that is the same thing, not a second feature. An album belongs to whoever made it, has a name and a created date, and you pick one of the pictures in it to be the cover. An album cannot be older than the person who made it, and the cover you pick has to be one of your own pictures -- you cannot point at a stranger's photo. Same goes for what is in an album at all: only your pictures go in your albums. The important bit people get wrong: a picture can be in several albums at once. My holiday photo is in 'Italy' and in 'Best of last year' and that is not two copies, it is the same photo.

There is a comments feature as well but it is barely used and I do not want it in this piece of work.

nl_description:
We stream ticketed live gigs. I have been asked to spec out the warehouse side and I think it is fairly clean, so this should be short. It got slightly less short once finance saw the draft.

Last year we ran 2,800 events for about 1.1 million registered viewers, and there were roughly 6 million stream sessions across them.

An act is the performer: a name, a home country, a genre code -- the act fixes both of those, they are not per event. An event belongs to exactly one act and has a title, a scheduled start, the duration in minutes it is meant to run for, whether it is ticketed or free, and the list ticket price. Run times average 95 minutes with a standard deviation of about 25, and list prices are spread pretty flatly from eight dollars up to forty-five.

Viewers register with an email, a country code and a date. The email is unique -- one address, one viewer, and support relies on that. When a viewer buys into a paid event we write a ticket: the event, the viewer, the purchase time, the price they actually paid, and the promo code if they used one. It is one ticket per viewer per event; we do not sell somebody the same gig twice, so that pair is as good a key as the ticket number. Comped tickets come through at zero and nothing is ever above forty-five, and no ticket is ever priced above the event's own list price or dated before the viewer registered. Promo codes are their own small reference -- the code, the discount percentage, and the window it is valid in -- and the code fixes all three of those. Discounts run between 5 and 100 percent, and we do hand out a few full-comp hundred-percent codes for press, which land the ticket at exactly zero. A code's window closes after it opens, and a ticket that names a code was bought inside that code's window, which is the check the last promotion drove straight through.

The watching itself: a session records the event, the viewer, when they joined and left, minutes watched, the peak bitrate they were served and the device type. Minutes watched decays exponentially at a rate of about 0.025 per minute, so forty minutes on average -- most people dip in and out. Nobody joins before the scheduled start, a session leaves after it joined, and the minutes watched never exceed the event's run time plus the thirty minutes of overrun we allow for an encore. Bitrate lives between 400 and 8000 kbps, but free events are capped: a session on a non-ticketed event never goes above 2500. Devices come out 46 percent mobile, 24 TV, 22 web, 8 tablet.

Chat is on per event -- who said what and when, plus a flag the moderators set when something has been pulled. Nothing is said before the event starts or before the viewer registered.

The part finance made me add is the payout. For each event we settle with the act: the gross ticket revenue we took, the share percentage that act is on, what we actually paid and the date we paid it. Shares run from 50 to 85 percent, so a payout never exceeds 85 percent of the gross and obviously never exceeds the gross itself, and we never pay before the event has started.

nl_description:
I run the reading app -- webcomics and translated manga, mostly. It is small: a hundred and ninety series, somewhere around eleven thousand chapters, and just under eight thousand people paying us.

A series has its title, whoever made it, the language it is in, where it is at -- ongoing, finished, or on hiatus -- and the date it first went up on us. All of that except the title is fixed by the series itself; the creator does not change halfway through and neither does the language. Most of what we carry is Japanese, about four in ten; Korean is another quarter or so, then English at a bit over a fifth, and a little Chinese. The creator is just a name to us. There are translation teams involved on a lot of these and they matter enormously to the readers, but all of that is handled over email and never touches the app.

Chapters sit under one series each, numbered, with the date they went up and the page count. No two chapters of the same series ever share a number -- that numbering is how readers find their place, so if you tell me the series and the number, that is one chapter and nothing else. Nothing goes up before the series itself did. Twenty-odd pages is normal -- twenty-two is about the average and they do not wander more than six either side of that. Anything under four pages we would send back, and the biggest we have ever taken was eighty. Some chapters are free and some sit behind coins: about half of what is up is free, a bit over a third costs three coins, and the ones the publishers make a fuss about cost five. If a chapter is free then obviously its price is nothing at all.

Readers -- subscribers, members, whatever you want to call them, it is the same person -- have a display name, the date they joined, whatever coins they have left, and which plan they are on. Balances cannot go below zero, and they are all over the place: most people are sitting on a handful of coins, and a few have thousands because they bought a big pack in a sale.

That is the other thing I forgot to write down: the coin packs. When somebody tops up we record it -- who bought, the day, how many coins it put on their balance, what the pack lists at and what they actually handed over, because in a sale those two are not the same. We never charge above the list price, and nobody tops up before they have joined.

When someone opens a paid chapter we take the coins and record it, so we know who unlocked what, when, and what it cost them -- and what it cost them is exactly the chapter's own price, never a penny different, whatever the support team thinks it saw. Opening a free chapter gets recorded the same way but charges nothing. Nobody unlocks a chapter before it was published or before they joined. Reads spike very hard the day a new chapter lands and then fall off a cliff, in case that matters for whatever you are sizing.
