nl_description:
Schema for the moderation console -- this is the internal tool, not the content firehose, so the volumes are tiny and I would rather have it normalised than fast: 240 moderators, about 60 live policies, 1,800 appeals filed since launch, and a couple of thousand audited decisions in the sampling table.

Moderators have an employee code, a hire date, a seniority level from 1 to 5 and a locale. The employee code is unique to the person, so it identifies a moderator on its own -- HR joins on it and we should not fight that. Queues have a name, the kind of content they hold and an SLA in minutes; the queue id fixes both the content kind and the SLA, and the SLAs are spread fairly evenly from fifteen minutes on the imminent-harm queue up to a full day for the low-severity backlog. A moderator is certified on some set of queues and a queue has many certified moderators, so that pairing gets its own row carrying the certification date, which is obviously never before the moderator was hired.

Shifts are new since the last revision and the workforce team needs them: a shift is one moderator working one queue, with a start timestamp, an end timestamp and the count of decisions made in it. A shift ends after it starts and never starts before the moderator was hired.

Policies carry a code, a title, a severity tier and a retired flag. The code is unique in the policy book and fixes the title and the tier. Tiers run 1 to 4, and the live book is roughly 20 percent tier 1, 34 tier 2, 28 tier 3 and 18 tier 4.

A content item is a UUID with its content kind, a submission timestamp, a hashed author identifier -- we never join back to the user service from in here -- the queue it landed in, and a report count. An item's content kind always matches the kind its queue holds, which is to say the kind is really a property of the queue and the copy on the item is convenience. Reports per item are Poisson with lambda about 1.7, and each report knows the item, when it came in, what kind of reporter filed it, and the policy cited.

A decision is one moderator on one item: a timestamp, an outcome, handling seconds, the policy applied, the queue it was worked from and an escalation flag. The queue on the decision is always the item's queue -- the routing does not move between the two -- but reporting wanted it inline. A decision is never stamped before the item was submitted or before the moderator was hired, and handling seconds never exceed the queue's SLA expressed in seconds, that is sixty times the SLA minutes; a decision that busts the SLA is a bug in the routing rather than a slow moderator. Outcomes split 49 percent keep, 34 remove, 9 age-gate, 8 escalate. Handling time is lognormal with log mean 3.6 and variance 0.7 -- median a bit over half a minute -- never under 2 seconds, and we cut anything past an hour as a stuck session. Anything decided on a tier-4 policy is escalated, no exceptions.

Appeals point at a decision with a filing time, an outcome and a resolution time; nothing is filed before the decision it appeals and nothing is resolved before it was filed. Audit samples point at a decision too, naming the auditor, who is another moderator, when it was audited, whether they agreed and a free-text note. The auditor is never the moderator who made the decision -- that was the finding from the first quality review and it is now a hard rule -- and an audit is never dated before the decision.

Enforcement is kept separate from the decision so we can re-issue it: an action code, a duration in days and when it was applied, never before the decision itself. The action codes are their own short reference list now, each with a description, whether the action can be reversed and the longest duration in days that action is ever allowed to run; an enforcement's duration never exceeds the ceiling its action code declares. Suspensions run one to thirty days; a keep decision can still get a bookkeeping enforcement row, and in that case the duration is zero. When we take an enforcement back, that is its own row against the enforcement -- when it was reversed, the reason and the moderator who reversed it -- and a reversal is never dated before the enforcement was applied.

Target model for the reservations, operations and revenue estate at a mid-size network carrier. Read this as the whole estate rather than one extract. It swallows four systems that presently reconcile by overnight file -- the schedule and fleet master, the reservation host, the departure-control and baggage side, and the loyalty ledger -- plus a revenue-accounting extract that nobody owns, and the reason we are doing it at all is that the joins between those four have never existed in one place. Sizing first, because it drives the partitioning: 1.3 million flights a year, just over 40 million coupons against them, about 58 million baggage scans, and the mileage ledger at roughly 120 million rows a year, which on its own is larger than everything else put together.

REFERENCE AND NETWORK. Stations are keyed on their IATA code and carry a name, a city, a country and a UTC offset as a float, because half a dozen of our stations sit on half-hour zones. Currencies are their own short list: the three-letter code, a description and the rate we hold against the US dollar, which is never negative and is exactly one for the dollar itself. Cabins are a small controlled list of a code and a description, and everything downstream that talks about a cabin points at that list instead of repeating the word. A route is an origin station and a destination station plus the great-circle distance in km, and no route begins and ends at the same station -- the old host allowed it and we carry three such rows today. Route popularity is brutally skewed: flight volume per route follows a Zipf law with an exponent around 1.2.

FLEET. Each aircraft type record holds the manufacturer, the certified seat count, the still-air range in km and the maximum take-off weight in kg. Individual airframes hang off the type by tail number with a delivery date and, once they are stood down, a retirement date, which is naturally never before the delivery date. The seat map is held per airframe: a seat number, the cabin the seat sits in and an exit-row flag. Seat numbers are unique within an airframe, so a tail number and a seat number together pin the seat down as surely as our own internal seat key does.

OPERATIONS. A flight is one dated operation of a route: the flight number, the flight date, the aircraft type the schedule was built on, the airframe actually assigned, scheduled and actual off-block timestamps, scheduled and actual on-block timestamps, the planned block time in minutes, the departure delay in minutes, an operational status and the observed load factor. Two things about that. First, the schedule is built by type months before an airframe is nominated, so the type sits on the flight in its own right; once an airframe is assigned, the type on the flight is of course that airframe's own type, and the current extract has managed to disagree with itself on precisely that. Second, a flight number keeps the same city pair for a whole season, so from the number alone you know the route. We never schedule a type onto a route longer than the type's certified range, which is the check the schedulers do by eye today. Load factor is a fraction between 0 and 1 and across the network is roughly Gaussian, mean 0.83, sd 0.09. Actual on-block is never before actual off-block. If a flight pushed back later than its scheduled off-block time then it carries a positive departure delay, and delay minutes are never negative. Any route beyond 6000 km is planned with at least 480 minutes of block time. Operational status codes are a short list with a description and a flag for whether that status counts as operating. Delays are logged as their own rows against a flight with a duration in minutes -- exponentially distributed, mean about 27 -- and an IATA reason code drawn from a coded list carrying a description and whether the reason is attributable to us.

CREW. Ranks are a list: the rank code, a description, whether it is a flight-deck rank, and the minimum logged hours the rank requires. A crew member has a home base station, a name, a staff number that is unique to the individual, a rank and a hire date. Type ratings are held separately -- the crew member, the aircraft type, the date the rating was awarded and the date it expires, always after the award -- because a rating that has lapsed is not a rating. Rostering onto flights is many to many: the flight, the crew member, the rank they operated in and the time they reported. The rank on a roster line is always the crew member's own rank, since we do not operate people above or below their rank, so it is strictly derivable and it is in there only because the roster reports read it there. Reporting time is never after the flight's scheduled off-block. Duty periods are separate from rostering, because flight-time-limitation reporting needs them whole: the crew member, a start, an end after the start, and the duty minutes, which come out roughly normal at 495 with an SD of 120 and are capped at 780 by the scheme.

RESERVATIONS. Tiers are a reference list with a code, a description, the qualifying miles for the tier and the free checked-bag allowance it confers. Passengers carry a name, a date of birth, a frequent flyer number that is unique to the passenger, and the tier they currently hold. The tier mix is about 71 percent base, 17 silver, 8 gold and 4 platinum. Sales channels are a list too, with a code, a description and the commission percentage we pay on that channel; the mix is about 46 percent direct web, 22 percent through the global distribution systems, 19 percent agency and 13 percent our own call centres. A booking is identified by its six-character PNR and records the lead passenger, when it was made, the channel it came through, the currency it was priced in, the total fare and a booking status. Fare classes are a small dimension: a one- or two-letter booking code, the cabin it sits in, a refundable flag and a change fee.

The coupon table is the many-to-many core: one row per PNR, flight and passenger, keyed on all three. It holds the fare class flown, the fare actually paid, the taxes paid, a coupon status, a checked-in flag, the seat allocated and any fee charged for that seat, the number of free checked bags on the coupon, and the tier the passenger held on the day of travel. That last one is frozen deliberately -- tiers move, and the bag allowance has to be reproducible two years after the fact -- so the allowance on a coupon follows from the frozen tier and from nothing else, and it is never below the allowance that tier confers. Coupon fares are log-normal, log-mean 5.4, log-variance 0.6, and no single coupon may be priced above the total on its own booking. Economy coupons price between 39 and 900. The cabin of the seat allocated always matches the cabin of the fare class flown; putting an economy coupon into a business seat is exactly the mess the current departure-control system permits.

Money against a booking splits two ways. Payments carry a method, an amount, the currency and when they were taken, and no single payment is larger than the booking total. Refunds carry an amount, a reason and when they were processed, and we never refund more than the fare on the booking. Ancillaries are a catalogue of their own -- seats, lounge, fast track, extra bag, pet in cabin -- with a product code, a description and a unit price, sold against a booking and a flight with a quantity, an amount and a sale timestamp. The amount is the unit price times the quantity, which sounds too obvious to write down and is the single most common defect in the extract we get today.

DEPARTURE CONTROL AND BAGGAGE. Check-in is its own event: the booking, the flight, the passenger, the station it happened at, the channel it came through (web, kiosk, desk, mobile), the timestamp and the number of bags dropped. Nobody checks in after their flight's scheduled off-block. Bags are tracked individually by tag against a booking and a flight, with a weight in kg, a priority flag and any excess fee charged; weight is normal around 18.6 kg with an SD of 5.4, we refuse anything over 32 kg, and anything over 23 kg attracts an excess fee. Every read of a bag is a scan row -- the tag, the scan point, the station and the timestamp -- and that feed is the only thing that can answer where a bag actually went. Mishandled bags are reported against the tag with a category (delayed, damaged, pilfered, lost), when it was reported, when it was resolved, which is never before it was reported, and the compensation paid, which runs from nothing up to 1500 and is always something on a bag we have declared lost.

LOYALTY. The mileage ledger posts against a passenger and, where there is one, a flight: a transaction type, the miles and when it posted. Accruals are positive and redemptions are negative, and the ledger is the only place either side is recorded. Award redemptions are held apart from the ledger row because they carry commercial detail the ledger does not: the passenger, the flight taken, the miles used, any cash component and when it was redeemed.

DISRUPTION. When we cancel a flight or delay one badly we declare a disruption event against it, with a type, when it was declared and when it was resolved, which is never before it was declared. Rebookings hang off the event: the event, the booking being moved, the flight it is coming off, the flight it is going to, when we moved it, and any compensation paid. An event is declared against exactly one flight, so the flight we are moving people off is fixed by the event and does not need looking up twice; the flight they are going to is never the same as the one they came off, which the current tool does not check; and a rebooking is never stamped before the event that caused it.

GOVERNANCE. Last, the audit trail, which is the reason the programme is funded at all: every change to any of this is a row naming the table, the record key, the action, the field, the old value, the new value, the staff member who made the change and when. On an update the old value must be populated. That was the finding.

Restating the hard numbers, because they get lost in prose: load factor 0 to 1; bag weight 0 to 32 kg; duty minutes at most 780; delay minutes never negative; economy coupon fares 39 to 900; mishandled-bag compensation 0 to 1500.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: just over 40 million coupons against them
the mileage ledger at roughly 120 million rows a year

nl_description:
We run 60-odd hotels and I am trying to spec out the reservation database properly before we hand anything to a vendor, so bear with the level of detail here.

Every property has a name, a city, a star rating and a total room count. We are mostly mid-market -- call it 12 percent three star, 58 percent four and 30 percent five. Within a property we sell room types rather than named rooms: a short code, how many people it sleeps and a base rate. The physical rooms exist too, each with a floor and a room number, and each one belongs to exactly one room type. Room numbers only have to be unique inside a property, so the property and the room number together identify a room. And because a room type is owned by one property, a room can never be typed against a room type from a different hotel -- that has happened twice during migrations and it is a mess to unpick.

Each property also has its own staff list. All I need there is a name and the department they sit in: housekeeping, front desk, food and beverage, maintenance. Nobody is on the books at two properties.

Reservations are the busy bit. A reservation is for one property, one room type and one guest -- the commercial team says customer and ops says guest, it is the same person, and all we hold on them is a name and an email, which is unique and is how we spot the same person coming back -- with a check-in date, a check-out date which is obviously after it, the night count, adults, children, a rate plan, a status, the nightly rate we quoted, the total amount, and when it was booked. Same rule as the rooms: the room type on a reservation always belongs to the property on the reservation, and so does the rate plan. Length of stay averages 2.4 nights and behaves like a count. The total amount is simply the nights times the nightly rate we quoted -- I know that sounds trivial, but the current system recalculates it three different ways and they disagree -- and it is heavily right-skewed, so log-normal is the sensible assumption. We never quote below the room type's base rate, whatever the season. Party mix is about 30 percent single adult, 52 percent two adults, 8 percent three and 10 percent four. We do not take a booking longer than 21 nights in this system, and obviously not shorter than one.

Rate plans belong to a property and have a name, a cancellation window in hours and a refundable flag. The non-refundable plans have a zero-hour window; the flexible ones give the guest somewhere between 24 and 72 hours. Anything booked on a non-refundable plan is prepaid, always, and we want that recorded on the reservation. And if the room type only sleeps two we cannot put more than two adults on the reservation.

We also keep seasons per property -- a name, a date range that has to run forwards, and the multiplier we apply to the base rate over that range.

Charges get posted to the reservation as they happen, and the charge types themselves are a central list we maintain: room, breakfast, bar, parking, laundry, each with a description, whether it is taxable, and the standard price we normally post it at. A posted charge carries the type, the amount and a timestamp, it is never posted before the reservation was booked, and it never comes out at more than half again the standard price for its type -- past that a manager has to raise it as something else.

Payments go against the reservation too: the method, the amount and when we took it. There is usually a deposit at booking and the balance at check-out, so more than one per reservation, and no single payment can be larger than the reservation total. About 88 percent is card, 8 percent cash and the rest bank transfer.

When someone cancels we write a row for it rather than just flipping the status: when they cancelled, how many hours before the arrival date that was, the fee we charged and what we handed back. Neither the fee nor the refund can exceed the reservation total, and inside 24 hours of arrival there is no refund at all whatever the plan says.

Housekeeping raise a task per room per day, with a date, a status, which staff member it went to and how long it took -- about 28 minutes on average, sd 9. We never send a housekeeper to a room in a different property from the one they work at, which the old rota system managed to do.

After check-out we email for a score out of five, so the review always lands on or after the check-out date. It is a 1 to 5 thing and it clusters high: 2 percent ones, 3 percent twos, 9 percent threes, 27 percent fours, 59 percent fives, plus an optional free-text comment and the time it came in. Volume-wise we are looking at roughly 400,000 reservations a year across the estate.

variance.basis: variance = ln(1 + CV^2) for CV in [0.324, 3.166], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=70)

ground_truth_moments.evidence: roughly 400,000 reservations a year across the estate

nl_description:
Right, so we have got the place in Lisbon and a smaller one in Porto now, and everything is still on paper and a shared spreadsheet, which is honestly a nightmare on changeover days. What I need is something that knows which beds are free. Both buildings go in, each with its own name and the city it is in, and that is all I want held about the buildings themselves.

Each building is split into dorms -- we call them rooms half the time, same thing -- and a dorm is anywhere from four to twelve beds, with a name on the door, and it is either mixed or women-only. Every bed has a label like 3B so the cleaners know which one we mean, and we do note whether it is a top or bottom bunk because people always ask.

When someone books, they are booking a bed, not a room. I need the arrival day and the departure day, how many nights, what we charged them a night, and where the booking came from -- about seventy percent is Hostelworld, the rest is our own site or people just turning up at the door. Prices swing with the season, sixteen to thirty-four euros a night, and if someone is staying a week or more we knock it down to a flat sixteen. Two weeks is the longest we will take, after that they need a proper rental. Most stays are short -- two nights, three nights, it averages out around two and a half. We take a ten euro deposit off everyone at the point of booking and note that down.

For the guests themselves it is just a name, an email, what country they are from and the year they were born, because we need to know if anyone is under eighteen. Nationality-wise, roughly four in ten are German, a quarter Australian, and the rest is a very long list of everywhere else.

Oh, and Elena does a walking tour on Tuesdays and a pub crawl on Fridays -- the walk is free, the crawl is twelve euros -- and she needs to know who has signed up for which one, so that wants to be in there somewhere too. Same person can do both, obviously.

We are small, mind. Maybe three thousand bookings a year between the two places.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: it averages out around two and a half
maybe three thousand bookings a year between the two places

nl_description:
I am the product owner at a European car hire outfit -- 340 branches, a fleet of about 22,000 and roughly 900,000 agreements a year. The current setup is two systems held together with a nightly file transfer, so we are re-modelling from scratch.

Branches need a name, a city, the airport code if it is an airport desk, and the opening and closing time, because after-hours returns are a whole separate mess.

We rent categories, not cars. A category has a code (ECON, COMP, INTER, PREM, SUV and so on), a description, a daily rate and a minimum driver age. Half the fleet is compact, a third intermediate, and the rest splits between economy, premium and SUV at roughly 8, 5 and 4 percent. The actual cars have a registration, a model year, an odometer reading and a home branch, and we sell them on once they hit 90,000 km, so nothing in the fleet is above that.

Customers we hold by name, date of birth, licence number and the country that issued it.

The agreement is the centre of the whole thing. It ties a customer to the booked category and to the specific car handed over, records the pickup branch and the return branch, when it was picked up, when it is due back, when it actually came back, how many days, the quoted total and the kilometres driven. Hires average just under four days and the distance driven is very long-tailed. We record the driver's age on the agreement itself, because the surcharge depends on it -- under 25 is a flat 12 a day. And we will not sign at all below the category minimum: most categories are 21, but premium and SUV are 25, and for those the driver has to be 25 or over. Nobody gets a car for more than 90 days.

There are two tariffs. The cheap one caps you at 1,500 km over the whole hire, the flexible one is unlimited, so there is a flag on the agreement and the cap only bites when it is set.

Extras -- child seats, sat nav, additional driver, winter tyres -- get added onto an agreement, several per agreement, and each extra has its own daily price.

Damage gets written up against the agreement with a severity, the time it was spotted and what the repair came to. Most of it is trivial; the average bill is about 340 but the shape is a long decay rather than a bell.

variance.basis: variance = ln(1 + CV^2) for CV in [0.324, 3.166], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=70)

ground_truth_moments.evidence: Hires average just under four days

nl_description:
Target data model for a 28-ship premium cruise operator; we are consolidating three legacy reservation systems onto one warehouse.

Ships carry a name, gross tonnage, passenger and crew capacity and a launch year. Cabins belong to a ship, sit on a numbered deck, have a cabin number and a berth count -- that berth number is load-bearing, because a booking's guest count can never exceed the berths in the cabin it holds. Cabin numbers repeat across the fleet but are unique within one hull, so a ship and a cabin number pin the cabin down as well as our own cabin key does. Cabin categories group cabins by class (inside, oceanview, balcony, suite) and each class carries exactly one base fare.

Crew are held per ship: a name, the position they hold, a nationality, a seafarer number that is unique to the individual, and the dates they signed on and signed off, the sign-off always after the sign-on. We do not model rotation any further than that; the manning agent owns it.

An itinerary is a reusable product: a name, a region and a night count, 2 to 21 nights, averaging around 7.4. Ports of call attach to an itinerary as a day-numbered sequence with scheduled arrival and departure times, departure never before arrival, and the same port shows up on many itineraries, so that is a proper association keyed on the itinerary and the port. No day number may fall beyond the last night of its itinerary, and no itinerary calls at two ports on the same day, so the itinerary and the day number identify the call. Ports themselves have a name, a country and a UN/LOCODE, which is unique and is the code the port agents actually quote.

A voyage -- marketing insists on calling them sailings, internally everything keys off voyage_id -- is one dated operation of an itinerary by a ship, with a departure date, a return date after it, and a recorded occupancy rate. A hull departs at most once on any given date, so the ship and the departure date identify the sailing just as well as the voyage key does. Note that occupancy is measured against double occupancy, so third and fourth berths push it above 1: expect roughly normal, mean 0.96, sd 0.04, and treat anything from 0 to 1.05 as valid rather than clamping at 1.

Bookings sit against a voyage and a cabin, with a lead guest, a booked-at timestamp, a guest count, the total fare, the deposit taken, the deposit percentage applied, a cancelled flag, the cancellation fee percentage and the number of days between booking and sailing. The cabin held is always a cabin on the hull operating that voyage, which the old Caribbean system did not enforce and which cost us two moves last season. The deposit taken is simply the total fare times the percentage applied -- state it explicitly, because two of the three legacy systems round it differently. Guest count is 2 on about 62 percent of bookings, 3 on 16, 4 on 14 and a single traveller on 8. Total fare is log-normal. Lead time decays exponentially with a mean near 120 days. Every guest travelling on a booking is enumerated in an association table keyed on the booking and the guest; guests themselves have a name, a date of birth, a nationality and a running loyalty night total, which never goes negative.

Deposit rules are firm: 15 percent when the booking is 90 or more days out, the full fare inside that. If a booking is cancelled within 60 days of sailing the forfeited share is between 50 and 100 percent. Money in against a booking is its own ledger -- a method, an amount and when it was taken, several rows per booking because the deposit and the balance land months apart -- and no single payment exceeds the total fare on the booking.

Shore excursions belong to a port and have a name, a price, a capacity and a duration in hours; they are sold per booking with a guest count and a sale timestamp. An excursion is never sold to more guests than are travelling on the booking, nor to more than the excursion's own capacity, and never before the booking itself was made.

Onboard spend posts against the booking as charge lines with an amount and a posting time, and the outlet is a proper dimension now rather than a free-text string: the ship it sits on, its name, an outlet type (bar, speciality restaurant, spa, shop, casino) and a flag for whether it is included in the fare. Anything posted against an included outlet posts at zero -- we still want the line for consumption reporting. A charge is never posted before the booking was made. Amounts are log-normal, and that is the monster table: about 90 million rows a year against 1.1 million bookings.

variance.basis: variance = ln(1 + CV^2) for CV in [0.324, 3.166], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=70)

nl_description:
I have been running the walking and cycling trips for eleven years now off a laptop and a wall planner and it is finally too much to hold in my head.

So. We have about a dozen trips we sell. Each one has a name, a proper write-up for the website, how many days it runs -- three days at the shortest, a fortnight for the Dolomites one -- and a rough idea of how hard it is, which honestly is just my own judgement, easy, moderate or tough. Prices are per person and run from around six hundred up to two thousand four hundred. There is a ceiling on the group size for every trip and it is never above fourteen; below four we cancel, it does not pay to run.

Each time we actually go, that is a departure -- the start date, which trip it is, who is guiding it, how many places have gone, and whether it is confirmed or cancelled. We tend to fill nine or so, give or take three, sometimes as few as four, occasionally we are full. Marek guides most of them and I have two freelancers I bring in when it clashes; I need their name, what languages they speak and their day rate.

Then the people. Clients, walkers, guests -- whatever you want to call them, it is one list: name, email, phone and which country they are from. Mostly British, a good number of Dutch and Americans, a scattering of everyone else. When someone books, it is onto a departure, and I need how many of them are coming, what they have paid so far, what is still outstanding, and the date they booked. Roughly half book as a couple, a quarter come on their own, the rest are threes and fours. Groups of six or more get ten percent off and I want that recorded rather than just baked into the price.

Hotels I will keep in my own spreadsheet. That is a separate headache and I do not want it anywhere near this.

It is not a lot of data, by the way. Maybe a hundred and forty departures and twelve hundred bookings in a year.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: maybe a hundred and forty departures

nl_description:
Notes for the developer doing our booking system. We are a 96-pitch touring park in North Wales, open March to October, and we take somewhere around four thousand stays a season, so nothing enormous.

A pitch has our own code on it (A1 through to F16), a type -- hardstanding, grass or fully serviced -- a flag for whether it has an electric hookup, the maximum unit length it will take in metres, which is six to twelve depending on where it sits, and its nightly rate. Rates run from 22 to 41 pounds. Anything with electric is at least 28.

Campers we hold as one record each: name, email, the vehicle registration because we need it for the barrier, and their club membership number if they have one.

A stay is one camper on one pitch: arrival date, departure date, the number of nights, how many adults, how many children, how many dogs, and what the whole thing came to. Our licence caps any single stay at 28 nights. Two dogs per pitch, no more than that. Between one and six adults on a pitch. Stays average about 3.2 nights and the pattern is the usual count-like spread you would expect. The total charge is right-skewed -- a lot of long weekends and then a handful of three-week stays. Adults come out at two on about two-thirds of stays, one on 12 percent, three on 8 percent and four on the remainder.

Payments go against the stay -- the method, the amount and the date we took it -- and there can be more than one per stay because we take a deposit up front and the balance on arrival. Around 82 percent goes on card, 11 percent cash and the remainder bank transfer.

nl_description:
My brother and I have five places now -- two in Shoreditch, one in Peckham, the Islington room and the new one -- and the booking situation has completely got away from us. Each site needs a name, roughly where it is, a phone line and how many it seats. The smallest is about forty covers; the Islington room is the big one at a hundred and twenty.

The bookings themselves: who it is for, which site, when they are coming (the date and the time together, obviously, not two separate things), when the booking actually came in to us, how many people, where it came in from -- about forty-five percent through the website widget now, a quarter on the phone, the rest walk-ins that we log after the fact -- and whether it is still live, cancelled, or they did not show. Roughly one in twenty just do not turn up, which is the thing that is actually costing us money, so I want that flagged plainly on its own and not buried in the status. It is the same fact twice, I know: if the status says no-show then the flag is on, and nothing else turns it on.

Whoever took the booking goes on it too. Each site has its own front-of-house lot and I only need a name and what they do -- host, manager, that sort of thing. Nobody works across two sites, which means that once you know who took a booking you already know which of the five it was for, so the site sitting on the booking as well is belt and braces. I still want it there, because that is how the managers read the sheet.

Party sizes. Twos are the bread and butter, near enough half of everything. Then fours at a bit over a fifth, threes maybe fifteen percent, sixes eight and the rest are eights and up. We will not take anything over twenty on the system -- past that it is a private hire and my brother handles it on email. And it should go without saying that we never seat a party bigger than the room holds, whichever room it is. A party of ten or more can only go into a room that seats a hundred or more, which in practice means Islington.

Eight and above we ask for a deposit, ten pounds a head, so a party of twelve is a hundred and twenty on the card before we hold anything. I want the money logged separately from the booking itself, because it moves about: what we took, when we took it, whether it was card or a transfer, and how much of it we gave back if they cancelled in time. We never take the deposit before the booking has come in, and we never hand back more than we took, though the number of times someone has argued about that.

For the people, we keep a name, a mobile, an email if they will give us one, and a notes field -- allergies, who the regulars are, and the two or three we would rather not have back. The mobile is how we look anyone up, so one number means one person and I do not want the same mobile sitting against two of them.

We do not need the actual table layout in here. The floor plan lives on a whiteboard and the managers like it that way.

It adds up though. Something like one point four million covers a year across the group.

nl_description:
Ground handling data model for a two-terminal hub. Roughly 310,000 aircraft movements a year and a little over 4 million service-task rows, so partitioning and retention matter more than usual here.

Carriers sit in a small dimension: IATA code, name, home country. Movement volume by carrier is extremely skewed -- two based airlines dominate and there is a very long tail of once-a-week charters. A Zipf law with an exponent near 1.35 fits the carrier mix on turnarounds well.

Stands carry a code, the terminal they belong to, the maximum wingspan they can accept (24 m up to 65 m, spread more or less uniformly across the apron) and whether a jetbridge is fitted.

A turnaround is the unit of work: one carrier, one stand, an aircraft registration, a flight number, the scheduled off-block time, the actual on-block and off-block timestamps, the resulting ground time in minutes and the departure delay in minutes. Contractual minimum turn is 20 minutes, and anything beyond 240 gets reclassified as a parking event, so ground time lives inside that window; it is roughly normal, mean 47, sd 14. Delay minutes decay exponentially with a mean near 14. Remote stands -- the ones with no jetbridge -- need bussing in both directions, so we plan those at 35 minutes minimum.

Task types are catalogued with a name, a standard duration and the certification level needed to perform them. Ground crew have a name, a shift pattern and a certification level of 1, 2 or 3, and the mix across the workforce is about 40/35/25. A service task instance ties one turnaround, one task type and one crew member, with start and completion timestamps and the actual duration in minutes -- log-normal, and never below one minute.

Equipment (tugs, belt loaders, GPUs, de-icers) is tracked by asset tag with a type, an in-service flag and a purchase date, and gets assigned to individual tasks with an assigned and a released timestamp.

nl_description:
I look after pricing at a travel insurance MGA and we are rebuilding the policy admin database, so I am writing down what I think it actually needs to hold.

Products first: a name, whether it is single-trip or annual multi-trip, the longest trip it will cover, the medical expenses limit and a base premium. The limits sit between 2 million and 10 million depending on which product it is.

The customer -- we say policyholder on the certificate and customer everywhere else, same person -- gives us a name, a date of birth, a country of residence and an email. We store the age at inception separately from the date of birth because that is what the rating actually uses, and the book averages about 44 with a spread of 15 years or so.

A policy (the certificate, again the same thing) ties a product to a policyholder: the start and end date, the trip length in days, the destination region, the premium charged, how many travellers are on it, whether pre-existing conditions were declared, when it was sold, the age loading applied, and the name of the agent who sold it. Trip length averages around 11 days and behaves like a count. Nobody gets more than 60 days on a single trip, and for anyone 65 or over we will not write more than 45. Over-65s also carry an age loading of at least 50 percent. Premium itself is log-normal. Destination-wise it is 58 percent Europe, 17 percent worldwide excluding the US and Canada, 15 percent full worldwide and 10 percent domestic.

Claims come in against a policy: a type, the incident date, what is being claimed, what we eventually paid, a status and the settlement date. Medical is 41 percent of claims, cancellation 28, baggage 19 and the rest miscellaneous. Amounts claimed are log-normal with a very fat tail. Declined claims settle at zero, obviously -- nothing paid at all.

We are writing about 620,000 policies a year and seeing maybe 45,000 claims against them.

nl_description:
I'm the manufacturing analyst for a two-plant vehicle assembly operation and I've been asked to spec out where our line-monitoring dashboards should read from, because right now every number comes straight off the PLC historian and nobody can join anything to anything.

Each plant has a code that everybody uses in conversation -- BRM1, and the newer one down in Puebla -- plus the city it sits in. A plant runs two or three assembly lines. A line has a name, a takt time -- the beat it's supposed to run to, in seconds -- and a declared station count, meaning the number of stations the line is signed off to run. Along a line sit the stations, numbered in order from one; our longest line gets up to 42 of them, and every station has a short code stencilled on the floor next to it. Those stencilled codes are unique across the whole operation, so if a supervisor reads me a code over the phone I can tell him which line it belongs to and what position it sits at without looking anything else up. Each station also carries the planned cycle the industrial engineers gave it, in seconds, and that planned cycle can never be longer than the takt of the line the station sits on -- if it is, the line physically cannot hold its beat. Nor can a station's position number run past the line's declared station count, which happens more often than you would think when somebody drops a station in and forgets the paperwork.

The thing that actually moves is a body-in-white, which by the end of the line is a vehicle. We identify it by VIN, and we know which model it's being built as, the date it was launched onto the line, and the timestamp it came off the end -- that last one is empty while the unit is still on the line, and when it is filled in it obviously cannot be earlier than the launch date. Only three models are running at the moment: a bit under half the volume is the sedan, roughly forty percent is the SUV, and the remainder are pickups.

The models want a place of their own. Today the model's proper name and its cycle allowance get retyped onto every single VIN row, which is exactly how we ended up with three spellings of the same SUV. What the industrial engineers actually keep is one sheet per model: the code everyone says out loud, the proper name, the cycle allowance in seconds they costed that model at, and the threshold in seconds past which the line-stop flag ought to be raised for it. Give me the code and every other number on that sheet follows from it. A model's threshold is never set below its allowance -- that would mean flagging cycles we budgeted for ourselves.

Every time a unit passes through a station we get a record -- when it entered, how long the cycle took, and which operator was manning that station. No record can be stamped as entering a station before that VIN was launched onto the line, and none after the unit came off the end of it. That is the check I would most like the database to do for me, because the historian gets both of them wrong. Operators belong to a plant, have a badge number that nobody shares, so the badge is as good as an internal ID, and work one of three shifts; days is the biggest at about forty percent of the roster, afternoons a bit over a third, nights the rest. The shifts themselves are three rows and nothing more -- the code, the time they start, and how many hours they run.

Cycle time is the number everybody stares at. The lines are set for 58 seconds and the actual spread is around six and a half seconds either side of that. If a cycle comes back longer than four minutes it isn't a slow cycle, it's a stoppage, and those get handled in a different system -- so nothing in here should be above 240 seconds, or negative for that matter. There's also a line-stop flag on the record. Pickups are genuinely slower to build, and the rule the plant floor uses is that on a pickup you don't raise the flag until the cycle passes 75 seconds.

On volume: we log somewhere around 40 million station events a year across the two plants, and three years of it has to stay queryable.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: we log somewhere around 40 million station events a year across the two plants

nl_description:
Handover notes for the MES replacement. I am the data architect who has carried this system for nine years and I leave in March, so this is the long version -- read the sizing first, because it decides the partitioning. Two sites, roughly 40k parts under control, 6k work orders a year, about 3M panel rows, 9M solder defect rows and 60M test result rows in the seven years of history we retain. The commercial side and the plant floor are only loosely coupled: purchasing talks to stores, stores talks to production, production talks to test, and sales only ever sees a work order and a shipment. Do not be surprised that the whole thing falls apart into five or six fairly independent islands -- that is the system, not an accident of the current design.

Sites and people first, because everything hangs off them eventually. Two sites, each with a site code, the city it is in and a country code. Staff carry a full name, a badge code that is unique and is what the shop-floor terminals key on, a role, an hourly rate -- it averages 31 dollars with a spread of about 6 -- the site they are attached to and the shift they normally work. Shifts are three rows and nothing more: the shift code, the time it starts, and its length in hours. Give me a shift code and the start time and the length follow from it.

Commercial. Customers have a name, an account code that is unique and is the thing the finance ledger keys on, and payment terms in days. A quote is raised for one customer and one part: the quoted quantity, the quoted unit price, the date it was quoted and the date it expires -- an expiry date is never earlier than the quoted date -- and a status. Quoted unit price is at least a cent, and we never quote a part below its own standard unit cost; the entry screen should stop anyone who tries.

A work order is for exactly one part and one customer, optionally against the quote it came from, with an ordered quantity, a released date, a due date that is never before the released date, a status, and a running quantity shipped that can never exceed the quantity ordered. If the order came off a quote, it may not be released for more than ten percent above the quoted quantity, and it cannot be released after the quote's expiry date. One costing rule we enforce at entry: if the part costs more than 50 dollars each, the order must be released for at least 25 pieces, because setup does not amortise below that. Every status change on a work order is written as its own event row -- the work order, the timestamp it changed, the status it moved from, the status it moved to, and the member of staff who did it. No such event can be stamped before the order was released.

A work order ships in one or more shipments, each with a shipped timestamp, a quantity shipped, a carrier code and a tracking number. A shipment cannot be dated before its work order was released and cannot be for more than the ordered quantity. Each shipment is invoiced exactly once -- give me the shipment and there is at most one invoice against it, which is precisely the relationship the current database gets wrong. An invoice carries the invoice date, a due date not earlier than it, the net amount, and the amount paid so far, which never exceeds the net amount. An invoice is never dated before the shipment it bills went out.

Engineering. Parts are the core entity: an internal id, the part number -- unique, and the only identifier anyone ever quotes at you, so it pins the row on its own -- a description, a type discriminator (RAW, COMPONENT, PCBA, ASSEMBLY), the standard unit cost, the current revision and a lifecycle status. Unit cost is log-normal with a log-mean of 0.4 and a log-variance of 1.8: most parts are worth cents, a handful are 400-dollar FPGAs. Parts nest into each other. A bill-of-materials line is a parent-part to child-part edge carrying the quantity per assembly and the reference designator, and the parent-and-child pair is the natural key for it. Depth is arbitrary -- a top-level assembly contains PCBAs, which contain components. Quantity per is at least 1 and never more than 500, and it is Zipf-like with an exponent around 1.6: overwhelmingly ones and twos with a long tail of decoupling caps placed two hundred to a board.

Revisions only move under an engineering change order. An ECO names the part, the staff member who raised it, the timestamp it was raised, the revision it goes from and the revision it goes to, an effective date that is never earlier than the raise, and a status.

Two more engineering artefacts, both hanging off a part. A placement program is what actually runs on a given SMT line: the part, the line, a program name, a revision, and the number of component placements it makes. The part, the line and the revision together identify a program -- that is how the programmers refer to them out loud. Under a program sit its feeder slots: the slot number, and which child part is loaded in it. Our machines have 120 slots numbered from one. A stencil also belongs to a part, with a stencil code unique on its own, the foil thickness in microns -- ours run 100 to 200 -- the strokes used so far and the stroke life limit. A stencil is scrapped the moment strokes used reaches the limit, so strokes used never exceeds the stroke life limit.

Purchasing and stores. Suppliers need a name, a country code and a quality rating. The same part normally has two or three approved sources, so that is a second composite-keyed association of part and supplier, carrying the quoted lead time in days, a price per thousand and a minimum order quantity. Lead time is exponentially distributed with a mean of 21 days, and we will not approve a source quoting past 180 days -- nor one whose price per thousand sits above 150 percent of a thousand times the part's own standard unit cost.

A purchase order goes to one supplier with a raised date, a promised date never earlier than it, a status and the buyer who raised it. Its lines each carry their own surrogate id. I know that looks redundant beside the purchase order and the line number, but goods receipts point at lines and I refuse to carry two-column foreign keys around the schema; the order-and-line-number pair still identifies a line uniquely and you should enforce that. A line names the part, the quantity ordered, the quantity received so far -- never more than the quantity ordered -- and the unit price. A goods receipt is against a purchase order and one of its lines, with a received timestamp, the quantity received and the reel lot code read off the label. Nothing can be received before the purchase order was raised, and no receipt can be for more than the line ordered.

Received material becomes a component lot: the part, the supplier, the goods receipt it arrived on, the date code, the quantity received, the quantity remaining -- which cannot exceed the quantity received -- an MSL rating from 1 to 6 and the floor life in hours that the rating implies. Every lot gets an incoming inspection recording the inspected timestamp, the sample size, the defects found, a disposition and the inspector. Sample size is at least one piece; a zero was typed in once and caused a fight that reached the general manager. Defects found cannot exceed the sample size, and a sample can never be larger than the quantity received on the lot it was drawn from. Dispositions run 96 percent accept, 3 percent deviate and 1 percent reject, and if even a single defect is found in the sample the disposition cannot be an accept.

Material leaves the stockroom against a work order: a stockroom issue names the lot, the work order, the issued timestamp, the quantity issued -- never more than the quantity received on that lot -- and who issued it. Nothing is issued against a work order before that order is released.

Production. An SMT line belongs to a site and has a line code and a rated placement rate in components per hour. A line is made up of equipment, each with an equipment code that is unique on its own, an equipment type and an install date. Maintenance events sit against equipment with a performed timestamp -- never earlier than the install date -- a maintenance type, the downtime minutes, the technician and the cost.

A work order is built across one or more production runs on a line. A run records the placement program and the stencil it used, a start time, an end time never earlier, the boards built -- averaging 480, and never fewer than one -- the boards scrapped, which cannot exceed the boards built, and the operator who ran it. A run cannot start before its work order was released. The program on a run must be a program for that same SMT line, and the stencil must be a stencil for the same part the work order is for. Both of those get violated by hand entry today and both are the sort of thing I want the database to refuse. Downtime inside a run is its own row: the run, the equipment that stopped, a started and an ended timestamp, a reason code and the minutes lost. Downtime cannot start before the run started, cannot end before it started, and the minutes lost are exponentially distributed with a mean of about 35.

Every panel off a run gets a serial number -- unique across both sites, so the serial pins the panel and tells you which run built it -- a built timestamp no earlier than the run start, and an AOI verdict: 94 percent pass, 5 percent fail, 1 percent sent back for a rescan. Traceability is the reason any of this exists at all: for each panel we record which component lots went into it, and the panel-and-lot pair is the key of that association.

Failing panels carry solder defects, each with a defect code, the component reference it was found at, and a detected timestamp never earlier than the panel was built. The defect codes are a catalogue in their own right -- the code, its category and its severity class -- and today the category and the severity class get retyped onto every defect row, which is exactly why the same code carries three different severities in the current database. Defect code frequency is brutally long-tailed: rank frequency fits a Zipf with an exponent near 1.4. If a defect's code is of the CRITICAL severity class, the panel's AOI verdict has to be a fail; a critical defect on a passed panel means somebody overrode the machine.

Panels are then tested. A test station belongs to a site and has a station code, the test type it performs and a calibration due date. A test result is a panel, a station, a tested timestamp, a verdict and the measured value; 91 percent pass, 7 percent fail, 2 percent are retests. A result cannot be dated before the panel was built, and -- this one is an accreditation requirement rather than a preference -- it cannot be dated after the calibration due date of the station it was taken on.

Failures go to rework: the panel, the technician, a started timestamp not earlier than the panel was built, a completed timestamp not earlier than the start, the rework minutes and an outcome. Rework minutes are log-normal, log-mean 3.0 and log-variance 0.7, so a twenty-minute median with a long tail, and they are never negative.

And finally returns. An RMA is raised by a customer against the shipment it went out on and, where we have it, the panel serial, with a returned timestamp never earlier than the shipment shipped, a failure mode and a disposition.

the boards built -- averaging 480, and never fewer than one
Lead time is exponentially distributed with a mean of 21 days
Shifts are three rows and nothing more

nl_description:
So we're a small brewery, six of us, and at the minute the whole thing lives in a shared spreadsheet that my head brewer keeps breaking. What we want is somewhere proper to put the brew records.

Right. We have recipes. Each one's got a name -- the pale ale is Harbour Light, the stout is Black Mole -- and there's only ever one of each, so the name does the job of a number round here. Say Harbour Light to anybody in the building and they'll tell you it's the pale ale and what strength it's meant to come out at, so the name carries the style and the target strength along with it. We set a bitterness target as well, although honestly nobody looks at that after the first couple of brews. Two out of every three batches we run are the pale ale, about a quarter is the stout, and the rest is whatever seasonal thing we've talked ourselves into that month.

Then every time we brew, that's a batch. Some of the lads call it a brew and Dave writes "lot" on the tank tags, it's all the same thing as far as I'm concerned. We want the date, how much we actually got into the tank, which tank it went into, and what it finished at strength-wise. The final ABV, if you want it in the trade's words. We aim for 5.2 percent and we're normally within about a third of a percent of that either way. Nothing we make is under 3.5 or over 7.5 -- that's just not what we do. The recipe's target is the thing to judge a batch against, mind: if one comes out more than half a percent off its own recipe's target, either side of it, then it isn't that beer any more and it doesn't go out under that name. Oh, and the stout we only ever do as a half batch, six hundred litres at the absolute most, because the tank we ferment that one in is the little one. And it goes without saying, but I'll say it because the spreadsheet cheerfully lets you do it: you cannot get more into a tank than the tank actually holds.

Tanks -- fermenters, if you want the proper word for them -- have names, we name them after dogs, and no two are called the same, so again the name's as good as a number. Each one's got a capacity in litres.

We write down the gravity it went into the tank at and the gravity it finished at. It only ever comes down, never up -- if the finish reads higher than the start then somebody's misread the hydrometer and I want that caught before it goes in the book. While it's fermenting someone goes round twice a day with the hydrometer and writes down the gravity and the temperature. Readings start around 1.050 when it's fresh and come down to about 1.010 when it's finished, and they're anywhere in between depending when you happen to look -- but no reading should ever come back higher than what that batch started at, and none of them can be dated before the brew day either. We hold the fermentation between 18 and 22 degrees, and that's the one thing we are genuinely strict about.

We also note which maltster the grain came from against each brew, for traceability, in case there's ever a problem with a sack of malt. There's only three or four suppliers we ever buy off, they've all got different names, so that's another one where the name identifies them.

It really isn't a lot of data. We do maybe 120 brews a year and we've got four years of history, so a few hundred batches and a few thousand hydrometer readings, that's your lot.

std.basis: coefficient of variation in [0.006, 0.682], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=117), applied to the stated mean

nl_description:
My grandfather started this dyehouse and we still run it much the same way, which is to say on paper. I'd like to get the shade records onto a computer before an auditor asks me for something I can't put my hands on.

What we do is dye cloth in lots. A lot is one drum-load: what fabric it was, what colour, the day it went in, and its weight in kilos. Lots run anything from forty kilos up to a couple of hundred, and it's fairly even right across that range -- depends entirely what the customer ordered. About half of everything through here is cotton jersey, a third is the poly-cotton blend, and the rest viscose.

The machines -- we call them drums, my father called them becks -- each have a name, and no two are called the same, so the name tells you which drum and what it takes. What it takes is the rated load. Ours go from fifty kilos up to three hundred. Now, the obvious thing, which the paper cards let you get wrong all day long: a lot can't weigh more than the rated load of the drum it went in. Less obvious and just as real -- you can't run a lot that's under a quarter of the drum's rated load either, because the cloth doesn't tumble properly and you get creasing, so nobody puts a forty kilo lot in the three hundred drum.

Once a lot comes out, one of the girls takes a swatch over to the light box and reads it against the customer's standard. That gives you a colour difference number -- delta E is what it says on the light box printout, and that's what the girls call it now -- and she puts the day she read it and her initials on the card. She reads it after the lot came out, not before, which sounds too obvious to say until you've seen the cards. Usually the number lands around six tenths, give or take a quarter.

The tolerance she judges it against isn't hers to pick -- it comes off the customer's standard, and it belongs to the colour rather than the lot. Every white in the building is judged to half, because on a white you can see everything; everything else is judged to one. Same colour, same tolerance, every single time, which is why writing it on each card is daft. Inside the tolerance she marks the card pass, outside it she marks it fail, and that's the whole of the decision. A lot that fails gets stripped and re-dyed and never goes out, but the number still goes on the card -- I've seen a two on a card, so don't go telling the computer the number can't be more than one. It can't be less than nothing, that's all.

We do about eight hundred lots a year and we keep three years of cards in the cabinet, and it's one card per lot -- one swatch, one reading, one line on the card, so if you've got the lot you've got the card. This is not a big job for a computer.

nl_description:
We're a forty-person job shop -- CNC turning and milling, mostly aerospace subcontract with some oil and gas -- and we're finally replacing a 1990s ERP we outgrew a decade ago. I've sketched out what I think the data looks like; you'll know better than me whether it normalises properly.

A job is one customer order line: their drawing number, how many pieces, the date the order came in, when it's due, what we quoted, and a priority code. A due date is never earlier than the date the order came in -- that one has been typed the wrong way round often enough that I want the system to refuse it. For customers I need the name, which is unique because we would never carry two accounts under one name, and the payment terms in days, which follow from the account. Quotes are all over the map -- the typical one is around thirteen hundred dollars, but there's a long right tail and a handful of jobs a year run into five figures. Log-normal, or it looks it. We don't take a job under one piece, and anything over about five thousand pieces we hand off to a production shop, so quantities live between those two.

Each job carries a routing: a numbered list of operations in order, never more than twenty of them, and the numbers are unique inside the job, so the job plus the operation number pins the operation down. Each operation is assigned to a machine and carries an estimated setup time, a per-piece run time, and a running count of pieces completed on it. That completed count can never exceed the job's quantity -- if it does, either somebody double-declared or the job grew and nobody told me. Setup averages about 45 minutes with maybe eighteen minutes of spread around that. Machines have a name -- they are all named differently, an old habit, and the name is what everybody quotes, so the type and the hourly rate follow from it -- a type, and that hourly rate. Roughly forty percent of the fleet is CNC mills, thirty percent CNC lathes, and the balance splits evenly between manual mills and surface grinders.

Machinists clock onto an operation and off it again, and when they clock off they declare good pieces and scrap. A clock-out is obviously not before the clock-on, and the good pieces on any single ticket can't be more than the pieces completed on the operation itself, since the operation total is the sum of the tickets against it. Scrap is usually one or two pieces on a ticket, sometimes zero, once in a while a proper disaster -- and it obviously can't be negative. For machinists I want a name and a skill level.

We also need what material went out to a job from the stores: the material code, the date it was issued, the weight in kilos, and the cost. On the big titanium jobs the material is most of the price, so it can't be an afterthought. The codes themselves come off the stores list, which carries a description and a cost per kilo against each code -- give me the code and both of those follow, and today they sit retyped on every issue line, which is why the same bar stock appears at three different rates in the old system. The cost on an issue is nothing more than the weight times that cost per kilo, and nothing is issued to a job before the order came in.

One rule that really matters. When a job comes in flagged as a rush, we won't allocate more than half an hour of setup to any operation on it. If it needs more than that, it isn't a rush job, it's a project, and it gets scheduled like one.

Volume is modest by your standards: around 900,000 time tickets over the fifteen years we'd migrate, half a million operations, a couple hundred thousand jobs.

nl_description:
Time-series store for a vibration-based condition monitoring programme spanning fourteen plants. Volume drives every design decision here: about 11,000 wireless sensors reporting every ten minutes, which comes to roughly 90 million reading rows a month and 1.2 billion a year, held hot for eighteen months. Partition on the capture timestamp.

Plants first, since assets roll up to them: a plant code that is unique and is what the SCADA tags are prefixed with, and the city it sits in. Give me the plant code and the city follows.

Assets are the monitored machines: an asset tag unique across the estate -- the tag alone tells you the machine and its class -- an asset class (PUMP, FAN, GEARBOX, MOTOR, COMPRESSOR), the plant, the installation date and the rated power in kW.

Each asset carries one or more sensors, each of which is a numbered channel on that asset, so the asset and the channel number together identify a sensor as unambiguously as its surrogate id does. A sensor row holds the channel number, the sensor type -- accelerometers and velocity transducers, mainly -- the sensor model it is, a firmware version, its own installation date, and the alert and trip thresholds in mm/s that apply to that channel. A sensor is never installed before the asset it monitors was, which the current system happily allows. The trip threshold on a channel is never below its alert threshold.

The sample rate in Hz and the saturation limit are properties of the sensor model, not of the individual sensor -- the model code, the manufacturer, the rate and the limit, one row per model -- even though today they sit retyped on all 11,000 sensor rows, which is how we ended up with two different sample rates recorded for the same hardware.

A reading is sensor, capture timestamp, RMS velocity in mm/s, peak g, and casing temperature. Nothing can be captured before its sensor was installed. On healthy equipment RMS velocity is tightly normal: mean 2.1 mm/s, standard deviation 0.6. The transducers saturate at 45 mm/s and cannot report a negative, so that is the check on the column. Casing temperature is normal around 46 C with a sigma of 7, and the sensors are only rated from -20 to 120 C.

Alerts are raised against a sensor and record the raise timestamp, a severity, the RMS value that tripped them, an acknowledgement flag and the timestamp of that acknowledgement. An alert only exists because a channel exceeded its own alert threshold, so the trigger RMS is never below the alert threshold of the sensor it was raised on, and no alert predates the installation of the sensor that raised it; and once the trigger RMS reaches that channel's trip threshold the severity is a TRIP, no discretion. An acknowledgement is never stamped before the raise, and if the acknowledged flag is set the acknowledgement timestamp has to be there. We precompute the elapsed hours since the previous alert on the same sensor, because reliability engineering wants MTBA straight out of the table rather than as a window function; that gap is exponentially distributed with a mean near 300 hours. Severity splits 72% warning, 24% alarm, 4% trip. Trigger RMS is non-negative by construction.

Per ISO 10816 the alarm threshold on our accelerometer channels is 4.5 mm/s, so any alert whose trigger RMS is above 4.5 on an accelerometer cannot be left sitting as a warning -- it is an alarm at least, and a trip if it has gone past the channel's trip threshold.

Where an alert turns into work, reliability engineering raises a maintenance action against it: the action type -- 55% inspections, 20% realignments, 18% bearing replacements, the remaining 7% full overhauls -- the timestamp it was raised, which is never before the alert it came from, a completion timestamp not earlier than that, the technician, the downtime hours (log-normal, log-mean 1.2, log-variance 0.6, and never negative) and the cost.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: about 11,000 wireless sensors reporting every ten minutes
Casing temperature is normal around 46 C
that gap is exponentially distributed with a mean near 300 hours

nl_description:
Quality engineering wants out of the paper-and-Access situation we're in, and I've been told to explain how inspection actually works here so you can tell me what it needs to look like underneath.

We mould plastic components. Each one has an SKU, a name, and a nominal weight in grams. The SKU is the handle for everything -- quote me an SKU and I can tell you the name and the nominal weight without opening a drawer. For each component quality writes an inspection plan; plans get revised over time, so a plan carries a revision label alongside the sample size it calls for and an AQL, and a component plus a revision label is enough to pick the plan out uniquely. The AQLs we're permitted to use run from 0.065 up to 6.5, and a sample size is at least one piece -- I've seen zero typed in and it caused a fight.

A plan lists the characteristics that get checked: a name, unique within that plan, a type -- dimensional, cosmetic or functional -- the nominal value, an upper and a lower spec limit, and the unit. Note the limits are stored as the actual numbers, not as a plus-or-minus, which means the nominal always sits between the lower and the upper limit. If it doesn't, somebody has entered the limits the wrong way round, and that has happened. The cosmetic ones don't really have a nominal but the form insists on one anyway.

Production hands over lots. A lot is a product, the press it ran on, the date it ran, how many pieces are in it, and which shift made it. Presses have a code of their own -- the code identifies the machine and tells you its tonnage -- and an install date, and obviously nothing was moulded on a press before it was installed. The shifts are a short list in their own right: the shift code, the time it starts and how many hours it runs, so the code carries the start and the length with it. Lot sizes are all over the place -- the median is around three thousand but it's badly skewed, some campaign lots are enormous, and no lot has fewer than one piece in it.

An inspection ties a lot to the plan revision that was used, plus who inspected it, when, and the disposition. The plan has to be a plan for the same component the lot is of, which sounds too obvious to write down until you have watched somebody inspect a housing against a bezel's plan. An inspection is never dated before the lot was produced. Nine times out of ten the disposition is an accept; about six percent go to rework and three percent are rejected outright. Inspectors have a name and a certification level.

Within an inspection each characteristic gets measured several times, and every measurement is stored with its value, the time it was taken, the gauge it was taken with, and whether it came in within spec. Gauges have a code, a gauge type and a calibration due date, and a measurement taken on a gauge after that gauge's calibration came due is not a measurement, it is a liability -- the auditor pulled us on exactly that. A measurement is also never timestamped before the inspection it belongs to was opened. Whether it is in spec is not a judgement call: over the characteristic's upper limit or under its lower limit and it is out, full stop. The one everybody watches is the critical bore diameter -- twelve millimetre nominal, the process sits right on twelve with a sigma of about four hundredths of a millimetre, and the print tolerance is plus or minus four hundredths, so a measurement of that characteristic has to land between 11.96 and 12.04.

Separately from the measurements, inspectors log the defects they find. We keep a coded catalogue -- defect code, category, severity class -- and the code owns the category and the severity, though right now both get retyped on every line, which is why the same code shows up as major on one sheet and minor on the next. Against each inspection we record the defect and the quantity found of it, at least one by definition, and typically a couple, call it two or three.

Anything rejected raises a corrective action: which inspection it came off, the timestamp it was raised, which is never before that inspection, the engineer who owns it, a description and the timestamp it was closed, which is never before it was raised.

There's a sampling rule out of the customer quality manual that we have to honour: any lot over ten thousand pieces must be inspected under a plan calling for at least two hundred pieces.

For sizing: roughly 400,000 inspections and eight million individual measurements across the five years we'd load.
