nl_description:
Small and tightly scoped: the calibration register for our metrology lab, run ISO 17025 style. About 900 gauges under control and maybe 2,000 calibration events a year, so five figures of rows in total. This is a correctness problem, not a volume one.

A gauge row is the asset number -- unique, etched on the tool, and the only handle anyone uses, so it pins the gauge and its type and resolution -- the gauge type (MICROMETER, CALIPER, DIAL_INDICATOR, BORE_GAUGE, HEIGHT_GAUGE), its resolution in mm, and its recall interval in days. Intervals are set per gauge and are spread roughly uniformly between 90 and 365 days.

A calibration event references the gauge and the reference standard used against it, and records the date performed, the technician, the as-found error in mm, an outcome, and the next due date. A gauge is calibrated at most once on any given day, so the gauge and the date performed identify the event. The next due date is not entered by hand and should not be: it is the date performed plus that gauge's own recall interval in days, and any row where those two do not agree is a data-entry error rather than a scheduling decision.

As-found error is normal, centred on zero, standard deviation 0.004 mm. Anything outside plus or minus 0.020 mm and the gauge is condemned rather than adjusted, so that is the hard limit on the column -- except on micrometers, where we hold plus or minus 0.005 mm and scrap outside that. An as-found error larger than the gauge's own resolution is not something you leave alone either: the tool has moved, and the outcome cannot be recorded as a plain pass. It is an adjustment at minimum.

Outcomes run 88% pass, 9% pass-after-adjustment, 3% fail.

Reference standards need a name, which is unique and carries the certified value and the uncertainty with it, the certified value in mm, and the stated uncertainty. Ours are all certified to better than two microns, and an uncertainty is non-negative by definition. The accreditation rule we work to is the usual four-to-one: the standard we calibrate a gauge against must have a stated uncertainty no worse than a quarter of that gauge's resolution, so the coarse bore gauges can be done against almost anything in the cabinet and the fine micrometers cannot.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: As-found error is normal, centred on zero, standard deviation 0.004 mm.

nl_description:
I do the scheduling for the plant -- fourteen hundred people across three buildings -- and I do it in Excel, which is the entire reason I'm sitting here.

Here's the shape of it. I've got employees. For each one I need the name, when they started, their hourly wage, and which department they sit in. Nobody is below the state minimum, which is seventeen twenty here, and I only mention it because the spreadsheet happily lets me type anything at all. Average is about twenty-four fifty an hour and most people are within four dollars of that either way.

The departments are worth writing down properly on their own, because at the minute I've got the same department spelled three ways. Each one's got a short code we all use, the proper name, and the building it's in -- and a department is in one building, that's fixed, so the code tells you the name and the building both.

Then there are the tickets people hold -- the auditor calls them skills, I call them tickets -- forklift, confined space, the two welding ones, food-safe handling. One person can have several of them and plenty of people hold the same one, and I need the date they certified. These things expire and I get audited on them, so I want the expiry date on there as well. And the expiry isn't something I decide: every ticket runs a set number of days from the day you certify -- the forklift one is three years' worth, confined space is two -- so the ticket tells you how long it lasts, and the expiry is just the certified date plus that many days. It's obviously after the certified date, and nobody certifies for anything before the day they started with us either.

Shifts come off patterns. A pattern has a name -- days, afters, nights, the weekend continental one, all different names -- a start time, and a length in hours, and the name is what I schedule off, so it may as well be the key.

Most of what I actually do is put a person on a pattern on a date, in a particular area of the floor. That's the bulk of it by a mile. Nobody gets put on a date before they started, though Excel has let me do it more than once. I record what they actually worked and how much of that was overtime, because payroll takes those numbers off me on a Monday. Be careful with those two: the overtime is part of the hours worked, not on top of them, so the overtime can never be more than the hours. And the way the overtime is worked out is simply whatever they worked beyond the length of the pattern they were on -- if the pattern's eight hours and they did nine and a half, that's an hour and a half of overtime, and if they didn't go past the pattern's length there's no overtime at all.

A shift is nominally eight hours and in practice it's a bit over -- eight and a bit, with somewhere under an hour of variation on it. Nine days out of ten there's no overtime at all; when there is, it's usually an hour, occasionally a whole extra shift, so across everybody it works out to about an hour on average. Nobody is on the floor more than twelve hours in a day and nobody gets more than four hours of overtime -- both of those are straight out of the union agreement. The packing crew are capped at two hours because of the noise exposure rules, which is a separate thing entirely and catches me out constantly.

And absences: who, what day, why, and whether I signed it off. Nothing before their start date there either. Just over half are sickness, about thirty percent is booked vacation, ten percent unpaid, and the odd bereavement.

We've got roughly two million shift rows going back to 2011, which is where Excel finally gave up on me.

std.basis: coefficient of variation in [0.006, 0.682], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=117), applied to the stated mean

ground_truth_moments.evidence: Average is about twenty-four fifty an hour
across everybody it works out to about an hour on average
We've got roughly two million shift rows

nl_description:
This is for the melt shop and the caster, and I'll warn you up front that the vocabulary round here is a mess -- people say heat, melt and charge for what I think are two or three different things, and I won't be able to fully untangle that for you.

The unit of production is a heat. It comes out of a furnace; we've got the big electric arc furnace and a smaller induction unit we mostly keep for specials, and each furnace has a name -- they're all named differently and the name is what everybody says, so the name gives you the type and the nominal tap capacity too -- a type, and that nominal tap capacity in tonnes. A heat records its heat number, the grade it was melted to, the crew that tapped it, when it was tapped, how much came out, the tap temperature and the electrical energy it took. The heat number is the thing everybody quotes down the phone and no two heats share one, so it tells you the furnace and the grade without any more digging. We don't tap more than the furnace's nominal capacity -- that's what nominal means round here, and the old system let you record 200 tonnes out of a 150 tonne furnace. The arc furnace taps somewhere between a hundred and a hundred and sixty-five tonnes; the induction one is a completely different animal and I'd rather you didn't hard-code anything for it. Tap temperature is the number the melters live by -- 1635 is the aim and they hold it to about a dozen degrees. Nothing below 1550 or above 1700 is real data, it's a thermocouple fault. High-carbon grades have to go out hotter: if the grade's target carbon is above four tenths of a percent, we tap at 1650 minimum.

Crews: a crew has a name, the shift code it works and the supervisor. Same as the furnaces, the crew names are all different so the name identifies the crew and tells you its shift.

Grades have a code, a family -- roughly seventy percent of our tonnage is plain carbon, twenty percent HSLA, the rest alloy -- and a target carbon. The code owns the family and the target carbon; at the minute both get written out again on every heat tag, which is why one grade shows up in two families depending which tag you read.

Into the furnace goes scrap and additions: shredded, busheling, pig iron, lime, ferro-alloys. Each material has a name, unique, which carries its class and its cost per tonne, and for a given heat we record how much of each went in. A heat obviously takes many materials and a material goes into many heats. The fluxes -- that's the lime and suchlike -- never come to more than five percent of the tap weight on a heat; if one does, somebody has keyed a tonnage in kilos.

Out of the furnace the steel goes to a ladle. Ladles have a number, no two alike, and we track how many heats the lining has done, because they go about 120 heats before we reline. Before it casts, the heat sits at the ladle furnace for treatment: which heat, which ladle, when the treatment started, when it ended -- never before it started, and never before the heat was tapped -- how much argon went through it, and the temperature after treatment. That temperature is always below the tap temperature; the steel loses heat in the ladle, it doesn't gain it. Treated steel comes out around 1580 with maybe ten degrees of spread.

A ladle feeds a casting sequence on one of the casters, and a sequence records when it started and how many strands were running -- between one and eight of them. Casters have a name, all different, which carries the machine type.

The sequence produces slabs. A slab belongs to a sequence and traces back to the heat it came from, and we keep its number -- unique, and it tells you the sequence and the heat -- the timestamp it was cast, which is never before its sequence started, its length, weight and a surface grade. No slab weighs more than the heat it came from, which sounds absurd until you see the transcription errors. Slabs run between eighteen and thirty tonnes, more or less evenly across that.

The surface inspectors mark defects on slabs: which slab, a defect code, a severity and when it was spotted, which is after the slab was cast. A critical one isn't a discussion -- the slab's surface grade goes to REJECT and it doesn't ship.

The lab pulls samples during the melt, so before the heat is tapped, and gives us back carbon, sulphur and manganese. Carbon comes in around 0.18 with a couple of hundredths of scatter on it. Sulphur has to be under three hundredths of a percent or the heat gets downgraded.

We also log delays against a furnace -- when it started, when it ended, the reason and the minutes lost. Most are short, twenty-five minutes on average, with the odd four-hour tap-hole repair. A delay never ends before it starts, which the paper log absolutely does not guarantee.

Oh, and the PLC historian dumps tag readings against each furnace -- tag name, timestamp, value. That's tens of millions of rows a day and honestly nobody has decided yet what we're keeping, but it needs somewhere to live.

std.basis: coefficient of variation in [0.006, 0.682], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=117), applied to the stated mean

nl_description:
Mediation and rating store for a national mobile operator. Volume drives the design: roughly 40 million voice records a day and another 12 million data sessions, so the event tables partition on start timestamp and everything else stays a narrow dimension.

Subscriber is keyed on a surrogate integer, with MSISDN and IMSI as varchars -- both unique to the individual, either one pins down the row on its own -- an activation date, a prepaid/postpaid boolean, and a mandatory rate plan reference. A plan row carries a short code that is unique in the plan book, a name, the monthly recurring charge as DECIMAL, the per-minute voice tariff and the per-megabyte data tariff; the plan book runs 5.00 to 60.00 a month and nothing sits outside it. The code determines the rest of the plan row outright, which is why finance keeps asking what the surrogate is for. Fraud screening reads a rolling daily call-attempt counter denormalised onto the subscriber row -- a count process, lambda near 6.

A voice CDR references the calling subscriber and the serving cell and holds the dialled B-number as varchar, the start TIMESTAMP, duration_seconds as INTEGER and the charged amount as DECIMAL. Two values are copied onto it at rate time and both are strictly derivable, which is the compromise I want written down rather than discovered: the subscriber's plan, because rating must not join back to a dimension being edited underneath it, and the serving site's region code, because that is what the partition pruner reads. The plan on a CDR is that subscriber's plan and the region on a CDR is that cell's site's region, always.

The switch discards anything under a second and force-releases at 7200, hence CHECK duration_seconds between 1 and 7200. Holding time is memoryless: no characteristic length, flat hang-up hazard once a call is up, and an exponential with a mean near 110 seconds tracks the observed curve. Nothing is billable before the subscriber existed, so a call's start timestamp is never earlier than that subscriber's activation date, and the same goes for messages and for data sessions. One deliberately slack rating check, slack by about the factor of sixty between seconds and minutes: a call's charged amount never exceeds its duration in seconds multiplied by the plan's per-minute tariff. It catches mediation faults by orders of magnitude, which is the only class of fault we have ever actually had.

Messaging gets its own thinner table -- sending subscriber, destination number, submit timestamp, and a segment count that is 1 to 6 by construction.

Data sessions carry the subscriber, the serving cell, an APN, an open and a close timestamp, uplink and downlink volumes in megabytes as FLOAT, and the charged amount. Volumes are only final once the session closes, and on a closed session two things hold: the close is never before the open, and downlink is at least uplink, because consumer traffic has never once been symmetric. Downlink volume is lognormal, log-mean 2.1, log-variance 1.6.

Cells hang off sites; a site carries latitude and longitude as FLOAT plus a region code, and a cell never moves site, so the cell identifies its site. Traffic per cell is brutally unequal, a few hundred cells taking most of it, and capacity planning models cell id as Zipf, exponent 1.4.

Two rating rules on prepaid. A call over 1800 seconds is charged at a flat out-of-bundle cap of 4.50 rather than per minute. And a prepaid subscriber's charge for one call never exceeds their plan's monthly recurring charge -- if mediation produces one it is a bug, and we have refunded that twice.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: roughly 40 million voice records a day

nl_description:
I run the provisioning side of a regional broadband outfit. We're in about four hundred thousand homes now across the west of the country, and the spreadsheets stopped coping roughly two years ago, so bear with me while I explain how the work actually flows.

Somebody signs up. Three in four do that online and the rest ring us, and we do want the signup channel written down, because the phone ones cancel less. We take a name, the address the service is going to, a contact number and an email. The address matters more than people outside think, because everything hangs off which exchange the property is wired back to, and there are a couple of hundred exchanges in our footprint. An exchange has a name, a code the engineers actually use on the ground, and whether it's been upgraded to fibre yet -- most have, not all. The code is the thing they say on the radio and no two exchanges share one, so if you've got the code you've got the exchange and you know whether it's fibre. When an order is taken the system stamps the serving exchange onto the order there and then, copied off the address, so nobody has to go and look it up again later.

Then the customer picks a package. There are four and we number them one to four in this order: Basic at 40 megabits, Family at 150, Pro at 500, and the gigabit one that we barely sell. Half the base is on Family, about a quarter on Basic, a fifth on Pro, and the rest is gigabit. Each package has its monthly price and a contract length, and those are only ever 12, 18 or 24 months. Package names are unique -- there's one Family and one Pro -- so the name gives you the speed, the price and the term. The headline speed gets written onto the order too, as the speed we've promised that customer, and it had better be the same number as the package says.

An order turns into an installation job. The job has a date, an appointment window with a start time and an end time -- meant to be two hours, so the end is always after the start -- one of our engineers on it, and an outcome: completed, failed, customer not home, that sort of thing. The appointment is never before the day the order was taken, obviously. Jobs get rebooked, so one customer can end up with three or four of them. Engineers work out of a depot and I want to know which depot somebody sits in, along with their name.

New thing since last year: at the end of a job the engineer runs a speed test on the line and we keep the number, with the time it was taken. It goes down against the job, and the order number gets written on it as well because that's what the customer quotes when they ring up complaining. A test is never dated before the appointment. And the number itself is what we get judged on -- if it comes in under eighty per cent of the speed we promised on that order, we have to send somebody back out, and I want the system to tell me rather than the customer telling me.

Two things bite us and I want the system to stop them. If the property is on an exchange that hasn't had the fibre upgrade, we cannot promise anything faster than 150 meg -- the order should just be refused. And nobody gets booked more than 45 days out; we write down how many days ahead each job was booked and that number must never go past 45, otherwise the order goes back to sales.

Last thing, and it's a sore point: installs take longer than we tell people. On paper it's a two hour slot. Real time on site averages nearer 145 minutes, and it's all over the place -- 40 minutes if there's a live socket already, most of a working day, eight hours say, when there's no duct into the property. A handful of very long jobs drag the average well above the typical one.

variance.basis: variance = ln(1 + CV^2) for CV in [0.324, 3.166], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=70)

ground_truth_moments.evidence: Real time on site averages nearer 145 minutes

nl_description:
Physical asset register covering two colocation halls. Call it 3,000 devices total, so row volume is irrelevant and normalisation wins everywhere.

The location hierarchy comes first. A site holds a data centre and has a name; a site has one or more halls; a hall is laid out in labelled rows of racks. Hall names are unique across the estate, and each hall records the per-rack power cap we contracted for -- Hall A is 8 kW a rack, Hall B is 12 -- so the hall name is enough to tell you the cap, and no hall in the estate is outside that pair. A rack belongs to exactly one row, carries a label that is unique within its row, is either 42U or 45U tall (CHECK rack_units between 42 and 45), has a design power envelope in kW as FLOAT, and records how many U are currently occupied. We also carry the hall on the rack itself, even though the row already tells you it, because every capacity report groups by hall and nobody wants a three-table join to get there; it is strictly the row's hall and must never say anything else. No rack's design envelope may exceed the contracted per-rack cap of the hall it stands in; occupied U obviously cannot exceed the rack's own height either, and audit has caught that one twice. Occupancy is unremarkably flat across the estate, anywhere between 8 and 40 U with no preferred value, so treat it as uniform.

Branch-circuit metering gives us a rack-level power reading: the rack, a read timestamp and the measured draw in kW. A reading above the rack's design envelope is a breach and pages the facilities team. Measured rack draw runs around 5.4 kW with a sigma of about 1.8 and is symmetric enough to treat as normal.

Devices mount into a rack at a start U position: servers, switches, PDUs, storage shelves. Each has an asset tag as varchar and a serial number, either of which identifies the device on its own, though we still carry a surrogate integer PK. Beyond that: a model reference, a lifecycle status and a measured power draw in watts. Measured draw sits tightly around nameplate -- normal, mean 340 W, sigma 95 -- and anything drawing more than 120 per cent of its model's nameplate rating is an audit exception, which is the check I want enforced in the data rather than in a spreadsheet.

A model is a dimension row: a model name that is unique in the catalogue and therefore determines the rest of the row, a form-factor height in U, a nameplate power in watts, and a foreign key to a manufacturer, of which we hold the name -- also unique -- and the support portal URL.

Devices are procured, and finance wants the trail. A purchase order has an order date, a supplier and a total value as DECIMAL; each PO has lines, and a line carries a line number, names the model, the quantity and the unit price. No line's unit price can exceed the whole order's total value divided by that line's quantity, which is the arithmetic version of the reconciliation finance does by hand. Every device points back at the line it arrived on.

Warranty is per device -- a start date, an end date that is always after the start, and a support tier. Tiers are their own short reference list: the tier code, a description and the contracted response time in hours, because that number was hard-coded into three different reports before I got here.

Cabling: a device exposes ports, each with a port name that is unique on that device, a speed in Gbps and a media type. Speeds are only ever 1, 10, 25, 40 or 100 Gbps and the estate is about 55 per cent 10G, 30 per cent 25G, 10 per cent 1G, 4 per cent 40G and 1 per cent 100G. A patch is a connection row with an A-end port, a B-end port and a cable label, both ends resolving to ports, and the two ends are never the same port.

Positional integrity, since audit keeps failing on it. A device's start U is never past the height of the rack it is in -- that is the real rule, and the 42-versus-45 mix is exactly why writing it as a literal 45 was wrong. For an active device the start U is at least 1. A device whose lifecycle status is DECOMMISSIONED has no meaningful position, and we encode that as start_u = 0 rather than a null.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: Measured rack draw runs around 5.4 kW with a sigma of about 1.8
Measured draw sits tightly around nameplate -- normal, mean 340 W, sigma 95

nl_description:
We're replacing a Jira-plus-Slack mess with something purpose-built for incident response, and I'd rather get the data model right before anyone writes screens. Scale: about 4,000 incidents a year, and something near 900,000 alert events feeding into them, so the alert side is where all the rows are.

Services own things. A service has a name, a tier -- we say tier 1 through tier 4, tier 1 being the customer-facing money paths -- and an owning team. Service names are unique, deliberately, so the name is enough to tell you the tier and who owns it. Roughly a tenth of services are tier 1, a fifth tier 2, and the rest splits about evenly between tier 3 and tier 4. Teams have a name and a Slack channel, and no two teams share a channel, so the channel identifies the team. Engineers belong to a team and have a phone number we page, which is unique to the person.

Severity is its own list rather than a string we retype everywhere, and this is the change I care most about. Each severity has a code, a description, the number of seconds we're allowed to take to acknowledge a page at that severity, and the number of seconds after which the pager repeats. Those numbers currently live in three different config files with three different values, which is exactly the argument I lost last quarter.

Alerts fire against a service. An alert carries a fired-at time, the rule name that produced it, a severity, and a flag for whether it auto-resolved; if it got promoted, it points at the incident it fed. A rule is bound to exactly one service, so the rule name tells you the service without looking anything else up. Most alerts never become incidents, and one that auto-resolved was never promoted, so it has no incident against it at all. Where an alert did feed an incident, it fired before the incident was declared -- that is what promotion means, and the old system managed to get it backwards. Across everything we see, roughly 5 per cent come in at SEV1, 12 per cent SEV2, 38 per cent SEV3 and the remainder SEV4.

An incident has a title, a declared-at time, a resolved-at time that is never before it, its own severity, the service it started on, the elapsed minutes to resolve, and a flag for whether it was escalated. We also copy the service's tier onto the incident, because the postmortem pack has to show the tier and I am not having it change under us when somebody re-tiers a service six months later -- but on the day it is written it is that service's tier and nothing else. Most incidents are shut inside the hour; a few drag on for days, and the mean elapsed time lands near 210 minutes, well above the typical one.

Several engineers get pulled into one incident and any engineer works plenty of incidents, so I need that pairing stored properly, with the role the person played on it -- incident commander, comms lead, subject matter expert. One row per person per incident, no duplicates.

On-call: each team runs a rotation of shifts, and a shift is a start and an end timestamp -- end after start -- plus the engineer holding the pager. A team has one shift starting at any given moment, so the team and the start time together pin down the shift. And you only ever hold the pager for your own team: the engineer on a shift always belongs to the team whose rotation it is, which the current spreadsheet cheerfully allows you to break.

Pages go out against a shift and reference the incident, with the time it was sent and how many seconds it took to be acknowledged. A page carries the severity the incident was at when we sent it, because incidents get upgraded and the acknowledgement target has to follow the severity at page time, not the severity we ended up at. A page is sent inside its shift -- not before it starts, not after it ends -- and never before the incident was declared. Acknowledgement time is a waiting time in the purest sense: somebody is either at their laptop or they are asleep, most acks land in well under a minute and the tail is long, mean about 95 seconds. Whatever the severity target says, nothing is allowed to sit unacknowledged past 900 seconds, because the pager re-fires at that point and the field can't hold more.

One escalation rule is non-negotiable: a SEV1 declared against a tier 1 service is always escalated, no judgement call. And the tier value itself is 1 to 4, nothing else.

variance.basis: variance = ln(1 + CV^2) for CV in [0.324, 3.166], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=70)

ground_truth_moments.evidence: something near 900,000 alert events feeding into them
the mean elapsed time lands near 210 minutes

nl_description:
Handover for the metering, rating and billing estate at a mid-size IaaS provider. Read this as the whole platform rather than one extract: it absorbs the four systems we run today -- the meter pipeline, the rating engine, the billing ledger and the support desk -- and it has to carry the change trail that last year's audit said we did not have. Sizing first, because it decides where the seams go: about 2.5 billion raw usage samples a month, pre-aggregated hourly before anything touches the billing tables, roughly 90 million hourly rollup rows a month, 40,000 invoices a month, and everything else in the thousands. One wide fact table, narrow dimensions around it, and four other subsystems that touch billing only through the invoice.

REFERENCE DATA. Regions are a short list -- a region code, a region name and the country the region sits in. Currencies likewise: the code, the currency name, and the number of minor units, because JPY has none and that has bitten our rounding twice; currency names are unique, as are region names, so either name gives you its code. Service families group what we sell: a family code, a family name and a flag for whether the family is reserved capacity rather than on-demand. A SKU is the priced unit: a SKU code that is unique across the catalogue and therefore fixes the rest of the row, the service family it belongs to, the region it is priced in, the unit it is measured in (vcpu-hour, GiB-month, request), and a unit price as DECIMAL. Anything in a reserved-capacity family is a reserved-instance SKU and priced under 0.05 per unit by definition. Volume pricing sits underneath the SKU as tiers: each tier has a minimum and a maximum quantity, the maximum always above the minimum, and a tier price that never exceeds the SKU's own unit price -- tiers discount, they never mark up.

ACCOUNTS AND IDENTITY. Accounts sit at the top: company name, the billing currency, a signup date, a payment status, plus a denormalised resource count we read for quota checks rather than counting live. That count is savagely top-heavy across the customer base -- a Zipf law with exponent 1.25 is what the capacity model uses. Each account has contacts, and a contact is a name, an email and the contact role they play (billing, technical, security). Under an account there are projects, each with a name that is unique inside that account, a region, a creation timestamp and a soft-delete flag. IAM users belong to an account and are identified by an email address that is unique platform-wide, with a creation timestamp and a disabled flag. A user can be granted access to several projects and a project has many users, with the role and the granted-on date recorded on the grant, exactly one grant row per user per project, and no grant ever predates the user it was issued to. Roles are their own short list: a role code, a role name and a privilege rank so that two roles can be compared without a case statement. API keys belong to a user: a creation timestamp, an expiry that is always after it, the timestamp it was last used -- never after it expires -- and a revoked flag.

RESOURCES AND METERING. Resource types are a coded list with a type name and the service family they meter into. A resource is what actually gets metered -- an instance, a bucket, a managed database. It belongs to a project, has a resource type, a creation timestamp, a termination timestamp once it is gone which is never before creation, and a SKU. Across the estate a little over half of resources are instances, about a quarter buckets, one in seven managed databases and the remainder everything else. Tagging is free-form: tags are key and value, a resource carries many of them and the same key shows up across many resources, one row per resource per key.

Meter samples arrive in batches. A batch records when it was received, how many samples it carried, how many we accepted -- never more than it carried, and the gap is the thing the pipeline dashboard actually plots -- and the region it came from. A batch runs around 4,200 samples, which behaves like a count of independent arrivals in a fixed window. The hourly rollup is the fact table: it references the resource, the batch it came out of, the hour bucket as a timestamp, and a quantity as FLOAT that is never negative, ever. It also carries the SKU, copied off the resource, because rating must not join through a dimension that support may be editing underneath it -- and being a copy, it is always that resource's SKU and nothing else. No rollup bucket is earlier than the creation of the resource it meters. For a running instance the hourly vCPU quantity is close to normal, 0.72 with sigma 0.21, once idle hours are excluded.

COMMITMENTS AND CREDITS. A commitment is a customer promising spend in a service family for a term: the account, the family, a committed amount as DECIMAL, a start and an end date with the end after the start, and a discount percentage. Drawdowns record consumption of a commitment against an invoice, with the amount drawn and the date -- and no single drawdown exceeds the whole committed amount, which is the arithmetic the finance team currently does in a spreadsheet. Credits are separate and simpler: a grant against an account with a granted amount, a remaining amount that is never above the granted amount, a reason code, the date granted and an expiry after it. Consumption of a credit is its own row against the grant and the invoice it was applied to, and a single consumption never exceeds what was granted.

RATING AND INVOICING. An invoice belongs to an account, covers a monthly period with a start and an end date -- end after start -- and carries a subtotal, a tax amount and a total as DECIMAL, a status, the currency, the date it was issued and a due date that is never before the issue date. The total is exactly the subtotal plus the tax amount; if those three ever disagree the ledger is wrong and I want it caught in the data. The currency on an invoice is the account's billing currency, copied for convenience, and the same is true of the currency on a payment. Monthly invoice totals are heavily right-skewed -- a handful of whales and a very long left mass -- and a lognormal with log-mean 7.4 and log-variance 1.9 fits well.

Line items are the rated rollups: each references the invoice and the rollup it rated, and carries the SKU, the quantity, the unit price applied and the resulting amount. The amount is the quantity times the unit price, exactly. The quantity is the rollup's quantity, copied, and the SKU is the rollup's SKU, so the rollup reference determines both. The unit price applied never exceeds the SKU's own unit price, because commitments and tiers only ever discount. Credits and adjustments are separate rows against an invoice with a reason code, a signed adjustment amount and a created-at timestamp.

Tax is held properly rather than as a rate hard-coded in the rating job. A tax rate is a region, a rate percentage, and the dates it is effective from and to; the region and the effective-from date together pin down the rate. A tax line on an invoice names the rate it used, the taxable amount and the tax amount, where the tax amount is the taxable amount times that rate's percentage and the taxable amount never exceeds the invoice subtotal. Tax is never negative, and for accounts billed in USD we do not levy it at all, so the tax amount on those invoices is exactly zero. And an account whose payment status is DELINQUENT cannot have invoices go out, so invoice status is forced to HELD for those accounts.

PAYMENTS AND DUNNING. A payment method belongs to an account: the method type, the last four digits, the date it expires and a default flag. A payment records the account, the method used, when it was paid, the amount, the currency and a status. Payments are allocated across invoices -- one allocation row per payment per invoice -- and an allocation never exceeds either the payment it comes from or the total of the invoice it lands on. Refunds hang off a payment with an amount that never exceeds the payment, a reason code and a refunded-at timestamp that is never before the payment was taken. Dunning is a stream of events against an invoice: an event type, when it occurred, and how many days overdue we were at the time, which is never negative and never before the invoice's due date.

QUOTAS AND SUPPORT. Quota limits are held per account per service family, one row each, with a limit value and the current value, and the current value never exceeds the limit -- that is the check the console is supposed to make and does not. Support plans are a short list: a plan code, a plan name that is unique, a monthly fee and the response target in hours we contract to. An account is on one support plan. A support case records the account, when it opened, when it closed which is never before it opened, a severity from 1 to 4, a subject, the hours to first response, and the support plan the account was on at the time -- we copy it because customers move plans and the SLA we are judged against is the one in force on the day. First response must beat that plan's response target. Case severity runs about 4 per cent severity 1, 16 per cent severity 2, 44 per cent severity 3 and the rest severity 4, and time to first response is a waiting time with a mean near 6 hours. Comments hang off a case with the user who posted, a posted-at timestamp never before the case opened, and the body.

GOVERNANCE. Budgets are per project: a monthly limit and an alert threshold as a fraction of it. A budget alert row records the budget, when it triggered and the observed amount, which by definition has reached the limit times the threshold. And the change trail: every change to any of this is a row naming the account, the user who made it, the table, the record key, the action, the field, the old and the new value and when. On an update the old value must be populated -- that is the audit finding, and it is the reason this rebuild is funded.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: roughly 90 million hourly rollup rows a month
the hourly vCPU quantity is close to normal, 0.72 with sigma 0.21
time to first response is a waiting time with a mean near 6 hours

nl_description:
Analytics store for our edge request logs. It is four things, honestly, and one of them is enormous: at peak we ingest around 60 million requests an hour, call it 30 billion rows a month before any rollup, and the other three are lookups hanging off it.

A zone is the customer-facing unit -- a hostname somebody has onboarded. Against it we keep the account reference on our side, the hostname itself, the date it was onboarded, and whether caching is switched on. No two zones share a hostname, so the hostname is as good as the id. Traffic across zones is absurdly unequal: the single busiest zone is something like 8 per cent of everything, the second is roughly half of that, and it keeps decaying in a textbook power law rather than tapering off. When we model zone rank we use a Zipf exponent of 1.15.

The POPs are the second lookup: a three-letter airport-style code that is unique and tells you everything else about the POP, a city, a country, and how many servers we have in it. That last one is anywhere from a dozen in the small ones to a couple of hundred in Frankfurt, spread pretty evenly across that range with no typical size.

The third is origins, which we've never modelled properly and it shows. An origin is the customer's own server that we go back to on a miss: which zone it belongs to, its hostname -- again unique, we insist on it -- whether we talk to it over HTTPS, and the timeout in milliseconds after which we give up. Timeouts are set somewhere between one second and a minute, so between 1,000 and 60,000. A zone can have more than one origin, which is exactly why the request row has to say which one it went to rather than us inferring it from the zone. Going the other way is fine: an origin belongs to a single zone, so the origin on a request tells you the zone the request was for, and those two had better agree.

Every request row points at the zone it was for, the POP that served it and the origin behind it, and records the timestamp down to the millisecond, the HTTP method, the URI path (which can be long), the response status, the bytes we sent, the cache result, how many milliseconds the origin took on the occasions we had to go back to it, and the total time we took end to end. The total is never less than the origin time -- it contains it. A request is never stamped before its zone was onboarded, which sounds obvious until you see what the old backfill did. Cache result is one of HIT, MISS, EXPIRED or BYPASS, and the split is about 82 per cent hits, 11 per cent misses, 4 per cent expired and 3 per cent bypassed.

Origin fetch latency behaves like any queueing wait -- no typical value, a flat hazard, mean about 180 ms. Bytes sent is wildly skewed the other way: mostly small JSON and HTML, with a fat tail of video segments, and a lognormal with log-mean 9.1 and log-variance 2.4 matches what we measure.

Rules that came out of schema review. Response status is only ever between 100 and 599, and bytes sent is never negative. When the cache result is a HIT the origin latency is zero, because we never left the POP. Anything that was not a HIT did go back, and it cannot have taken longer than that origin's own timeout -- if it did we would have cut it off, so a row like that is a bug in the logger. And if caching is switched off on the zone, everything for it comes back BYPASS.

I'm trying to get a proper database behind our hosted phone product before we onboard any more resellers, because right now half of it lives in the billing system and half in the switch config and the two disagree.

Start with the resellers, since they're the reason for all this. We sell through about forty of them; for each we hold the company name and the commission percentage we've agreed, and every business customer we have came in through exactly one of them.

A business customer -- we say tenant internally, sales insists on calling them accounts, it's the same thing -- has a company name, a billing contact and a status, and sits under a reseller and on a package. There are three packages and we number them one to three: Starter, Business, Enterprise. Each has a monthly price and the number of simultaneous calls it allows: Starter gets 10, Business gets 50, Enterprise is unmetered which we store as 999. Package names are unique so the name gives you the price and the cap. Most tenants are on Business, about a fifth are on Starter and one in ten on Enterprise. We also hold the concurrent call cap on the tenant itself, because the provisioning script reads it there and I'm not rewriting the provisioning script -- but it is copied straight off the package and it must always match.

Under a tenant you get extensions. An extension is somebody's desk line: an extension number, a display name, a voicemail PIN, and the device it's registered to. Extension numbers only have to be unique inside one tenant -- everyone has a 100 -- so it takes the tenant and the number together to identify a line. Devices are the desk phones and softphones and they belong to a tenant too, so a MAC address (unique, obviously, it's a MAC), a model and a firmware version. An extension is only ever registered to a device belonging to its own tenant, which the current setup does not stop and which caused the incident in March. Plenty of extensions have no device yet, which the current setup can't even represent.

Numbers are separate from extensions and this is where everyone gets confused. We buy DIDs in blocks from carriers and point them at extensions. A DID has the E.164 number, which is unique across the whole platform, the carrier we got it from, a monthly cost, the tenant we bought it for, and which extension it currently routes to. And the extension it routes to always belongs to the tenant the number was bought for -- the tenant on the number is really just that extension's tenant, we only keep it because unrouted numbers still have to be billed to somebody. Carriers we barely track -- a name and our account number with them, that's the lot.

Then the calls. Every leg gets logged: the tenant, the extension involved (new, that -- the old logger only had the numbers, which is why nobody could ever report per-desk), the from and to numbers, when it started, when it ended, how long it rang before anyone picked up, the talk time, and how it ended -- the disposition, we call it: answered, busy, no answer, failed. Roughly two thirds are answered, an eighth busy, a fifth no answer and a couple of per cent outright failed. The leg's tenant is the extension's tenant, same story as the numbers. The end is never before the start. We're doing something like a million and a half legs a month across all tenants now.

Talk time is the classic shape where most calls are short, there's no typical length, and a few go on forever; the average sits around three and a half minutes. Ring time before answer behaves the same way, averaging about nine seconds, and the switch gives up at sixty so it never exceeds that. There's a MOS score too, which the vendor hands us on a 1 to 5 scale, and in practice we sit just above 4 with not much spread either side. And a leg that wasn't answered has zero talk time, obviously -- that one keeps getting violated by the switch and it drives our reporting mad.

There's an IVR thing as well that a few of the bigger tenants use, menus and options and so on, but nobody has agreed what we're storing for it so leave it out for now.

std.basis: coefficient of variation in [0.006, 0.682], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=117), applied to the stated mean

ground_truth_moments.evidence: We sell through about forty of them
a million and a half legs a month across all tenants now
we sit just above 4 with not much spread either side

nl_description:
We're a small outfit -- fourteen shops around the region, we sell airtime and handsets for two of the big networks. My son set us up a spreadsheet years back and it has become a disaster, so we'd like something proper built.

What we genuinely need to know is what stock is where. A handset is a physical thing with that long IMEI number printed on the box -- no two the same, that's the whole point of it -- a make, a model, what we paid for it and what we're asking for it, and it sits in one particular shop. There'll be three or four hundred handsets across the shops at any one time. One thing worth knowing: a model only ever comes from the one make. A Galaxy is always a Samsung, nobody else makes one, so if you've written the model down you've written the make down whether you meant to or not.

There are SIM cards too, thousands of them, but we buy those in bags of fifty and frankly we just count them -- the accountant only wants the long ICCID number written on the docket when one actually goes out with a customer, so that's the one place it needs to live, and a given SIM only ever goes out the once.

Every shop has a name, the high street it's on, and a manager. The names are all different -- we name them after the town -- so the name is as good as any number you'd give it. What I'd love is to glance at a shop and see what it's holding and what it shifted last week.

We should keep the customers as well, or at least the ones who buy something. A name and their mobile number, and the number is what we go on when somebody comes back in about a fault, because nobody can ever remember which shop they bought it from and the number always finds them.

Selling works like this. Somebody comes in, buys a handset, maybe a SIM with it, maybe just a SIM. We note which shop the sale happened in, who served them, and the customer. The sale itself has the date, what they actually paid, and the payment method, cash or card -- it's about sixty forty card to cash these days, a bit more card if anything. Two things that ought to be impossible and currently aren't: the person who served them has to actually work in that shop, and the handset has to be one that was sitting in that shop, not one on the other side of the county.

On the money. Handsets go out at a markup, so what we're asking is never below what we paid. What the customer actually pays can be under the asking price -- we knock a bit off for cash, everyone does -- but it can never be under what the handset cost us plus a fiver, because that fiver is the whole business. Average selling price is somewhere around 210 pounds, though we've had the odd thousand-pound flagship go out the door, and those few big ones pull the average up above what a typical sale looks like. Nothing at all leaves below 40 pounds, that's the floor we agreed.

The refurbished ones are a headache. They come back to us, we test them, some go out again cheaper. So a handset needs to say what condition it's in, new or refurbished -- about a fifth of what we're holding at any time is refurbished -- and a refurbished one we never ask more than 400 for however nice it is.

Staff, last thing -- about thirty of us including the part-timers. I don't think we need much beyond a name, which shop they're at, and whether they're part-time, because the rota is somebody else's problem.

variance.basis: variance = ln(1 + CV^2) for CV in [0.324, 3.166], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=70)

ground_truth_moments.evidence: Average selling price is somewhere around 210 pounds

nl_description:
This is for the fault side of a regional transmission network -- microwave links, fibre spans, and the power and environmental kit at each site. About 1,800 sites, and we take in something like two hundred thousand alarms a month, so it isn't big data, it's messy data.

Sites are the anchor. Each has a site code that's unique and is what everybody actually says out loud, a name, a grid reference, and a criticality band from 1 to 5 where 1 is the worst thing to lose. Most sites end up band 3 or 4 -- call it 40 per cent band 3 and 35 per cent band 4 -- with 5 per cent band 1, a tenth band 2 and the last tenth band 5. Sites sit in regions and a region has an area manager; region names are unique, so the name tells you whose region it is. The site record also carries a daily alarm count that the trending dashboard reads; it sits around 3.7 and behaves like a count of independent events in a fixed window.

Equipment is installed at a site, each piece with a serial number that's unique to it, a type, a commissioning date and a software version, and it comes from a vendor. Vendors are worth holding properly now that there are five of them: a name, unique, and the support contact we're supposed to ring. Nothing can alarm before it was commissioned, which sounds too obvious to write down until you've seen what the migration loaded. Links join two sites, an A-end and a B-end -- never the same site at both ends -- and carry a capacity in Mbps and a media type, microwave or fibre.

Alarms come off equipment, and because the correlation engine needs it fast, each alarm is also stamped with its site directly rather than being resolved through the equipment every time; that stamped site is the equipment's site and must never say otherwise. An alarm has a raise time, a clear time once it clears, the minutes it took to clear, a severity from the vendor MIB, a probable cause, flags for flapping, for suppressed and for whether we ticketed it, and the ticket it rolled onto. Behind the codes there are alarm definitions -- the code itself, a human-readable description, a default severity, and whether the alarm is suppressible at all. Probable causes are their own short list too: the cause code, a description and a category, because the same cause turns up under a dozen different alarm codes and we report on the category. A definition maps to exactly one probable cause; the alarm carries the cause as well because the engine groups on it, but it is always the definition's cause. On a normal month about 60 per cent of what arrives is warnings, 25 per cent minor, 11 per cent major and 4 per cent critical.

Self-clearing alarms clear on their own schedule with no characteristic duration -- the ones still up after an hour are no more likely to clear in the next minute than the fresh ones -- and the mean time from raise to clear is 22 minutes. A clear is obviously never before the raise.

When something is real we open a fault ticket against the site: an opened time, a closed time no earlier than it, a fault class, the field team it went to, a resolution note, and the hours it took to restore. Several alarms usually roll onto one ticket, and an alarm we ticketed was raised before the ticket was opened -- that's the whole point of the alarm. Field teams have a name that's unique, a base depot and a headcount, and depots are now a list of their own with a name and the town they're in, because two teams share the Colwyn depot and the old free-text field had it spelled three ways. Individual technicians we've started holding as well: a name, a badge number that's unique to the person, and the team they're on. Time to restore averages 4.5 hours with a standard deviation of about 2.1 and is roughly symmetric around that. Nothing is allowed to sit open beyond 30 days -- 720 hours -- because the KPI system force-closes it.

If a truck rolls we log a site visit against the ticket: which team went, which technician led it, when they arrived, when they left, and which parts they consumed and how many of each. A visit never arrives before its ticket was opened, never leaves before it arrived, and the technician who led it is always on the team that was sent -- we've had visits logged with someone from a different team on them and nobody could explain it. Parts come from a stores catalogue keyed on the part number, with a description and a unit cost; a visit can burn several part numbers and a part number turns up on many visits, but only one line per part number per visit. Each line carries the quantity used and the line cost, and the line cost is the quantity times that part's unit cost -- if it isn't, somebody has been editing costs. Lines are small, one or two parts typically, averaging about 1.6.

Planned work is tracked apart from all this: maintenance windows have a start and an end after it, the site, an owner and an approval state, and alarms raised inside a window are meant to be suppressed. Which leads to the one rule I keep having to explain: if the alarm's definition says it isn't suppressible, then it cannot come back marked suppressed, window or no window. The other one is escalation -- a critical alarm at a band 1 site is always ticketed.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: the mean time from raise to clear is 22 minutes
Lines are small, one or two parts typically, averaging about 1.6

nl_description:
I have ended up running IT support here almost by accident. We're a 320-person architecture practice and there is no IT department beyond me and two contractors who come in on Tuesdays. At the moment, when somebody's laptop dies they walk over and tell me and I write it on a pad. That is the entire system.

What I want is somewhere to log the thing that came in: who reported it, when, a line or two about what it is, and how urgent it is. We get somewhere between forty and sixty of these a week, so a few thousand a year, we are not talking about a mountain of records.

The what-it-is-about part should be a proper list rather than me typing it differently every time. There are six and I'd number them in this order: printers, the network, the CAD licences, email, hardware, and "other", which is most of it if I'm honest -- about thirty per cent lands in other, hardware is a bit under a fifth, printers and network are around fifteen per cent each, email a little over a tenth and the CAD licences a tenth. Each of those has a name -- all different, obviously -- and a target turnaround in hours that I set when we agreed all this and have not touched since, so the name of the category tells you its target. No target is more than the fortnight. The target also gets copied onto the ticket when it's logged, because the partners want the target that applied printed on the report and I don't want it moving if I ever do change one. It's the category's target and nothing else.

For each one I need to know who is dealing with it and whether it's still open. Things get handed between the three of us fairly often and I'd like that history rather than just the current name, because at the moment nobody can tell me who had it last Thursday. So every assignment of a request is its own little record: the request, who it went to, when they picked it up and when they handed it on. Nobody can be given a ticket before it was reported, nothing is handed on before it was picked up, and -- this one is embarrassing -- it should stop me assigning a ticket to the very person who raised it, which I have absolutely done.

And I want to be able to answer how long things took, because the partners ask and I never have a number. So the ticket needs when it was closed, never earlier than when it came in, and the elapsed hours. My gut says most get sorted the same day but a handful drag on for weeks -- the licence renewals especially, those are hostage to the vendor. If I had to put an average on it I'd say around eleven hours of elapsed time, which sounds far too high until you remember it's the licence ones pulling it up; the typical one is much quicker than that.

People: everyone is already in the staff list for payroll, so I only need their name, their payroll number, which studio they sit in, and whether they're a partner. The payroll number is the one thing that's guaranteed unique so that's what I'd key off. That partner flag matters, because anything a partner raises gets treated as high priority and there's no arguing about it. Studios should be their own little list as well -- there are five, each with a name and the floor it's on, and no two share a name.

On urgency: roughly one in twenty is what I'd call an emergency, about a quarter are high, and the rest splits fairly evenly between normal and low.

Equipment is the other half of the story. Maybe half these tickets are about one specific machine and I would love to link them up, but the asset list lives in a different spreadsheet that facilities own and I am not taking that on as well -- so at most I want the asset tag written down against the ticket and they can keep the rest.

One thing I want the system to shout about: nothing should be sitting open past a fortnight. Call it 336 hours.

variance.basis: variance = ln(1 + CV^2) for CV in [0.324, 3.166], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=70)

ground_truth_moments.evidence: there are five, each with a name and the floor it's on
If I had to put an average on it I'd say around eleven hours of elapsed time

nl_description:
Right, so I look after the collection side of things for the borough -- bins, basically. There's about ninety-two thousand properties on our patch and every one of them sits on a round, which is what we call the route a lorry does on a given day of the week. Some of the lads say runs instead of rounds, same thing. We hold the address and the postcode for each property and which round it's on, and a note of what sort of property it is, because the mix is mostly houses but there's a good chunk of flats and they behave completely differently. The rounds are split across two depots, Kingsmead and the little one out at Fenn Lane, and each round has a name that nobody outside the depot understands, things like NE3 Tuesday. The name isn't random, mind -- the day's in it and the depot's in it, so if you show me a round name I can tell you straight off which depot it goes out of and which day of the week it runs, no need to look anything up. And the rounds are drawn on the postcodes, so a given postcode only ever sits on the one round. A crew is assigned to a round -- that's a driver and either one or two loaders, so two or three bodies, never more than that because there isn't room in the cab -- and each crew has a name on the rota, usually the driver's.

Every property has its bins, and this is where it gets fiddly, because a house might have four of them. The black one is general waste, the blue is your dry recycling, then there's the green garden waste bin which people pay a subscription for, and food caddies. If I look at every bin we've got out there, roughly four in ten are black, another four in ten blue, about one in seven is a green garden one and the little bit that's left is caddies. They come in different sizes too -- the caddies are only twenty-three litres and at the other end we've got the big communal bins on the flats which are eleven hundred. We record when each bin was delivered to the property, because people do ring up asking.

The lorries weigh each lift now, which is new and honestly a bit of a headache. An average bin comes in around eleven and a half kilos, give or take four either way. There's a hard limit -- the lifting gear won't take anything past ninety kilos, full stop -- and with the food caddies in particular, if one comes in over about twelve kilos then somebody's put the wrong thing in it and the crew are told to leave it and tag it. The supervisors have another check they use, which is the weight against the size of the bin: rule of thumb is a kilo for every ten litres, so if a lift that actually got emptied comes back heavier than a tenth of that bin's litres, somebody's put rubble or soil in it and we go and have a word. Every lift gets logged against the bin and against the round, with the time it happened, and there's a yes-or-no on whether it actually got emptied, because sometimes the bin's blocked in or contaminated and we go away again. And a lift can't be dated before the day we dropped the bin off at the property, which sounds too obvious to say until you see what the old system let through.

Then there's the missed bin reports. Residents ring up or use the form on the website, and we log it against the property with the time it came in and a reason -- blocked access, crew error, resident put it out late, that sort of thing -- and the time we closed it off, which is never earlier than the time it came in, whatever the spreadsheet used to say. It's steady, that: any given round will pick up about six of these in a week, week in week out. Now the important bit is assisted collections. If somebody's registered as assisted -- elderly, disabled, whatever the reason -- the crew have to go into the garden, fetch the bin and put it back where they found it. And if we miss one of those we're supposed to be back within twenty-four hours. Everybody else it's three working days, seventy-two hours, and between you and me we don't always hit that either. The target hours sitting on the report is just read straight off whether the property is assisted or not -- there's no judgement in it, it's one or the other.

All in we do something like nine million lifts a year, which is a lot of rows to keep.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: about ninety-two thousand properties on our patch
An average bin comes in around eleven and a half kilos
All in we do something like nine million lifts a year

nl_description:
This is the library management system for a county service -- twelve branches plus a mobile, and the mobile behaves like a branch as far as the data goes, so it gets a flag rather than a table of its own. Members are attached to a home branch and to a membership category, and the category is what drives the rules: how many items you can have out, and for how long. Both of those follow from the category code alone, which is why they have no business being copied onto the member. Allowances run from six items on a junior card up to thirty for a school or institutional borrower. Roughly speaking our membership is 62% adult, 22% junior, 13% concession and 3% institutional. On the member themselves we hold the usual -- name, date of birth, email, and the date they joined.

We distinguish the title from the physical copy, and that matters, because a popular title might have forty copies spread across branches, each with its own barcode, the date we bought it and a condition grade. Barcodes are unique across the whole service, so a barcode on its own identifies a copy, and a copy belongs to exactly one branch. A title has its text, an ISBN, a year of publication, and a publisher -- we hold publishers separately because we negotiate supply with them, so a publisher name and the town they publish from. An ISBN is enough by itself to pin down the title text, the year of publication and the publisher; that is rather the point of an ISBN.

Titles have authors, and a fair number have several -- editors, translators, illustrators -- so that is a proper many-to-many, with the contribution role recorded on the link itself: the role is a property of that particular title-and-author pairing, not of the author. We also tag titles against subject headings from a controlled list, each heading being a code and a name, and the name follows from the code. A title usually carries three or four headings, so that is another many-to-many.

Loans hang off a copy and a member: when it went out, when it is due, when it came back, and how many times it has been renewed. The due date is always later than the moment it went out, and a return, where there is one, is never earlier than the borrowing. Nor can a copy go out before the date we acquired it -- the current system does not check that and it shows. Renewals average a bit under one per loan. Juniors are capped at two renewals; adults get up to five.

Reservations are placed against the title rather than a specific copy, with a pickup branch and a status, and there is a 75p charge to reserve which is waived for junior cards -- those come through at zero, and nothing goes above the 75p in either direction.

Copies move about. When a branch wants a title that is held somewhere else we send the copy over, and we log the move: which copy, the branch it left, the branch it is bound for, when it went and when it arrived. It never arrives before it was sent, and the branch it is going to is never the branch it came from, which again sounds too obvious to write down until you look at what is in the table.

Overdues raise a fine against the loan, with the date it was raised and the date it was paid if it has been: median is about three pounds with a long right tail up to the twenty-pound replacement charge, and nothing above that. Fines get paid at a desk and sometimes in instalments, so a payment is a row in its own right -- which fine, how much, when, the method, the branch it was taken at, and the member of staff who took it. A single payment is never for more than the fine it is against. Staff are attached to one branch and carry a role, and money is only ever taken at the branch the member of staff belongs to, which is how the till gets reconciled.

One thing worth flagging for sizing. Borrowing is wildly top-heavy. If you rank titles by lifetime loans it is a clean power law with an exponent somewhere around 1.6 -- a few hundred titles carry an enormous share of circulation and the tail barely moves. We are at about 310,000 members and 4.2 million loan records going back to 2009.

variance.basis: variance = ln(1 + CV^2) for CV in [0.324, 3.166], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=70)

ground_truth_moments.evidence: a popular title might have forty copies spread across branches

nl_description:
Handover note for the reporting replica of the national case management estate. I am the data architect on the migration and this is the shape of it as it actually is, not as the old diagram claims. Volumes set the partitioning, so those first: 2.1 million live case files plus fourteen years of archive, roughly 14 million hearings, and documents are the monster at north of 60 million rows. The audit trail runs about double the documents.

Reference data before anything else, because almost every join lands on it and none of it is large. Court tiers are a lookup -- a tier code, a tier name, and the route an appeal from that tier takes; the code fixes both of those, which is the entire reason the lookup exists. A court carries a short court code, a name, and a tier code. A courtroom belongs to exactly one court and never moves between them, so the room determines its court, and it holds a room label, a seating capacity and a flag for whether it is a secure dock room. Capacities run from six in a district judge's room up to about 120 in the big crown courtrooms. Judicial offices are their own lookup: an office code, the office title that goes with it, the tier the office sits at, and whether the post is salaried or fee-paid, all three following from the code. An officer then has a name, an appointment date and exactly one office code, because an officer holds one office at a time.

Case types are reference data too -- a code, a name and the jurisdiction the code belongs to, which follows from the code. Procedural tracks are a lookup of code, name and the maximum minutes a hearing on that track may be listed for. Case statuses are a lookup of code, name and a flag for whether the status is terminal.

The root entity is the case file: the court it was issued in, a case reference, a case type code, a track code, a current status code, the filed date, a disposal date once there is one, a derived duration in days and a hearing count. The reference is constructed out of the issuing court's own code, so the reference determines both the case and the court, and they should not be treated as independent. Duration in days is nothing but the filed and disposal dates subtracted, kept only because the reports want it. A disposal never predates the filing. Status changes are held as their own history -- case, new status, the timestamp, the officer who made the change -- which is new; today we overwrite. Cases also get transferred between courts: the case, the court it left, the court it went to, the date and a reason code, and the receiving court is never the sending court.

Parties are their own entity with a name and a kind flag for person versus organisation, because the same party recurs across cases. Party roles are a lookup -- role code, role name, and a flag for whether the role is the initiating one, both determined by the code -- and case-to-party is many-to-many keyed on case and party, carrying the role code and the date the party joined the case, with the pair fixing the role. Legal representation sits on top of that: a firm, identified by name and SRA number, represents a given party in a given case, so that association keys on case, party and representative with the retainer date as payload, and those three together fix the retainer date. SRA numbers are unique, so an SRA number identifies the firm and its name by itself.

Hearings are where the current model is wrong and the replica fixes it. A hearing belongs to a case and carries a hearing type code, an outcome code, the timestamp it was listed at, the minutes it was scheduled for and the minutes it actually took, and it is never listed before the case was filed. Hearing types are a lookup of code, name and a default length in minutes that the code fixes. Outcome codes are a lookup carrying a description and a flag for whether that outcome disposes of the case, again following from the code. The courtroom and the judge are NOT attributes of the hearing, which is what we do today and it is the source of half our reconciliation problems. They belong to the sitting. A sitting is a courtroom, a presiding officer, a date, a session marker and a start and end time, and it ends after it starts. A listing then places a hearing into a sitting with a position in the list, a slot start, a slot end and the minutes allotted; a hearing is listed into one sitting, so the hearing determines the sitting, and the sitting determines its room and its judge. A slot ends after it starts, sits inside its own sitting's start and end times, and is never allotted less time than the hearing was scheduled for. Listing slots run from a fifteen-minute directions appointment to a full 480-minute day, and a hearing on the small claims track is never listed longer than an hour. Actual duration is roughly normal, mean 62 minutes, sd 25. Hearings per case is Poisson with lambda about 2.4. Adjournments hang off the hearing -- the date it was adjourned, a reason code, whether it is part-heard, and the next hearing date, which is always later than the adjournment itself. Where a party needs an interpreter we book one against the hearing with a language code, a supplier, the minutes booked and a cost, and we book at least the scheduled length, never less.

Criminal work needs the offence catalogue, which is the most heavily joined reference table we have: an offence code, its description, the maximum sentence in months and whether it is indictable. All three follow from the code -- that is what a catalogue is for -- and the maxima run from zero for fine-only offences up to 1200 months, which is how we hold life. A charge is then a case, a party, an offence code, the offence date, the charge date, a plea, a verdict and a sentence in months. A charge is never dated before the offence, a sentence is never negative, and a sentence never exceeds the maximum held against its own offence code. Charging is heavily concentrated: rank offence codes by volume and you get a Zipf with an exponent near 1.4.

Orders and judgments. Order types are a lookup of code, name and a flag for whether that type of order must be sealed, the flag following from the code; where it must be sealed, the order carries the seal. An order is a case, the officer who made it, an order type code, the date it was made and the seal flag. A judgment is a case, the officer, the date, a kind, a reserved flag and an awarded amount that is never negative, and no judgment is dated before its case was filed.

Documents. Document types are a lookup of code, name and the retention period in years, which the code fixes. A document is a case, a document type code, the party who filed it, a filed timestamp and a page count of at least one; page counts are long-tailed, log-mean 2.4 with log-variance 1.1. Bundles are assembled for a hearing: the case, the hearing, when it was prepared, a total page count and whether it has been lodged. Bundle contents are a junction of bundle and document carrying a tab number and the start page within the bundle, and a start page never runs past the bundle's own page count.

Enforcement. Warrants are a case, a party, the issuing officer, a type, an issue date, an execution date and an executed flag; once executed, the execution date is on or after the issue date. Fees are a lookup of fee code, description and standard amount, with the amount following from the code. A fee payment is a case, a fee code, an amount, a paid timestamp and a remission flag; the amount never exceeds the standard amount for that code, and where remission was granted it comes in strictly below it. There is no issue fee in the criminal jurisdiction, so criminal fee rows come through at zero. Fines are a different thing from fees and sit against the party as well as the case: an imposed date, the amount imposed, a surcharge, the amount paid down so far and a collection status. Amount imposed is log-normal, log-mean 5.0, log-variance 0.8. Paid to date never exceeds the amount imposed, and instalments are rows of their own against the fine -- amount, timestamp, method -- with no single instalment larger than the fine it is paying down.

Appeals go on the file: the case, the appellant party, the court receiving the appeal, an appeal type, the lodged date, an outcome and a decided date. Nothing is appealed before it has been disposed of, and nothing is decided before it was lodged.

Last, the audit trail, which is not optional for us: every change against a case file writes a row with the case, the user name, an action code, a timestamp and the entity that was touched.

Two more measured splits for the generator: case type comes out 46% civil, 24% family, 22% criminal and 8% tribunal, and disposal time is lognormal on log-days with mu 5.2 and sigma-squared 0.9.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: Actual duration is roughly normal, mean 62 minutes, sd 25
Hearings per case is Poisson with lambda about 2.4

nl_description:
Driver licensing registry -- a rebuild of the core record. I will be honest up front that the medical side is where the requirements are still soft, so treat that part as indicative.

A driver record keys on the driver number and carries surname, forenames, date of birth, sex and current postcode. A driver may hold more than one licence record over time -- provisional, full, exchanged foreign -- each with an issue date, an expiry date and a status code. Entitlement categories are reference data: code, description, minimum age. A licence carries a set of those categories with valid-from, valid-to and an optional restriction code, and that is a composite key on licence and category rather than a repeating group on the licence. Minimum ages across the reference table run from 16 to 24.

Applications are the transactional side: driver, application type, received and decided timestamps, decision code, the applicant's age at the point of application, and a fee. Fees are effectively three-valued -- 34, 43 and 62 pounds -- splitting about 55 / 31 / 14. A first provisional car application cannot be taken from anyone under seventeen. Every application from someone seventy or over has to be referred for medical review; medical declarations hang off the application with a condition code, a declaration date and that referral flag.

Theory tests attach to an application: test centre, timestamp, score out of fifty, pass flag. Scores are near-normal, mean 41.3, sd 7.8.

Endorsements attach to a licence -- offence code, offence date, points, expiry date. Points come out 3 in about 72% of cases, 6 in 19%, 9 in 5% and 11 in the remainder, and the statutory range is 3 to 11. Disqualifications sit on the driver rather than on the licence, because a ban survives the licence being surrendered: start date, length in months (Poisson-ish, mean about 8.5) and a reason code.

Motorist volumes: 52 million driver records, 9 million applications a year, endorsements north of 30 million. We also hold tachograph card data but that is out of scope for this piece.
