nl_description:
Planning. OK so the thing we are trying to get off a spreadsheet is the development management caseload -- applications, or submissions, or cases. People here call them all three and mean the same thing.

Somebody applies, usually through an agent rather than in person, and honestly the agent is the one we end up emailing, so we want their name on the applicant record along with whether they are acting. The application lands against a site, and the site is a physical thing with an address, a ward and an area. Most of them are tiny -- a back garden, a shopfront -- but every so often there is a fifteen-hectare allocation, so the size distribution is horribly skewed, tiny median and a very long tail. On the application itself there is a reference code, a type (householder, minor, major, listed building consent, that sort of list), the date it came in, the target date, and eventually a decision and a decision date. Most things get granted -- call it four in five -- around one in eight refused and the rest withdrawn before we get to them.

Each one has a case officer. They sit in teams and they each carry a caseload in the mid-thirties, plus or minus about nine, and obviously that cannot go negative.

Consultation is the bit that generates the volume. Neighbours, the parish, statutory consultees like the Environment Agency -- each response has a type of respondent, whether they object or support or are neutral, and a date. A typical application picks up three or four responses, though a controversial one picks up hundreds.

Determination clock: eight weeks for the ordinary stuff, thirteen for a major. So a major is allowed ninety-one days and everything else fifty-six, and that is what we get measured on, so we hold the days it actually took.

Conditions get attached when we grant -- there is the text of the condition and a type. And appeals, if the applicant does not like the answer: date lodged, appeal type, outcome, date decided.

Oh, and the conservation area thing. If a site is in one then it cannot be signed off by an officer, it has to go to committee, so we record who it was decided by. That is a flag on the site rather than on the application.

We are looking at something like 4,000 applications a year and about fifteen years of history to migrate, so a few hundred thousand rows once you count consultation responses.

nl_description:
Food safety team, district council. We keep a register of every food business in the district -- about 2,700 of them -- and we are the ones who publish the hygiene ratings, so the data ends up public and it needs to be right.

A premises has a trading name and an address, a business type, and a risk category we assign, A through E. The types come out roughly a third restaurants and cafes, a quarter retailers, getting on for a fifth takeaways, an eighth pubs, and then small numbers of schools and care settings and a handful of manufacturers. The operator is held separately from the premises, partly because one company can run six chip shops and partly because operators change while the premises stays put -- we hold the operator name, whether it is a company or a sole trader, and the company number where there is one. We also keep the date the premises registered with us.

Inspections: which premises, which officer, the date of the visit, and then the three scores that make up the rating -- hygiene, which is out of 25, structure, and confidence in management, which runs 0 to 30 and is honestly all over the place, more or less flat across the whole range. Those three combine into the 0 to 5 rating that goes on the sticker in the window. Our distribution is about 62% fives, 19% fours, 11% threes, 5% twos, 2% ones and the odd zero.

Each inspection also sets the interval until the next one, in months. Category A premises get revisited at six months or less. And anything that comes out with a one or a zero, we are back inside three months whatever the category says.

Where things are bad enough we take enforcement action off the back of the inspection -- the type of action, the date it was issued and the date they complied. We manage maybe 1,600 visits a year and enforcement is a couple of hundred of those.

Officers carry a qualification code, which matters because only some of them can sign off a prohibition.

Register of electors, national scale. Four entities in the core and I want them right, because everything downstream joins through them.

Polling district is the geographic spine: district code, ward, parliamentary constituency, and the polling station it maps to. Households sit in a district and key on UPRN -- address line, postcode, the number of registered electors at the property, and the date the canvass form came back. Occupancy is Poisson-ish with lambda 1.9, legitimately zero for voids, and I would cap it at 30 for the HMOs. The lag in days between the canvass form going out and a response arriving is close to exponential with a rate of about 0.07 per day, so a fortnight on average.

Electors hang off the household: elector number, surname, forenames, date of birth, age in years, nationality code, franchise code, registration date, absent vote type and the open-register opt-out flag. Franchise splits roughly 93% G, 3% E, 2% K and 2% L. Absent voting is 79% none, 19% postal, 2% proxy. There is also a status on the elector, full or attainer. Minimum registration age is 16 and I would bound the top at 115; attainers are exactly 16 or 17 by definition, so that is a conditional bound rather than a global one.

Canvass contacts are the audit trail -- household, channel, timestamp, responded flag. Where a property comes back with zero occupants we stop posting to it and send a personal visit instead.

Sizing: 46 million elector rows, 25 million households recanvassed annually, and contacts run three to four times that.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: the lag in days between the canvass form going out and a response arriving is close to exponential with a rate of about 0.07 per day, so a fortnight on average

nl_description:
I have been doing housing options here for nine years, so I will just tell you how it actually works rather than what the policy says, and you can make of it what you like.

Someone comes in, or more often rings, and we take their details. Might be a single lad sofa-surfing at his mate's, might be a family of six in a two-bed. Whatever the situation, we treat it as one household with one lead person -- that is whose name and phone number goes on it -- and we note how they are housed at the moment, whether that is private rented, staying with family, temporary accommodation, or we have accepted them as homeless. And the size of the household, and how many bedrooms we reckon they need. The average family on our list is a bit over two people. Bedroom need, if you look across the whole list, is nearly half of them needing a one-bed, around a third on two, one in six on three, and a handful needing four. We do not advertise anything bigger than a four-bed, so four is the ceiling both on what they can ask for and on what we can offer.

Then they go on the list. They get a band -- that is the priority thing, A down to D -- and the date they registered, and a points total, and a flag for whether they are still active, because people find something themselves and do not think to tell us. The points are the bit nobody understands, including me some days. Most people are sitting somewhere around the two hundred mark, but there are people up in the thousands because of medical awards and time spent waiting, and it cannot go below zero, obviously. And the one hard rule I can give you for certain: if we have accepted a household as homeless, they go into band A. That is statutory, there is no discretion in it.

When something comes up we make an offer. That sits against their entry on the list -- the address of the place, how many bedrooms it has, the date we offered it, and then the outcome. Roughly six in ten accept, coming on for three in ten turn it down, and the rest just never get back to us at all, which is its own kind of answer. If they refuse, we are supposed to record why, though whether that always happens is another matter.

We have got about nineteen hundred households on the list at any one time and we only let around two hundred and forty places a year, which is the whole tragedy of the thing in one sentence. There is usually a support worker involved on the more complicated cases but that is all in a different system that I do not touch.

nl_description:
I am a trustee and I also end up running the fundraising database because nobody else will, so bear with me, this may wander.

There are two halves to what we do. Money comes in from the public, and money goes out again as grants to small community groups. They are quite different animals and the system we have smushes them together very badly at the moment.

The giving side first. We have got somewhere north of four hundred thousand people on the supporter file -- donors, givers, supporters, I use all three words and they are all the same people. For each one we hold the name, the address and postcode, an email where we have got one, the date of their first gift, whether they have signed a Gift Aid declaration, and how they have asked to be contacted, which we have to respect now. Then every gift is a row of its own: who gave it, which appeal it came in on, how much, when, how they paid, whether it is a standing order or a one-off, and the Gift Aid we can claim on it. If somebody has signed a declaration then there is Gift Aid on the gift, always -- it is twenty-five pence in the pound and it is a quarter of our income, so if that figure is sitting empty on a declared donor then something has gone wrong.

Gift sizes. The typical one is about eighteen pounds, but the shape of it is that long-tailed thing where the average is much higher than the middle because of a handful of enormous ones. The biggest single gift we ever had was two hundred and fifty thousand, from an estate, and the website will not take anything under a pound. Payment mix is about four in ten by direct debit, a third on cards, one in nine cash -- that is the collection tins -- a small amount still by cheque, bless them, and the rest through payroll giving. Our regulars give roughly every three months, but that average hides an awful lot of variation: loads of very short gaps and then a long straggly tail of people who give once a year at Christmas and that is that.

Appeals -- campaigns, whichever word you prefer -- have a name, a channel, a start and end date, and a target.

Now the grants side. We run three programmes, each with an annual budget and a maximum award. Groups apply to a programme: how much they are asking for, when they applied, then a panel score out of a hundred which averages out in the low sixties, and a decision, and what they actually got in the end. No single grant goes above fifteen thousand. We hold the group itself separately because they come back to us year after year -- name, charity number, region, and their annual income. That last one matters, because we only fund small organisations: anything turning over more than a quarter of a million we turn down and point elsewhere.

There are volunteers as well but they are on a spreadsheet in the office and I would leave them out of this for now.

nl_description:
Small rescue centre, two of us on the admin side. I have built bits of this in Access before so I roughly know what I want, I am just not sure where some of it ought to live.

An animal comes in -- intake, admission, whatever you want to call it -- and we record the name we give it, what it is, breed if we can tell, sex, a rough age because a lot of them are strays and nobody knows, weight, the date it came in and the reason. Species mix over a year is a bit over half cats, a third dogs, a small number of rabbits, and then the odd guinea pig or bird which I would just lump in together. Weight is the awkward one: the typical animal through the door is six or seven kilos, but you have got a two-kilo kitten and a forty-kilo lurcher in the same column, so it is very skewed. Ages we cap at twenty-two, which was a cat, and nothing sensible goes below zero.

Length of stay -- we hold it as a number of days in care -- is the thing the trustees always ask about. Half of them are gone inside a month, but a handful of the older dogs are with us the best part of a year, so it is that decay shape, mean somewhere around thirty days. There is also an outcome on the animal: adopted, returned to owner, transferred on, died.

Adopters we hold separately -- name, postcode, phone, whether the home check passed, and whether there are children in the house. That last one is there for a reason. Some animals are flagged as not suitable for a home with children, and if an animal carries that flag we will not place it with an adopter who has kids. Full stop, no exceptions, and I would like that enforced rather than left to whoever is on the desk.

The adoption itself links the animal and the adopter with a date, the donation they paid, and a flag for if the animal came back to us. The donation is forty-five pounds for a cat, and between a hundred and twenty and a hundred and eighty for a dog depending on age, and occasionally nothing at all when it is an old animal going to a long-standing supporter, so zero up to a hundred and eighty overall.

We take in maybe eight hundred animals a year and we have got about six years of records, so this is not a big database, it just needs to be a correct one. We use foster carers for the under-eights too but they are a different conversation.

nl_description:
Design note for the settlement store we are replacing. The unit of account is the supply point, keyed on its MPAN, and each one carries an address with postcode, a profile class and a GSP group because settlement needs both, plus the date it was energised and a flag for whether the site has PV on it. Which GSP group a supply point falls into follows from its postcode -- we hold both and they have never disagreed -- and the MPAN is unique, so it identifies the supply point on its own. GSP groups are a short reference list in their own right: the group code, the region name it goes by, and the distribution loss factor settlement applies to that group. Loss factors run between 1.00 and 1.12 and are spread fairly evenly across that band.

A supply point normally has exactly one meter fitted at a time, identified by serial number, with an install date and a firmware version, and we care which of three generations it is -- SMETS2 covers about 72 per cent of the estate, SMETS1 another 21, and the residual 7 per cent are still legacy mechanical units. Serial numbers are unique across the estate, so a serial pins down the meter and the supply point it sits on, and firmware strings are generation-specific, so a firmware version tells you the generation without looking anything else up. A meter is never installed before its supply point was energised. Meter exchanges are their own event against the supply point: the meter coming out, the meter going in, the date of the swap, the closing register read in kWh and a reason code. The outgoing and incoming meters on an exchange are never the same meter, and the incoming meter's install date is the swap date or later. Legacy mechanical meters cannot report at interval level, so any half-hourly row we hold against one is flagged ESTIMATED rather than actual.

Interval data is the volume driver: per meter, per half hour, the import kWh, an export figure for the sites with PV, and a quality flag. At 2.1 million metered supply points that is a bit over 100 million rows a day. Consumption per interval is log-normal with log-mean -1.0 and log-variance 0.8, and is never negative. Import and export are mutually exclusive within a half hour -- if there is any import on the row then the export figure is zero. A half hour stamped earlier than the install date of the meter it is filed against came off the meter that was replaced, so it is flagged ESTIMATED too. We also sample supply voltage off the smart meters -- a timestamp and a volts reading -- which sits normally around 239.5 V with a standard deviation of 4.1; anything outside the statutory 216.2 to 253.0 V envelope is a compliance event. No sample is stamped before the install date of the meter that produced it.

Contracts bind a supply point to a tariff for a date range and record the payment method. The end date, once there is one, is never before the start date, and the tariff has to be in effect when the contract begins, so the tariff's effective-from date is on or before the contract start. A tariff has a code, a type, a standing charge and day and night unit rates in pence, effective from a date; each code belongs to exactly one type. On the ECONOMY_7 type the night rate must land between 7.5 and 12.0p and is never above the day rate. Billing periods roll consumption up per contract with the period dates, the total kWh, the day and night halves of that total, the amount due and an estimated flag. The two halves add back to the total exactly, and the night half has never run above 60 per cent of it. A period ends after it starts and cannot begin before its contract does; a period running past the contract end date is the final settlement run and is always flagged estimated. Period totals average 705 kWh with a standard deviation near 240, and a period totalling more than 6,000 kWh must be settled on actual reads, never estimated.

Right, so what we're after is something to replace the spreadsheets the billing team have been nursing since forever.

Everything hangs off the account. An account has a reference we quote on letters, the account holder's name, wherever they want the post sent, when they came on to us, and how they pay -- direct debit, card, or the ones who still send cheques. The reference is the thing people read down the phone and no two accounts share one, so if you have the reference you have the account. Most people here say customer, some of the older staff say account holder, it's the same thing, don't build two of them.

Then there's the property itself, which is not the same as the account, because landlords hold accounts for places they don't live in. For each property we hold the address, what kind of place it is -- roughly a third are terraces, a bit over a quarter semis, about 22 per cent flats and the rest detached -- how many people live there, which averages out at about 2.4 and nobody has ever put down fewer than one or more than a dozen, and crucially whether it's on a meter or not. We spent two years deduping the addresses so there's one property per address now, and that's the handle everyone searches on. Metered ones have a meter fitted, and for that we want the serial, the date it went in and the size of the pipe in millimetres. Serials are stamped at the factory so no two are alike, and from a serial you can get straight to the meter and the property it's sat in. I suppose in theory a big place could have two meters but I've honestly never seen it.

The readings themselves are nothing much: which meter, the date, the number off the dial, and where the reading came from -- our own reader, the customer phoning it in, or the estimating routine. We carry the reading before it along on the same row, because the usage is the difference between the two and the girls in billing want to see both. Dials only go forwards, so the new number is never below the one we're carrying, and nothing gets read before the meter was fitted, obviously.

Bills are the thing people ring up about. A bill belongs to an account and to a property, covers a period with a start and an end and a number of days on it, states the volume used in cubic metres, what's owed, and whether it's open, paid or in dispute. The end of a period always comes after the start of it. Metered properties get a bill every quarter and there is never less than 84 days of usage on one and never more than 98. Unmetered properties are charged off the rateable value instead, so there is no volume figure on those bills at all -- it sits at zero. A typical quarter's usage on a metered place is about 27 cubic metres, give or take 11, and volumes are obviously never negative. Most bills come out around 130 pounds but the tail goes a long way up -- we have estates with swimming pools on them.

Payments come in against a bill with the date, the amount and how it arrived. Part payments are completely normal so one bill can have several against it, but the system won't take one bigger than the bill is for, and it won't take a token tenner off a four hundred pound bill either -- there's a floor at a tenth of the bill. Nothing gets paid before the bill goes out, which is the end of the period it covers.

When somebody won't pay we log the dispute: which bill, the day it was raised, what they say the problem is, the team it's landed with and the day it was settled if it has been. The reason decides the team -- anything about the meter reading goes to revenue, anything about a leak goes to the network lot, we don't get to choose. A dispute is never raised before the bill was issued and never settled before it was raised.

Oh, and there's a hardship discount scheme -- I don't know the rules well enough to tell you how it works, someone in revenue would have to explain that bit.

Volume-wise we bill around 1.6 million properties, so it's several million bills a year and rather more payments than that.

nl_description:
Notes from the asset-data workshop -- what the new network model has to hold.

We're organised by district. A district has a name, a region code and a rough population served (that number only ever appears in board packs, so don't over-think it). District names are unique and a district has never been moved between regions, so the name is enough to tell you the region.

The physical asset is the main, which we track as segments. A segment sits in a district, is fed at one of the pressure tiers -- low, medium and intermediate, each with a name and a nominal pressure in bar, and the tier name is the thing that fixes the nominal pressure -- and has a material, a diameter in millimetres, a length in metres, the year it was laid and a condition grade from 1 to 5. Grades run roughly 12 per cent at 1, 31 at 2, 34 at 3, 17 at 4 and 6 at 5. Materials are their own short list now rather than free text on the segment: a material code, a description, the expected life in years we plan against, and a flag for whether that material is on the replacement programme. We also carry a due year on each segment, which is nothing more than the year it was laid plus the expected life its material gets -- the planners wanted it stored rather than worked out every time. The replacement mains we lay are all PE, and those are always between 63 and 180 mm; the old cast iron and ductile stuff can be far wider. Segment lengths are log-normally spread, log-mean about 4.4 with log-variance 0.9. Nothing in the ground predates 1850 and obviously nothing is laid later than 2026.

The replacement programme itself needs modelling because finance keep asking. A scheme has a code, a name, a start and an end date after it, a budget and the spend against it so far, and the spend never goes over the budget -- if it's going to, it gets re-approved as a new scheme. A scheme covers many segments and a segment can come back round in a later scheme, so that pairing is a thing in its own right: it carries the metres we planned to replace on that segment, the metres actually completed, the planned start and the date the work actually finished. You can't plan more metres than the segment is long, you can't complete more than you planned, a segment's planned start is never earlier than the scheme's own start date, and the completion follows the planned start.

Pressure is stepped down at the governor stations -- some of the field teams call them regulator stations, it's the same asset. Each belongs to a district and has a reference, an inlet pressure in bar, an outlet in millibar and a commissioning date. The reference is unique, so it identifies the station. Outlet sits around 75 millibar with a standard deviation of about 8. Telemetry gives us a reading per station every few minutes -- a timestamp, the inlet in bar and the outlet in millibar as measured. Nothing is stamped before the station was commissioned. A measured outlet never runs more than 10 per cent above the station's design outlet, and a measured inlet never drops below 70 per cent of the station's design inlet; either of those is an alarm, not a data point. Separately the stations get walked: an inspection is a station, the crew that went, the date, an outcome and the date the next one falls due, which is always after the visit. Nobody inspects a station before it was commissioned.

Service connections branch off a segment to a premises, with a premises reference, a connection type and a connection date. The premises reference is one-to-one with the connection -- we split any premises that needed two. There are roughly 1.1 million of them on our patch.

Leak reports are the operational side: which segment, when it came in, how we heard about it, a severity and the gas-in-air percentage the operative measured. Around 400,000 a year. About six per cent are the immediate-risk A1 kind, another 19 per cent are A2 and all the rest are B. An A1 is never logged on a reading below 20 per cent gas in air, and an A1 has to be attended within the hour -- that's regulated, not an internal target.

A repair job comes off a report and records which crew went, when it started and finished, the response time in minutes and what it cost. Nothing starts before the report came in and nothing finishes before it started. Response averages about 50 minutes with the usual long tail behind it, and the money is similar in shape -- log-normal, log-mean around 7.55 with log-variance 0.7.

Crews -- the older lads say gangs -- have a name, a depot and a headcount, and each crew holds a set of qualifications. Depots are a table now too: a name, the district they sit in and a postal address. Crew names are unique across the business and a crew has never been moved between depots, so the name gives you the crew and its depot. A qualification has a code, a description and a renewal interval in months; the code is unique and pins down both the description and the interval, and no certificate we recognise runs longer than 60 months. We need the certified date and the expiry date against each crew-and-qualification pairing, with the expiry after the certification, because that pairing is exactly what the auditors ask to see.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: There are roughly 1.1 million of them on our patch.

nl_description:
I run the O and M side for a solar portfolio and honestly the reporting is held together with string, so bear with me.

We've got about 140 plants. People here use plant, site and farm interchangeably, don't read anything into which one you hear. For each one we want a name, roughly where it is, how big it is, when it switched on, and the reference of its grid connection. No two sites share a grid connection reference -- that reference is how the network operator knows which site they're talking about, so it's as good as the name. Site names are unique too, and a site plainly doesn't move, so if you've got the name you've got the site and where it is. They run from about 5 megawatts up to 50 and they're spread pretty evenly across that range -- no clustering at either end, we've got as many little ones as big ones.

Inside a site the thing that matters is the inverters. Who made it, what it's rated at, when it went in, and whether it's behaving. Ratings go from a hundred kilowatts right up to four megawatts depending on the vintage. When we loaded the old spreadsheets we backfilled the missing install dates off the site switch-on date, so nothing is dated earlier than the day its site went live. At any one time about 93 in a hundred are running normally, five in a hundred are running derated for one reason or another, and the odd couple per cent are properly offline.

Every inverter reports in every five minutes -- what it made, the light reading, the panel temperature and the air temperature the same logger picks up. That is the bulk of the data by a mile; across the portfolio it came to something like 60 million rows last month alone. Nothing reports before the inverter was installed. The light readings are the ones the analysts argue about: on a good summer noon we're north of 900, and averaged over daylight it works out somewhere around 340 with a huge amount of scatter, easily 200 either side. Whatever else it is, it can't be negative and we have never recorded above 1200. Generation obviously can't go negative either, and there's a hard ceiling on it that's just arithmetic: five minutes is a twelfth of an hour, so a window can never hold more than a twelfth of the inverter's rating in kilowatt hours. Anything above that is the meter lying to us. On the ones flagged derated the ceiling is tighter still, half of that -- a twenty-fourth of the rating -- because that's what derating means in practice, and when one is properly offline the windows come through as flat zero. Panel temperatures have hit minus fifteen in a cold snap and gone over seventy in a heatwave -- call it minus twenty to eighty-five and you'll cover everything we've ever seen. Whenever there's any light at all the panel is warmer than the air around it; if it isn't, the sensor has come loose.

When something trips we raise a fault against the inverter: when it came in, the code, the wording that goes with that code -- it comes out of the manufacturer's manual and it's the same words every time for a given code, we just print it on the report -- when it cleared, and how long the thing was out for. Nothing is raised before the inverter was installed and nothing clears before it was raised. Most clear inside an hour or two, a few drag on for days, and the average works out around three and a half hours. Anything on an inverter rated over 2 megawatts we have committed contractually to have back inside 48 hours, no excuses.

The bigger jobs go out to the maintenance firm we're contracted to rather than our own techs. We just hold their name and a phone number -- one number per firm, and the names are all different -- and we note against the fault which firm dealt with it.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: it came to something like 60 million rows last month alone.
averaged over daylight it works out somewhere around 340
the average works out around three and a half hours.

nl_description:
Small internal schema for the wind fleet -- 82 turbines, around 2,000 work orders a year, maybe 300 component swaps, so nothing here needs partitioning or archival.

Turbines are the root asset: surrogate integer key plus the asset tag the techs actually quote, the model, hub height in metres (the fleet spans 60 to 120), rated output in kW and a commissioning date. The asset tag is unique, so it stands in for the surrogate. Three models only -- 45 per cent are the 3600 kW machine, 40 per cent the 2300, and the remaining 15 per cent are the old 850 kW units -- and since the rating is a property of the model, not of the individual machine, the model alone fixes the rated output on any row you look at.

Technicians have a staff reference (unique, and the only thing the roster system knows them by), a name, a grade and an HV certification flag. The flag is not independent: certification comes with the grade, so every technician on a given grade carries the same value. Also a joining date, because we back-loaded eleven years of orders and half of them came out attributed to people who had not started yet -- no order opens before its technician joined.

Work orders hang off a turbine and a technician with open and close timestamps, a work type of SCHEDULED, CORRECTIVE or INSPECTION in roughly a 55/38/7 split, labour hours, parts cost and an integer priority from 1 to 4 weighted 8/22/45/25 with 1 the most urgent. Labour hours are log-normal, log-mean 1.6 and log-variance 0.7; anything below 0.25 or above 400 is a keying error and should fail the check constraint. Scheduled work never carries a priority better than 3, so on those rows priority is always 3 or 4, and a priority 1 order is only ever signed off by an HV-certified technician. Close never precedes open, and nothing is opened against a turbine before that turbine was commissioned.

Component types are a reference list rather than free text: a surrogate key, the part code the stores system uses, the component name, the expected life in running hours we plan replacement against, and the list unit cost. The part code is unique and pins down both the name and the expected life.

Where a part is actually swapped out we record it against the work order -- the component type, its serial, the date, the running hours the part had on it when it came out, and whether we put a warranty claim in. Serials are unique per swap and carry the part code in them, so a serial identifies both the swap and the component type. Those hours cluster normally, mean about 41,000 with a standard deviation near 9,000, and we have never seen a part run past a quarter over its expected life -- the condition monitoring catches them first. Anything that comes out short of half its expected life goes in as a warranty claim, that is the rule the supplier agreement gives us. A swap is never dated before its work order opened, and the parts cost on the order is at least the list cost of the component that came out of it.

Handing over the data model brief for the new CPO platform. I'm a product owner, not a DBA, so treat the shapes as intent rather than gospel.

We are one operator among several and we need the others in the model too, because of roaming: an operator has a name and a country code. Roaming works as a pairing -- for any home operator and host operator combination we hold the date it took effect and the commission the host takes, which is capped at 25 per cent and obviously can't be negative. A given pair appears exactly once.

Sites belong to an operator and carry a name, a latitude and longitude, a postcode, an opening date and a running count of sessions in the month. Site names repeat across operators (everyone has a Retail Park One) but within an operator they are unique, so the operator and the name together identify the site. That count is wildly skewed -- a handful of sites do enormous volume and there is a very long tail of sites doing one or two a week. It's a proper power law with an exponent around 1.5.

Each site has charge points, which are the physical EVSEs: a reference, a maximum power anywhere from 3.7 kW up to 350, a connector type (CCS just over half, Type 2 about 36 per cent, CHAdeMO 9, Tesla the remainder), a commissioning date and a status. The EVSE reference is globally unique and has the site code baked into it, so from a reference you can get to both the unit and its site. Nothing is commissioned before its site opened.

On the customer side, drivers register with an email, a registration date and a home postcode; the email is the login so no two drivers share one. A driver can have several vehicles -- make, model, usable battery size and the maximum DC rate the car will accept -- and several RFID cards, each with a UID, an issue date and an active flag. The battery size and the DC limit are properties of the make and model rather than of the individual car, so two drivers with the same make and model always show the same figures. Card UIDs are unique and a card is never reassigned to another driver, so the UID tells you the card and its owner. No card is issued before its driver registered.

Sessions are the fact table: which charge point, which card, which vehicle, which tariff plan, start and end, energy delivered, peak power, duration in minutes and what we billed. Tariff plans belong to an operator and carry a name, a per-kWh price, a session fee and an idle fee per minute; a plan name means the same per-kWh price wherever you find it, and within an operator the name identifies the plan. Energy delivered is log-normal, log-mean 2.8 and log-variance 0.6, and durations are exponential with a mean near 45 minutes. On the rapid units -- 50 kW and above -- a session essentially always lands between 5 and 100 kWh. A session ends after it starts, never begins before the unit was commissioned or before the card was issued, cannot draw more than the unit is rated for, cannot deliver more energy than the car's battery holds, and we never draw more than the car will take: if the vehicle's DC limit is under 50 kW then peak power on that session stays at or below 50, and in general peak power never exceeds the vehicle's DC limit. What we bill is at least the energy times the plan's per-kWh price, because the session fee goes on top of that.

The chargers stream meter values through the session -- a timestamp, the instantaneous power, the energy delivered so far and the car's state of charge as a percentage. This is the volume: it dwarfs the session table. A meter value sits inside its session's window, its power reading never exceeds the peak power we recorded for the session, the running energy never exceeds the session total, and state of charge is a percentage so it lives between 0 and 100.

Drivers can also reserve a unit ahead of arriving. A reservation is against a charge point and a card, with the time it was made, the window it holds (from and until, and the until is after the from), and a status. Nothing is reserved for a window starting before the reservation was made.

Faults are raised against a charge point with a category, a raise and a resolve time and the hours it was down. Nothing is raised before the unit was commissioned and nothing resolves before it was raised.

Drivers get a monthly invoice covering a period, with the issue date, the total and the number of sessions on it -- and if they charged nothing that month they still get a zero invoice. The period ends after it starts and we issue on or after the period end. Which sessions landed on which invoice is a thing we have to be able to show the regulator, so that pairing is held explicitly with the amount that went on the line; a line never carries more than the session was billed, because roaming commission comes off it.

Scale: about 1.4 million sessions a month across roughly 38,000 connectors, and the session table is already past 40 million rows.

std.basis: coefficient of variation in [0.006, 0.682], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=117), applied to the stated mean

ground_truth_moments.evidence: durations are exponential with a mean near 45 minutes

nl_description:
We're a small housing association and we've inherited a heat network that we don't really have any systems for.

There are four blocks on the scheme, just under 900 flats in total, all fed from the one energy centre behind the shops. That's a couple of gas boilers and a CHP engine, but for our purposes it's just a name and the year the thing was commissioned. The scheme has a name and it sits in one town. Scheme names are unique -- ours is the only one called what it's called -- so the name is enough to tell you the town and which energy centre we mean. I gather other associations run several schemes each, so whatever you build shouldn't assume there is only ever the one.

For each flat we need to know which scheme it's on, its flat number, which block it's in, the floor area and the tenure. The flat number has the block letter on the front of it -- B14 is block B -- so you can always work the block out from the number, and no two flats on a scheme share a number. About 62 per cent are social rent, 29 per cent leasehold, and the rest are privately rented out by leaseholders who moved away. The flats average around 58 square metres and most are within fifteen either way -- the smallest is a 22 square metre studio and the biggest is a 140 metre maisonette.

In every flat there's a heat interface unit, one each, no more. The contractors call it a HIU, the residents call it the box in the cupboard, and the old paperwork calls it a substation, which confuses everybody. We need the model, when it was fitted and when it was last serviced, and that service date is obviously never earlier than the day the thing went in. The metering firm reads them for us -- I don't think we need to hold anything about them, they just send us a file every month.

The servicing itself I do want logged properly, because we got caught out at the last audit with nothing to show. Every visit against a unit: the date, the engineer who came, what they found, and when the next one falls due, which is always later than the visit. Nobody visits a unit before it was fitted, and the last-serviced date we carry on the unit is just the most recent visit, so no visit is ever dated after it.

Charging is monthly and per flat: how much heat they used, the standing charge, the usage charge and the total. The total is the standing charge and the usage charge added together and nothing else -- there are no other lines on it. Usage can't be negative, and if it comes through as zero -- empty flats between lets, mostly -- then the usage charge has to be zero too, though the standing charge still applies. The usage charge works out at fifteen pence a unit at the absolute worst, so if it's ever come in above that against the heat used, something's gone wrong in the calculation. We also sanity check the heat against the size of the place: nothing has ever come in above about twelve units per square metre in a month, and when it does we go and look for a leak. A typical month is somewhere near 270 units of heat but the winter ones are far bigger than that, it's very skewed. And the council tenants' standing charge is capped by the management agreement: it cannot go above twelve pounds in a month, whatever we end up doing with the leaseholders.

variance.basis: variance = ln(1 + CV^2) for CV in [0.324, 3.166], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=70)

ground_truth_moments.evidence: The flats average around 58 square metres

domain: Wholesale Energy Trading and Grid Balancing
nl_description:
Handover for the balancing and wholesale book. Read this as the whole estate, not one extract: it swallows three Access databases, the credit spreadsheet risk have been running off a laptop, and the settlement reconciliation pack, and it has to carry the audit trail the last REMIT review said we did not have. Eight loosely-joined parts of the business end up in here -- reference data, credit and collateral, the physical asset register, market data, the balancing mechanism, the trading book, settlement and invoicing, and the compliance trail -- and they touch each other in a handful of places rather than everywhere. Volumes for sizing: 17,520 settlement periods a year per market, a few hundred thousand bid-offer rows a month, around 2 million acceptances on the book, about 90,000 bilateral trades a year, and the weather feed at roughly 4 million observations a month, which on its own is larger than everything except the acceptances.

REFERENCE DATA. Currencies are a short list -- the code, the currency name and the number of minor units, since the settlement engine rounds on it. FX rates are held per from-currency, to-currency and rate date, one row per combination and the rate is never negative. Markets are the outer dimension: a code, a name, the settlement granularity in minutes, the currency the market clears in and the timezone name we localise against. The market code is unique and pins down the granularity and the currency, which is why nobody should be copying either onto anything else. A market is divided into grid zones, each with a zone code, a zone name and a transmission loss factor that lives between 0.90 and 1.10; the zone code is unique across all markets and determines both the market it belongs to and its loss factor. Fuel types are a list too, keyed on the fuel code, carrying the fuel name, the carbon intensity in kg per MWh and a renewable flag; fuel names are unique in their own right, so a name gets you back to the code and the intensity. Fuel mix across the register is wind 31 per cent, CCGT 24, solar 15, battery 14, hydro and biomass 6 each, nuclear 4.

COUNTERPARTIES AND CREDIT. Credit ratings are a reference list: a surrogate key, the rating code, the agency the rating comes from, a rank order from 1 to 22 with 1 the strongest, and the maximum unsecured exposure we will carry against that rating. The rating code determines all three of those. Counterparties carry a legal name, an LEI, a credit limit, an onboarding date and their current rating; the LEI is unique and identifies both the counterparty and its legal name. No counterparty's credit limit exceeds the maximum unsecured exposure its rating allows -- that is a hard control and it is the one the spreadsheet kept breaking. Admission to a market is held per counterparty per market with the admission date and the collateral posted against it, exactly one row per pairing, and nobody is admitted before they were onboarded. Collateral postings are separate and individually tracked: the counterparty, the market, the date posted, the amount, the instrument type (cash, letter of credit, parent guarantee) and the date it was released if it has been. Nothing is posted before the counterparty was onboarded and nothing is released before it was posted. Margin calls are their own event -- the counterparty, when we called, the exposure at the time, the amount we asked for, when it was met and a status. A call only goes out once exposure has passed the counterparty's credit limit, we never ask for more than the exposure itself, and the met timestamp is never earlier than the call. Where the status says met there is always a met timestamp. Exposures at call time are log-normal, log-mean 13.4 with log-variance 1.2. Every change to a credit limit is journalled with the effective-from, the effective-to after it, the previous and the new limit -- which are never the same value, or it would not be a change -- and who approved it. Nothing takes effect before the counterparty was onboarded.

PHYSICAL ASSETS. A site has a name, the grid zone it connects into, a latitude and longitude, the connection capacity in MW that the connection agreement gives it, and a commissioning date; site names are unique and a site does not move zone, so the name gives you the zone. Balancing units -- BMUs, or just units in most of the desk's vocabulary -- belong to a counterparty and sit at a site, with a reference, a fuel type, a maximum export in MW, a minimum stable level which is never negative and never above the maximum export, and the date they were registered. The BMU reference is unique and tells you which counterparty owns the unit. A unit's maximum export never exceeds the connection capacity of the site it sits on, and a unit is never registered before its site was commissioned or before its counterparty was onboarded. Dynamic parameters are versioned against the unit: an effective-from, the run-up and run-down rates in MW per minute, the minimum zero time in minutes and the notice to deviate in minutes. No parameter set takes effect before the unit was registered. Planned outages are held with an outage reference (unique), the unit, a start and an end after it, the capacity still available during the outage -- which cannot exceed the unit's maximum export -- and an outage type, split roughly 62 per cent planned maintenance, 26 per cent forced and 12 per cent restricted.

MARKET DATA AND FORECASTS. Settlement periods belong to a market, are numbered 1 to 48 within the day, and hold a start timestamp, the cash-out system price, the day-ahead price for the same period and the net imbalance volume. The market and the period start together identify the period. System price averages about 78 with a standard deviation near 41, day-ahead sits a little lower at 71 with a standard deviation of 33, and net imbalance is centred on zero with a standard deviation around 240 MW. When the system is long -- net imbalance above zero -- cash-out has always come in at or below the day-ahead price for that period; that is an observed invariant of the cash-out formulation and the analysts rely on it. Note that people will say half-hour when they mean settlement period. Demand forecasts are issued against a settlement period, several times over, with an issue timestamp, the forecast MW and whichever model version produced it; nothing is issued after the period it forecasts has started, and forecasts run around 32,000 MW with a standard deviation of 6,000. The versioning is currently a free-text mess and I would leave it that way for now. Weather comes in per zone: an observation timestamp, wind speed in m/s (mean 8.2, standard deviation 3.6), temperature in Celsius (mean 10.5, standard deviation 6.4) and irradiance in W/m2, which sits between 0 and 1200 like everyone else's.

BALANCING MECHANISM. Bid-offers are submitted per unit per period with a direction, a pair number, a volume in MWh, a price per MWh and a submission time; the unit, the period and the pair number together are the natural key. Direction splits about 55 per cent offer to 45 per cent bid. On the OFFER direction the price is allowed to run from minus 100 up to a cap of 4,000 per MWh; bids are not bounded that way. Nothing is submitted after its period has started -- that is gate closure. A half hour is half an hour, so the volume offered can never exceed half the unit's maximum export in MWh. An acceptance references a bid-offer and records an acceptance reference (unique), when it was accepted, the accepted volume and the resulting cashflow. The accepted volume never exceeds the volume that was offered, nothing is accepted before it was submitted, and since a bid is a request to turn down, the cashflow on an accepted BID is never positive to us. Physical notifications are per unit per period with the notified MW, a submission time and a final flag; the notified level never exceeds the unit's maximum export, is never submitted after the period starts, and where it is above zero it is never below the unit's minimum stable level. Availability declarations are the same shape -- unit, period, the MW declared available and when it was declared, one row per unit and period -- with the declared figure capped by the unit's maximum export and declared before the period starts. Metered volumes come back after the fact, one row per unit and period with the metered MWh and a source, and again a half hour cannot hold more than half the unit's rating.

WHOLESALE TRADING. Traders have a staff reference (unique and the only handle HR give us), a name, a desk, a per-trade limit in MWh and a joining date. The limit is set by the desk, not by the individual, so everyone on a desk carries the same number. Books have a code, a name, the desk that owns them and a base currency, and the book code determines the desk and the base currency. Brokers are just a name and their commission in basis points. A trade sits against a market, a counterparty, a book, a trader and (where it went through one) a broker, with a trade timestamp, a delivery start, a delivery end after it, a volume, a price per MWh, the notional, the broker commission, a side, the currency and a status. Sides run about 51 per cent buy to 49 per cent sell. The notional is the volume times the price, exactly -- if it is not, someone has keyed a leg wrong. Broker commission never exceeds ten basis points of the notional. Trade volumes are log-normal, log-mean 3.0 and log-variance 1.1, no trade exceeds the trader's own per-trade limit, nothing is traded before the counterparty was onboarded or after delivery has started, and counterparties on a credit line below a million are hard-limited to 500 MWh per trade. Confirmations are tracked per trade: when we sent it, when they confirmed it, the method and whether it matched -- sent no earlier than the trade, confirmed no earlier than sent. Amendments are journalled too: the trade, when it was amended, the field changed, the old and new values -- which differ, or there was no amendment -- and who did it, never before the trade itself.

SETTLEMENT AND INVOICING. Charge codes are a reference list with a surrogate key, the code, a description and a credit flag, and the code determines both. A settlement run is per market with a run type (initial, interim, final), the period range it covers with the end after the start, when it ran and a status; a run never executes before the end of the range it settles. Settlement lines are the output: the run, the counterparty, the settlement period, the charge code, a volume and an amount. A line's settlement period never falls before the start of the range its run covers. On a charge code flagged as a credit the amount is never negative. Invoices are raised off a run per counterparty with an issue date, a due date after it, the total, the currency and a status, and nothing is issued before its run executed. Which settlement lines went onto which invoice is held explicitly, because the disputes team live in that join, and the amount on the pairing is the line's own amount unchanged. Payments come in against an invoice with the date, the amount, a method and a reference; part payment is normal so there can be several, none dated before the invoice was issued and none for more than the invoice total. Disputes sit against an invoice with a raise timestamp, who raised it, the amount disputed, a reason code, a resolution timestamp and an outcome. Nothing is disputed before the invoice was issued, nothing resolves before it was raised, and you cannot dispute more than the invoice is for.

COMPLIANCE AND AUDIT. Every bilateral trade has to be reported to the regulator, so a submission row per trade with the submission timestamp, the regulator's reference and a status; nothing is submitted before the trade was struck. Users have a username (unique), a name, a role code, a created date and a disabled date once they have gone, which is always after they were created. Finally the audit log: the user, the table name, the record key, the action and the timestamp, and no log row predates the user that wrote it. That last table is the one the review actually asked for.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: System price averages about 78 with a standard deviation near 41
day-ahead sits a little lower at 71 with a standard deviation of 33
net imbalance is centred on zero with a standard deviation around 240 MW.
forecasts run around 32,000 MW with a standard deviation of 6,000.
wind speed in m/s (mean 8.2, standard deviation 3.6)

nl_description:
Scoping note for the outage reporting rebuild. Written by me, an analyst, so treat the modelling as indicative and shout if I've got a cardinality wrong.

The network side we only need shallowly. Substations get a name, an operating voltage, a count of how many feeders come off them, a region and the control room that runs them; voltages on our patch run from 6.6 kV up to 132. Substation names are unique and a substation belongs to one region, and the region is what decides the control room -- there is exactly one room per region, so if you know the region you know the room and there is no point holding the pairing anywhere else. Feeders -- half the control room says circuits, it's the same object -- belong to a substation and have a reference, a count of customers connected and a flag for whether they are overhead or underground. The reference has the substation code as its first four characters, so a feeder reference identifies both the feeder and the substation it comes off. Customers per feeder averages about 420.

An outage is raised against a feeder: start, restoration time, a cause, whether it was planned, how many customers it hit, the duration in minutes and a flag for whether we lost the whole circuit. Restoration never precedes the start, and an outage cannot hit more customers than its feeder has connected to it -- we had 1,200 rows failing that in the old system, which is half the reason we are doing this. Anything taking out 80 per cent or more of the feeder's connected customers counts as a whole-circuit loss and gets flagged as one; that threshold is in the reporting guidance. Causes break down roughly as weather 31 per cent, equipment failure 27, third-party damage 18, vegetation 12, animals 7 and unknown 5. Restoration averages around 80 minutes -- most are quick but there's a fat tail of multi-day ones after storms. We don't log anything shorter than three minutes, and the customers-affected count is never negative.

Calls come in against an outage: when it came, the number they rang from, the channel (phone is still 58 per cent, web 27, app 13 and the rest social) and the postcode they gave us. Nobody rings about an outage before it starts, whatever the control room say. About 600,000 calls a year against roughly 190,000 outages.

Dispatches are per outage -- a crew reference, when they were sent, when they arrived and the travel time. Nothing is sent before the outage started and nobody arrives before they were sent. Travel averages 34 minutes with a standard deviation of about 15. We don't hold a crew register in this system; the reference is just whatever resource management gave us.

The other thing we badly need is the estimated restoration time and its history, because at the moment we overwrite it and then cannot answer what we told people at eight in the morning. So: an update row per revision against the outage, with the timestamp, the estimate we published and who published it. One update per outage per timestamp, no duplicates. An update is never stamped before the outage started, and the estimate it carries is always later than the moment we published it.

Planned shutdowns we notify in advance, and that needs recording per household: the outage, the account reference, the date we sent the notice and how we sent it. Advance means advance -- the notice date is on or before the outage start, and if it isn't, we are in breach.

Compensation is the bit the regulator cares about. A payment sits against an outage with the account reference, the amount, when it was paid and a reason code. One payment per household per outage, so the outage and the account reference together are as good as the payment's own key. Nothing is paid before the supply came back on. Anything over twelve hours triggers at least 75 pounds a household under the guaranteed standards. Planned shutdowns we notify in advance and no compensation is due on those, so where a payment does get raised against a planned job the amount comes through as zero.

I run the retrofit scheme for the borough and at the moment it lives in two spreadsheets and my head, which is why I'm here.

The way it works is somebody gets referred to us -- usually by the advice centre, sometimes they just ring up. We take their name, the address and postcode, whether they own the place or rent it and off whom, what they earn in a year, and the EPC band off the register. One record per address, we're strict about that, because we had the same bungalow in three times last year. Eligibility is income-based: we can only take referrals from households under 31 thousand a year, that's the funder's line not ours. Most of the people we see are somewhere around twenty-two thousand, with a tail running up towards the ceiling. We note the date they first came to us too, because the funding is annual and we have to report against it.

The referrals themselves need holding one by one rather than just the first one, because people come back -- once for the loft, then again two winters later when the boiler goes. So per referral: who sent them to us, the date it came in, whoever took the call, and whether we accepted it or turned it away and why. Nothing is dated before the household first came to us, by definition.

Once a referral is accepted a surveyor goes out and writes the place up. That's the assessment: the date, who did it, the EPC score they measured, how many measures they're recommending and what they reckon the whole lot will cost. The visit can't be before the household came to us. An assessment gets its own reference but in practice the household and the date of the visit pin it down -- nobody surveys the same house twice in a day.

The money comes out of annual pots. A pot has a name, the funder behind it, the year it runs for, how much is in it and how much we've committed so far, and the committed figure never goes over the pot -- when we get close, we stop taking referrals. A pot name always belongs to the same funder. The name and the year together identify the pot, since the big ones come round again every year with the same name. There's also a rule I've been told is non-negotiable: no single job may draw more than a tenth of the pot it's charged to.

Then we fit things. People here say measure, upgrade or just job depending who's talking -- it's all the same thing. Every job comes off an assessment -- we don't fit anything the surveyor hasn't written up -- and it's charged to one of the pots. Roughly a third of what we do is loft insulation, a quarter or so cavity wall, then heat pumps at about 17 per cent, solar panels 13, and the expensive external wall stuff makes up the rest. For each one we record what it was, when it went in, what it cost us, how much of that was grant, who fitted it, and the guarantee in years. The grant never comes to more than the job cost -- we can't hand back more than we spent. The guarantee is a property of what you fit rather than who fitted it: loft and cavity always come with twenty-five years, heat pumps seven, solar ten -- though I wouldn't swear the field is always filled in on the older rows. Nothing is fitted before the survey that recommended it, or before the household came to us. Costs are all over the place: the typical job is around three thousand but a heat pump with a new cylinder is ten times that, and we've agreed with the funder that we don't go more than 30 per cent over the surveyor's estimate for the property without going back for re-approval. Heat pump grants top out at seven and a half thousand and can't be negative -- that's a hard funder rule. And the very worst homes, the band G ones, get a minimum of five thousand towards the work whatever we end up fitting.

Every job gets inspected afterwards -- that came out of the audit. The inspection is against the job: the date, the inspector, whether it passed, a note of what needs putting right and the date it has to be put right by. Nobody inspects before the work went in, the put-right-by date is after the visit, and if it failed there has to be a note saying why -- a blank note on a failed inspection is exactly what got us in trouble.

We ring people six months afterwards. That gives us a date, a satisfaction score out of five, what they reckon they've saved as a percentage, and whatever else they said. Nobody is rung before they were referred. Scores are good -- about 42 per cent give us a five, 36 a four, 14 a three, and only a handful come in at one or two. The saving figure is self-reported so it's anywhere between nothing and, well, it can't sensibly be more than a hundred per cent.

Numbers are small: about 380 homes in three years, so a few hundred measures and a similar number of follow-up calls. Nothing that needs a big machine.

We don't hold anything about the installers as such beyond the name -- they're all on the framework and procurement manages that list, not us.

nl_description:
Right, I'll try and explain it the way it works rather than the way you'd want it written down.

We're 360 hectares up on the wolds, sixty-two fields, and every field has a name because that's how everyone talks about them -- Long Meadow, Chapel Piece, Stone Close. No two of them share a name, never have, you'd have chaos otherwise: tell me a name and I'll tell you which field it is, how big it is and what it's sat on. Average field is a shade under six hectares, the smallest is barely one and the biggest is twenty-two. Soil matters more than anything else: about half of it is heavy clay and the rest is sand over chalk, and they behave like two different farms.

Each year a field gets one crop drilled into it, one and one only, so the field and the year between them pin down exactly which crop we're talking about -- and I want the drilling date and the harvest date sat against that. Harvest comes after the drilling, which isn't a rule so much as how the world works, but your computer won't know that. Out of every ten fields in a year, five would be wheat, two oilseed rape, two barley and one beans, and now and again one sits fallow. Everything comes over the weighbridge so I know the tonnes off each field to a decimal place, and I work in tonnes a hectare when I'm comparing years -- wheat here averages about eight point six, we've had six in a bad year and just under eleven in a cracking one. Eleven to the hectare is the ceiling on this farm whatever's in the ground, so if the tonnes off a field ever work out at more than eleven times that field's hectares, somebody's fat-fingered the weighbridge and I want telling.

Then there's what we put on. Fertiliser, sprays, seed -- each application goes onto one field for that year's crop, on a date, at a rate per hectare, and it costs what it costs. Mind, the product name tells you which of the three it is -- I don't have to stop and think whether Liberator is a spray, the name says spray, and it always will. I buy off two or three merchants, each with their own name and no two called the same, and I want to see who sold me what, what they quoted and what I actually paid, because the invoice and the quote are never the same number and it's never the invoice that's the smaller one. Sprays are the fussy ones: a spray only ever goes on after the crop's drilled and before it's cut, so those dates want checking back against the drilling and the harvest.

Grain doesn't go straight off the farm. There are four sheds, each one with a name and each one holds so many tonnes -- the name's enough, tell me it's the Dutch barn and I know that's four hundred and eighty tonnes -- and I need to know what's sitting in which shed at any given time, which obviously can't be more than that shed holds. Then it goes out on lorries -- twenty-nine tonne loads, near enough, three hundred loads a year -- out of one of the sheds, off one field's crop, and every load has a ticket with the moisture on it. Nothing leaves before it's been cut, and no lorry goes out with more on it than the shed it came from would hold in the first place. The mill knocks money off over fifteen percent so nothing should be leaving here above that, and they pay us a bit extra when a wheat load comes in under fourteen, so those tickets want flagging as premium. It's not a big pile of data, a few thousand rows a year at the very most.

Last thing. The agronomist walks the fields every fortnight through the spring and writes half a page of notes each time, and those notes need to hang off the visit so I can find them again.

nl_description:
Spec for the herd system that replaces the Access database that finally gave up. 620-cow Holstein-Friesian block-calving unit. Every reference list in here follows the same pattern -- surrogate integer PK, plus whatever short code or name the stockmen already use as a unique natural key -- because the old database keyed on the codes and we spent two years chasing renames.

The cow is the anchor entity: surrogate integer PK plus her official ear tag as a unique 14-character natural key, with breed, birth date and a herd status flag. Her dam is usually in the herd as well, so that is a nullable self-referencing FK, and a dam is by definition born before her daughter. One cow has many lactations, and a lactation carries its sequence number, the calving date and the dry-off date; the sequence number is unique within the cow, so cow plus sequence number identifies a lactation just as surely as the surrogate does, and the calving date follows from that pair. Dry-off is after the calving. Every calving that produces a live calf gets a calf row against the lactation: its own ear tag, sex, birth weight in kilos, birth date, and the service it came from. Birth weights run 25 to 60 kilos, mean around 42 with an sd of 5, and heifer calves are about 49 percent of them. The registered sire on the calf is strictly the sire of that service -- it is derived, we keep it because the breed society export wants everything on one row -- and the calf is obviously born after the service date.

Services -- inseminations, if you want the word that goes on the breed society form -- hang off the cow and point at a sire from the bought-in bull catalogue, which we hold with a unique sire code and its predicted transmitting ability for milk. Service outcome is held, returned or aborted -- about 55 percent hold to first service, 35 percent return and the rest abort.

The volume driver is the parlour. Two rotaries, named, with 60 and 50 stalls respectively -- the name gives you the stall count -- three milkings a day, so roughly 680,000 cow-milking rows a year and we retain seven years. Each of those rows is a timestamped yield in litres plus the conductivity reading off the meter, with FKs to both the cow and the parlour. Per-cow daily yield averages 31.5 litres across the three milkings with a standard deviation near 7, which per session is a mean of 10.5 and an sd of 2.6. Anything the meter reports below zero or above 30 litres for one session is a sensor fault, so 0 to 30 is the hard domain on that column.

Tanker collections are a separate daily row: volume, butterfat, protein, bactoscan and the price per litre we were paid. Butterfat runs a 4.05 percent mean with sd 0.22, and on this breed protein always comes back under the butterfat figure -- if a collection ever reports otherwise the lab has transposed the two, which happened twice last year. The contract floors milk price at 0.28 a litre and it has never been above 0.52.

Somatic cell counts come back monthly per cow in thousands per ml and are heavily right skewed -- lognormal, log-mean about 4.4, log-variance 0.55. Any cow with an SCC reading over 400 has her mastitis follow-up flag set.

Health events point at an event type from a short list which carries a description, a treatment flag, and the statutory milk withdrawal in days for that treatment. The withdrawal recorded on an event is at the vet's discretion, but for anything flagged as a treatment it is never shorter than the statutory figure held on its type -- that is the residue rule and it is the one the milk buyer audits. While a cow has a withdrawal against her the milking rows are not saleable, which is a flag on the session row.

Feeding is five diets, each with a unique ration name that tells you its dry matter kilos and its cost per head per day, and a cow is on exactly one at a time, so a dated cow-to-ration assignment with start and end dates, end never before start.

One migration rule that applies across the whole thing: every dated row hanging off a cow -- calving, service, cell count, treatment, ration assignment -- is on or after that cow's own birth date. The Access database was full of ones that were not.
