nl_description:
I do the reporting for a broiler business and I'm rebuilding the whole thing off spreadsheets, so bear with me on the details.

There are 14 grow-out farms with 96 houses between them. The farms belong to growers who are contracted to us -- some growers have more than one farm, but a farm never moves between growers, and farm names are unique across the business, so the farm name on its own tells me whose it is. Grower names are unique too, and against each grower sits the base rate per bird per week we agreed with them.

Now, the rate that actually gets paid is a bit more awkward than that. It is negotiated with the grower but it lands on the house, because the newer tunnel-ventilated houses are on a higher rate than the old naturally-ventilated sheds. So I hold the ventilation type and the pence per bird per week on the house itself, along with the house number on the farm -- house numbers only run 1 upwards within each farm, so it takes the farm and the number together to say which house you mean. When we place a batch we copy the house's rate onto it so the payment run has one row to read, and that copy is always the same number the house is on. If it ever is not, somebody has edited it by hand.

The thing everyone actually cares about is the batch. I call it a flock, the field guys call it a crop, the old reports say batch -- it is one and the same. A flock lives in one house, starts on a placement date with a head count of day-old chicks, and finishes when the last bird is caught, so the catch date is never before the placement date. Typical placement is 28,000 birds, give or take a thousand. Chicks come from one of four hatcheries and we want to know which. Breed is nearly all Ross 308 with about a tenth Cobb.

Somebody walks each house every day and writes down the day number (day 1 through to about day 42), how many birds died that day, the average bird weight off the sample scales, the house temperature and how much water went through the meter. One sheet per flock per day, so the flock and the day number between them identify the sheet and give me its calendar date. No sheet is dated before the placement. Daily mortality on a healthy flock is low, about 22 birds out of the 28,000, and since it is a straight count a Poisson at lambda 22 is what I have been using and it fits; anything over five percent of the placement in a single day is not mortality, it is a disaster or a typo, and either way I want it flagged. Temperature is meant to sit between 30 and 34 in the first week and be down between 19 and 23 from day 35 onwards. That daily sheet is the big table -- 96 houses, 42 days, eight or nine crops a year, five years of history, so a couple of million rows.

Feed arrives by lorry into the bins outside the house. Each delivery is a tonnage of one feed type -- starter, grower or finisher -- at a price per tonne, and it lands somewhere between the placement and the catch, because there is nothing to feed outside that window.

At the end the birds go to one of two processing plants and one kill sheet comes back per flock: the date, how many birds were delivered, the total dead weight, how many were rejected and the reject percentage that gets worked out from it. Since there is only ever one, the flock tells me the sheet, the plant and the kill date. The kill is on or after the placement, obviously. You cannot deliver more birds than you placed, and you cannot reject more than you delivered -- both of those got through the spreadsheets more than once. Total dead weight has a physical ceiling as well: this bird does not dress out over 2.6 kilos, so the weight on a sheet is never more than 2.6 times the birds delivered. Reject percentage is meant to stay under one percent. Average finished bird is 2.45 kilos live with a standard deviation of about 0.2.

Vet visits produce a medication record against the flock with the product and its withdrawal period, and the treatment date is inside the crop window like everything else. The withdrawal period is a property of the product rather than the visit -- the same product always carries the same number of days, and I would rather it was not typed in fresh each time. Any medicine with a withdrawal period of seven days or more means the kill sheet is held for review before we invoice.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: Daily mortality on a healthy flock is low, about 22 birds out of the 28,000
Average finished bird is 2.45 kilos live

nl_description:
Right, so. Eighteen hectares under vine on the south slope and a winery in the old barn, and the whole lot lives in my notebook plus a spreadsheet my daughter set up that nobody else understands.

The vineyard is in blocks. Parcels, plots, whatever you want to call them -- I say block, my father said parcel, it's the same thing. Every block has its own name and no two are the same, so the name is enough: say Chapel Bank to me and I'll tell you it's Pinot Noir on SO4, two and a bit hectares. Each one is planted to a single variety on a single rootstock in a particular year, and I know its size, its row spacing and how many vines are in it. We plant about four thousand vines to the hectare and it has never once been over five thousand, so if the vine count comes out at more than five thousand times the hectares somebody has counted rows instead of vines. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are most of it, roughly a third each, then Bacchus about a fifth and a bit of Pinot Meunier we're still not sure about.

Picking runs over about three weeks in October. A picking is one block on one day -- tell me the block and the day and I know exactly which picking you mean, we've never gone at the same block twice in a day. We weigh the bins as they come in, so a picking's weight is in kilos, a bin holds about four hundred kilos and a picking is anywhere between five and thirty bins. Fifteen tonnes to the hectare is the outer limit of what this slope can physically give, so a picking weighing more than fifteen thousand kilos for every hectare in that block is a weighbridge error, not a miracle. Someone takes a sugar reading and the acid at the same time, and I write down whether the fruit looked clean or whether there was rot in it. Sugar comes in anywhere from fifteen to twenty-four brix, and anything over twenty is too ripe for the sparkling so I mark that fruit for still wine there and then. The pickers are a gang from an agency and I do need to know which worker was on which picking and for how many hours, because they're paid by the hour and there are always arguments about it.

Then the fruit goes into a tank or a barrel and becomes a lot. This is the bit that's hardest to explain. A lot might be one block's fruit, or it might be three or four pickings blended together, and one picking can end up split across two lots -- so it isn't one to one in either direction, and I write down what share of the blend each picking was. Every lot gets a code of its own -- no two lots have ever shared one -- and the date I started it, and nothing that happens to that lot afterwards can be dated before I started it: no reading, no sulphur, no racking, no sample off it, no bottling. Every lot sits in a vessel and I know what each vessel is and what it holds -- they're all named, and the name tells you whether it's a tank or a barrel and how many litres, they run from a thousand litres up to eight thousand. You obviously cannot have more wine in a vessel than the vessel holds, which the spreadsheet lets me do and shouldn't. Lots move about -- racked off, blended, bottled -- and I write the movements down with the volume each time, and you can't move more out than there was in the lot to start with. Each lot is red or white, which matters below.

Ferments get logged twice a day, temperature and density, one reading per lot per time so there's never two of them fighting each other. They sit in the low twenties mostly, twenty-two ish, swinging a few degrees either side, and if a red goes over thirty I have to do something about it quickly. Sulphur additions get written down too with the milligrams a litre, because the legal ceiling on total sulphur is two hundred.

Bottling happens in runs. A run is one lot going into one product, the product being the label and the vintage -- the 2024 Classic Cuvee, that sort of thing, and there's only ever one of each label-and-year pair. A lot only ever goes into the one label as well; we don't split a lot across two wines, it makes the paperwork impossible. We get so many bottles out of a run and a few get broken. A thousand litres is about thirteen hundred bottles, so the bottles filled off a run never come to more than one and a half times the litres that were in that lot, and breakages have never got above two percent of the run. Then it sells: which wine, how many bottles, which channel it went out through and what it came to. Nothing leaves here under eight pounds a bottle, not even to the merchants, so the money on an order is always at least eight times the bottles on it. More than half the orders are people at the cellar door taking a case or two, restaurants are maybe a quarter and the rest is the two merchants. Most orders are tiny and a merchant order can be several hundred bottles, so the sizes are very lopsided. We're small -- forty thousand bottles a year, a few thousand orders -- so it isn't a big database, but the traceability has to be right, because if there's a problem I have to get from a bottle back to the block.

There's also a bloke who comes and takes samples off the lots for the lab over in Kent. I suppose his results have to sit somewhere but I don't know what we'd keep besides the date and the number.

nl_description:
Data platform for a 12-hectare glasshouse tomato nursery. Small schema, very large data, and the whole design question is the telemetry.

The site is divided into 48 compartments, each with its own floor area in square metres, a glass type (single, diffuse or hortiglass) and the identifier of the climate computer that controls it. One computer drives several compartments, but only ever compartments of the same glass type, because the control strategy is written per glass -- so the computer identifier settles the glass type on its own. Everything else keys off the compartment on a surrogate integer.

A compartment carries one crop at a time, so the compartment and the planting date together identify a cycle. We open a fresh cycle at each planting, holding the cultivar as a short code, the planting date, the date the crop is finally cleared -- never before the planting -- the plant density we went in at, the head count that gave us, and the cumulative marketable yield when it comes out. Density is set anywhere between 2.4 and 3.1 plants per square metre and in practice it is spread flat across that band; since 3.1 is the hard ceiling, the head count on a cycle never exceeds 3.1 times its compartment's floor area, and that is the check that catches a density typed into the count field.  A full eleven-month cycle lands around 68 kilos per square metre with a standard deviation of about 5.

Telemetry is the problem child. Nine sensors per compartment logging every minute is roughly 227 million rows a year and we hold three years, so it wants monthly partitioning on the timestamp. A row is the compartment, the timestamp, which sensor type produced it, the float value, and a daylight boolean the climate computer hands us for free. One row per compartment, per sensor type, per minute -- that triple is the natural key and the surrogate exists only for the partitioned index. Note the daylight flag is a property of the compartment and the minute, not of the sensor: all nine rows for a given compartment and timestamp carry the same value, and it is duplicated nine times over as things stand.

The sensor type list is keyed on its short code and carries a description, the unit of measure, and the credible instrument band as a low and a high value -- a reading outside its own type's band is an instrument fault rather than data, and that check has to read the band off the type row rather than have thresholds compiled into a view, which is how CO2 ended up clamped at the old 1000 ppm ceiling for a year. CO2 is credible between 420 and 1100 ppm, relative humidity between 30 and 95 percent, and so on down the list; they all live on the type row.

The mix of rows is nowhere near even: air temperature is 30 percent of rows, relative humidity 22, CO2 18, PAR 12, slab moisture 10, and the remaining 8 percent is everything else. Air temperature carries an agronomic setpoint band on top of the instrument band, and that one does depend on the daylight flag: 18 to 26 degrees during daylight, 16 to 19 at night.

Picking is recorded against the crop cycle: the date, the graded class, the weight in kilos and a truss count -- one line per cycle per day per class, so those three identify the pick. Picks fall inside the cycle window, on or after the planting and on or before the clearance. A truss does not weigh more than 600 grams even on the best week, so the weight on a line never exceeds 0.6 times its truss count. By weight it comes out around 62 percent class 1, 30 percent class 2 and 8 percent waste.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: Nine sensors per compartment logging every minute is roughly 227 million rows a year
A full eleven-month cycle lands around 68 kilos per square metre with a standard deviation of about 5

nl_description:
It's a trout farm, spring-fed. Twelve ponds and four raceways -- I call the whole lot ponds when I'm talking, but the raceways are concrete and the ponds are earth and that difference matters for the paperwork, so whatever you build wants to know which is which and what each one is called. They've all got their own name and no two are the same, so the name is all you need: say Top Raceway to me and I know it's concrete without thinking about it.

What I actually need is to stop losing track of the fish. Stock arrives as fry, mostly from the hatchery down the road but not always, goes into one pond as a batch with a count and a date -- one lot into one pond on one day, we've never split a delivery -- and comes out fifteen or sixteen months later at a pound and a half or so. The date they come out is obviously after the date they went in, which the spreadsheet does not stop me getting wrong.

While they're in there, three things get written on the board by the pond and they may as well all go on the same daily line -- one line per pond per day, and if there are two for the same pond and day then somebody's written it up twice. First, what's died -- mostly it's a handful a day, it climbs when the water's warm and drops right off in winter, and if a heron finds us it's a bad week. Second, feed: I count in sacks, a sack is twenty-five kilos, and a big pond gets through a couple of sacks a day in summer and hardly anything in the cold, so anywhere between nothing and two. Third, the water -- temperature and oxygen, taken at the same time. The spring comes up around twelve and the top ponds can touch eighteen in a heatwave; I've seen twenty once in ten years and never below about four. Above eighteen they stop eating so I have to cut them right back to half a sack. Oxygen mustn't go below six or you're in real trouble.

Once a month I net out thirty fish off a pond, weigh them, put them back, and the average goes on that same day's line.

Sales are to two smokehouses and to people at the gate, and there's a chap who takes the small ones for restocking fishing lakes. It's not a lot -- maybe two hundred sales a year, and a few thousand records in the whole thing once you count the daily lines. I just want a list of what went out of which batch, how many kilos, who had it and what they paid. Nothing sells out of a batch before the fry went in, and nothing after the pond's been emptied either. And there's a limit to what you can get out of a batch: a fish is seven hundred grams at the absolute outside, so if a sale claims more kilos than seven-tenths of the fish that went into that batch, it's wrong. On price, nothing has ever left this farm under four pound a kilo, not even to the smokehouses, so the money on a sale should always come to at least four times the weight on it.

The vet has been here once in eight years so I'm not fussed about that side of it.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: maybe two hundred sales a year

nl_description:
Handover notes for the replacement traceability and performance store on the chilled ready-meals site. Read this as the whole estate, not one extract: it absorbs the four systems we run today -- purchasing, the line MES, the quality LIMS and the despatch book -- and it has to carry the change history the last BRC audit said we did not have. Sizing: three lines, about 1.1 million retail units a week, 340 live SKUs, five years of retention, and the checkweigher feed on its own is bigger than everything else in here put together.

SUPPLY BASE. Approved suppliers, each with a name that is unique across the base, an approval status, a current audit score out of 100 and the date approval started. A supplier delivers from one or more of its own sites, each with a site name, a country code and the certification scheme that site holds. Audits are their own history: which supplier, the date, which of our people audited it, the score awarded and the outcome. An audit recorded as a pass never carries a score under 70 -- the old system let one through and that is how we ended up in this rebuild. Ingredients carry a unique ingredient code, a name, a unit of measure, a shelf life in days and a storage class of ambient, chilled or frozen; the code is the natural key and gives you all of that. Allergens are their own short list -- code, name, and whether the allergen is declarable on pack -- and an ingredient can carry several of them, which is a genuine many-to-many and gets a composite key on ingredient plus allergen code rather than a surrogate.

PURCHASING AND GOODS IN. A purchase order has a unique order number, goes to one supplier site, is raised on a date by a named buyer, and carries a required-by date that is never earlier than the date it was raised. Its lines are one per ingredient on that order, so the order and the ingredient together are the key, with a quantity ordered in kilos and the agreed price per kilo. Goods in writes one receipt per delivery against the order line: the supplier, the ingredient, the arrival timestamp, the supplier's own lot code, the quantity in kilos, the probe temperature on arrival, an accepted flag, a use-by date and, where it was turned away, a rejection reason from a coded list which also says whether that reason is chargeable back to the supplier. A supplier's lot code is unique within that supplier, so supplier plus lot code is the pair a recall query enters the data on, and it must behave as a key. Where a receipt is accepted, the quantity may exceed the ordered quantity on its line by no more than five percent -- goods in is allowed that tolerance and nothing beyond it -- and the use-by date is always after the arrival timestamp. Anything not accepted must have a rejection reason recorded, which the old system did not enforce and which is why our reject analysis is worthless. Two hard rejection rules are enforced right there at goods in: a chilled ingredient probing above 5 C is rejected, and anything from a supplier whose audit score is under 70 is rejected regardless of temperature.

PRODUCT AND RECIPE. SKUs sit in product groups; a group has a unique group name and the storage class the whole group is held at. A product carries its SKU code, its group, a name, a retail price, a target pack weight in grams and the weekly unit volume we plan against -- the SKU code identifies the product and gives you its name and target weight. Each product has one live packaging specification: the film type, the tray material, how many units make a case, and the absolute minimum pack weight for that spec. Recipes are versioned per product, each with a version number, an effective date and the person who approved it, and the product with the version number together identify the recipe and settle its effective date. A recipe is only ever approved by the technical manager, which is a job title check on the approver. A recipe line is a set of ingredients with a kilo quantity per batch, and that is the other real many-to-many, so again a composite key on recipe plus ingredient.

PEOPLE. Departments have a name and a cost centre code. Employees sit in one department with a unique payroll number, a full name, a job title and a hire date -- payroll number is the natural key and tells you the department. Training is held per employee: the course name, the date it was completed and the date the completion lapses, which is always after the completion, and nothing is recorded as completed before the person was hired.

MANUFACTURING. Three production lines, each with a name unique on site, the department that owns it and a rated units-per-hour figure; the line name is enough to get you the department and the rating. Shift patterns are a short list with a name and planned hours. A shift is one line on one date working one pattern -- those three identify it -- with a start and end timestamp, end after start, and a supervisor. A run is one recipe on one line inside one shift, with start and end timestamps, the units produced and the giveaway percentage, which sits between 0 and 8 percent. A run's window is inside its shift's window, and the line on the run is by definition the line the shift was on -- the shift already determines it, and that column was inconsistent in the old MES extract, which is the whole reason I am flagging it. No run has ever run past 24 hours, so the units produced can never beat the line's rated hourly rate times 24. Traceability is the association between a run and the specific receipts consumed in it, with the kilos drawn from each, and that is the table a recall query walks; the kilos drawn from a receipt obviously cannot exceed the kilos that receipt brought in. Downtime is an event against the run with a coded reason (the reason list carries a description and a planned/unplanned flag), a start, an end and a duration in minutes; a downtime event sits inside its run's window and ends no earlier than it started.

QUALITY. Check types are a coded list carrying a description, a critical flag, and the lower and upper limit for that check -- the chill-temperature type holds 0 and 5, metal detection holds its own, and so on. That is the point of the table: a passing check reads its limits off the type row rather than off a threshold compiled into a report, which is how chill checks were being signed against the wrong band for a quarter. A QC check is per run, typed, timestamped inside the run window, with the operator who did it, a measured value and a pass flag; a check recorded as a pass has its measured value inside its own type's limits. Checkweigher sampling is the row-count driver: one pack weight sample every 90 seconds per line, timestamped inside the run window, which is tens of millions of rows over the retention window. On a nominal 400 gram pack the samples come out at 402 grams mean with an sd of 6, and no individual pack may be under 385 grams. Micro tests are separate and slow: a sample date against the run, the organism tested, the result in cfu per gram and the date it was reported back, which is never before the sample was taken and never before the run started. Non-conformances are raised against a run by a named person with a raised timestamp, a closed timestamp not before it, a category, the units affected and a disposition; the units affected cannot exceed the units the run produced.

ENGINEERING. Equipment is inventoried per line with a unique asset number, an equipment type and an installed date -- the asset number gives you the line. Calibrations are a history per item of equipment: when it was calibrated, when the next one falls due, who did it and whether it passed. The next-due timestamp is after the calibration, and nothing is calibrated before the equipment was installed.

DESPATCH. Customers have a name and a unique account code, and deliver-to sites under them with a site name and a postcode. A despatch note goes to one customer site with a timestamp, the vehicle registration and a total case count. Its lines are one per run shipped on that note, keyed on the note and the run, with the case count from that run -- a line's cases never exceed the note's total, and a note is never timestamped before the run on it finished, which the despatch book let through routinely.

GOVERNANCE. Customer complaints come in against a product and a customer with a date, a category and the units affected, which is at least one. Product recalls are their own record: the product, when it was raised, the reason, the units recalled and when it was closed, closed never before raised. And the change history the audit asked for: every change to any of this is a row naming the table, the record key, the action, the field, the old and the new value, the employee who made the change and when. On an update the old value must be populated. That is the finding, and it is what funded this.

FITTED DISTRIBUTIONS. Arrival temperature runs a 3.2 C mean with an sd of 1.1. Weekly unit volume per SKU is savagely skewed -- a Zipf with an exponent around 1.25 fits the rank curve better than anything else we have tried. About 40 percent of checks are metal detection, 25 percent chill temperature, 20 percent seal integrity and 15 percent organoleptic. Complaint categories split roughly 45 percent foreign body, 30 percent quality, 15 percent packaging and 10 percent labelling. Supplier audit scores cluster high, normal-ish around 84 with an sd of 8.

We run four markets a week across the county. Tuesday in the market square, Thursday on the leisure centre car park, Saturday is the big one, and there's a Sunday one at the garden centre that's new and we'll see if it survives the winter. Each of those runs on its own day at its own venue and has its own name that nobody would confuse -- tell me the name and I can tell you the day, the venue and how many pitches will fit, because the square takes forty, the car park twenty-eight and the garden centre only sixteen. Every time one of them happens it's a separate market day with its own date, so a market plus a date is one market day and no more than one, because that's what everything else hangs off. On each market day I write down how many pitches we actually booked in, and that can't be more than the venue holds -- we oversold the garden centre twice in the summer and had two traders standing in the car park.

The people who sell are members of the co-op. I call them stallholders, the committee minutes call them traders, the lottery grant paperwork insists on 'vendor' -- all the same people. About 140 on the books though only sixty-odd turn out in a given week. Each one trades under a name of their own that nobody else uses, and that name tells you what they sell. Each one pays an annual membership, and then a pitch fee on the day.

Fees go by frontage. There's a little price list on the wall: a three-metre pitch is eighteen pounds, a six-metre is thirty. Most take the three, maybe a third want the six. That list is the thing I want held in one place, because the committee puts the prices up every couple of years and I am not going back through nine hundred booking rows to do it -- the fee on a booking should just be whatever the list says for the frontage that trader took. First two markets for a new trader are free, though, that's the taster deal, so the booking sheet carries a count of how many markets that trader has done and if it's one or two there's no fee at all and the list doesn't come into it. And one booking per trader per market day -- if there are two, someone has entered it twice.

Every market day I need who booked in, how much frontage they took, whether they wanted power, whether they actually turned up, and what they took. Power is only for the hot food units, so a booking with power on it is always one of the prepared food traders and never a grower or a craft stall. The takings are voluntary but most of them tell us because it goes in the funding report, and it is wildly uneven. Your average grower does two or three hundred quid on a Saturday, the man with the paella pan can do two thousand on a good day, and there's a candle woman who barely clears forty. Two or three stalls account for most of the money on the site. If they didn't turn up there's nothing to declare and the takings go in as a nought. And when they did turn up, nobody has ever declared less than the pitch fee they paid -- if that happens the committee wants a word, because either the figure's wrong or the stall isn't viable.

Some of them use our card readers under the till-share scheme, and every one of those transactions comes through to us with its amount and we pass the money on less our commission, which is two pence in the pound -- so the commission on a transaction is always less than the amount and never more than two percent of it. That's what makes this bigger than you'd think -- with the years of individual card transactions we're at roughly half a million rows.

Produce type matters because of the funding: we have to report what proportion of stalls are growers and meat versus prepared food versus crafts. It's about half growers, a third prepared food, and the rest crafts and the occasional charity stall.

Two more things. If a trader no-shows twice in a season they lose their booking priority, so we keep a running count of no-shows against them and a flag for whether they've still got priority -- and that flag is just the count, there's no judgement in it. And there are volunteers who put the barriers out. They ought to be on a list of their own with the date they signed up and whether we've had them checked, and then their shifts against the market day with the hours, since we're meant to report volunteer time. One shift per volunteer per market day, nobody does more than eight hours in a day, and nobody is down for a shift on a market day before the date they signed up.

nl_description:
I'm doing the data side for a machinery hire business. Six depots, about 480 machines on fleet, and we go back to 2016, so it's just under 400,000 hire lines and roughly 1.6 million engine-hour readings pulled off the telematics -- those readings are a table in their own right, one row per machine per timestamp with the hours off the box, and they are most of the row count in the whole system. Nothing enormous, but well past what the spreadsheet it currently lives in can cope with.

A machine sits at one depot -- each depot has a name, no two the same, and the county it's in, so the depot name is enough to place it. A machine has an asset number stamped on the frame, which is unique and tells you both the machine and the depot it lives at, plus a type, a make and model, the year it was built and its engine hours, which only ever tick up. Nothing on fleet is older than 2006; that's policy, we trade them out before that. Each machine also carries a list day rate. A make and model is only ever the one type of machine, by the way -- a Manitou is a telehandler wherever it happens to be parked -- so if the type and the model ever disagree on a row it is the type that has been typed in wrong. Just under half the fleet is tractors, a fifth telehandlers, trailers about 15 percent, mowers a tenth and the rest is odds and ends -- toppers, rollers, a couple of chippers.

The machine types are a short list of their own with a description, and the important thing on that list is the rate floor for the type. A tractor never goes out under 180 a day whatever anyone has typed on the rate card, because below that we're subsidising the customer, and there's a floor for each of the other types too. Those numbers belong on the type list rather than in a rep's head or a report -- no machine's day rate is ever below the floor its type carries, and that is the check I want.

Customers, which some people here call accounts and the invoices call customer, have a name that is unique on the ledger, are either contract or cash, and we hold a credit limit against them. A hire -- the yard calls it a job, the rate card calls it a rental, same record -- is one machine out to one customer with the date it went, the date we expected it back, the date it actually came back, the hours it did while it was out, the discount applied, what we charged, and how far we delivered it. Neither the expected return nor the actual return is ever before the day it went out. Contract accounts come off list at a flat 15 percent and that gets written onto the agreement as the discount. We won't deliver further than 120 km. Average delivery is about 34 km with a fair spread either side of it, call it 18. Hours on a hire average 50 but the shape is a decay curve -- masses of one and two day jobs, then a long thin tail of six-week silage jobs, and six weeks is the longest we have ever let one run, so the charge on an agreement cannot beat forty-two times the machine's own day rate. Nor can it beat the account's credit limit; we don't let a job out that would take them over it.

Servicing: every machine has a history of services and breakdowns against it, with the date, what kind of service it was, the engine hours when it happened, whether it was a breakdown rather than a scheduled one, and the cost. Most of those invoices are a couple of hundred pounds but there's a fat tail -- the odd four-thousand-pound gearbox -- so it's a lognormal shape, log-mean around 5.5 and a log-variance about 1. Since the hour clock only goes up, neither a service nor a telematics reading can carry more hours than the machine is currently showing.

Insurance claims exist but leave them out for now, and there's an operator involved on some hires where we supply the driver, which I haven't thought through yet.

We're rebuilding the order history for an agricultural inputs distributor -- seed, fertiliser, crop protection -- trading out of 22 branches across the country. The reason we're doing it at all is size: about 31 million order lines since 2004, growing by roughly 1.8 million a year, and the current warehouse takes eleven minutes to answer 'what did this grower buy last spring'.

The line is the grain of the thing. One line is one product to one account on a date -- that combination happens exactly once, we merge them at entry if a rep keys the same product twice for the same grower on the same day -- with a tonnage, the price per tonne we actually charged, a discount, and the delivery week they asked for. Weeks are numbered one to fifty-two and that is how the entire logistics side talks. I'll be honest, there is no proper order header in the source system, just lines that happen to share a date and an account, and I've never been sure whether we should invent one.

Products carry a code, which is unique and is what the reps quote down the phone -- give me the code and I can tell you the category and the pack size without looking anything else up -- plus the pack size in kilos, a list price per tonne, and for the fertilisers a nitrogen percentage, which runs from nothing at all up to 46 percent for straight urea. You cannot buy less than one bag, so a line's tonnage is never below its product's pack size expressed in tonnes. By line count, fertiliser is about 42 percent, seed 30, crop protection 20, and the last 8 percent is everything else -- lime, netting, twine.

The categories themselves want to be a proper list, not a text field, because two things hang off them: a description for the reports, and the price floor for the category. Fertiliser's floor is 190 a tonne and it is a hard floor -- sales cannot override it -- and the other categories have their own. No product's list price is ever set below the floor its category carries, and no fertiliser line is ever charged under 190 a tonne.

On what we actually charge: we never charge above list, and the deepest anyone is authorised to go is thirty percent off list, so the price on a line always lands between seventy percent of the product's list price and the list price itself. Anything outside that band went in through a back door.

Accounts (the reps say growers, finance says customer, it's the same entity) belong to a home branch, which has a name -- unique, so the name gives you the region -- and a region, and each account has a status and the hectares they farm. The average is about 180 hectares, the median nearer 120, and a handful of estates are over five thousand, so it's a long right tail -- lognormal, roughly 4.8 on the log scale with a variance around 0.9. That hectarage is worth holding properly because it is also a sanity check: nobody spreads more than three tonnes of fertiliser to the hectare in a season, so a fertiliser line for more than three times the account's hectares is a decimal point in the wrong place, which is how we once delivered 4,000 tonnes of ammonium nitrate to a smallholding.

Line sizes have a similar shape: median about three and a half tonnes, with everything from a single 25-kilo bag up to a 600-tonne blanket fertiliser order, so log-mean around 1.25 and log-variance about 1.1.

One more commercial rule needs baking in rather than living in someone's head. Any line of 24 tonnes or more earns the bulk discount, six percent, which we want written on the line itself; anything under 24 tonnes carries no discount at all. So the tonnage on its own settles the discount -- there is no judgement in that column and there should be no way to type one in.

Right, so we're a two-branch estate agency -- my father started it in 2018 and I took over the sales side of it last year. Nothing fancy. At any one time we have somewhere around a hundred and eighty houses on our books, and across the whole eight years we have sold maybe two and a half thousand, so we are really not drowning in data here; the problem is more that the same house exists in four different notebooks. The properties are the heart of it -- everything else hangs off them.

For every house, or property if you want the word off the particulars, that we take on I want the street address and the postcode held apart from each other, because the postcode is how we do our local price comparisons. Then the style of house it is -- roughly a third of what we handle is semi-detached, a quarter terraced, about a fifth detached and the rest are flats. Bedrooms obviously; we have never listed anything smaller than a one-bed and the biggest we ever had was six. The asking price, the date the instruction came in, and the EPC band, which sellers always forget to send us.

Asking prices sit around two hundred and eighty-five thousand as a typical figure, but there is a long tail upwards -- we did a farmhouse at 1.4 million in 2023 and that one number ruins every average I try to work out. We have never taken on anything below sixty thousand, that is a floor we hold to.

Viewings are the bit that goes wrong most. A viewing has to say which house it was for, which of our negotiators took it, the applicant's name and a phone number, the date and time, and whatever feedback came back afterwards. I also want a marker for whether it was a second viewing, because those are the ones that actually convert. The applicant's phone number is the thing we tell people apart by -- same number, same person -- so if a number turns up with a different name attached to it then somebody has mistyped one or the other, and I want that catchable. And nobody can view a house before we have the instruction on the system, so a viewing date and time is never earlier than the instruction date for that house.

For the negotiators themselves we only need their name, which branch they sit in, their mobile, and the date they started with us. The mobile is unique to the individual because we hand the phones out ourselves, so the number identifies the negotiator on its own -- handy, because half of what comes in off the answering service is just a number. We pay a length-of-service bonus and I am forever digging that start date out of old contracts.

Offers come in against a house. We write down the applicant's name, the amount, the day it was made, whether they have anything of their own to sell (chain-free buyers, we love those), how many days after the instruction it landed, and the status it ended up at. An offer obviously cannot be dated before the instruction came in. We also do not pass anything on that is under sixty per cent of what we are asking for the house -- it wastes the seller's afternoon and it insults them -- so every offer we record sits at or above sixty per cent of the asking price. On average it takes about thirty-four days from us putting a house up to the first offer landing, although some go the same afternoon and some sit for half a year.

When one actually goes through, that is worth its own record. It points back at the offer we accepted, and it carries the price we agreed, the day we exchanged, the day it completed and our commission fee. Completion is never before exchange, and exchange is never before the day the offer was made. The agreed price is never above the asking price -- if it looks like it is, somebody has typed a number into the wrong box. And the commission fee is one and a half per cent of the agreed price as standard and has never gone above three per cent of it, not even on the ones that sold well under asking, where the sellers always try it on. A house only ever sells once through us; we do not do resales, so there is at most one of these per house.

Oh, and the one rule Dad never broke: if a house has been on the market with us more than seventy days and nothing has happened, the asking price gets cut. So I need to know how long each one has been on and whether we have already reduced the price once.

nl_description:
We are a lettings and management outfit, nine and a bit thousand properties under management across the north west, and the honest truth is our current system was built for about four hundred. There are getting on for two million rent transactions sitting in it now and it takes forty seconds to open a statement.

Start with the clients, by which I mean the landlords -- half the office says landlord and half says client and they are the same person. We hold their name, a correspondence address, a mobile, an email, their tax reference for the non-resident ones, and the date they came to us. The tax reference is only on some of them but where we have it, it is unique to that landlord, so it will do as a way of spotting the same person entered twice, which happens more than I would like. We also hold the management fee percentage we agreed with them -- most are on ten per cent of what we collect, the fully managed ones are on twelve, and twelve is the ceiling, we have never charged more than that. Some of them own one flat and one of them owns two hundred and eleven.

Then the properties themselves, each one belonging to a landlord: the address, the number of bedrooms, whether it is furnished, the EPC rating, and whether it is licensed as an HMO because the council are very keen on that at the moment.

A tenancy is the agreement that sits on a property. Start and end dates, the monthly rent, the deposit, what kind of agreement it is, and the date the deposit was protected. A property can only have one tenancy starting on any given day, so the property and the start date between them pin down which agreement you mean. The end date is always after the start date, and the deposit protection date is never before the start -- we have thirty days from the start to protect it and we do not miss that, whatever else we miss. Nearly all of ours are standard assured shortholds -- about six in a hundred are company lets and there is a small slice, call it eight per cent, that are licences for the HMO rooms. The rent averages around eleven hundred and fifty a month and most of the book is within a couple of hundred either side of that. On a normal assured shorthold the deposit is capped at five weeks' rent, which works out at about a month and a half's rent and in practice means we never hold more than about fifteen hundred pounds; company lets are not capped at all so those can be anything. It used to be six weeks before the rules changed, so you will see older numbers in the data that look wrong and are not.

Everybody named on the agreement gets recorded separately -- name, date of birth, mobile, email, and whether we have completed their right to rent check. They are each attached to the one tenancy they signed.

Rent payments are per tenancy. Date received, amount, how they paid, and how many days late it was. Obviously nothing is ever received before the tenancy started -- if you see one, the payment has been keyed against the wrong agreement, and that has happened where the same tenant renews. Anything more than a fortnight late and a notice goes out, and we need to know for each payment whether that notice was actually sent, because a tribunal will ask.

Repairs get logged against the property rather than the tenancy, which I know is annoying, but that is how the maintenance lads work. Date reported, what is wrong, how urgent, the date it was finished, what we quoted and what it ended up costing. Nothing is finished before it was reported. A tenancy generates about two and a half repair jobs in a year on average -- some years none at all, and then a boiler goes and you get five in a fortnight. Most jobs are small and there are a handful every year that cost more than all the small ones put together.

The contractors themselves want to be a proper list rather than a name typed into the job, which is what we do now and it is why the same firm appears eleven times spelled eleven ways. A firm has a company name, the trade they do -- and it is one trade each, a plumber is not also a roofer on our list, so the firm name tells you the trade -- their hourly rate, and whether they are Gas Safe registered. Anybody we send on a gas job has to be Gas Safe registered, no exceptions, and that is the check I most want the system to make for me. There is a minimum charge of an hour on everything, so no job ever comes back costing less than the firm's hourly rate. And where a job does come in over what was quoted, it is never more than ten per cent over -- past that they have to come back and ask.

Last bit, the statements, which is where I started. Once a month per landlord we produce one: which month it covers, the rent we collected, the management fee we took, the repairs we deducted and the net we paid them, plus the date we paid it. One statement per landlord per month, that is a rule. The fee is never more than twelve per cent of the rent collected, the repairs we deduct never come to more than the rent we collected in the first place, and the net paid never exceeds the collected rent less the fee. And we pay after the month has closed, so the payment date is always later than the month the statement is for.

nl_description:
Lease admin platform, commercial landlord group. Four hundred buildings, eleven thousand demised units, 8,500 live leases; the service charge apportionment table is the fat one at roughly 3.5 million rows after fifteen years of quarterly runs.

Buildings hang off a holding entity, one entity to many buildings, and the entity carries a name and its company number, which is unique and is the thing the auditors match on. Buildings carry name, address, year of practical completion, total lettable area in sqm. Each building subdivides into demised units: unit reference, net internal area, floor level, planning use class. Unit references are unique across the estate and are prefixed with the building code, so a unit reference resolves to its building on its own. No unit's net internal area exceeds the lettable area of the building it sits in -- trivially true and yet violated 41 times in the current extract, because the areas were loaded from two different surveys.

Use classes are a reference list, not a free text field: the code, a description and a flag for whether that class obliges us to grant a break. Tenant covenants are held apart from leases because the same covenant re-lets -- legal name, company number, covenant strength grade, guarantor name where there is one.

A lease is one unit to one covenant: term commencement, term in whole years, the term expiry date, contractual annual rent, review pattern, a tenant break flag, repairing obligation, and the rent deposit we hold. We also carry the use class on the lease itself, which is strictly the unit's use class and must agree with it -- the unit determines it, and the two have drifted apart where units were amalgamated. Expiry is always later than commencement. Term is an integer 1 to 25, nothing longer exists on this book, and it clusters on the round numbers -- 34 per cent at five years, 29 at ten, 18 at fifteen, 12 at three, the last 7 at twenty-five. Rent is log-normal, log-mean 11.6, log-variance 1.1. Net internal areas are log-normal too, log-mean 5.4, log-variance 0.9. Standing rule from our solicitors, and the reason the flag on the use class list exists at all: where the class obliges a break, the lease carries a break clause, and the flag on the lease is whatever the class says. B8, storage and distribution, is the one that bites.

The rent deposit is capped at six months' rent, so it never exceeds half the contractual annual rent. Where the covenant strength grade is C -- our weakest band -- we always take a deposit of at least a quarter of the annual rent; that is a credit committee rule and there are no exceptions to it.

Break options are child rows on the lease rather than a single date, because a lease can have several: the break date, the notice period in months and whether it was exercised. A break date always falls after commencement and on or before expiry, and the notice period is never less than six months.

Reviews are child rows on the lease too -- review date, passing rent before, reviewed rent after, uplift percentage, whether it went to third party determination. These are upward-only, institutional leases, so the reviewed rent is never below the passing rent. A review date falls after commencement and before expiry. Uplifts average 8.5 per cent, standard deviation near 4.

Apportionments are per lease: charge year, certified quarter, apportioned percentage, demanded amount. One row per lease per charge year per quarter, and the percentage is what varies. The percentage is bounded 0 to 100 and a run whose per-building total exceeds 100 gets rejected. A demanded service charge never exceeds the lease's contractual annual rent -- if it does, the apportionment is wrong, which is how we discovered the 2019 run had been certified against the wrong building.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: the service charge apportionment table is the fat one at roughly 3.5 million rows

nl_description:
I look after reporting for a main contractor -- civils and fit-out, turnover about ninety million, twenty-odd live jobs at any time. I have been asked to write down everything we actually track before the new system gets specified, because at the moment it is four systems that do not speak to each other plus the commercial team's spreadsheets. This is going to be long. Read it as the whole estate rather than one module: the commercial side, the programme, the labour, the buying, the plant, the quality file and the safety file all end up in here, and they only really touch each other at the job.

Sizing first. Twenty to twenty-five live jobs, four years of history, and the volumes are wildly uneven between the parts. We book roughly six hundred thousand timesheet lines a year, so that is a couple of million rows on its own and by far the fattest table. Order lines are the next biggest at maybe four hundred thousand. Everything else is in the thousands or the low tens of thousands, and some of the reference lists have a dozen rows in them and will never grow.

CLIENTS AND JOBS. Clients have a name, the sector they are in, and which of our account managers owns the relationship. Sector is its own short list -- public bodies, private developers, utilities -- with a description against each and, importantly, the standard retention percentage that sector's contract form gives us: three per cent on public work, five on the private and utility jobs. Nobody remembers that until the final account, which is exactly why it should sit in a list and not in somebody's head. We also stamp the sector on the job itself, which is strictly redundant since the client already tells you the sector, and the two have disagreed in the old extract more than once; they must match, and the client determines it.

A job -- the commercial team's paperwork and every contract we sign call it a project, and it is one and the same thing, I am not going to win that argument -- belongs to one client and carries a job name, a job code which is unique across the business and is what everybody actually quotes, the site address, the contract value, when we started on site, the practical completion date, the stage it is at, the retention percentage, and the defects liability period in months. Practical completion is never earlier than the start on site. Retention is never above ten per cent, and it always equals the standard retention percentage for the job's sector. Stages are another short list, with a description and an order number so reports sort properly. Contract values are all over the place -- the middle of the range is around 3.2 million but we have done a 40 million spine road and a 90 thousand pound shopfront in the same year, so it is very much a long-tailed thing.

COMMERCIAL. Variations against a job: what changed, when it was submitted, the valuation amount we applied for, the amount that was finally agreed, and the status. Once one is agreed, the agreed amount is never above the amount we applied for -- the client's surveyor does not hand money back.

Monthly valuations, also per job: the valuation number, which is numbered from one within each job so the job and the number together tell you the period end date, then the period end date itself, the gross amount, the retention held, the amount previously certified and the net due. The net due is the gross less retention less what has already been certified, so it is never more than the gross amount minus the retention held. The previously certified figure is never above the gross. Where a job is on the standard five per cent, the retention held is never more than five per cent of the gross. And if we have applied for more than has already been certified, there is by definition something net due.

Payment certificates come back one per valuation: the certified amount, the date it was certified, the date it falls due and the date it was actually paid. The certified amount never exceeds the net due we applied for. Neither the due date nor the paid date is ever earlier than the certified date -- we have rows in the old system where they are, and they are all keying errors. Retention releases sit against the job: release date, released amount and which release stage it is. Nothing is ever released before practical completion.

PROGRAMME. A job breaks into work packages: package name, planned start and planned finish, the actual start and actual finish once they happen, a percent complete figure the site manager updates on a Friday, and the package value. Planned finish is never before planned start and actual finish is never before actual start. Percent complete only ever runs 0 to 100 although you would not believe how often somebody types 110, and across the book at any moment it is spread pretty evenly across that whole range. Once a package reads 100 per cent there has to be an actual finish date against it.

Under a package sit the programme activities: activity name, the planned duration in days, planned start and planned finish, and the float days off the planner's file. An activity is never planned to start before the package it belongs to. Progress updates are their own rows against the package -- the update date, the percent complete reported and who updated it. The figure held on the package is the latest of these, so no individual update ever reports more than the package does.

SUBCONTRACT AND LABOUR. Trades are a coded list with a description and a flag for whether the trade is high risk. Subcontractors are a shared list, not per job: company name, their trade, whether their CSCS checks are verified, when their insurance runs out, and the date we prequalified them. The insurance expiry is always later than the prequalification date, or the prequalification was a fiction. The same firm turns up on lots of our jobs and a job has thirty or forty of them, so the appointment is its own thing: which firm on which job, the package value and the date they were appointed. That pairing is unique, we never appoint the same firm to a job twice. A firm's package value on a job is never more than the job's contract value, and we never appoint a firm on a date later than its insurance expiry.

Operatives belong to a subcontractor: name and trade card number, and the card number is unique to the man so it identifies him on its own. Before anybody goes on site there is a site induction: which operative, which job, the date he was inducted, the date that induction expires and who inducted him. The expiry is always after the induction. Then timesheets -- the operative, the package, the work date, the hours worked and the overtime hours within them. A normal day is about 8.6 hours with a spread of an hour and a half either way, we do not allow anybody to book more than twelve hours on one date, and the overtime hours can obviously never exceed the hours worked on that line.

PROCUREMENT. Suppliers are a list: name, whether they are approved, and when that approval expires. Materials are a list too: material name, the unit of measure it is bought in, and whether it is hazardous. Units of measure are their own tiny list of a code and a description, and a material is only ever bought in one of them -- tonnes or square metres or linear metres, never both for the same material. Purchase orders are raised against a job: the supplier, the raised date, the order value, the status and who approved it. An order value is never above the job's contract value. Each order has lines, numbered within the order: the material, the quantity ordered, the unit rate and the line amount, which is just the quantity times the rate and should never be anything else. A very small number of materials account for most of the lines we ever raise -- rebar, concrete, blockwork -- and the rank frequency is a long tail, close to Zipf with an exponent around 1.4.

Material deliveries come in against an order and against the package they are for: the delivered date, the quantity delivered, the tonnage and the ticket reference off the weighbridge. Nothing is ever delivered before the order that bought it was raised, whatever the site says.

PLANT. Plant items are held centrally: a plant description, a serial number that is unique to the machine, the date of its last thorough examination and the date the next one is due, which is always after the last. Hires put a plant item on a job: hire start date, hire end date, the weekly rate and the hire cost. The end is never before the start, and because the minimum charge is one week the hire cost is never below the weekly rate. Weekly rates average about 620 pounds with a spread of a bit over 200. Plant inspections are separate from examinations and happen on site: the item, the date, whether it passed, a defect note and who inspected it. A fail has to carry a defect note -- that is the rule the current system silently lets through. And an inspection we have recorded as passed is only meaningful if it happened on or before the next examination due date; past that the certificate has lapsed and a pass is not a pass.

QUALITY. Inspection types are a coded list with a description and a flag for whether the type is a hold point. Quality inspections are raised against a package: the type, the date inspected, whether it passed and the inspector name. We never inspect a package before it has actually started on site. Where one fails we raise a nonconformance off it: the raised date, a description, the closed date and the rework cost. It cannot be raised before the inspection that found it, and it is not closed before it was raised. Separately, at handover, defect items are logged against the job and the package: raised date, description, the target date to put it right and the date it was actually rectified. The target date is always after the raised date and nothing is rectified before it was raised.

HEALTH AND SAFETY. This is the one the board actually reads. Severity is a list: the grade, a description, and whether that grade is RIDDOR reportable -- grades 3 and 4 are, 1 and 2 are not, and the flag belongs on the list rather than being retyped. Incidents are logged against a job with a date, the severity grade, whether it is RIDDOR reportable, how many days were lost and who reported it. The reportable flag on the incident is whatever the severity list says for that grade, full stop. About sixty-eight per cent are grade 1 near misses, twenty-one per cent grade 2, nine per cent grade 3 and the last two per cent grade 4. Lost days are never negative.

Toolbox talks are recorded per job: the date, the topic, the attendee count and who delivered it. There is always at least one attendee or the talk did not happen, and fourteen or so is typical. Permits to work are per job as well: the permit type, the subcontractor it was issued to, when it was issued and when it expires, and who issued it. Permit types are a list with a description and the maximum duration in hours the type allows. A permit always expires after it was issued.

AUDIT. Last thing, and it is a condition of the new contract rather than something we want: every change to any of the above is a row naming the table, the record key, the action, the field name, the old value, the new value, who changed it and when. On an update the old value has to be populated, otherwise the trail is worthless, and that is precisely the finding that got this rebuild funded.

nl_description:
So my patch is hard FM across about nine hundred buildings -- schools, a couple of leisure centres, offices, the lot. The reason I am even in this meeting is the meter data. Every bit of plant with a meter on it reports every fifteen minutes and that is something like sixty million readings a year, and the spreadsheet approach died about three years ago.

Sites: name, which region they fall in, and floor area. Site names are unique and, because of how the contract was carved up, the region follows from the site -- tell me the site name and I can tell you whose numbers it lands in. Region matters because the regional managers all want their own.

Every site has kit on it -- assets, plant, whatever you want to call it. Air handling units, lifts, boilers, chillers. We hold what type it is, the year it went in, how critical it is, which is a flag the client sets, and the replacement cost off the asset register. Critical kit is the stuff where the building stops if it stops.

The meters want separating out from the kit, which is the thing we got wrong last time. A meter sits on a piece of plant, and it has its own serial number -- unique, they come off the manufacturer's plate -- and the date it was installed. Then a reading is just the meter, the timestamp and the consumption in kilowatt hours, and nothing is ever read before the meter was installed, which sounds obvious and yet the migration produced about eleven thousand of them. Typically it is around forty units on a fifteen minute read, give or take fifteen, but the leisure centres in January are a different animal entirely. Consumption is never negative -- if it is, the meter has rolled over and that is a different conversation.

Then the jobs. Some of the team say job, the helpdesk say ticket, the contract says work order, they are the same thing and I would like to stop arguing about it. A job is raised against a piece of kit. We need when it came in, what the caller said, how urgent it is, when it was closed, how long the response took, the labour hours booked, what it cost, and whether we took a deduction on it. Nothing is closed before it was raised.

Urgency -- priority, on the contract, and that is the word I will use because it is the word the client uses -- is banded one to four, and the priority bands want to be a proper little list of their own, with a description and, against each band, the response target in hours -- four hours on a band one, twenty-four on a two, and so on out to a week. That number is the number we are held to and it has been retyped into three different reports with three different answers, which is exactly why it belongs in the list. On a band one we simply never exceed the target, that is a contractual absolute. On the others, if the response goes past the target for its band then we are paying a deduction and the job has to be marked as such -- that is the report the client keeps asking for and we cannot produce. Nearly everything comes in as a three -- call it sixty-three per cent -- with seventeen per cent fours, sixteen per cent twos and only about four in a hundred coming in as ones. And anything raised against critical kit comes in as a one automatically, the helpdesk has no say in it.

On money: labour is charged at forty-two pounds an hour, so whatever a job costs it is at least the labour hours on it times forty-two. There is a callout charge on top of that from every firm, so a job never comes in below the firm's callout rate either. And the rule the client wrote into the contract is that we never spend more putting a thing right than it would cost to replace it -- once a job has gone past the bare callout charge, it is capped at the replacement cost of the kit, and past that it stops being a repair and goes to them as a capital item. Job costs are mostly small with a nasty tail: a door closer is forty quid and a chiller compressor is fifteen thousand.

The interesting thing, and the other report we cannot produce, is that the callouts are not spread out at all. A tiny number of assets -- the old AHUs at the two big sites, mainly -- soak up most of the jobs we raise in a year, and the overwhelming majority of the kit on the register never generates a single one. It is a very long tail and every average I quote them is meaningless because of it.

Jobs go to contractors. We need the firm's name, their trade -- one trade each on our list, so the name gives you the trade -- and their callout rate. They are a short list and I do not want to build a whole procurement module.

Last thing, planned maintenance. Each bit of kit has one service schedule, no more: how often it is due in months, which runs from monthly at the most frequent out to annual at the least, when it was last done and when it is next due, which is obviously after the last one.

a.basis: within the range of Zipf exponents the specifications state (n=30)

nl_description:
There are five of us. Two directors, two Part 2s and Jean who does everything else, and we have been going since 2011, so call it four hundred jobs all in and a few thousand drawings in the archive. It is not a lot of information. It is just in nine hundred folders on a NAS and Jean is retiring.

The unit of work is -- well, we call it a job, the invoices call it a commission and the directors say project, and it is one thing. Whatever it is called, we want the client's name, the title we gave the scheme, the town the site is in, how far up the RIBA stages it got, whether the fee was fixed or a percentage or time-charged, what fee we agreed, the date the enquiry first came in, the date we were actually instructed, and how much we have invoiced against it to date. The instruction is never earlier than the enquiry -- sometimes it is the same afternoon and sometimes it is nine months later and twice it has been two years. On the fixed-fee jobs, what we have invoiced to date never goes above the fee we agreed; that is the whole point of a fixed fee and yet it is the thing I most want the system to stop us doing.

Fees are wildly uneven. Most of what we do is a domestic extension worth a few thousand -- nine grand is about the middle of it -- but every couple of years one lands that is worth six figures and then the year looks nothing like the year before. On the fixed-fee ones we have a floor of two and a half thousand; below that it is not worth opening a file, and that has been the rule since about 2016. There is no such floor on the time-charged work, we will do a two-hour appraisal for a builder if we like him.

Most jobs die at stage 3. That is just the reality of planning work -- you get consent and the client goes off to a contractor who does the technical package. If I had to put numbers on it, about a tenth of the jobs stop at stage 1, one in seven at stage 2, a good third and a bit at stage 3, a bit over a fifth at stage 4 and the remaining sixth run through to stage 5.

The five of us -- the staff, if we are being formal about it, and the staff list is what this really is -- need writing down properly too, because at the moment a timesheet line just has a name typed on it. So, per member of staff: the person's name, which is unique enough among five people to identify them, what role they are -- director, Part 2, administrator -- the date they started here, and their charge-out rate. The rate goes with the role and not with the person: both directors are charged out at the same rate, both Part 2s at theirs. If we ever take on a third director he is on the director rate whether he likes it or not, so it is the role that fixes the rate.

Drawings hang off the job. Number, title, revision letter, the date it was issued and the scale it was drawn at. A given drawing number at a given revision letter was issued once and once only -- that pairing is the thing everybody quotes on site and it has to pin down a date. Nothing is ever issued before we were instructed, obviously. That is the bit that actually causes arguments -- somebody issues revision C to the contractor and the structural engineer is still working off B.

And time. Who, what day, how many hours, which job, and what we charge for the line. A full day usually comes out at six or seven chargeable hours once you take out the phone calls -- six and a half is about right, and it varies by a couple of hours either side. Nothing over twelve, if someone books fourteen hours they have fat-fingered it. Nobody books time to a job before the enquiry came in, and nobody books time before the date they started here, which sounds absurd until you migrate a spreadsheet. We bill in whole hours with a minimum of one, so the charge on a line is never less than that person's charge-out rate, and there is a floor of forty-five pounds an hour across the practice, so it is never less than forty-five times the hours either.

We also used to write down which planning officer was handling each application, and honestly it was the single most useful thing we ever recorded, but it lived in an individual's head and I do not know what to do with that.
