nl_description:
Cost management database, QS practice. Only a few thousand cost plans, but the bill of quantities lines underneath them come to roughly two million rows, and those are what need modelling properly instead of living in workbooks.

Client organisations at the top: name, procurement route. A cost plan belongs to one of them -- project reference, version number, base date, gross internal area in sqm, total estimate. We reissue four or five times over a scheme's life, and the project reference with the version number is what identifies a plan; the internal id is a surrogate we added when the workbooks went into the database.

Plans decompose into elements keyed on NRM code, with element name, elemental cost and the cost per square metre derived from it. The NRM code fixes the element name -- it is a published standard, 2.5 is always Roofs -- and where our data disagrees with that it is because somebody typed over the name, which happens most weeks. No element costs more than the whole plan's total estimate, which sounds too obvious to write down until you have seen an element loaded against the wrong plan.

Under each element sit the bill items: description, measured quantity, unit of measurement, rate applied, extended amount, and which library rate it was priced off. The extended amount is the measured quantity times the rate applied and nothing else -- there is no rounding fudge in it. An item's extended amount never exceeds the cost of the element it sits under. And we never apply a rate below the library unit rate for the resource it was priced from; discounting below the library is a commercial decision that goes through a partner, not through the bill. Item amounts are log-normal, log-mean 7.6, log-variance 2.1 -- thousands of trivial items and a handful carrying the bill.

Two reference libraries, neither of them keyed to a plan: resource rates, held on resource code plus type -- that pair is what determines the unit rate, and we carry an internal id alongside only because the bill items point at it -- with the unit rate itself and an effective-from date; and the TPI, a dated index value per month that we rebase to, where the month determines the value and the id is again a surrogate.

Tenders come in against a plan -- contractor name, submission date, tender sum, compliance flag. Tender sums are log-normal, log-mean 15.1, log-variance 1.2. Nothing is submitted before the plan's base date. The compliance rule is arithmetic rather than editorial: a tender we mark compliant sits within ten per cent above the plan's total estimate, and one that comes in further above than that is not compliant, whatever the covering letter says.

Interim certificates likewise: certificate number, valuation date, work done to date, the amount previously certified, and retention. Certificates are numbered within the plan, so the plan and the certificate number give you the valuation date. Retention is never negative and never more than five per cent of the work done to date. The work done to date never exceeds the plan's total estimate, the previously certified figure is always strictly below the work done to date -- it is a to-date series, it only goes one way -- and nothing is valued before the base date.

Risk allowances are per plan too -- description, a band of LOW, MEDIUM or HIGH, and the allowance as a percentage. Allowances run anywhere from 1 to 12 per cent and are flat across that interval, no clustering; on anything banded HIGH we will not sign off below 7.5.

One check I want in the data rather than in somebody's head: over 15,000 sqm of gross internal area, economies of scale mean no element should exceed 2,500 per square metre. If one does, it is mis-measured or the area is wrong, and that has embarrassed us twice.

std.basis: coefficient of variation in [0.006, 0.682], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=117), applied to the stated mean

nl_description:
Six self-storage sites, and I have been asked to sketch the model before we talk to developers. Scale is genuinely small -- about 2,700 units across the six and a little under 9,000 agreements since the first site opened in 2014.

A facility has a name, the town it is in, how many units it holds and the date it opened. The names are all distinct and each one is in exactly one town, so the facility name gives you the town -- we have never had two sites in the same place and if we did we would rename one.

Units belong to a facility and each one has a reference like B-114, a size, the floor level (ground is 0, we go up to 2 at Warrington), whether it is climate controlled, and the current list price per month. The letter on the front of the reference is the site code, so a unit reference is unique across all six and tells you which facility it is at without a lookup -- that was deliberate and it is the one thing the original spreadsheet got right. We only sell five sizes, deliberately, because it keeps the site plan simple: 25, 50, 75, 100 and 200 square feet. The 50s are the workhorse at about a third of the estate, the 25s a bit over a fifth, the 75s not quite a fifth, the 100s about a sixth, and the 200s the remaining eight per cent. List prices average near 96 pounds a month with a spread of maybe 38 either way -- a climate-controlled ground floor 200 and a second floor 25 are not the same product at all. Which is the reason for our one hard pricing rule: a ground floor unit that is climate controlled never goes out below 120 a month, whatever a walk-in offers us.

Customers are just name, email, phone and the date they first signed up. The email is how we tell them apart -- one email, one customer, and the system should refuse a second account on the same address, which it currently does not.

An agreement links one customer to one unit -- start date, end date if they have gone, the monthly rate they actually pay, whether they are on autopay, and how much insurance cover they took. A unit can only have one agreement starting on any given date, so the unit and the start date together identify the agreement. The end date is after the start date. Nobody starts an agreement before the date they signed up as a customer -- the sign-up is the walk-in or the web enquiry and the agreement comes after it, even if it is only twenty minutes after.

On the rate: it is not always the list price, but it is never above it, and we do not go more than twenty per cent under it either. Anything deeper than that needs a manager and gets done as a rent-free month instead, which is a different thing we handle badly. Cover starts at a thousand and we cap it at twenty-five thousand, above which the insurer wants a survey.

Billing is monthly against the agreement, and every payment is a row of its own: the due date, the amount due, the date it was paid, the amount paid and the payment method. The amount due is just the monthly rate on the agreement -- we do not put anything else on it, no fees, no insurance, that all goes through a different ledger -- and nothing is ever due before the agreement started. We never take more than was due on a line. Where the customer is on autopay the money leaves on the due date itself, so the paid date and the due date are the same; it is only the manual payers who drift.

The number I care about most is how long people stay. Average is around nine months, but the shape is a decay curve -- most are out inside a month or two after a house move, and then there is a hard core in the same unit since 2015. So put the tenure in months on the agreement.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: a little under 9,000 agreements since the first site opened in 2014
List prices average near 96 pounds a month

nl_description:
Portfolio is fourteen purpose-built student blocks, just over eleven thousand beds, and the operational data volume is dominated by one thing: door access. Every swipe on every door is logged and across the estate that is somewhere around forty million events a year. Everything else is small by comparison -- bookings are eleven thousand a year, instalments maybe forty thousand.

A residence has a name, a city, its bed count, and the university we hold the nominations agreement with. Universities want to be their own list, because we deal with the same handful of them over and over and because two of them have merged since we signed: a university has a name, which is unique and is how everybody refers to it, and the city it is in. Note that the university a resident actually attends is not always the one we have the nominations agreement with for that block, so those are two separate pieces of information and we have been conflating them for years.

Inside a residence there are flats -- flat number, floor, and how many bedrooms the flat contains, which can never be more than the bed count of the whole residence, obviously -- and inside a flat, the bedrooms themselves. Each bedroom has a room reference, the band it is sold in, whether it is ensuite, and the weekly rent. The room reference carries the flat number in it, so from a room reference you can tell which flat it belongs to; that is a convention the original developer set and we have stuck to it.

Bands are a proper list rather than a text field, because each band carries a description and, more importantly, the minimum weekly rent we are allowed to sell it at. There are three: Classic, Premium and Studio, about 52 per cent Classic, 31 Premium and 17 Studio across the estate. Studios are the exception to everything -- the floor on a studio is 240 a week, they are the margin, and the floors on the other two bands are much lower. The point of holding the floor against the band is that the sales team stopped being able to undercut it. No bedroom is ever priced below the floor for its band. Weekly rents average around 189 pounds with a standard deviation of roughly 42.

Residents -- students, tenants, whatever the sales team is calling them this week -- have a name, the university they actually attend, their year of course, and whether they are an international student.

A booking puts one resident in one bedroom for an academic year, and a given bedroom is only ever let once in a given academic year, so the room and the year together identify the booking. It carries the academic year, the contract length in weeks, the weekly rate agreed, a flag for whether a guarantor is required, whether the deposit has been paid and the deposit amount, plus the total contract value. Contracts are either 44 weeks or 51 weeks and nothing else, which makes the arithmetic easy: about seven in ten are the 44-week ones. The total contract value is just the weekly rate multiplied by the contract weeks -- it is stored because every report wants it and nobody wants to recompute it. The deposit is one week's rent, so where a deposit has been paid the deposit amount is the weekly rate they agreed. On the rate itself, we will discount up to ten per cent off the bedroom's rent for an early booker, and never more than that, and obviously never above the bedroom's rent either.

International students always need a UK guarantor -- that comes from the finance policy, not from us, and there are no exceptions to it. Where one is required we hold the guarantor properly: their name, their relationship to the resident, whether they are UK based and an email to chase.

Rent goes out in instalments against a booking: due date, amount due, the date it was received, the amount received, and whether it landed late. Nothing negative in the received column, even for the refunds, we handle those separately and badly. We never receive more against an instalment than was due on it, and no single instalment is ever billed for more than the whole contract value. If the money came in after the due date then it was late, and the flag has to say so -- that is the check I want, because at the moment the flag is set by hand and it is wrong about a fifth of the time.

Doors are their own register now: which residence the door is in, the door reference and whether it is an external door. Door references are unique across the estate and have the block code in them, so a door reference tells you the residence. Access events are then per resident per door -- when it happened, and whether entry was granted. We also stamp the residence on the event, which is strictly the door's residence and must agree with it. Denied swipes matter, that is usually somebody who has not paid or a lanyard that has gone walkabout.

Maintenance jobs are raised against a bedroom: when it was reported, what is wrong, how urgent it is, when it was completed and what it cost. Nothing is completed before it was reported. Costs are mostly trivial -- a light fitting, a blind -- with the occasional shower pump that eats the month's budget, so it is a long-tailed thing rather than an average.

Incidents get raised against a residence, and against a resident where we know who it was: when it was reported, what category, whether it is resolved and when it was resolved, which again is never before it was reported. A block generates about four or five of them a month on average, more in freshers' week, obviously.

nl_description:
This is the valuation stack, and I will be honest that half of it is well defined and half of it is whatever the last contractor left behind.

The well-defined half. We hold a property record per UPRN -- postcode, the address as a single text blob because we never managed to parse it, property type, floor area, build year and tenure. Sales come off the registry against a UPRN: sale date, price, and a new-build flag. That is 29 million addresses in the record table and the automated model runs over all of them monthly, so the estimate table is the one that hurts -- it is tens of millions of rows a run, each with the run date, the model version, a point estimate and a lower and upper bound. The bounds bracket the point estimate, so where the upper is above the lower at all, the upper is at or above the point and the lower at or below it. Model versions are a table in their own right now, with the date the version was trained and its mean absolute error as a percentage, because we were carrying the version as a free-text string and nobody could say what any of them meant. No estimate is ever dated before the version that produced it was trained. Median sale price on the index is a bit over 228,000, so log-mean 12.33, and the log-variance is about 0.42.

Surveyors: name, RICS number, grade, region. The RICS number is unique to the individual and identifies them on its own. A valuation is one surveyor against one property -- instructed date, inspection date, the basis of valuation, the market value reported, a confidence score which is a fraction between 0 and 1 sitting around 0.78 with a standard deviation of about 0.11, a defect count, and the reinstatement cost for insurance purposes. The basis of valuation is a coded list -- market value, investment value, reinstatement and so on -- carrying a description and a flag for whether that basis requires a physical inspection; where it does, there has to be an inspection date. An inspection is never dated before the instruction. The reinstatement figure is a rebuild cost, not a market figure, and the QA team's sanity check is that it never comes in below sixty per cent of the market value reported on the same valuation.

A typical inspection also turns up one or two defects worth writing up, so the count of them belongs on the valuation itself, and the defect rows carry a category, a severity grade and an estimated remedial cost. Severity is a graded list of three with a description and, against each grade, the minimum remedial cost that qualifies for it -- grade 3 is our top severity and it is defined by cost, anything we grade a 3 is more than five thousand pounds to put right, and that is what makes it a 3 rather than a judgement call. So no defect's remedial cost estimate is below the minimum for the grade it has been given.

Every valuation gets a second pair of eyes. A review holds which surveyor reviewed it, the date, the value they agreed and the review outcome. The reviewer is never the surveyor who did the valuation, which is the whole point, and a review is never dated before the inspection. Where the reviewer's agreed value differs from the reported market value at all, it still has to sit within ten per cent either side of it; outside that band the outcome is a referral and the case is reopened.

Now the messy half. Comparables -- the surveyors say comps, the report template says comparable evidence, the schema calls them something else again. A valuation cites several other properties as evidence and the same property gets cited across many valuations, so it is genuinely both ways round, and the pair carries the percentage adjustment applied and the weight the surveyor gave it. Weights are a fraction from 0 to 1. Adjustments centre on nothing much -- mean zero, standard deviation around 6 per cent -- and, obviously, a valuation never cites its own subject property as a comparable, which the old loader allowed and which is why two of last year's reports were nonsense.

Instructions come from lenders -- a lender being a name and a panel tier. Panel tiers are their own small table with a description and the contractual SLA in hours: tier 1 lenders are on 48 hours, the rest are looser and it belongs in the table rather than in a report. The instruction sits against a valuation with the time it came in, the tier, the SLA in hours, the product type and the time we returned it. We stamp the tier on the instruction as well as holding it on the lender, which is redundant -- the lender determines the tier -- and they must agree; likewise the SLA hours on the instruction are whatever the tier says. Nothing is returned before it was received.

Fees are invoiced per instruction, one invoice each: the fee amount, the VAT amount, the date invoiced and the date paid. Fees average about 285 pounds with a spread of 90. VAT is twenty per cent of the fee and is stored because the finance system wants it that way. An invoice is never dated before the instruction it bills was received, and never paid before it was invoiced.

We also keep a monthly regional index series -- region, month, index value -- which is what we revalue the book against; a region and a month together give you exactly one index value, the numeric series id on it is just a surrogate the last contractor added. There is an EPC feed landing on the same box that nobody has opened since 2023 and I am ignoring it here. Floor areas are supposed to be square metres, incidentally, and a chunk of the older rows are clearly square feet, and we have never cleaned it.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: 29 million addresses in the record table

domain: Amateur Football League Fixtures and Results
nl_description:
Backing store for a regional amateur football league, eleven divisions, currently being lifted off a pile of Access files.

Divisions are a reference table in their own right now rather than a string on the club record: eleven rows, each with a name and the tier it sits at, and the names are unique, so the division name tells you the tier. TEAM is keyed on an integer team_id and holds the club name, the year the club was founded, the division it plays in, and a reference to its home ground. A club never moves division anywhere in the history we hold, so the club name determines the division too, which is the one denormalisation I will defend.

Grounds are their own entity -- two or three clubs share a pitch -- and a ground carries a name, unique across the league, and a licensed capacity. Nothing in the league is licensed below 250. Under 2,000 the ground is all-seated, and we hold that as a flag on the ground rather than recomputing it in six reports.

MATCH is the interesting one. It points at the season it belongs to (a season is just a label like 2024-25 plus its opening and closing dates, and the label is unique so it determines both), at the ground it was played on, and at TEAM twice: home_team_id and away_team_id, both foreign keys into the same table, which is the bit every ORM tutorial skips. The two are never the same club. Fixtures are always staged at the home club's own ground, so the ground on the match is strictly the home team's home ground -- keep the column because it makes the queries readable, but it is derivable and the Access export disagreed with itself about it. Kick-off is a TIMESTAMP and has to fall inside its season's opening and closing dates.

home_goals and away_goals are non-negative integers, and goals for one side in one match are Poisson with lambda 1.4. Attendance is lognormal in log space, mean 6.1, variance 0.8. We never record a gate above the ground's licensed capacity. At an all-seated ground we cap the recorded gate at 1,800 on top of that. And where a ground is not all-seated the safety certificate limits us to half the licensed figure, so a gate above half of capacity there is a keying error, not a bumper crowd.

There is a flag on the match for whether it was a cup tie, because only cup ties go to extra time. Every goal also gets its own row, against the player who scored it -- and we do not record own goals separately, so the scorer always plays for one of the two clubs in that match -- and the minute it went in, so minute is an INTEGER in 1..120 to allow for extra time -- and a goal after the 90th minute belongs to a cup tie by definition. A player belongs to one team; we store the name, the position, a squad number between 1 and 99 which is unique inside his own club, and the age at registration -- normal, mean 26.5, sd 5.1. Positions run roughly 10 per cent goalkeeper, 32 per cent defender, 34 per cent midfielder, 24 per cent forward.

Volumes: 900 teams, 14K players, 400K matches back to 1994, about 2.6M goal rows.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: age at registration -- normal, mean 26.5, sd 5.1
goals for one side in one match are Poisson with lambda 1.4

domain: Gym Chain Membership and Group Classes
nl_description:
I run operations for a gym chain -- forty-one sites, two more opening before Christmas. It is all spreadsheets and it is falling over, so bear with me while I explain how the thing actually works.

People join. They pick one of our packages -- Off-Peak, Standard, Premium, and a Student one -- and each package has a monthly price and says whether it is one gym only or all of them. Premium is 54.99 a month and Standard is 34.99. The Student one is never more than 25, that is a rule marketing gave us and I have stopped arguing. The package name is the price, if you follow me: tell me the package and I can tell you what it costs and whether it gets you into all the sites, so I do not want that typed in anywhere else. Every member is tied to a home gym even though the Premium lot can walk into any site. For a member we need the name, the email -- we key off the email, no two people share one -- the date of birth and the date they signed up. A site is just a name and a town, and no two sites are called the same thing; we made that rule after the Bradford business.

Each site has one or two studios in it. A studio has a name and a capacity, which is simply how many bodies fit in the room, and the biggest room we own holds forty. A studio only ever belongs to one site, so once you know the studio you know the site, and I would rather not have the site written down twice.

Memberships are not forever and that is what the spreadsheets cannot cope with. Someone joins in March on Standard, upgrades to Premium in May, freezes in July because they are away, cancels in November. We need all of that as history -- when it started, when it ended if it has, what state it is in, and which package it was on -- not just where they stand today. An end date is always after the start date, and a membership never starts before the day the person signed up with us, both of which the spreadsheet cheerfully lets us get wrong.

Classes are messier. We run spin, yoga, HIIT, boxing, aquafit and a couple of others; each of those is a kind of class with a bit of blurb and a normal length, spin is 45 minutes and yoga is an hour, and the kind tells you the length. Then a real class happens: six o'clock on a Tuesday at the Leeds site, spin, in one of the studios, one named instructor taking it, a length, and a capacity. Those capacities average around 24 and vary either side by about 7, and they are never above 40, because that is our biggest studio -- and obviously a class cannot have a bigger capacity than the studio it is being held in. We do not schedule a class longer than the normal length for its kind either. Spin is the exception on numbers -- it is limited by bikes and nobody has more than 24 of those.

Members book onto a class, and the same person obviously cannot book the same class twice. You cannot book one after it has started, either, which the website used to allow, and nobody books one before the day they signed up with us. Afterwards we mark them as attended or a no-show -- that is the attendance on the booking -- and no-shows are about one in six and they are killing us.

Instructors are freelance. Each has an hourly rate somewhere between 22 and 45 depending on what they hold, spread fairly evenly across that, and each is only signed off to teach certain kinds of class -- the yoga people cannot take boxing, so a class only ever gets an instructor who is signed off for the kind of class it is. Each one is based at a site but covers others.

We settle up with the instructors monthly, and it is a claim per class: which class, which instructor, the month it is for, the hours they are claiming and what we actually paid them. Two rules there and I care about both. The instructor on the claim has to be the instructor who took that class -- last April we paid the wrong Sarah. And what we pay is never more than their hourly rate times the hours claimed, which sounds obvious, and yet.

Then there is ordinary gym use, nothing to do with classes: the turnstile logs who came in, which site, and when. Nobody comes through before the day they signed up, so if you see that it is bad data. That table is the monster -- about 250,000 a month across the chain and we keep two years of it.

Payments are monthly direct debit, and each one hangs off the membership it is paying for rather than just off the person, because otherwise we cannot say which package the money was for -- and the member on the payment is the member on that membership, needless to say. Amount, the date, and whether it went through -- roughly 4 per cent bounce. Around 60,000 people are paying us right now.

Oh, and the kit, since I am told it has to live somewhere. Every bit of equipment on the gym floor: which site it is at, what it is, the day we bought it, when it was last serviced, and how many months we are meant to leave between services. It cannot have been serviced before we bought it, which happened twice in the old sheet and nobody noticed.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: about 250,000 a month across the chain
Around 60,000 people are paying us right now.

nl_description:
I am the data lead at a race-timing outfit -- we do chip timing for road races, about 1,100 events a year across Europe. Here is roughly how I think about the model.

An event is the thing on the calendar: a name, a date, a host city. A name and a date together pin down the event; we have two Berlin events on different dates and one name reused by a different organiser. Inside one event there can be several races -- a marathon, a half, a 10K, sometimes a kids' fun run. Each race has its own distance in kilometres (42.2, 21.1, 10, 5), its own start time and its own entry fee. Fees run from 25 to 95 euros depending on the distance and are spread pretty evenly across that, and inside a single event the fee is a function of the distance -- two 10Ks at the same event never cost different amounts, the organisers would never hear the end of it.

Big races go off in waves rather than all at once. A wave has a letter, its own start time and a cap on how many entries we will put in it, and a wave letter is unique inside its race. A wave never goes off before the race's own start time. Every entry is assigned to a wave, and because a wave belongs to exactly one race, the wave on an entry tells you the race -- we still carry the race on the entry and the two have to agree.

A runner is a person and we keep them across events: name, date of birth, gender, and the club they run for if they run for one. A club has a name and a country, and a name is only unique within a country -- there are four Harriers in as many countries. Club sizes are wildly top-heavy: a handful of big city clubs supply an enormous share of the entries and there is a very long tail of clubs with two members each. That matters a lot when we generate test data.

An entry is one runner in one race. It has a bib number, which is between 1 and 99999 and is unique inside the race, the age group we assign, and once they have run, the gun time and the chip time in seconds plus a finish status. About 94 per cent finish, 4 per cent are DNF, and 2 per cent never start. The gun clock starts when the horn goes and the chip clock starts when you cross the mat, so a chip time is never slower than the gun time for the same entry, and the gap between them is never more than 20 minutes, which is the longest it has ever taken to clear a start pen. If someone does not finish we store a chip time of zero rather than a null -- a decision made in 2011 that we are stuck with. Marathon finishers average about four and a quarter hours with a spread of roughly 45 minutes either side. Nobody has ever run a marathon under 2h02, so any chip time below 7,320 seconds on the 42.2 is a mat error and we reject it. Half marathons and anything shorter have a four-hour cut-off, so for a race of 21.1 km or less we will not accept a chip time above 14,400 seconds.

The volume comes from splits. A race has timing points -- start mat, 5K, 10K, halfway and so on -- each with a name that is unique within the race and the distance along the course where it sits, which obviously cannot be further out than the race distance itself. Every runner crossing every mat is a row holding the elapsed seconds, which is never negative, and for anyone who actually finished no split can be later than that entry's own chip time. Six or seven mats per runner gives us north of 20 million split rows a year and about 90 million sitting in the warehouse, on top of 3.4 million entries.

a.basis: within the range of Zipf exponents the specifications state (n=30)

ground_truth_moments.evidence: about 1,100 events a year across Europe

domain: Cycling Club Ride Platform and Club Estate
nl_description:
Schema notes and handover for the club's ride-logging platform, which is now the whole estate rather than the activity feed it started out as. Read it as five things bolted together -- the telemetry ingest, the club calendar, the racing side, the coaching side, and the shop and insurance paperwork the committee lives in. They barely touch each other, which is exactly why the old one-database-per-feature answer has to go. 'Activity' and 'ride' mean the same thing in every conversation you will have here, and the code says ride.

Sizing first, because it drives the partitioning: 61,000 riders, 240,000 bikes, 1.9 million rides a year, and the raw telemetry on top of that at about 40 million trackpoints a week, which on its own dwarfs everything else in this document.

REGIONS AND MEMBERSHIP. Regions are a short reference list -- a region code, the region name, and the country it sits in -- so the code determines both and nothing else should be carrying a region string. A club has a name, unique across the federation so the name identifies the club, a founding year, and the region it is affiliated to. Riders are the people: a display name, an email that is unique to the individual, a date of birth, a sign-up timestamp, a body weight in kg and an FTP in watts. FTP is normal, mean 238, sd 46. Weights below 40 or above 140 are rejected on ingest. Each rider sits on one membership tier; the tier list carries a code, a description, the annual fee and whether the tier includes insurance, and the fee lives there rather than being copied onto every payment row. Clubs and riders are genuinely many-to-many: a rider can be in several clubs, a club has many riders, and the association itself carries a role, the date they joined and the date they left if they have left, so it is a junction keyed on (club_id, rider_id).

Racing licences are separate from membership and people confuse the two constantly. Licence categories are a reference list with a code, a description, the minimum age and whether a medical is required. A licence row holds the rider, the category, a licence number that is unique across the federation, the date it was issued and the date it expires, which is always after it was issued.

EQUIPMENT. Bike types are a short list -- road, gravel, mountain, TT -- each with a description and the minimum frame weight the type may legally be built to. About 62 per cent of bikes are road, 20 per cent gravel, 10 per cent mountain, 8 per cent TT. A bike belongs to a rider and carries its type, its frame weight in kg, the date it was purchased and the date it was retired once it is stood down, which is after the purchase date; a frame weight under the type's own minimum is a keying error and we block it on save. Components fitted to a bike are tracked because the workshop bills off them: the component type, the date it was fitted, the service interval in km and the distance since it was fitted, which is never negative and is never allowed past the interval -- that is the point the workshop job gets raised. Service records are their own history against the bike: the date it was serviced, which is never before the bike was purchased, the workshop name, the odometer reading in km and the cost. Head units are registered per rider with a make, a model, a firmware version and the date they were registered, because the firmware version explains about half of the bad files we get.

ROUTES. A route has a name, a distance, a total elevation gain, the rider who created it, and where it is a variant of another route a pointer at the parent route it was cut from -- a variant is always shorter than its parent, and that self-reference is the bit the last two ORMs got wrong. A route is cut into segments, each with a name, a length in metres, an average gradient percent which we clamp to the range -15 to 30 because sign errors happen constantly, its position along the route, and a surface. Surfaces are a reference list of their own: a code, a description, and whether the surface is sealed. No segment is longer than the route it sits on.

INGEST AND TELEMETRY. Every file arrives as an upload row: the rider, the head unit it came off, the upload timestamp, the file format, the byte size and a status. A ride then references its rider, the bike used, the upload it came from, and a route where we can match one -- often we cannot. It carries a start timestamp, a distance, a moving time, an elapsed time, an average power and its own elevation gain. Ride distance is lognormal, log-mean 3.5, log-variance 0.6. Moving time can never exceed elapsed time. The bike on a ride always belongs to the rider who logged it. Where we did match a route, the logged distance sits within a tenth of the route's own distance, so anything below nine tenths of it is a bad match and we drop it. Laps come straight off the head unit: one row per lap with a lap number counting from one, a distance, an elapsed time and an average power, and no lap is longer in time or further in distance than the ride that contains it. Inside a ride there is also one row per segment crossed, holding the time the effort started -- never before the ride's own start -- the elapsed time, which cannot be longer than the ride's own elapsed time either, and the average power for that effort. Effort counts per segment are viciously Zipfian with an exponent around 1.3: the town-sign sprint has millions of them, the farm track has four. Two sanity rules live there. A segment shorter than 1,000 m has never legitimately taken more than 300 seconds. And on anything averaging 8 per cent or steeper the effort's average power comes in at 200 W or more, because you cannot soft-pedal up it. Raw trackpoints are one per second per ride with latitude, longitude, heart rate, power and cadence. Heart rate is normal, mean 138, sd 18, and anything outside 30 to 230 bpm is a strap dropout rather than a person. Cadence is normal, mean 84, sd 12.

CLUB CALENDAR. Qualifications are a reference list with a code, a description, and whether holding it permits leading a group ride; riders hold them many-to-many, with the date it was awarded and the date it expires. A club schedules a group ride on a route at a time, with a pace group (A, B or C -- what those actually mean is a perennial argument), a named leader, and a maximum number of riders, which runs between 4 and 30 and is never above 12 for an A group because nobody shepherds more than that at pace. Riders sign up, again many-to-many, with a status and the time they signed up; a confirmed signup is never timestamped after the ride was scheduled to roll out. Signups split roughly 72 per cent confirmed, 11 per cent waitlisted, 17 per cent cancelled.

RACING. Race categories are a reference list: a code, a description, and the minimum licence category the category admits. A race event is hosted by a club on a date in a region, with a name and an entry limit. Inside one event there are several races, each with a name, a category, a distance, a start time and an entry fee. An entry is one rider in one race on one bike -- and the bike has to be the entering rider's own -- with a bib number between 1 and 999 that is unique inside that race, the date they entered, and a status. Results are one row per entry and only ever one: the finishing position, the finish time in seconds, and the points awarded. Finish times are lognormal, log-mean 8.6, log-variance 0.2.

COACHING. Coaches are staff rather than riders: a name, an accreditation level and the date they joined. A coaching plan ties a coach to a rider between a start date and an end date after it, with a weekly hours target. Below the plan sit planned workouts, each with the date it is scheduled for, a workout type, a target duration in seconds and a target power. When a rider actually does one we record the completion against the ride that satisfied it, with the date it was completed -- never before the workout was scheduled -- and a compliance percentage.

SAFETY AND FINANCE. Incident types are a reference list with a code, a description, and whether the type is reportable. An incident is raised against a ride with its type, when it occurred, when it was reported -- never before it occurred, and it has to be reported at all if the type is reportable -- a description, and whether an injury was reported. An insurance claim comes off an incident with the rider, the date it was submitted -- never before the incident itself occurred -- the date it was settled, the amount claimed and the amount settled; a settlement is never dated before the submission and never pays out more than was claimed. Claim amounts are lognormal, log-mean 6.2, log-variance 0.9. Subscription payments are annual: the rider, the tier, the amount, the date paid and a status -- and a payment that went through is for exactly the tier's annual fee, no rounding, no goodwill. About 97 per cent go through. The shop is small but it is in scope: kit products with a product code unique in the catalogue, a product name, a unit price and the stock on hand; orders against a rider with the date ordered, the date dispatched which is never earlier than the order, an order total, and a discount amount that never exceeds a quarter of that total; and order lines holding the product, the quantity ordered, the quantity dispatched -- never more than was ordered -- and the unit price charged, which never exceeds the catalogue price.

GOVERNANCE. Last piece is the audit trail the committee asked for after the leaderboard argument: every change names the table, the record key, the action, the field, the old value and the new value, the rider who made the change, and when it changed. On an update the old value has to be populated, and today it is not.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: Heart rate is normal, mean 138, sd 18

nl_description:
Right, so this is for the leisure centre pool. The council wants it computerised and I have been told to write down how the booking works, which I have never done before, so it might be a bit all over the place.

We have got six lanes. Depending on the hour the pool is either general swimming, or lane swimming, or it is a lesson, or the aqua-aerobics lot have it. Whatever it is, it is a slot on a particular day at a particular time with a price on it, and we write down how many people we will let in the water for that one. Only one thing is ever on in the pool at once, so the day and the time between them tell you which slot it is and what sort of slot it is. Never more than thirty in the water in total, and for lessons it is a lot tighter, eight, because that is what the teacher can watch. We also note how many lanes that slot is using, and obviously that cannot be more than six or fewer than one. Prices run from the 2.30 concession up to about eight quid for the aqua class, all sorts in between.

The lessons have a teacher. I do not need much about them beyond who they are and what level they are qualified to, but we do have to be able to say which teacher took which lesson, because parents ask. If it is a lesson there is always a teacher against it.

Then the people. We call them swimmers, the till system calls them customers, and the council's letter calls them users -- it is all the same person. Name, a phone number, which is how we look them up so no two share one, whether they live in the borough, and what sort of concession they get. The concessions are a list the council hands us: a short code, what it is called, and the fixed price where there is one -- so the code tells you the price. Pensioners are 2.30 no matter which slot it is; that is fixed by the council and it never changes. Roughly half of our lot pay full whack, about a quarter are pensioners, and the rest is students and children, rather more students than children.

A booking is one of them against one of the slots. When they booked it -- and you cannot book a slot after the day it is on, which the old form let people do -- which concession they claimed at the till, because it is not always the one on their record, how much they actually paid, and how many are in the party, because it is usually just the one person but every so often a family turns up on one booking, four or five of them. Very lopsided, that. A party can never be bigger than what we said we would let in the water for that slot. And whatever they paid, it is never more than the slot price times the number in the party -- that is the most we could possibly be owed. Where the concession they claimed has a fixed price, that is what they pay, no arguing.

It is not a big operation. Maybe nine hundred people on the list, a couple of thousand bookings in a month, and the whole thing currently lives in a ring binder and a Google Sheet that Denise looks after.

a.basis: within the range of Zipf exponents the specifications state (n=30)

ground_truth_moments.evidence: maybe nine hundred people on the list

nl_description:
Product analytics at an esports tournament platform. I will describe the model the way I understand it and the engineers can correct my types afterwards.

We support several game titles. A title has a publisher and a number of players per side, and that number drives a surprising amount of downstream logic. Title names are unique, so the name is as good as the id. Each title has its own set of maps, and a map is really just a name hanging off a title -- unique within that title, so two titles can both have a Dust.

Titles also ship patches, and we care because the meta moves under us. A patch belongs to a title, has a version string that is unique within the title, and the date it went live. A match records the patch it was played on, and no match is ever scheduled earlier than the date that patch went live -- when we see one, it is the ingest guessing.

Players have accounts: a handle, which is unique across the platform, a country, when they signed up, and an MMR that the matchmaker maintains. MMR is normally distributed, centred on 1500, standard deviation around 320. Anti-cheat sits over the top: a penalty row against an account with the penalty type, a reason in free text, the date it was issued and the number of days banned. Zero days means it was only a warning, and we do record it that way. A penalty is never dated before the account was created, obviously.

Teams -- the community says orgs, or squads, same thing -- have a name, a short tag that is unique across the platform, a region and a founding date. The regional split is roughly APAC 34 per cent, EU 30, NA 22, SA 9, MEA 5. A team's roster is many-to-many against accounts, because an account moves between teams over time, and each roster row says what role they play, when they joined -- never before the team was founded -- and whether they are a starter or a sub. Tournament participation works the same way: a tournament has many teams and a team enters many tournaments, and that association is where the seed and the final placement live.

A tournament belongs to a title and has a prize pool, a start date, a format and an entry fee, which is zero for most of the open ones and never negative. A tournament is then split into stages -- group stage, upper bracket, playoffs -- and a stage has a name, its number in the sequence, and a start date that is never before the tournament's own. Stage numbers are unique inside the tournament.

A match sits inside a stage, and since the stage belongs to a tournament the stage tells you the tournament. We do still carry the tournament on the match for query convenience, and it had better agree with the stage -- in the first version it did not, twice. A match is between two teams -- and yes, both of those point at the same team table, which caused us a lot of grief in the first version -- and the two are never the same team. It has a scheduled time, a best-of number between 1 and 7, and a winning team, which is always one of the two teams that played. Within a match, each game records which map it was on, its number in the series -- unique inside the match, and never higher than the match's best-of -- how long it lasted, and who won it -- and the game's winner is one of the match's two teams, same as the match winner is. Game duration is lognormal, log-mean 7.3, log-variance 0.35. Anything with a prize pool of a million or more is never a single game -- best-of-three at absolute minimum.

Per game per player we keep kills, deaths, assists and damage. Kills average about 7.5 per player per game and behave like a Poisson count. None of kills or deaths ever goes negative, which sounds obvious until you see what the ingest does with a crashed server.

Broadcasts are their own thing now that we run our own channels. A broadcast covers a match on a platform, in a language, with a named caster, and it has a start and an end after the start; a broadcast never starts before its match was scheduled. We sample the viewer count every ten seconds while a broadcast is live, so every sample carries the time it was taken -- which sits inside that broadcast's start and end, or it is garbage -- and the concurrent viewers, which are lognormal, log-mean 9.1, log-variance 1.4.

And there is a payouts table -- which tournament, which team, how much, and the date it went out, which is never before the tournament started. In a million-dollar event no single cheque is under 500 dollars, and no single cheque is ever more than half the pool either, because we always pay at least the top two.

Volume: roughly 90 million player-game stat rows a season, and the viewership samples are the same order of magnitude.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: MMR is normally distributed, centred on 1500, standard deviation around 320.
Kills average about 7.5 per player per game
Volume: roughly 90 million player-game stat rows a season

nl_description:
Handicap and scoring store for a members' golf club running WHS.

A course has a name, unique here since we only own two of them, a par and a hole count -- we own an 18 and a 9. Each course carries several tee sets, one per colour, so the course and the colour together identify the set, and the tee set is what holds the numbers that matter: course rating, slope rating, and total yardage. Slope is 55 to 155 by definition and is essentially uniform across that band in our data. No set we hold is under 4,100 yards.

The holes are modelled properly this time rather than as a number on the score row. A hole belongs to a course and carries its number, its par -- 3, 4 or 5, there is nothing else out there -- and its stroke index, 1 to 18. The course and the hole number together identify the hole.

A member has a name, a join date, a gender, a current handicap index and the WHS category, an integer 1 to 5, which is derived from the index and from nothing else: two members on the same index are always in the same category. Anyone at 5.4 or better is category 1. Indexes across the membership are normal, mean 16.2, sd 7.4, and the rules do not permit an index below -10 or above 54.

A round references the member and the tee set played. It stores the date, which is never before the member's join date, the gross score, the adjusted gross, the computed score differential, and the round type -- about 78 per cent of rounds are social and 22 per cent competition. Gross scores are normal, mean 91, sd 11. The adjusted gross is the gross with the per-hole cap applied, so it never comes out above the gross itself. Off the forward tees, meaning any tee set under 5,200 total yards, an adjusted gross above 120 is not credible, so the stored adjusted gross is capped at 120 there.

Below a round sits one row per hole: the hole it was played on, the hole number carried alongside it because every report we have asks for it and it has to agree with the hole, the strokes, and the putts. Putts per hole are Poisson, lambda 1.9, and a putt is a stroke, so putts never exceed strokes on the same row. For handicap purposes we will not record more than five over the hole's own par, which is the cap the committee settled on.

Handicap revisions are their own history table -- member, effective date, the new index and the reason it changed -- because auditors ask. A member gets at most one revision on any given date, and no revision predates the member's join date.

About 2,300 members, 340K rounds since 2009, just over 5 million hole rows.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: Indexes across the membership are normal, mean 16.2, sd 7.4
Gross scores are normal, mean 91, sd 11
Putts per hole are Poisson, lambda 1.9

nl_description:
We are a small sports academy, after school and weekends, and I have been asked to explain what we need to keep track of. I am not technical so this will be in my own words.

The kids are the main thing. We call them players, or athletes if we are being posh, and there are about two hundred and forty of them on the books across roughly ninety families. For each one we need the first and last name, when they were born because everything here is age-banded, which sport they do, and any medical bits -- inhalers, allergies, that sort of thing, written out longhand because it never fits in a box. Football is the big one, getting on for half of them. Netball and athletics are about a fifth each and the rugby lot are whatever is left.

Every child has a grown-up attached -- guardian is the word on the county's form, so let us use that. Mum, dad, gran, sometimes a foster carer -- we just need who they are, a mobile, an email, and what they are to the child, because if a kid goes over on an ankle we are not ringing round guessing. The mobile is how we tell them apart; two guardians never share one. One guardian often has two or three kids with us.

The kids are grouped into squads -- Under-9 girls' netball, that kind of thing -- and a squad has one coach running it, a name, its age band and the sport. The name says it all, mind: if you read me the squad name I can tell you the age band and the sport without looking anything up. A child is only ever put in a squad for their own sport, which sounds obvious but the old spreadsheet let us do it. We never put more than twenty in a squad, and under six is not worth running so we do not. If it is one of the volunteer dads taking the squad rather than a paid coach we keep it to a dozen at most, because they are not insured for more than that. For coaches we need the name, whether they are volunteer or paid, and the expiry on their background check -- that one is not optional, the county asks for it every year.

We train in three or four places -- venues, if you want the word the council uses -- the school hall, the astro, the leisure centre up the road. Each venue has a name, which is unique, an address, and a capacity, meaning how many kids it will safely take. We do not put a squad in a place that holds fewer than the squad's own limit; that was the fire officer's point and it is fair enough.

A squad trains on a schedule. Each training session is a date, a start time, the place, and the duration in minutes -- normally ninety, though about a third of them are just the hour. We also write down which coach actually took it, because it is not always the squad's own coach when somebody is away, and whoever took it has to have a background check that has not expired by the date of the session. For every session we tick each child off as there, not there, or late -- the attendance sheet, and the status on it is present, absent or late. Most turn up, somewhere around four in five, a bit over one in ten just does not appear, and there is always a handful arriving late.

The money side is simple. We send the families an invoice monthly: the amount, the month it is for, how many sessions we are billing for, the date we sent it, and the date they paid it if they have. One invoice per family per month, so the family and the month tell you the amount. It works out at six pounds a session, so the amount never comes to more than six times the number of sessions billed, and it lands anywhere from thirty to sixty pounds depending on how many the child is down for -- and obviously never a negative number. They cannot have paid it before we sent it, and if it is marked paid then there had better be a date against it.

Oh -- there is a physio who comes in on Thursdays, but she does her own paperwork and none of it comes near us.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: there are about two hundred and forty of them on the books across roughly ninety families.

nl_description:
I am a personal trainer, one-man band, and I want to get off paper.

Twenty-eight clients on the books at the moment. For each one I want the name, a mobile number, what they are actually after -- weight loss, strength, marathon prep, whatever they told me in the consult -- when they started with me, how many sessions they have got left in the tank, and what I charge them an hour. The rate is not the same for everybody: if they have bought a block of ten up front it is forty an hour, otherwise it is fifty, and I need the system to know which of those they are on. Sessions left cannot go below zero; that is the whole point of tracking it.

The blocks themselves want writing down properly, because at the moment they are on the back of an envelope. A block is a client buying a batch up front: the date they bought it, how many sessions it was for, how many of those they have used, and what they paid me for it. Used can obviously never be more than they bought. A block is always forty a session, so what they paid is the number of sessions times forty, and nothing gets bought before the client started with me.

Then the sessions themselves. Date and time, how long, where -- their house, the park, or the unit I rent on Fridays -- whether it was off a block or paid one-off, and whether it actually happened. Most do, call it seven in eight; about one in twelve gets cancelled and the odd one is a straight no-show, maybe one in twenty-five -- that is the status on the session. And what I charged for it, because a cancellation inside 24 hours still gets billed and I want to see that in black and white. An hour is the standard, a fair few do forty-five minutes, and I do a handful of half-hour top-ups -- call it six in ten, three in ten, one in ten. Nothing under half an hour and nothing over ninety minutes, and since ninety minutes is the longest I do, what I charge for a single session never comes to more than one and a half times their hourly rate. No session is dated before the client started, and a session that came off a block is never dated before that block was bought.

Last bit is the measurements. Every four to six weeks I weigh them, do the calipers and take a resting heart rate, and none of that is ever dated before they started with me either. My lot average around seventy-eight and a half kilos with a fair spread, twelve or thirteen kilos either way, and body fat sits around twenty-five per cent give or take six and a half. I will not write down a body fat reading under 4 per cent, that is the calipers lying to me.

Two thousand sessions in the diary since I started, so it is small -- I just want it searchable.

std.basis: coefficient of variation in [0.006, 0.682], the full range exhibited by stated spread parameters (n=117), applied to the stated mean

nl_description:
Notes for whoever builds the new system at the climbing centre. I am the duty manager and I know just enough SQL to be dangerous, so treat the shapes as suggestions and the rules as gospel.

Start with the walls, since everything hangs off one. A wall has a name -- Cave, Slab, the Arch and so on, all unique -- a height in metres, and a flag for whether it is a bouldering wall. Nothing in the building is over 16 metres and nothing under 3. The bouldering walls only ever carry boulder problems; you cannot put a lead line on a four-metre wall.

The walls have things on them. We call them routes, the boulderers call them problems, and the setters write 'lines' on the whiteboard -- it is one concept and I genuinely do not care what you name it. Each one lives on one of the walls, has a grade, a hold colour so people can find it, the date it went up, and the date it came down if it has come down yet, which is obviously after it went up. Some are boulder problems, some are lead, a few are top-rope only: about seven in ten boulder, two in ten lead, the rest top-rope. We write down who set it -- they are all staff and their details already sit in the rota system, so a name in a field is enough on our side.

Climbers register once. Display name, which the app makes them pick unique so it is as good as an id, the date they registered, when their waiver runs out -- always after they registered -- and what they are to us: a member, a day-pass punter, or a student rate. Roughly 58 per cent members, 34 per cent day pass, 8 per cent student.

Logging is the interesting part. A climber logs an ascent of a route: when they logged it, how many goes it took, and the style. Attempt counts are savagely long-tailed -- most things go first or second try, but there is always somebody forty attempts into a project -- Zipf-ish with an exponent around 1.8. It is at least one attempt by definition, and if the style is recorded as a flash then it is exactly one attempt, because that is what the word means. Two more things about the timestamp on an ascent: it is never before the route went up, it is never after the route came down where the route has come down, and nobody logs anything on an expired waiver, so it is never after their waiver runs out either.

Separately, the door scanner logs visits: the time in, the time out after it, and the minutes between. Session length averages about ninety-five minutes but the tail is long -- students park themselves in here all afternoon -- so it is exponential rather than anything symmetric. Nothing shorter than five minutes counts as a visit, and anything over ten hours is the scanner having missed the exit. A visit cannot be before the climber registered and cannot be after their waiver has run out, same as an ascent -- the turnstile is supposed to enforce that and does not.

We are busy: around 11,000 registered climbers, 300,000-odd visits logged, and about 1.4 million ascent rows, because the app nags people to log.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: Session length averages about ninety-five minutes

nl_description:
Data model for the EDC back end of a phase III oncology programme; I am specifying it, not asking whether we need it. One row per protocol at the top, with its code, title, phase and therapeutic area -- the protocol code is unique and is what the sponsor's systems key on, so the code alone hands you the trial row, its phase and its therapeutic area. Every activated site hangs off exactly one protocol: ninety-odd sites across fourteen countries, each with a site name, a country, an activation date, the enrolment cap we agreed with the site, and a running enrolled count that must never overtake that cap. A site has one principal investigator who, in this system, never appears at more than one site, so the site pins the investigator as tightly as the investigator pins the site. Arms belong to the protocol rather than to a shared lookup, because the dose text is protocol-specific; there are two per protocol, treatment and control, randomised 2:1, so allocation lands at 0.667 treatment / 0.333 control and the arm row carries that weight along with the planned dose in mg per cycle.

Roughly 42,000 subjects, each pinned to one site and one arm, carrying consent date, age at consent (INTEGER, protocol window 18 to 89), sex, baseline ECOG performance status on the usual 0-4 integer scale, baseline weight in kg -- normal, mean 71.4, sd 14.8 -- and the number of days from consent to first dose, which is exponential with rate about 0.11. Nobody consents at a site before that site is activated. Visits are child rows on the subject: cycle number 1 through 12, protocol nominal day, actual date, completion status. Nothing about a subject predates consent, so a visit's actual date is never earlier than the subject's consent date. The nominal day is not per-subject data at all -- the protocol schedule fixes it from the cycle number, and every visit at cycle 3 anywhere in the programme carries the same nominal day -- but it is written on the visit row because that is what the CRF exports.

Dosing is recorded per visit: the visit, the arm the dose was given under, the administered dose in mg, the timestamp, and a reduction reason. No dose is stamped before the visit it belongs to. A dose never exceeds the planned dose on that arm, and where it comes in under the planned dose there has to be a reduction reason recorded. Toxicity reductions in this programme are floored, so an administered dose is also never below half the arm's planned dose -- anything lower is a discontinuation, not a reduction.

A visit may collect specimens with a collection timestamp and a draw volume in mL; a specimen is never stamped before the visit it was taken at. Specimen types are a small reference list -- blood, biopsy, urine -- each with a description and the nominal volume in mL for that type of draw, and a draw is never more than the nominal volume for its type nor less than a tenth of it. Specimens fan out to assay results -- analyte code, numeric value, unit, lab flag -- and each result names the central laboratory that produced it, since we use three of them and audit needs the lab's accreditation on file; lab names are unique, so the name is as good a key as the id. Each result also names the reference range it was read against -- always the range for that same analyte at that same laboratory, the analyte code and the lab id sit on both rows and they have to agree -- and those ranges are held per laboratory per analyte with a lower limit and an upper limit, the upper always above the lower. A value above its range's upper limit is flagged HIGH and one below the lower limit is flagged LOW; that is arithmetic the extract should not be re-deriving at query time. Note the unit is a property of the analyte at a given laboratory rather than of the individual measurement, even though it is written on every result row. Result values are log-normal, log mean 1.1 and log variance 0.8. That table is the volume driver: about 4.6 million rows.

Safety data attaches to the subject, not the visit. Adverse events carry a MedDRA preferred term, the system organ class that term rolls up into -- the preferred term determines the class, MedDRA is a fixed hierarchy and we do not get to choose -- a CTCAE grade 1-5, onset and resolution dates, a seriousness boolean and an outcome; observed grade mix is 46 / 31 / 15 / 6 / 2 percent from grade 1 upward. An event never resolves before it onset, and never onsets before the subject consented. Grade 5 means death, so grade = 5 forces outcome 'FATAL'. Separately, a grade 3 or worse event in a subject who was 75 or older at consent sets the geriatric dose-review flag. Concomitant medications are also per subject: drug name as free text, indication, start and stop, and a stop that is populated is never before the start; we only hold medications from consent onward, so no start date precedes the consent date either. Protocol deviations are recorded against the visit where they happened, with a category, a narrative and a report date that is never earlier than the visit's actual date; a deviation on a visit whose completion status came back 'MISSED' always takes category 'VISIT_NOT_DONE'.

Handover for the replacement LIMS in the clinical genomics service. Read this as the whole estate rather than one extract: it swallows the three systems we run today -- the accessioning spreadsheet, the run tracker on the sequencer share, and the interpretation database -- and it has to carry the audit trail the last accreditation visit said we did not have. Sizing, because it drives the partitioning: about 14,000 clinical orders a year against roughly 16,000 biosamples, 2,400 sequencing runs, and the variant call table on its own is past 60 million rows and grows by 9 million a quarter, which is bigger than everything else here put together.

CLIENTS, CONSENT AND PANELS. Work comes in from ordering clients -- referring trusts, research institutes and a couple of commercial labs -- each with a client name, an institution type, a country, and the start and end date of their contract, the end never earlier than the start. A sequencing project sits under exactly one client and carries a project code that is unique across the service, so the code on its own hands you the project, its PI name and the client it belongs to; it also carries the consent type it was opened under, the date it opened and the date it closed -- a project never closes before it opened, and it never opens before its client's contract started. Consent types are a short coded list with a description and two flags: whether research use is permitted and whether we may recontact. Test panels are the catalogue we actually sell: a panel code that is likewise unique, a panel name, a gene count, a list price and a turnaround target in days, and the code fixes the target and the price. Panel membership is many to many against the gene list -- a gene sits on several panels and a panel carries hundreds of genes -- so the membership row is keyed on the panel and the gene together and records whether the gene is core to that panel. Genes are held once, with an HGNC symbol that is unique, the chromosome they sit on and a transcript length in bp; the symbol therefore tells you the gene and its chromosome.

ORDERS AND SAMPLE RECEIPT. A clinical order names the project and the panel requested, with the timestamp it was ordered, the timestamp we received it -- never before it was ordered -- a priority, an order status, and the turnaround in days we stamp on it when it closes. Turnaround has to beat the target held on the panel; that number belongs in the panel row rather than hard-coded in a report, which is how we came to quote three different figures to the same trust last year. An urgent order has to land inside half of that same target. No order is received before its own project opened, either. Biosamples arrive against an order with an external sample ref, a tissue type, the timestamp the material was collected, the timestamp we received it (never before collection, and never before we received the order it came in against), a DNA concentration in ng/uL, a volume in uL, a RIN between 1.0 and 10.0, and an accession status. Tissue types are their own list with a description, a flag for whether the material is FFPE, and the minimum input mass in ng we ask for. FFPE material is degraded, so an FFPE biosample is only accessioned at all when its RIN is 2.0 or better.

EXTRACTION AND LIBRARY PREP. Extractions run in batches. A batch carries a protocol name, a start and a finish timestamp with the finish never before the start, a sample count, and the lead scientist who ran it. Each extraction row names its biosample and its batch and holds the input mass in ng, the eluate volume in uL, the yield in ng, and who performed it -- and in this lab a batch is worked end to end by its lead, so the performer on an extraction is always the batch's own lead. Keep the column because the bench sheet has it, but understand it is derivable from the batch and it has been inconsistent in the old export. An extraction never takes more mass in than the biosample actually holds, which is that sample's concentration multiplied by its volume. Libraries are prepped one or more per extraction: the prep kit, the input in ng, the achieved insert size in bp, an index barcode, the molarity in nM, the prep date and who prepped it. Prep kits are a reference list with a description, the vendor, the target insert size in bp and the minimum input in ng the kit is validated down to. A library is never prepped below its kit's minimum input, and never above what its own extraction actually yielded, and the achieved insert size has to sit within twenty percent either side of the kit's target -- above 1.2 times the target or below 0.8 times it and the library goes back for a re-prep.

REAGENTS. Reagent lots are tracked per kit with a lot number that is unique and has the kit code in it, the date received, the expiry date (always later than receipt), the quantity received and the quantity remaining, which can never exceed the quantity received. Every draw is a consumption row naming the lot, the library it went into, the quantity used and the timestamp it was consumed -- and a lot is never consumed after its expiry date, nor before it arrived, nor for more than the quantity that lot arrived with. That pair of rules is what closed our last CAPA.

INSTRUMENTS AND RUNS. Instruments carry a serial number that is unique to the machine, an install date, a retirement date once they are stood down -- after the install date, naturally -- and a running total run count. Each instrument is of an instrument model, and the model list is short: a description, the vendor, the maximum read length and the lanes per run, so the model fixes both of those and nothing on the instrument row should be restating them. Maintenance is an event row per instrument: the event type, when it was performed, the engineer who did it, whether it passed, an engineer note, and the date the next one falls due, which is always later than the one just done, and no maintenance predates the machine's own install date. A maintenance event that did not pass has to carry an engineer note, and that is the one rule the current tracker silently lets through. A sequencing run names its instrument and its operator and carries the run folder, a start and a finish timestamp (finish never before start), the chemistry, the read length, the cycle count and a run status; no run predates the install date of the machine it ran on, and the run folder is unique on the share and has the machine in its name, so from the folder you know both the run and the instrument. Everything here is paired-end, so the cycle count is never less than twice the read length. Lanes hang off the run, numbered from one, each with a cluster density in thousands per mm2, a Q30 fraction, the total reads and the reads passing filter, which plainly cannot exceed the total. On S4 chemistry we hold lanes to a Q30 of at least 0.85, capped at 1.0. Libraries are pooled across lanes many to many, so the pool membership row is keyed by lane plus library together and carries the intended fraction of the pool, a fraction between 0 and 1. Anything that went wrong on a run is a deviation row -- the run, a category, when it was raised and who raised it, a narrative, and when it was resolved, never before it was raised -- and nothing is raised against a run before that run started.

ANALYSIS. An analysis job names the run, the library and the pipeline version, with a submitted and a completed timestamp (completed never before submitted), an exit status, and the CPU hours it burned. A job is never submitted before the run it reads has finished. Pipeline versions are their own record: a version tag, the date it was released, the reference build and a validated flag. Clinical work only ever completes on a validated version, and enforcing that is half the reason the table exists. Alignment metrics are stored per job -- mean coverage, duplicate rate, total read pairs, mapped read pairs which are never more than the total, callable fraction, and a QC status. QC status goes to FAIL whenever the duplicate rate exceeds 0.30, and equally whenever fewer than seventy percent of the total read pairs mapped.

VARIANTS AND INTERPRETATION. Variant calls are the volume table. Each names its analysis job and the gene it falls in, plus a chromosome, a position, ref and alt allele, genotype, the depth (never negative), the alt depth which cannot exceed the depth, the allele fraction in [0, 1], a QUAL score and a filter status. The chromosome is written on the call as well even though the gene already fixes it -- the VCF has it in every row and we kept it. Anything under depth 10 gets filter status LOW_DEPTH. Calls per gene are savagely uneven, Zipf-like with an exponent about 1.35, because the long genes dominate. Anything we intend to report is classified: an ACMG class, an evidence summary, who classified it and when, and who reviewed it and when. A review never predates the classification and is never done by the person who classified it. A call classified PATHOGENIC always has a reviewer named.

REPORTING AND SIGN-OUT. A clinical report is issued against the order -- one report per order, so the order pins the report -- with the timestamp it was issued, which is never earlier than the timestamp we received the order, who drafted it, who signed it out, and a report status. A report is never signed out by the person who drafted it, and an issued report is only ever signed out by someone holding the consultant clinical scientist qualification, which is the one flagged in the qualification list as permitted to sign out. Which classified variants a report carries is many to many, keyed on the report and the classification together, with a flag for whether that finding is the primary one.

BILLING. Charges are posted against the order with a billing code, an amount, a discount amount and a posting date, and nothing is posted before we received the order. Billing codes carry a description and a list amount; a charge never exceeds its code's list amount, and the discount we are permitted to give is capped at half of that list amount.

PEOPLE. Lab staff have a name, a registration number unique to the individual, a joining date, an active flag and a primary qualification. Qualifications are their own list with a description, a seniority rank and the sign-out flag mentioned above. Behind the primary one we hold every competency a staff member holds, keyed on the person and the qualification, with the date it was awarded and the date it expires, the expiry always after the award, and nothing awarded before the person joined -- a lapsed competency is not a competency. Training courses are separate from competencies: a course name, when it was completed and when the completion lapses, again after completion, and again never before they joined.

AUDIT. Every change to any of this is an audit row naming the table, the record key, the action, the field, the old value and the new value, the staff member who made the change and when. On an update the old value must be populated. That is the accreditation finding, and it is the reason the rebuild is funded.

Fitted distributions from the current systems: DNA concentration is log-normal, log mean 3.1 and log variance 0.6. RIN sits at 8.1 with an sd of 0.9. Mean coverage is normal at 38.5 with an sd of 6.0. Allele fraction for heterozygous calls clusters near 0.48 with an sd of 0.09. Turnaround in days is log-normal, log mean 2.5 and log variance 0.35. CPU hours per job are log-normal too, log mean 2.1 and log variance 0.5. Order priority splits 78 percent routine, 18 percent urgent and 4 percent critical. ACMG classes come out 41 percent benign, 22 percent likely benign, 28 percent VUS, 6 percent likely pathogenic and 3 percent pathogenic.
