RIN sits at 8.1 with an sd of 0.9
Allele fraction for heterozygous calls clusters near 0.48

nl_description:
Spec for the regional air-quality archive we are rebuilding off the old flat files. A monitoring station has a station code that is unique across the network, a site classification, lat/long, elevation and a commissioning date; the code is what the national return keys on, so it settles both the station and its classification. Across the 214 stations the classification mix is about 42 percent urban traffic, 33 percent urban background, 18 percent rural background and 7 percent industrial.

Each station hosts one or more analysers, and an analyser measures exactly one pollutant, so the analyser row carries its station, its pollutant, a model, a serial number that is unique to the box, a non-negative detection limit and a top of scale. The top of scale is always above the detection limit, and it is never below the statutory limit value of the pollutant the analyser is on -- an instrument that saturates below the limit value cannot record the exceedance we bought it to record, and we have two of those in the field today. Pollutants are a small reference table: a pollutant code, a reporting unit, the statutory limit value, and the averaging period in hours, which is never below 1 or above 24. The unit and the limit value belong to the pollutant code and to nothing else.

The fact table is the hourly measurement against the analyser -- one row per analyser per hour, so the analyser and the timestamp together identify the observation without needing the surrogate id at all -- with the concentration, a QC flag, the co-located ambient temperature and a validated boolean. Concentrations are strongly right-skewed and log-normal, log mean 2.9 with log variance 0.55; ambient temperature is normal, 14.2 C with sd 8.6. A row may only be marked validated if its concentration lies inside the recording envelope of the analyser that produced it -- at or above that analyser's detection limit and at or below its top of scale. Raw rows outside that band stay in the archive but never get the validated tick, and the old loader compared them against a pair of hard-coded numbers instead of the instrument's own, which is the bug that started this rebuild.

Analysers get span-gas calibrations: a timestamp, the span gas concentration, the percent drift (kept within plus or minus 10, and normally distributed around zero with sd 1.4) and a pass boolean. Drift beyond 5 percent is a fail by definition. Span gas is dosed inside the instrument's own recording range too -- at or above its detection limit and never above its top of scale.

Reporting completeness is its own record now, because the funders ask for it monthly: one summary row per analyser per month with the month start, the hours we expected, the hours we actually captured -- which plainly cannot be more than we expected -- and a reportable flag. A month where the captured hours came in below three quarters of the expected hours is not reportable, full stop.

Finally, exceedance alerts point at the offending observation and carry a severity, a raise timestamp -- never earlier than the observation it was raised on -- and whether the authority was told; where the observed concentration is above 150, notification is mandatory. Volume: 38 million observation rows today, plus about 4.5 million a year.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: Across the 214 stations the classification mix is about 42 percent urban traffic, 33 percent urban background, 18 percent rural background and 7 percent industrial.
ambient temperature is normal, 14.2 C with sd 8.6.
kept within plus or minus 10, and normally distributed around zero with sd 1.4

nl_description:
Notes toward the schema for the state seismic network's analysis database. Stations are identified by network code plus station code -- that pair is what every exchange format uses and it identifies the station on its own, the surrogate id is ours alone -- with lat/long, elevation and a vault type: posthole, tunnel, surface vault, we have not standardised that vocabulary yet.

Channels hang off the station: a channel code, a sample rate in Hz, a gain, an azimuth in degrees and a dip. The station plus the channel code is likewise unique. Every channel names the sensor model it is running, and the model list is worth holding properly because it is where the instrument's own limits live -- a description, the manufacturer, a nominal sensitivity, the minimum and maximum sample rate the sensor is rated for, and a strong-motion flag. A channel is never configured outside the rated band of its own sensor model, which is a check the current config loader does not do and it is how we ran a broadband at 200 Hz for six weeks. The channel row also still carries the free-text sensor type string from the old dataless files; it is redundant now, because the model settles it, but the analysts grep on it. Sample rates across the network are roughly 20 Hz for 18 percent of channels, 40 Hz for 24 percent, 100 Hz for 51 percent and 200 Hz for the remaining 7 percent, and a channel whose model is flagged strong motion is never run below 100 Hz.

Events carry an origin time, hypocentre lat/long, a depth from 0 to 700 km (and depth is essentially exponentially distributed with a mean near 12 km, so rate about 0.083), an event type, a single-letter location quality and the location RMS residual in seconds. An event with an RMS residual worse than 1.5 seconds never gets quality 'A', whatever the analyst thinks of it.

Phase picks are the volume -- past 240 million rows -- each tying an event to a channel with a phase label, an arrival time, a timing uncertainty in seconds that is log-normal with log mean -2.3 and log variance 0.4, a polarity, and the initials of whoever made the pick. A pick never arrives before the origin time of the event it is attached to. One phase per channel per event, so the event, the channel and the phase label together identify the pick and its arrival time.

Magnitudes are separate rows per event so ML, Mw and mb can coexist -- one row per type per event, which is what makes the type plus the event the real key -- with the value between -2.0 and 9.5, the contributing station count, an uncertainty, and a preferred flag. Gutenberg-Richter means magnitude is exponentially distributed with rate about 2.3. An estimate built from fewer than three stations is never preferred, nor is one whose uncertainty is above 0.5, and a local magnitude ML is never preferred for an event deeper than 300 km.

Waveform segments record the channel, the event they were cut for, a start time, a duration in seconds, a sample count and the archive path; one segment per channel per start time. A segment cut for an event starts no later than that event's origin time, because the pre-event window is the whole point. The sample count is the duration times the channel's sample rate, and since 20 Hz is the floor anywhere on this network a segment never holds fewer samples than twenty times its duration in seconds.

We also keep a log of channel outages -- when the channel went dark, when it came back, which is never before it went dark, and why, though the why is free text and nobody fills it in consistently.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: depth is essentially exponentially distributed with a mean near 12 km
Phase picks are the volume -- past 240 million rows

nl_description:
I look after the herbarium here and honestly the current arrangement is a card index plus three spreadsheets that disagree with each other, so we would like something proper.

What we hold is sheets -- pressed, dried plants glued to card -- a bit under nine thousand of them, which is small by herbarium standards but it is a hundred and forty years of work. Every sheet gets an accession number when it comes in, and no two sheets have ever shared one, so if you have the accession number you have the sheet and there is nothing else to look up. We write down when it was collected, what state the sheet is in (good, fair, poor -- roughly six in ten are good, three in ten fair, and the rest we would rather nobody handled), how tall the pressed specimen is on the card, and whether it is a type. A type is the actual sheet the original published description was based on, which makes it irreplaceable. Heights are mostly around thirty or thirty-one centimetres because that is the size of the card; the smallest scraps are two centimetres of moss and the tallest thing we have folded onto a sheet is about a hundred and twenty.

Then there is the name -- the botanists say taxon and I have given up arguing, so use their word -- which has to be its own thing, because names change and plenty of sheets share a name -- family, genus, species, who published it, and the common name if it has one. And the genus settles the family on its own; every Quercus is in the beech family whether the label says so or not, so we should not be writing the family down twice and getting two answers. Three families account for a third of the whole collection and then there is an enormous tail of families we hold one or two sheets of, so the count of sheets per taxon is as lopsided as it gets.

And where it came from, the locality as the collectors write it on the label: a place name, the region, the country, the latitude and longitude if the label bothered to say, and the altitude. We keep one row per place and we spell the place name one way, so the place name gives you the region and the country -- that was the whole reason for splitting it out, because the spreadsheets had the same valley in two countries. Most of our collecting is lowland, a couple of the Andean sheets are up over four thousand metres and there is one from a salt flat twenty metres below sea level.

Collectors are the awkward part. A sheet often has more than one person on the label -- a lead collector and whoever was with them -- so you cannot just put one name on the sheet. We need to be able to say which people collected which sheet and what each of them was doing, and for each collector we keep their institution and roughly when they were active, meaning the year they started. And nothing should ever come out saying a person collected a sheet before they started collecting; we have two of those in the spreadsheet at the moment and both are typos. Something else: when a botanist collects a plant they usually press several duplicates to send to other herbaria, and we note how many went out. It is usually one or two, sometimes five or six.

Last thing, and it matters for insurance -- we lend sheets to other institutions. We keep a short list of the places we lend to: the institution, the city, the country, and the longest we will let that particular place keep something, because we trust the big national herbaria for a good deal longer than a university that has lost two things. A loan record says which sheet, which of those institutions borrowed it, when it went, when it is due back -- which is obviously after it went out -- when it actually came back, which is never before it went out either, and what state it was in when it did. Nothing goes out before it was collected, which sounds too obvious to write down until you meet the row we have for a sheet collected in 1962 and lent in 1957. Loans are written for a number of days, normally about a hundred and eighty, and never for more days than that institution's own limit allows. If it came back later than the date it was due, the record gets ticked as overdue, and that is the report the registrar actually reads. And a type never physically leaves the building. If somebody wants a type we send photographs, and the loan record gets ticked as photographs only. Same for anything we have marked poor -- photographs only, no argument.

nl_description:
We are the research office, and the reporting we owe the funders is currently three people with spreadsheets, so here is what we think we need. Start with people: every researcher sits in one department, and we hold their ORCID -- which is unique to the person and is honestly a better handle than our own internal id -- plus career stage, appointment date and their h-index, which we refresh from Scopus; it is a stored number, not something we compute. Departments roll up into faculties, so a faculty is its own record with a faculty name, the dean and a headcount, and each department carries its own headcount too. A department's headcount can obviously never be larger than the headcount of the faculty it sits in, and the fact that we have three spreadsheets where it currently is larger is roughly why we are doing this. Department names are unique across the university, so the name tells you the department and which faculty it belongs to.

Grants are the centre of it. A grant is awarded by one funding agency -- we keep the agency name, which is unique, its country, its type (national council, charity, industry, EU) and its overhead rate, and the rate is a property of the agency, not of the individual award -- and has one lead researcher, a title, an awarded amount, the overhead amount we are allowed to charge on top, start and end dates with the end after the start, a duration in months and a status. Durations run between 6 and 60 months in practice. Awards are wildly spread: median around 220 thousand, from small travel awards up to programme grants in the tens of millions, so log-normal with a log mean near 12.3. Whatever the agency's rate says, the overhead amount never comes to more than a third of the awarded amount -- that is a university rule and it overrides the funder's arithmetic. Anything awarded over 2 million needs council sign-off, and for a charity funder that threshold drops to half a million.

The complication is that a grant has several investigators, not just the lead, each with a role and an FTE fraction between 0.05 and 1.0, so that has to be its own thing keyed on the grant and the person together. Grants involving people also need ethics approval before they can spend: an approval record carries a reference that is unique, the committee that issued it, the date it was approved and the date it expires, the expiry after the approval. No grant starts before its approval is in place, so the approval date is never later than the grant's start date, and the approval has to still be live at that point, so its expiry falls after the start date too. Nobody is an investigator on a grant that started before they were appointed, either -- we have two of those and both are data entry.

Money. Each grant is broken into budget lines -- one line per spend category, so the grant and the category together identify the line -- with a budgeted amount and a spend-to-date that we roll up nightly and which must never exceed the budgeted amount on that line. Individual expenditure rows are posted against the grant and against the budget line they draw on, with a category, an amount and a posting date. No single expenditure exceeds the budgeted amount of the line it is posted to. The category is written on the expenditure as well as on the line, which is redundant -- the line already fixes it, and where the two disagree the line wins. Nothing is posted before the grant starts or after it ends. Equipment purchases just come through as one of those categories; we do not track assets separately.

Then publications -- about 340,000 records and 900,000 authorship links, which is why authorship also has to be keyed on the paper and the person, with the author position and whether they were corresponding. A paper sits in one journal (journal name, ISSN, publisher, impact factor, an open-access flag, and the APC list price the journal advertises) and carries a DOI, a publication date, an article type -- we lump journal articles, conference papers and preprints in the same place -- and a citation count. The ISSN is unique, and it settles the publisher and the impact factor on its own; the DOI likewise identifies the paper and the journal it came out in. Impact factor is never negative and is log-normally spread. Citation counts are never negative and about as skewed as data gets: Zipf-ish with an exponent around 1.6, a handful of papers with thousands of citations and most of them under five. The article processing charge actually paid is recorded on the paper, it never exceeds the journal's advertised APC list price, and if the journal is not open access that charge should be zero. Papers acknowledge grants, and a paper can acknowledge several while a grant gets acknowledged by many, so that link is keyed on both as well.

Progress reporting: each grant has milestone reports with a due date, a submitted date, an outcome and a reviewer score on a 1-5 scale -- mostly 4s at about 44 percent, then 24 percent 5s, 22 percent 3s, 7 percent 2s and 3 percent 1s. A report due date always falls inside the grant, so never after the grant's end date, nothing is submitted before the grant started, and a report handed in after its own due date is recorded with outcome 'LATE' regardless of what the reviewer thought of it.

nl_description:
This is for the reserve's collaring work, and I should say up front that I am a field ecologist, not a database person. We put transmitters on animals and we need to stop losing the data in spreadsheets.

So, the animals first. Each one we handle gets a field name -- usually something the team makes up, Notch, Big Mama, that sort of thing -- and we have never given two animals the same one, so the field name is as good as any number for finding the animal again. We record the species, the sex, roughly how old we think it is, its body mass in kilos from when we had it down, and the date of that first capture. Weights: the cows come in around forty kilos and the bulls more like fifty-five, so call it high forties on average with maybe ten kilos of spread either way. The smallest we have ever collared was a yearling at twelve kilos and the biggest bull went ninety-five. We also need to know whether the animal is still alive as far as we know, because that changes what we do with its collar.

Now the collars. People here say collars, tags, transmitters, units -- it is all the same object. Each one has a serial on the housing and a type, and the serial has the type in it because the maker puts a prefix on, so really the serial tells you the type and we should not be typing the type in twice. The types themselves are worth writing down properly, because the maker gives us numbers for each one and those numbers are what we argue about: a description, what the housing weighs in grams, the shortest interval it can be programmed to, and how many days the maker claims the battery will last. We have never had one beat that claim, not once.

The deployment record needs to say which animal the collar went on, the day it was fitted -- never before that first capture, because we do not collar an animal we have not had down -- the day it came off, which is obviously not before the day it went on, and who did the fitting, usually one of the rangers and sometimes the vet; just the name is fine, we are not building a staff directory. The collar is programmed to take a position every so many hours, mostly every six, which is four fixes a day, though about a fifth of the units are on twelve and a few of the old ones only manage one a day. You cannot program one tighter than the shortest interval the maker allows. The battery lasts the better part of a year if we are lucky, less in the wet season, so we note how many days we got out of it -- usually somewhere around two hundred and eighty, give or take a couple of months.

There is one rule we will not bend, and it is the ethics committee's rule not ours: the collar must not weigh more than three percent of what the animal weighs. So a forty-kilo cow can carry twelve hundred grams of hardware and not a gram more, and the two numbers we compare are the housing weight on the collar type and the weight we had for the animal when it was down.

When a collar comes off there is a reason recorded, and one rule there is absolute: if we have confirmed the animal dead, that collar record closes as recovered off the carcass, no other reason is allowed.

Then the positions themselves, which is the big pile -- we are at just under three hundred animals across eleven seasons and a few hundred thousand fixes. Each fix is a time, a latitude and longitude, how many satellites the unit saw, how good it reckons the position is in metres, and the battery voltage at the time. A collar reports once per scheduled time, so the collar and the timestamp together are enough to find the fix. Nothing is ever recorded before the collar was fitted or after it came off, though the spreadsheet has a few of those from testing units on the office roof. Most fixes see seven or eight satellites, and if it saw fewer than four we mark the fix as dodgy so the analysts drop it. One more thing: we only work in the one reserve, so every position should fall between 24.5 and 21.8 degrees south -- anything outside that is a glitch, not an animal.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: usually somewhere around two hundred and eighty, give or take a couple of months

nl_description:
Materials lab, mechanical testing group. Right now every test goes into a workbook per project and nobody can answer 'show me all the quench-and-tempered material that failed elongation'. Here is roughly what we hold.

Stock arrives as batches -- supplier, heat number, receipt date, mass in kg -- and each batch is one alloy grade, where the grade record is just the grade code, the alloy family and the nominal density. The grade code is unique and settles the family and the density. The heat number is unique too, because it is the mill's number for that melt, and it tells you which batch and therefore which grade you are looking at.

Batches get heat treated: a process name, a soak temperature, a soak time in minutes, a quench medium and the date it went through the furnace, which is never before the batch arrived. For the study work we deliberately sweep soak temperature uniformly between 820 and 960 C, and the furnaces themselves will not go outside 500 to 1200.

Specimens are machined out of a batch and tagged with the treatment they went through; each one has a specimen code that is unique, a geometry, a gauge diameter between 3 and 25 mm, a gauge length, the machining date, and a stamped condition code. You cannot machine a specimen before the stock arrived, and you cannot machine it before the treatment it is tagged with went through the furnace either, though the old workbooks have both. These are proportional specimens, so the gauge length is always at least four times the gauge diameter.

The stamped condition -- as-received, annealed, or quench-and-tempered -- matters because the acceptance bands differ, and those bands are now their own little table rather than three numbers in a macro: a description, the minimum and maximum yield we will accept for material in that condition, and the minimum elongation. As-received material should yield between 250 and 380 MPa, quench-and-tempered between 400 and 620, and that table is the only place those numbers should live. Across everything we have tested, yield comes out around 345 MPa with sd 22, UTS around 512 with sd 30, and elongation 24.5 percent with sd 4.1, and elongation is physically between 0 and 60.

A tensile test names the specimen, the frame it ran on and the acceptance condition it was judged against -- which is of course the specimen's own stamped condition, so it is derivable, but the report writer wants it on the test row and we have had it disagree -- plus the timestamp, the strain rate, yield, UTS, elongation, the operator's initials and a result status. A test is never run before its specimen was machined, nor before the frame's own last calibration date. Yield and UTS have to sit inside the accepted band for that condition, UTS is by definition never below yield, and anything whose elongation comes in under the minimum elongation for its condition goes to status 'REVIEW' automatically.

The frames are their own record: a name that is unique, a load cell capacity in kN, the manufacturer, the last calibration date and the date the next calibration falls due. Nothing is tested on a frame past its calibration due date -- that is the finding from the last audit. The small frames under 100 kN can only be driven quasi-statically, so a test on one of those runs at 0.001 per second or slower.

Hardness is separate because we take several indents per specimen, numbered from one, so the specimen and the indent number together identify the reading: a method, the indent number, the load in kgf and the value, which sits around 178 with sd 12 and can physically be anywhere from 20 to 950.

Broken tensile specimens sometimes get a fractography write-up against the test -- fracture mode, an image path on the share, and free-text observations. Scale is modest: about 4,200 specimens and 11,000 indents.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: sits around 178 with sd 12 and can physically be anywhere from 20 to 950

nl_description:
Survey ops here. The thing I want modelled is the frame archive -- people call them frames, exposures or images and it is all one object, so pick a word and stick to it.

We tile the sky into fields; a field has a name, a tile number, its centre in RA and Dec, the galactic latitude, and a running count of how many times it has been visited, which averages about a dozen a season. Tile numbers are unique and the field name is just the tile number dressed up, so the tile number settles the name.

Observing is organised into seasons, and I want the season as a record of its own rather than a string on every frame: a season label, the date it opened, the date it closed -- after it opened, obviously -- and the visits per field we were budgeted for. The label is unique and pins the dates. Every frame belongs to a season as well as to a field, and a frame's start time has to fall inside its season, which sounds too obvious to state until you see what the loader did with the frames taken in the changeover week.

Every frame belongs to one field and one filter. There are five filters, u g r i z, and each carries a band code, its own central wavelength and a photometric zero point, so they are worth their own record rather than a bare code on the frame; the band code fixes the wavelength and the zero point. On the frame itself we log the start time, the exposure length, airmass, seeing, sky background and the limiting magnitude we reached, plus a quality flag. A field, a filter and a start time between them identify a frame -- we cannot point at the same field through the same filter twice in the same instant.

Nearly all frames are 30 seconds -- call it 55 percent -- with 30 percent at 90 and the rest the long 300 second ones. Airmass is between 1.0 and 2.5 by scheduling. Seeing typically comes in around 1.15 arcseconds and it is skewed, because a bad night is far worse than a good night is good, so log-normal rather than Gaussian -- log mean about 0.14, log variance about 0.10. Sky background is all over the place depending on the moon and I would not put a number on it. If seeing is worse than 2.5 or airmass over 2.0, the frame gets flagged 'BAD'. And we do not believe a limiting magnitude fainter than the zero point of the filter it was taken through; that is the pipeline lying to us, and the number should never come out past it.

Then the detections, which are the volume: 210,000 frames and about 4 million source rows. Each detection points at the frame it came out of and has its own RA and Dec, a magnitude and a magnitude error, an extended-source flag, and a bitmask of processing flags whose meaning honestly lives in the pipeline code rather than anywhere documented. Magnitudes pile up near the survey limit, mean about 21.4 with sd 1.6, and nothing outside 12 to 24.5 is real. Detections off a frame flagged BAD are not published, and we carry that as a flag on the detection rather than working it out at query time. Nor do we publish anything fainter than the limiting magnitude of the frame it came off -- if the frame only went to 22.1 then a 23rd magnitude source on it is noise -- and nothing with a magnitude error above 0.2 goes out either.

The observers also keep a night log in a wiki, which is not part of this.

ground_truth_moments.evidence: which averages about a dozen a season
Seeing typically comes in around 1.15 arcseconds

nl_description:
I run the shift schedule and the logbook for the beamline, so I have been asked to describe what we actually need to keep -- which is not the physics, the physics people have their own systems, but the record of the running.

Start with the shifts, because that is my half of it. We cover the beamline in eight-hour shifts and every shift has a leader, and shifts do not overlap, so the time a shift began is enough to tell you which shift you mean. For each one we keep when it began, when it ended -- after it began, thank you -- the leader's name and how many people were on crew. Just names, we are not making a staff system out of this.

A run is what we call a stretch where the beam was on and we were recording. People say run, fill, spill, sometimes 'the file' when they mean the run, and they all end up meaning the run as far as we are concerned. We number them, no number ever gets used twice, and we are at about eighteen hundred and fifty since the beamline came back up. Every run happened during one shift, and it has to sit inside that shift: it never starts before the shift started and it never ends after the shift ended. We also write the shift leader's name on the run itself, which is silly now I say it out loud, because the shift already tells you who was leading -- but the old logbook pages have it and the physicists grep for names, so it stays, and where the two disagree it is the shift that is right.

For each run we write down when it started and when it stopped, which is never before it started, what energy the beam was at, what target was in, how much charge went through the target by the end of it, what quality we give the run -- good, suspect or junk -- and then a free-text comment, which is where the actual story lives. Energy is mostly 12 GeV, that is nearly half our runs, then a good chunk at 10.6, some at 6.4 and a handful of low-energy ones at 2.2. Nothing above 13 and nothing below half a GeV has ever been taken here. Charge is very lumpy -- most runs get a few tens of microcoulombs but the aborted ones get almost nothing, so the spread is enormously skewed, log-normal if you want a name for it. If a run got less than one microcoulomb it is junk, full stop.

Then there are the detector subsystems -- the drift chambers, the calorimeter, the Cherenkov and so on. Each of those has a name, which is unique and is what everybody actually says, the group responsible for it, how many channels it has, and its nominal high voltage. Names being unique means the name gives you the group and the nominal voltage, and I would rather it lived there than in six spreadsheets. Nothing here has more than two hundred channels.

The part I think is the hard part: for every run, every subsystem has a status. Whether it was actually in the readout, how many dead channels it had that night, what voltage it was really set at, and a note. So it is one entry per run and subsystem together. Dead channels are usually two or three, occasionally a lot more, and obviously a subsystem cannot have more dead channels than it has channels, which the current spreadsheet cheerfully allows. Nobody ever runs a subsystem above its nominal voltage either -- the real setting is at or under the nominal, and it starts from zero. If a subsystem was not in the readout at all we just put zero dead channels for it rather than leaving it blank. And a run is only ever called good if every subsystem was in the readout -- if the calorimeter was out, the best that run gets is suspect. Roughly seven in ten runs come out good, about two in ten suspect and one in ten junk.
